aetheogamous.d: Propagated in an unusual way; cryptogamous

aethogen.d: A compound of nitrogen and boro&unr_;, which, when heated before the blowpipe, gives a brilliant phosphorescent; boric nitride

aethrioscope.d: An instrument consisting in part of a differential thermometer. It is used for measuring changes of temperature produced by different conditions of the sky, as when clear or clouded

affabrous.d: Executed in a workmanlike manner; ingeniously made

affamish.d: To afflict with, or perish from, hunger

affecter.d: One who affects, assumes, pretends, or strives after

affectibility.d: The quality or state of being affectible

affectuous.d: Full of passion or emotion; earnest

affiliable.d: Capable of being affiliated to or on, or connected with in origin

affordment.d: Anything given as a help; bestowal

affronte.d: Face to face, or front to front; facing

affronter.d: One who affronts, or insults to the face

affy.d: To confide (one's self to, or in); to trust

aflaunt.d: In a flaunting state or position

afoam.d: In a foaming state; as, the sea is all afoam

african wild dog.d: a dog (Lycaon pictus) with mottled fur found in Africa, notable for the strong social structure of its family groups

after-mentioned.d: Mentioned afterwards; as, persons after-mentioned (in a writing)

after-note.d: One of the small notes occur on the unaccented parts of the measure, taking their time from the preceding note

after-sails.d: The sails on the mizzenmast, or on the stays between the mainmast and mizzenmast

after-wit.d: Wisdom or perception that comes after it can be of use

aftercast.d: A throw of dice after the game in ended; hence, anything done too late

aftergame.d: A second game; hence, a subsequent scheme or expedient

afterwise.d: Wise after the event; wise or knowing, when it is too late

agamist.d: An unmarried person; also, one opposed to marriage

agaty.d: Of the nature of agate, or containing agate

aggeneration.d: The act of producing in addition

aggeration.d: A heaping up; accumulation; as, aggerations of sand

aggroupment.d: Arrangement in a group or in groups; grouping

aggry.d: Applied to a kind of variegated glass beads of ancient manufacture; as, aggry beads are found in Ashantee and Fantee in Africa

agminal.d: Pertaining to an army marching, or to a train

agnoiology.d: The doctrine concerning those things of which we are necessarily ignorant

agnus scythicus.d: The Scythian lamb, a kind of woolly-skinned rootstock. See Barometz

agonothete.d: An officer who presided over the great public games in Greece

agonothetic.d: Pertaining to the office of an agonothete

agrappes.d: Hooks and eyes for armor, etc

agricolist.d: A cultivator of the soil; an agriculturist

agriologist.d: One versed or engaged in agriology

agrise.d: To shudder with terror; to tremble with fear

agrom.d: A disease occurring in Bengal and other parts of the East Indies, in which the tongue chaps and cleaves

aguilt.d: To be guilty of; to offend; to sin against; to wrong

aich's metal.d: A kind of gun metal, containing copper, zinc, and iron, but no tin

aid-de-camp.d: An officer selected by a general to carry orders, also to assist or represent him in correspondence and in directing movements

ailuroidea.d: A group of the Carnivora, which includes the cats, civets, and hyenas

air poise.d: An instrument to measure the weight of air

air stove.d: A stove for heating a current of air which is directed against its surface by means of pipes, and then distributed through a building

air-built.d: Erected in the air; having no solid foundation; chimerical; as, an air-built castle

air-slacked.d: Slacked, or pulverized, by exposure to the air; as, air-slacked lime

airball.d: A throw at the basket that completely misses, not even hitting the rim.  Compare swoosh and nothing but net

ajouan.d: The fruit of Ammi Copticum, syn. Carum Ajowan, used both as a medicine and as a condiment. An oil containing thymol is extracted from it. Called also Javanee seed, Javanese seed, and ajava

ajour.d: of or pertaining to objects which are pierced or decorated with an openwork pattern

al segno.d: A direction for the performer to return and recommence from the sign &unr_

alabama period.d: A period in the American eocene, the lowest in the tertiary age except the lignitic

alacrify.d: To rouse to action; to inspirit

aladinist.d: One of a sect of freethinkers among the Muslims

alamire.d: The lowest note but one in Guido Aretino's scale of music

alamodality.d: The quality of being à la mode; conformity to the mode or fashion; fashionableness

alatern.d: An ornamental evergreen shrub (Rhamnus alaternus) belonging to the buckthorns

alb sunday.d: The first Sunday after Easter Sunday, properly Albless Sunday, because in the early church those who had been baptized on Easter eve laid aside on the following Saturday their white albs which had been put on after baptism

albert ware.d: A soft ornamental terra-cotta pottery, sold in the biscuit state for decorating

albication.d: The process of becoming white, or developing white patches, or streaks

albification.d: The act or process of making white

albolith.d: A kind of plastic cement, or artificial stone, consisting chiefly of magnesia and silica; -- called also albolite

alborak.d: The imaginary milk-white animal on which Mohammed was said to have been carried up to heaven; a white mule

album graecum.d: Dung of dogs or hyenas, which becomes white by exposure to air. It is used in dressing leather, and was formerly used in medicine

albuminin.d: The substance of the cells which inclose the white of birds' eggs

alburn.d: The bleak, a small European fish having scales of a peculiarly silvery color which are used in making artificial pearls

albyn.d: Scotland; esp. the Highlands of Scotland

alcaid.d: A commander of a castle or fortress among the Spaniards, Portuguese, and Moors

alcaldia.d: The jurisdiction or office of an alcalde; also, the building or chamber in which he conducts the business of his office

alcarraza.d: A vessel of porous earthenware, used for cooling liquids by evaporation from the exterior surface

alcyonic.d: Of or pertaining to the Alcyonaria

alcyonium.d: A genus of fleshy Alcyonaria, its polyps somewhat resembling flowers with eight fringed rays. The term was also formerly used for certain species of sponges

alcyonoid.d: Like or pertaining to the Alcyonaria

aldermanity.d: Aldermen collectively; the body of aldermen

aldermanlike.d: Like or suited to an alderman

ale silver.d: A duty payable to the lord mayor of London by the sellers of ale within the city

alebench.d: A bench in or before an alehouse

aleberry.d: A beverage, formerly made by boiling ale with spice, sugar, and sops of bread

alectorides.d: A group of birds including the common fowl and the pheasants

alegge.d: To allay or alleviate; to lighten

alepole.d: A pole set up as the sign of an alehouse

alestake.d: A stake or pole projecting from, or set up before, an alehouse, as a sign; an alepole. At the end was commonly suspended a garland, a bunch of leaves, or a “bush.”

alethiology.d: The science which treats of the nature of truth and evidence

alethoscope.d: An instrument for viewing pictures by means of a lens, so as to present them in their natural proportions and relations

alexipharmical.d: Of or relating to an alexipharmic or alexipharmac; warding off poison; antidotal; prophylactic

alexiterical.d: Resisting poison; obviating the effects of venom; alexipharmic

alfet.d: A caldron of boiling water into which an accused person plunged his forearm as a test of innocence or guilt

alfione.d: An edible marine fish of California (Rhacochilus toxotes)

algarovilla.d: The agglutinated seeds and husks of the legumes of a South American tree (Inga Marthae).  It is valuable for tanning leather, and as a dye

alicant.d: A kind of wine, formerly much esteemed; -- said to have been made near Alicant, in Spain

aliene.d: To alien or alienate; to transfer, as title or property; as, to aliene an estate

alimentariness.d: The quality of being alimentary; nourishing quality

alimentiveness.d: The instinct or faculty of appetite for food

alkalamide.d: One of a series of compounds that may be regarded as ammonia in which a part of the hydrogen has been replaced by basic, and another part by acid, atoms or radicals

alkali flat.d: A sterile plain, containing an excess of alkali, at the bottom of an undrained basin in an arid region; a playa

all saints.d: The first day of November, called, also, Allhallows or Hallowmas; a feast day kept in honor of all the saints; also, the season of this festival

allfours.d: A game at cards, called “High, Low, Jack, and the Game.”

allhallow eve.d: The evening before Allhallows. See Halloween

allhallown.d: Of or pertaining to the time of Allhallows. [Obs.] “Allhallown summer.” Shak. (i. e., late summer; “Indian Summer”)

allineation.d: Alignment; position in a straight line, as of two planets with the sun

alliteral.d: Pertaining to, or characterized by alliteration

allnight.d: Light, fuel, or food for the whole night

alloo.d: To incite dogs by a call; to halloo

allophylic.d: Pertaining to a race or a language neither Aryan nor Semitic

alloquy.d: A speaking to another; an address

alloxanate.d: A combination of alloxanic acid and a base or base or positive radical

alloxanic.d: Of or pertaining to alloxan; -- applied to an acid obtained by the action of soluble alkalies on alloxan

alluminor.d: An illuminator of manuscripts and books; a limner

almadia.d: A bark canoe used by the Africans

almagra.d: A fine, deep red ocher, somewhat purplish, found in Spain. It is the sil atticum of the ancients. Under the name of Indian red it is used for polishing glass and silver

almond furnace.d: A kind of furnace used in refining, to separate the metal from cinders and other foreign matter

almude.d: A measure for liquids in several countries. In Portugal the Lisbon almude is about 4.4, and the Oporto almude about 6.6, gallons U. S. measure.  In Turkey the “almud” is about 1.4 gallons

alogian.d: One of an ancient sect who rejected St. John's Gospel and the Apocalypse, which speak of Christ as the Logos

alopecist.d: A practitioner who tries to prevent or cure baldness

alopius.d: type genus of the family Alopiidae; in some classifications considered a genus of the family Lamnidae

alpha paper.d: A sensitized paper for obtaining positives by artificial light. It is coated with gelatin containing silver bromide and chloride

alphitomancy.d: Divination by means of barley meal

alphonsine.d: Of or relating to Alphonso X., the Wise, King of Castile (1252-1284)

alpist.d: The seed of canary grass (Phalaris Canariensis), used for feeding cage birds

alternat.d: A usage, among diplomats, of rotation in precedence among representatives of equal rank, sometimes determined by lot and at other times in regular order. The practice obtains in the signing of treaties and conventions between nations

alto-cumulus.d: A fleecy cloud formation consisting of large whitish or grayish globular cloudlets with shaded  portions, often grouped in flocks or rows

alum root.d: A North American herb (Heuchera Americana) of the Saxifrage family, whose root has astringent properties

alveary.d: A beehive, or something resembling a beehive

amarantaceous.d: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, the family of plants of which the amaranth is the type

amatungulu.d: a very large closely branched South African shrub (Carissa grandiflora) of the dogbane family having forked bright green spines, white flowers, shiny leaves, and red berries.  Also called natal plum

amauropelta.d: a genus of epiphytic or terrestrial ferns of America and Africa and Polynesia

amber room.d: A room formerly in the Czar's Summer Palace in Russia, which was richly decorated with walls and fixtures made from amber.  The amber was removed by occupying German troops during the Second World War and has, as of 1997, never been recovered.  The room is being recreated from old photographs by Russian artisans

amber seed.d: Seed of the Hibiscus abelmoschus, somewhat resembling millet, brought from Egypt and the West Indies, and having a flavor like that of musk; musk seed

amber tree.d: A species of Anthospermum, a shrub with evergreen leaves, which, when bruised, emit a fragrant odor

ambigu.d: An entertainment at which a medley of dishes is set on at the same time

amblygon.d: An obtuse-angled figure, esp. and obtuse-angled triangle

amblypoda.d: A group of large, extinct, herbivorous mammals, common in the Tertiary formation of the United States

amboyna wood.d: A beautiful mottled and curled wood, used in cabinetwork. It is obtained from the Pterocarpus Indicus of Amboyna, Borneo, etc

ambreate.d: A salt formed by the combination of ambreic acid with a base or positive radical

ambreic.d: Of or pertaining to ambrein; -- said of a certain acid produced by digesting ambrein in nitric acid

ambs-ace.d: Double aces, the lowest throw of all at dice. Hence: Bad luck; anything of no account or value

american protective association.d: A secret organization in the United States, formed in Iowa in 1887, ostensibly for the protection of American institutions by keeping Roman Catholics out of public office. Abbrev. commonly to A. P .A

ametabolian.d: Of or pertaining to insects that do undergo any metamorphosis

aminol.d: A colorless liquid prepared from herring brine and containing amines, used as a local antiseptic

amioid.d: Like or pertaining to the Amioidei

amioidei.d: An order of ganoid fishes of which Amia is the type. See Bowfin and Ganoidei

amissibility.d: The quality of being amissible; possibility of being lost

ammite.d: Oölite or roestone; -- written also hammite

ammonitoidea.d: An extensive group of fossil cephalopods often very abundant in Mesozoic rocks. See Ammonite

amnicolist.d: One who lives near a river

amnigenous.d: Born or bred in, of, or near a river

amoebaeum.d: A poem in which persons are represented at speaking alternately; as the third and seventh eclogues of Virgil

amoebea.d: That division of the Rhizopoda which includes the amoeba and similar forms

amorphozoa.d: Animals without a mouth or regular internal organs, as the sponges

amorphozoic.d: Of or pertaining to the Amorphozoa

amotus.d: Elevated, -- as a toe, when raised so high that the tip does not touch the ground

amovability.d: Liability to be removed or dismissed from office

ampere foot.d: A unit, employed in calculating fall of pressure in distributing mains, equivalent to a current of one ampère flowing through one foot of conductor

ampere hour.d: The quantity of electricity delivered in hour by a current whose average strength is one ampère.  It is used as a unit of charge quantity; the Ampere hour is equal to 3600 coulombs.  The terms Ampère minute and Ampère second are sometimes similarly used

amphibiotica.d: A division of insects having aquatic larvæ

amphicome.d: A kind of figured stone, rugged and beset with eminences, anciently used in divination

amphidromical.d: Pertaining to an Attic festival at the naming of a child; -- so called because the friends of the parents carried the child around the hearth and then named it

amphigen.d: An element that in combination produces amphid salt; -- applied by Berzelius to oxygen, sulphur, selenium, and tellurium

amphigonic.d: Pertaining to amphigony; sexual; as, amphigonic propagation

amphipneust.d: One of a tribe of Amphibia, which have both lungs and gills at the same time, as the proteus and siren

amphiprostylar.d: having columns at both ends but not on the sides

amphirhina.d: A name applied to the elasmobranch fishes, because the nasal sac is double

amphitropal.d: Having the ovule inverted, but with the attachment near the middle of one side; half anatropous

ampyx.d: A woman's headband (sometimes of metal), for binding the front hair

amuletic.d: Of or pertaining to an amulet; operating as a charm

amvis.d: An explosive consisting of ammonium nitrate, a derivative of nitrobenzene, chlorated napthalene, and wood meal

amyelous.d: Characterized by lack of the spinal cord

amygdalic.d: Of or pertaining to almonds; derived from amygdalin; as, amygdalic acid

amylate.d: A compound of the radical amyl with oxygen and a positive atom or radical

an 't.d: An it, that is, and it or if it. See An, conj

anabaptistic.d: Relating or attributed to the Anabaptists, or their doctrines

anabaptistry.d: The doctrine, system, or practice, of Anabaptists

anabaptize.d: To rebaptize; to rechristen; also, to rename

anacamptic.d: Reflecting of reflected; as, an anacamptic sound (and echo)

anacamptically.d: By reflection; as, echoes are sound produced anacamptically

anacardic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, the cashew nut; as, anacardic acid

anacharis.d: A fresh-water weed of the frog's-bit family (Hydrocharidaceae), native to America.  Transferred to England it became an obstruction to navigation.  Called also waterweed and water thyme

anachorism.d: An error in regard to the place of an event or a thing; a referring something to a wrong place

anachronize.d: To refer to, or put into, a wrong time

anacoenosis.d: A figure by which a speaker appeals to his hearers or opponents for their opinion on the point in debate

anadrom.d: A fish that leaves the sea and ascends rivers

anaerobies.d: Microörganisms which do not require oxygen, but are killed by it.  See obligate anaerobes under anaerobes

anagasta.d: a genus of moths whose larvae are flour moths

anaglyptographic.d: Of or pertaining to anaglyptography; as, anaglyptographic engraving

anaglyptography.d: The art of copying works in relief, or of engraving as to give the subject an embossed or raised appearance; -- used in representing coins, bas-reliefs, etc

anakim.d: A race of giants living in Palestine

anallagmatic.d: Not changed in form by inversion

anallantoic.d: Without, or not developing, an allantois

anallantoidea.d: The division of Vertebrata in which no allantois is developed. It includes amphibians, fishes, and lower forms

anamese.d: Of or pertaining to Anam, to southeastern Asia

anaptychus.d: One of a pair of shelly plates found in some cephalopods, as the ammonites

anarthropoda.d: One of the divisions of Articulata in which there are no jointed legs, as the annelids; -- opposed to Arthropoda

anarthropodous.d: Having no jointed legs; pertaining to Anarthropoda

anaseismic.d: Moving up and down; -- said of earthquake shocks

anatifa.d: An animal of the barnacle tribe, of the genus Lepas, having a fleshy stem or peduncle; a goose barnacle. See Cirripedia

anatiferous.d: Producing ducks; -- applied to Anatifæ, under the absurd notion of their turning into ducks or geese. See Barnacle

anatomism.d: The application of the principles of anatomy, as in art

anatreptic.d: Overthrowing; defeating; -- applied to Plato's refutative dialogues

anatropal.d: Having the ovule inverted at an early period in its development, so that the chalaza is as the apparent apex; -- opposed to orthotropous

anchor shot.d: A shot made with the object balls in an anchor space

anchor space.d: In the balk-line game, any of eight spaces, 7 inches by 31/2, lying along a cushion and bisected transversely by a balk line. Object balls in an anchor space are treated as in balk

anchor watch.d: A detail of one or more men who keep watch on deck at night when a vessel is at anchor

ancile.d: The sacred shield of the Romans, said to have-fallen from heaven in the reign of Numa. It was the palladium of Rome

ancome.d: A small ulcerous swelling, coming suddenly; also, a whitlow

ancony.d: A piece of malleable iron, wrought into the shape of a bar in the middle, but unwrought at the ends

andorra la vella.d: The capital city of Andorra.  Population (2000) = 22,390

androcephalous.d: Having a human head (upon an animal's body), as the Egyptian sphinx

andromede.d: A meteor appearing to radiate from a point in the constellation Andromeda, -- whence the name

andropetalous.d: Produced by the conversion of the stamens into petals, as double flowers, like the garden ranunculus

androtomous.d: Having the filaments of the stamens divided into two parts

androtomy.d: Dissection of the human body, as distinguished from zoötomy; anthropotomy

anemonic.d: An acrid, poisonous, crystallizable substance, obtained from, the anemone, or from anemonin

anemorphilous.d: Fertilized by the agency of the wind; -- said of plants in which the pollen is carried to the stigma by the wind; wind-Fertilized

angelicalness.d: The quality of being angelic; excellence more than human

angelify.d: To make like an angel; to angelize

angelize.d: To raise to the state of an angel; to render angelic

angelot.d: A French gold coin of the reign of Louis XI., bearing the image of St. Michael; also, a piece coined at Paris by the English under Henry VI

angienchyma.d: Vascular tissue of plants, consisting of spiral vessels, dotted, barred, and pitted ducts, and laticiferous vessels

angiomonospermous.d: Producing one seed only in a seed pod

angioneuropathy.d: Neuropathy of the neurons innervating blood vessels. Called also Angioneurosis, Vasomotor neurosis, Vasoneurosis

angiosporous.d: Having spores contained in cells or thecæ, as in the case of some fungi

angiostomous.d: With a narrow mouth, as the shell of certain gastropods

angle of entry.d: The angle between the tangent to the advancing edge (of an aërocurve) and the line of motion; -- contrasted with angle of trail, which is the angle between the tangent to the following edge and the line of motion

anglemeter.d: An instrument to measure angles, esp. one used by geologists to measure the dip of strata

anglicity.d: The state or quality of being English

anglo-saxonism.d: A characteristic of the Anglo-Saxon race; especially, a word or an idiom of the Anglo-Saxon tongue

angola pea.d: A tropical plant (Cajanus indicus) and its edible seed, a kind of pulse; -- so called from Angola in Western Africa. Called also pigeon pea and Congo pea

angustation.d: The act of making narrow; a straitening or contacting

angusticlave.d: A narrow stripe of purple worn by the equites on each side of the tunic as a sign of rank

anhele.d: To pant; to be breathlessly anxious or eager (for)

anient.d: To frustrate; to bring to naught; to annihilate

anilic.d: Pertaining to, or obtained from, anil; indigotic; -- applied to an acid formed by the action of nitric acid on indigo

animadversal.d: The faculty of perceiving; a percipient

animadversive.d: Having the power of perceiving; percipient

animalculism.d: The theory which seeks to explain certain physiological and pathological phenomena by means of animalcules

animastic.d: Pertaining to mind or spirit; spiritual

animose.d: Full of spirit; hot; vehement; resolute

anisodactyla.d: A group of herbivorous mammals characterized by having the hoofs in a single series around the foot, as the elephant, rhinoceros, etc

anisopleura.d: A primary division of gastropods, including those having spiral shells. The two sides of the body are unequally developed

anisopoda.d: A division of Crustacea, which, in some its characteristics, is intermediate between Amphipoda and Isopoda

anisotrope.d: Not isotropic; having different properties in different directions; thus, crystals of the isometric system are optically isotropic, but all other crystals are anisotropic

anito.d: In Guam and the Philippines, an idol, fetich, or spirit

anlaut.d: An initial sound, as of a word or syllable

annats.d: The first year's profits of a spiritual preferment, anciently paid by the clergy to the pope; first fruits. In England, they now form a fund for the augmentation of poor livings

annelidous.d: Of the nature of an annelid

annodated.d: Curved somewhat in the form of the letter S

annotine.d: A bird one year old, or that has once molted

annualist.d: One who writes for, or who edits, an annual

annueler.d: A priest employed in saying annuals, or anniversary Masses

annulary.d: Having the form of a ring; annular

annuloida.d: A division of the Articulata, including the annelids and allied groups; sometimes made to include also the helminths and echinoderms

annulosa.d: A division of the Invertebrata, nearly equivalent to the Articulata. It includes the Arthoropoda and Anarthropoda. By some Zoologists it is applied to the former only

annumerate.d: To add on; to count in

annwfn.d: the other world; land of fairies

anomural.d: Irregular in the character of the tail or abdomen; as, the anomural crustaceans

anophyte.d: A moss or mosslike plant which cellular stems, having usually an upward growth and distinct leaves

anoplothere.d: A genus of extinct quadrupeds of the order Ungulata, whose were first found in the gypsum quarries near Paris; characterized by the shortness and feebleness of their canine teeth (whence the name)

anserated.d: Having the extremities terminate in the heads of eagles, lions, etc.; as, an anserated cross

ant egg.d: One of the small white egg-shaped pupæ or cocoons of the ant, often seen in or about ant-hills, and popularly supposed to be eggs

ant-bear.d: An edentate animal of tropical America (the Tamanoir), living on ants. It belongs to the genus Myrmecophaga

ant-cattle.d: Various kinds of plant lice or aphids tended by ants for the sake of the honeydew which they secrete; plural of ant cow. See Aphips

antanaclasis.d: A figure which consists in repeating the same word in a different sense; as, Learn some craft when young, that when old you may live without craft

antanagoge.d: A figure which consists in answering the charge of an adversary, by a counter charge

antecommunion.d: A name given to that part of the Anglican liturgy for the communion, which precedes the consecration of the elements

antemosaic.d: Being before the time of Moses

antemural.d: An outwork of a strong, high wall, with turrets, in front of the gateway (as of an old castle), for defending the entrance

antenicene.d: Of or in the Christian church or era, anterior to the first council of Nice, held a. d. 325; as, antenicene faith

antepredicament.d: A prerequisite to a clear understanding of the predicaments and categories, such as definitions of common terms

antestature.d: A small intrenchment or work of palisades, or of sacks of earth

antestomach.d: A cavity which leads into the stomach, as in birds

antetemple.d: The portico, or narthex in an ancient temple or church

antherogenous.d: Transformed from anthers, as the petals of a double flower

anthobranchia.d: A division of nudibranchiate Mollusca, in which the gills form a wreath or cluster upon the posterior part of the back. See Nudibranchiata, and Doris

anthokyan.d: The blue coloring matter of certain flowers. Same as Cyanin

anthorism.d: A description or definition contrary to that which is given by the adverse party

anthozoic.d: Of or pertaining to the Anthozoa

anthracomancy.d: Divination by inspecting a burning coal

anthracometric.d: Of or pertaining to an anthracometer

anthrax vaccine.d: A fluid vaccine obtained by growing a bacterium (Bacillus anthracis, formerly Bacterium anthracis) in beef broth. It is used to immunize animals, esp. cattle

anthrenus.d: A genus of small beetles, several of which, in the larval state, are very destructive to woolen goods, fur, etc.  The common “museum pest” is Anthrenus varius; the carpet beetle is Anthrenus scrophulariæ. The larvæ are commonly confounded with moths

anthropidae.d: The group that includes man only

anthropolite.d: A petrifaction of the human body, or of any portion of it

anthropomancy.d: Divination by the entrails of human being

anthropomorphite.d: One who ascribes a human form or human attributes to the Deity or to a polytheistic deity

anthropomorphology.d: The application to God of terms descriptive of human beings

anthroponomics.d: The science of the laws of the development of the human organism in relation to other organisms and to environment

anthropopathite.d: One who ascribes human feelings to deity

anti-gallican.d: Opposed to what is Gallic or French

antiae.d: The two projecting feathered angles of the forehead of some birds; the frontal points

antialbumid.d: A body formed from albumin by pancreatic and gastric digestion. It is convertible into antipeptone

antibillous.d: Counteractive of bilious complaints; tending to relieve biliousness

antiburgher.d: One who seceded from the Scottish Burghers (1747), deeming it improper to take the Burgess oath

antichronical.d: Deviating from the proper order of time

antichronism.d: Deviation from the true order of time; anachronism

basipterygoid.d: Applied to a protuberance of the base of the sphenoid bone
