bishop's-weed.d: An umbelliferous plant of the genus Ammi

bishop's-wort.d: Wood betony (Stachys betonica); also, the plant called fennel flower (Nigella Damascena), or devil-in-a-bush

bishoplike.d: Resembling a bishop; belonging to a bishop

bissell truck.d: A truck for railroad rolling stock, consisting of two ordinary axle boxes sliding in guides attached to a triangular frame; -- called also pony truck

bitheism.d: Belief in the existence of two gods; dualism

biting in.d: The process of corroding or eating into metallic plates, by means of an acid. See Etch

bitumen process.d: Any process in which  advantage is taken of the fact that prepared bitumen is rendered insoluble by exposure to light, as in photolithography

bituminate.d: To treat or impregnate with bitumen; to cement with bitumen

bivial.d: Of or relating to the bivium

blaberus.d: a genus of insects consisting of giant cockroaches

black flags.d: An organization composed originally of Chinese rebels that had been driven into Tonkin by the suppression of the Taiping rebellion, but later increased by bands of pirates and adventurers. It took a prominent part in fighting the French during their hostilities with Anam, 1873-85

black hamburg.d: A sweet and juicy variety of European grape, of a dark purplish black color, much grown under glass in northern latitudes

black snake.d: A snake of a black color, of which two species are common in the United States, the Bascanium constrictor, or racer, sometimes six feet long, and the Scotophis Alleghaniensis, seven or eight feet long

black spanish.d: One of an old and well-known Mediterranean breed of domestic fowls with glossy black plumage, blue legs and feet, bright red comb and wattles, and white face. They are remarkable as egg layers

black-jack.d: A name given by English miners to sphalerite, or zinc blende; -- called also false galena. See Blende

black-mouthed.d: Using foul or scurrilous language; slanderous

blackfriar.d: A friar of the Dominican order, so named because wearing the black mantle of the Dominicans; -- called also predicant and preaching friar; in France, Jacobin. Also, sometimes, a Benedictine

blacksalter.d: One who makes crude potash, or black salts

blackwater state.d: Nebraska; -- a nickname alluding to the dark color of the water of its rivers, due to the presence of a black vegetable mold in the soil

bladefish.d: A long, thin, marine fish of Europe (Trichiurus lepturus); the ribbon fish

blanch holding.d: A mode of tenure by the payment of a small duty in white rent (silver) or otherwise

blanchard lathe.d: A kind of wood-turning lathe for making noncircular and irregular forms, as felloes, gun stocks, lasts, spokes, etc., after a given pattern. The pattern and work rotate on parallel spindles in the same direction with the same speed, and the work is shaped by a rapidly rotating cutter whose position is varied by the pattern acting as a cam upon a follower wheel traversing slowly along the pattern

blanchimeter.d: An instrument for measuring the bleaching power of chloride of lime and potash; a chlorometer

blanket clause.d: A clause, as in a blanket mortgage or policy, that includes a group or class of things, rather than a number mentioned individually and having the burden, loss, or the like, apportioned among them

blazing-star.d: any of various North American plants of the genus Liatris having racemes or panicles of small discoid flower heads

blea.d: The part of a tree which lies immediately under the bark; the alburnum or sapwood

blendous.d: Pertaining to, consisting of, or containing, blende

blendwater.d: A distemper incident to cattle, in which their livers are affected

blenk.d: To blink; to shine; to look

blesser.d: One who blesses; one who bestows or invokes a blessing

blewit.d: an edible agaric (Tricholoma personatum) that is pale lilac when young

bleyme.d: An inflammation in the foot of a horse, between the sole and the bone

blind reader.d: A post-office clerk whose duty is to decipher obscure addresses

blink beer.d: Beer kept unbroached until it is sharp

blirt.d: A gust of wind and rain

blissom.d: To be lustful; to be lascivious

blocage.d: The roughest and cheapest sort of rubblework, in masonry

block book.d: A book printed from engraved wooden blocks instead of movable types

blocking course.d: The finishing course of a wall showing above a cornice

blond metal.d: A variety of clay ironstone, in Staffordshire, England, used for making tools

blood-boltered.d: Having the hair matted with clotted blood

bloodstick.d: A piece of hard wood loaded at one end with lead, and used to strike the fleam into the vein

bloodstroke.d: Loss of sensation and motion from hemorrhage or congestion in the brain

bloodwite.d: A fine or amercement paid as part of a settlement for the shedding of blood; also, a riot wherein blood was spilled

bloody hand.d: A hand stained with the blood of a deer, which, in the old forest laws of England, was sufficient evidence of a man's trespass in the forest against venison

blote.d: To cure, as herrings, by salting and smoking them; to bloat

blowen.d: A prostitute; a courtesan; a strumpet

blue bonnet.d: A broad, flat Scottish cap of blue woolen, or one wearing such cap; a Scotchman

blue hen state.d: The State of Delaware; -- a popular sobriquet. It is said, though the story lacks proof, to have taken its origin from the insistence of a Delaware Revolutionary captain, named Caldwell, that no cock could be truly game unless the mother was a blue hen, whence Blue Hen's Chickens came to be a nickname for the people of Delaware

blue-grass state.d: The Sate of Kentucky; -- a nickname alluding to the blue-grass region, where fine horses are bred

blue-green alga.d: any of a group of photosynthetic microorganisms possessing characteristics of both bacteria and plants.  When classed as bacteria, they are assigned to the Cyanobacteria; when classed as plants, they are assigned to the Cyanophyta.  They are now known to be prokaryotic, and are usually called cyanobacteria in technical contexts.  See cyanobacterium

blue-john.d: A name given to fluor spar in Derbyshire, where it is used for ornamental purposes

blue-skylaw.d: A law enacted to provide for the regulation and supervision of investment companies in order to protect the public against companies that do not intend to do a fair and honest business and that offer investments that do not promise a fair return; -- so called because the promises made by some investment companies are as boundless or alluring as the blue sky, or, perhaps, because designed to clear away the clouds and fogs from the simple investor's horizon

blue-veined.d: Having blue veins or blue streaks

bluepoll.d: A kind of salmon (Salmo Cambricus) found in Wales

bluff-bowed.d: Built with the stem nearly straight up and down

bluff-headed.d: Built with the stem nearly straight up and down

bluffy.d: Having bluffs, or bold, steep banks

boat shell.d: A marine gastropod of the genus Crepidula. The species are numerous. It is so named from its form and interior deck

boat-tail.d: A large grackle or blackbird (Quiscalus major), found in the Southern United States

boation.d: A crying out; a roaring; a bellowing; reverberation

boatwoman.d: A woman who manages a boat

bob-cherry.d: A play among children, in which a cherry, hung so as to bob against the mouth, is to be caught with the teeth

bocal.d: A cylindrical glass vessel, with a large and short neck

bockelet.d: A kind of long-winged hawk; -- called also bockerel, and bockeret

bockey.d: A bowl or vessel made from a gourd

bod veal.d: Veal too immature to be suitable for food

bogie engine.d: A switching engine the running gear and driving gear of which are on a bogie, or truck

bogsucker.d: The American woodcock; -- so called from its feeding among the bogs

bois durci.d: A hard, highly polishable composition, made of fine sawdust from hard wood (as rosewood) mixed with blood, and pressed

boistous.d: Rough or rude; coarse; strong; violent; boisterous; noisy

bojanus organ.d: A glandular organ of bivalve mollusca, serving in part as a kidney

bold eagle.d: an Australian eagle (Aquila audax), which destroys lambs and even the kangaroo

boletic.d: Pertaining to, or obtained from, the Boletus

bolis.d: A meteor or brilliant shooting star, followed by a train of light or sparks; esp. one which explodes

bolty.d: An edible fish of the Nile (genus Chromis)

bombardman.d: One who carried liquor or beer in a can or bombard

bombardo.d: Originally, a deep-toned instrument of the oboe or bassoon family; thence, a bass reed stop on the organ. The name bombardon is now given to a brass instrument, the lowest of the saxhorns, in tone resembling the ophicleide

bombastry.d: Swelling words without much meaning; bombastic language; fustian

bombazet bombazette.d: A sort of thin woolen cloth. It is of various colors, and may be plain or twilled

bombic.d: Pertaining to, or obtained from, the silkworm; as, bombic acid

bombolo.d: A thin spheroidal glass retort or flask, used in the sublimation of camphor

bombylious.d: Buzzing, like a bumblebee; as, the bombylious noise of the horse fly

bon silene.d: A very fragrant tea rose with petals of various shades of pink

bonasus.d: The aurochs or European bison. See Aurochs

bonchretien.d: A name given to several kinds of pears. See Bartlett

boncilate.d: A substance composed of ground bone, mineral matters, etc., hardened by pressure, and used for making billiard balls, boxes, etc

bond-servant.d: A slave; one who is bound to service without wages

boniform.d: Sensitive or responsive to moral excellence

bonify.d: To convert into, or make, good

bonnaz.d: A kind of embroidery made with a complicated sewing machine, said to have been originally invented by a Frenchman of the name of Bonnaz. The work is done either in freehand or by following a perforated design

bonnet head.d: small harmless hammerhead shark (Sphyrna tiburio) of the southern United States and West Indies, having a spade-shaped head; abundant in bays and estuaries

bonnet rouge.d: The red cap adopted by the extremists in the French Revolution, which became a sign of patriotism at that epoch; hence, a revolutionist; a Red Republican

book muslin.d: A kind of muslin used for the covers of books

bookmate.d: A schoolfellow; an associate in study

booly.d: A company of Irish herdsmen, or a single herdsman, wandering from place to place with flocks and herds, and living on their milk, like the Tartars; also, a place in the mountain pastures inclosed for the shelter of cattle or their keepers

boomdas.d: A small African hyracoid mammal (Dendrohyrax arboreus) resembling the daman

boomorah.d: A small West African chevrotain (Hyæmoschus aquaticus), resembling the musk deer

boomslange.d: A large South African tree snake (Bucephalus Capensis). Although considered venomous by natives, it has no poison fangs

boothale.d: To forage for booty; to plunder

borachte.d: A large leather bottle for liquors, etc., made of the skin of a goat or other animal. Hence: A drunkard

boracous.d: Relating to, or obtained from, borax; containing borax

boraginaceous.d: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a family of plants (Boraginaceæ) which includes the borage, heliotrope, beggar's lice, and many pestiferous plants

boragineous.d: Relating to the Borage tribe; boraginaceous

borborygm.d: A rumbling or gurgling noise produced by wind in the bowels

bord service.d: Service due from a bordar; bordage

bordelais.d: Of or pertaining to Bordeaux, in France, or to the district around Bordeaux

bordland.d: Either land held by a bordar, or the land which a lord kept for the maintenance of his board, or table

bordlode.d: The service formerly required of a tenant, to carry timber from the woods to the lord's house

bordman.d: A bordar; a tenant in bordage

bordrag.d: An incursion upon the borders of a country; a raid

borele.d: The smaller two-horned rhinoceros of South Africa (Atelodus bicornis)

boroughmaster.d: The mayor, governor, or bailiff of a borough

borrel.d: Coarse woolen cloth; hence, coarse clothing; a garment

bosporian.d: Of or pertaining to the Thracian or the Cimmerian Bosporus

botocudos.d: A Brazilian tribe of Indians, noted for their use of poisons; -- also called Aymborés

bottle-nose.d: A grey cetacean of the Dolphin family, of several species, as Delphinus Tursio and Lagenorhyncus leucopleurus, of Europe

bottlegrass.d: a European foxtail naturalized in North America; it is often a troublesome weed

bougie decimale.d: A photometric standard used in France, having the value of one twentieth of the Violle platinum standard, or slightly less than a British standard candle.  Called also decimal candle

boultel.d: A molding, the convexity of which is one fourth of a circle, being a member just below the abacus in the Tuscan and Roman Doric capital; a torus; an ovolo

boutefeu.d: An incendiary; an inciter of quarrels

bouts-rimes.d: Words that rhyme, proposed as the ends of verses, to be filled out by the ingenuity of the person to whom they are offered

boviform.d: Resembling an ox in form; ox-shaped

bovinae.d: a term essentially coextensive with the genus Bos, including cattle, buffalo, and sometimes kudu; -- it is not used technically

bow hand.d: The hand that holds the bow, i. e., the left hand

bow net.d: A trap for lobsters, being a wickerwork cylinder with a funnel-shaped entrance at one end

bow-bells.d: The bells of Bow Church in London; cockneydom

bow-pen.d: Bow-compasses carrying a drawing pen. See Bow-compass

bow-pencil.d: Bow-compasses, one leg of which carries a pencil

bow-saw.d: A saw with a thin or narrow blade set in a strong frame

bowable.d: Capable of being bowed or bent; flexible; easily influenced; yielding

bowbell.d: One born within hearing distance of Bow-bells; a cockney

bowdlerisation.d: the deletion of all passages considered to be indecent

bower bird.d: An Australian bird (Ptilonorhynchus violaceus or Ptilonorhynchus holosericeus), allied to the starling.  The male constructs singular bowers or playhouses of twigs and decorates them with bright-colored objects to attract females; the satin bird

bower-barff process.d: A certain process for producing upon articles of iron or steel an adherent coating of the magnetic oxide of iron (which is not liable to corrosion by air, moisture, or ordinary acids). This is accomplished by producing, by oxidation at about 1600° F. in a closed space, a coating containing more or less of the ferric oxide (Fe2O3) and the subsequent change of this in a reduced atmosphere to the magnetic oxide (Fe2O4)

bowl-legged.d: Having crooked legs, esp. with the knees bent outward

bowssen.d: To drench; to soak; especially, to immerse (in water believed to have curative properties)

box tail.d: In a flying machine, a tail or rudder, usually fixed, resembling a box kite

box-iron.d: A hollow smoothing iron containing a heater within

box-number.d: the mailing address to which answers to a newspaper ad can be sent

boxen.d: Made of boxwood; pertaining to, or resembling, the box (Buxus)

brachioganoidei.d: An order of ganoid fishes of which the bichir of Africa is a living example. See Crossopterygii

brachycatalectic.d: A verse wanting two syllables at its termination

brachyceral.d: Having short antennæ, as certain insects

brachygrapher.d: A writer in short hand; a stenographer

brachyptera.d: A group of Coleoptera having short wings; the rove beetles

brachypteres.d: A group of birds, including auks, divers, and penguins

brachystochrone.d: A curve, in which a body, starting from a given point, and descending solely by the force of gravity, will reach another given point in a shorter time than it could by any other path. This curve of quickest descent, as it is sometimes called, is, in a vacuum, the same as the cycloid

brachytactyly.d: abnormal shortness of fingers and toes

brad awl.d: A straight awl with chisel edge, used to make holes for brads, etc

bragget.d: A liquor made of ale and honey fermented, with spices, etc

bragly.d: In a manner to be bragged of; finely; proudly

brahmo-somaj.d: A modern reforming theistic sect among the Hindus

bramah press.d: A hydrostatic press of immense power, invented by Joseph Bramah of London. See under Hydrostatic

branch pilot.d: A pilot who has a branch or commission, as from Trinity House, England, for special navigation

brancher.d: That which shoots forth branches; one who shows growth in various directions

branchiogastropoda.d: Those Gastropoda that breathe by branchiæ, including the Prosobranchiata and Opisthobranchiata

branchiostege.d: The branchiostegal membrane. See Illustration in Appendix

brand goose.d: A species of wild goose (Branta bernicla) usually called in America brant. See Brant

brand spore.d: One of several spores growing in a series or chain, and produced by one of the fungi called brand

brant-fox.d: A kind of fox found in Sweden (Vulpes alopex), smaller than the common fox (Vulpes vulgaris), but probably a variety of it

breadcorn.d: Corn of grain of which bread is made, as wheat, rye, etc

break-circuit.d: A key or other device for breaking an electrical circuit

breastband.d: A band for the breast. Specifically: (Naut.) A band of canvas, or a rope, fastened at both ends to the rigging, to support the man who heaves the lead in sounding

breastfast.d: A large rope to fasten the midship part of a ship to a wharf, or to another vessel

breastheight.d: The interior slope of a fortification, against which the garrison lean in firing

breastknot.d: A knot of ribbons worn on the breast

breastplow.d: A kind of plow, driven by the breast of the workman; -- used to cut or pare turf

breastwheel.d: A water wheel, on which the stream of water strikes neither so high as in the overshot wheel, nor so low as in the undershot, but generally at about half the height of the wheel, being kept in contact with it by the breasting. The water acts on the float boards partly by impulse, partly by its weight

breathful.d: Full of breath; full of odor; fragrant

breech action.d: The breech mechanism in breech-loading small arms and certain special guns, as automatic and machine guns; -- used frequently in referring to the method by which the movable barrels of breech-loading shotguns are locked, unlocked, or rotated to loading position

breech pin.d: A strong iron or steel plug screwed into the breech of a musket or other firearm, to close the bottom of the bore

breech sight.d: A device attached to the breech of a firearm, to guide the eye, in conjunction with the front sight, in taking aim

breedbate.d: One who breeds or originates quarrels

brelan.d: A French gambling game somewhat like poker

brelan carre.d: In French games, a double pair royal

brelan favori.d: In French games, a pair royal composed of 2 cards in the hand and the card turned

breloque.d: A seal or charm for a watch chain

brennage.d: A tribute which tenants paid to their lord, in lieu of bran, which they were obliged to furnish for his hounds

brenschluss.d: the time at which the engines of a rocket stop firing; the termination of the firing of the rocket engines, whether due to intentional shutdown of the engines or exhaustion of the fuel.  This term was used mostly in the early days of rocketry when only one firing sequence occurred for rockets, which were used as ballistic missiles or for experiments in rocketry or atmospheric science

bretwalda.d: The official title applied to that one of the Anglo-Saxon chieftains who was chosen by the other chiefs to lead them in their warfare against the British tribes

breviloquence.d: A brief and pertinent mode of speaking

bribeless.d: Incapable of being bribed; free from bribes

bric-a brac.d: Miscellaneous curiosities and works of decorative art, considered collectively

brickellia.d: genus of herbs of SW America having usually creamy florets followed by one-seeded fruits in a prominent bristly sheath

bridalwreath.d: a shrub (Spiraea prunifolia) having copious small white flowers in spring

bride-ale.d: A rustic wedding feast; a bridal. See Ale

brideknot.d: A knot of ribbons worn by a guest at a wedding; a wedding favor

bridestake.d: A stake or post set in the ground, for guests at a wedding to dance round

bridge-ward.d: A bridge keeper; a warden or a guard for a bridge

bridgepot.d: The adjustable socket, or step, of a millstone spindle

bridgetree.d: The beam which supports the spindle socket of the runner in a grinding mill

bridle iron.d: A strong flat bar of iron, so bent as to support, as in a stirrup, one end of a floor timber, etc., where no sufficient bearing can be had; -- called also stirrup and hanger

brie cheese.d: A kind of soft French cream cheese; -- so called from the district in France where it is made; it is milder than Camembert; -- called also fromage de Brie, Brie and brie (uncapitalized)

brigue.d: A cabal, intrigue, faction, contention, strife, or quarrel

brinjaree.d: A rough-haired East Indian variety of the greyhound

bristle-shaped.d: Resembling a bristle in form; as, a bristle-shaped leaf

broad-side.d: to collide with the broad side of

broadbean.d: an Old World upright plant grown esp. for its large flat edible seeds but also as fodder

broadmouth.d: One of the Eurylaimidæ, a family of East Indian passerine birds

broadseal.d: To stamp with the broad seal; to make sure; to guarantee or warrant

brocken specter.d: A mountain specter (which see), esp. that observed on the Brocken, in the Harz Mountains

broggle.d: To sniggle, or fish with a brog

bromalin.d: A colorless or white crystalline compound, (CH2)6N4C2H5Br, used as a sedative in epilepsy

bromatologist.d: One versed in the science of foods

brome grass.d: A genus (Bromus) of grasses, one species of which is the chess or cheat

bromidiom.d: A conventional comment or saying, such as those characteristic of bromides{2}; a bromide{3}

bromlife.d: A carbonate of baryta and lime, intermediate between witherite and strontianite; -- called also alstonite

brompicrin.d: A pungent colorless explosive liquid, CNO2Br3, analogous to and resembling chlorpicrin

brompton's mixture.d: A mixture containing morphine and cocaine, and sometimes other narcotic substances, such as heroin, in an alcoholic solution, administered mostly to terminally ill patients, especially cancer patients, to relieve severe pain.  Its use is not universally accepted as good medical practice

broncho-pneumonia.d: Inflammation of the bronchi and lungs; catarrhal pneumonia

brontotherium.d: A genus of large extinct mammals from the miocene strata of western North America. They were allied to the rhinoceros, but the skull bears a pair of powerful horn cores in front of the orbits, and the fore feet were four-toed. See Illustration in Appendix

brontozoum.d: An extinct animal of large size, known from its three-toed footprints in Mesozoic sandstone

bronze steel.d: A hard tough alloy of tin, copper, and iron, which can be used for guns

bronzine.d: A metal so prepared as to have the appearance of bronze

bronzist.d: One who makes, imitates, collects, or deals in, bronzes

broom rape.d: A genus (Orobanche) of parasitic plants of Europe and Asia. They are destitute of chlorophyll, have scales instead of leaves, and spiked flowers, and grow attached to the roots of other plants, as furze, clover, flax, wild carrot, etc. The name is sometimes applied to other plants related to this genus, as Aphyllon uniflorumand Aphyllon Ludovicianum

brother german.d: A brother by both the father's and mother's side, in contradistinction to a uterine brother, one by the mother only

browbound.d: Crowned; having the head encircled as with a diadem

brown bill.d: A bill or halberd of the 16th and 17th centuries. See 4th Bill

brown race.d: The Malay or Polynesian race; -- loosely so called

brownist.d: A follower of Robert Brown, of England, in the 16th century, who taught that every church is complete and independent in itself when organized, and consists of members meeting in one place, having full power to elect and depose its officers

brownwort.d: A species of figwort or Scrophularia (Scrophularia vernalis), and other species of the same genus, mostly perennials with inconspicuous coarse flowers

browpost.d: A beam that goes across a building

browsewood.d: Shrubs and bushes upon which animals browse

browspot.d: A rounded organ between the eyes of the frog; the interocular gland

bruisewort.d: A plant supposed to heal bruises, as the true daisy, the soapwort, and the comfrey

brunonian.d: Pertaining to, or invented by, Brown; -- a term applied to a system of medicine promulgated in the 18th century by John Brown, of Scotland, the fundamental doctrine of which was, that life is a state of excitation produced by the normal action of external agents upon the body, and that disease consists in excess or deficiency of excitation

brushiness.d: The quality of resembling a brush; brushlike condition; shagginess

brustle.d: To crackle; to rustle, as a silk garment

bryozoum.d: An individual zooid of a bryozoan coralline, of which there may be two or more kinds in a single colony. The zoœcia usually have a wreath of tentacles around the mouth, and a well developed stomach and intestinal canal; but these parts are lacking in the other zooids (Avicularia, Oœcia, etc.)

buansuah.d: The wild dog of northern India (Cuon primævus), supposed by some to be an ancestral species of the domestic dog

bubbling jock.d: The male wild turkey, the gobbler; -- so called in allusion to its notes

buccan.d: A wooden frame or grid for roasting, smoking, or drying meat over fire

buccinoid.d: Resembling the genus Buccinum, or pertaining to the Buccinidæ, a family of marine univalve shells. See Whelk, and Prosobranchiata

buccinum.d: A genus of large univalve mollusks abundant in the arctic seas.  It includes the common whelk (Buccinum undatum)

buck's-horn.d: A plant with leaves branched somewhat like a buck's horn (Plantago Coronopus); also, Lobelia coronopifolia

buck-basket.d: A basket in which clothes are carried to the wash

buckety.d: Paste used by weavers to dress their webs

buckler-headed.d: Having a head like a buckler

buckstall.d: A toil or net to take deer

bucranium.d: A sculptured ornament, representing an ox skull adorned with wreaths, etc

bude burner.d: A burner consisting of two or more concentric Argand burners (the inner rising above the outer) and a central tube by which oxygen gas or common air is supplied

bude light.d: A light in which high illuminating power is obtained by introducing a jet of oxygen gas or of common air into the center of a flame fed with coal gas or with oil

buffalo nickel.d: A United States five-cent coin minted from 1913 to 1937 having an image of an American bison (“buffalo”) on its reverse, and an American Indian on the obverse

buffel duck.d: A small duck (Charitonetta albeola); the spirit duck, or butterball.  The head of the male is covered with numerous elongated feathers, and thus appears large.  Called also bufflehead

bufferhead.d: The head of a buffer, which recieves the concussion, in railroad carriages

buffle-headed.d: Having a large head, like a buffalo; dull; stupid; blundering

bulau.d: An East Indian insectivorous mammal (Gymnura Rafflesii), somewhat like a rat in appearance, but allied to the hedgehog

bull brier.d: A species of Smilax (Smilax Pseudo-China) growing from New Jersey to the Gulf of Mexico, which has very large tuberous and farinaceous rootstocks, formerly used by the Indians for a sort of bread, and by the negroes as an ingredient in making beer; -- called also bamboo brier and China brier

bull fly.d: Any large fly troublesome to cattle, as the gadflies and breeze flies

bull trout.d: In England, a large salmon trout of several species, as Salmo trutta and Salmo Cambricus, which ascend rivers; -- called also sea trout

bull's-nose.d: An external angle when obtuse or rounded

bull-necked.d: Having a short, thick and muscular neck like that of a bull

bullantic.d: Pertaining to, or used in, papal bulls

bullbeggar.d: Something used or suggested to produce terror, as in children or persons of weak mind; a bugbear

bullcomber.d: A scaraboid beetle; esp. the Typhæus vulgaris of Europe

bullen-nail.d: A nail with a round head and short shank, tinned and lacquered

bullirag.d: To intimidate by bullying; to rally contemptuously; to badger

bullist.d: A writer or drawer up of papal bulls

bullition.d: The action of boiling; boiling. [Obs.] See Ebullition

bullsnake.d: any of several large harmless rodent-eating North American burrowing snakes of the genus Pituophis.  They include the gopher snake and pine snake

bulse.d: A purse or bag in which to carry or measure diamonds, etc

bultel.d: A bolter or bolting cloth; also, bran

bultow.d: A trawl; a boulter; the mode of fishing with a boulter or spiller

bumbelo.d: A glass used in subliming camphor

bunch-backed.d: Having a bunch on the back; crooked

bunji-bunji.d: an Australian timber tree (Flindersia schottiana) whose bark yields a poison

bunkbed.d: A type of multiple bed in which the individual beds are arranged one above the other.  It is used to save space in crowded quarters

bunodonta.d: A division of the herbivorous mammals including the hogs and hippopotami; -- so called because the teeth are tuberculated

bunyon.d: An enlargement and inflammation of a small membranous sac (one of the bursæ muscosæ), usually occurring on the first joint of the great toe

buprestidan.d: One of a tribe of beetles, of the genus Buprestis and allied genera, usually with brilliant metallic colors. The larvæ are usually borers in timber, or beneath bark, and are often very destructive to trees

bur fish.d: A spinose, plectognath fish of the Allantic coast of the United States (esp. Chilo mycterus geometricus) having the power of distending its body with water or air, so as to resemble a chestnut bur; -- called also ball fish, balloon fish, and swellfish

burgall.d: A small marine fish; -- also called cunner

burgess-ship.d: The state of privilege of a burgess

burggrave.d: Originally, one appointed to the command of a burg (fortress or castle); but the title afterward became hereditary, with a domain attached

burghbote.d: A contribution toward the building or repairing of castles or walls for the defense of a city or town

burghbrech.d: The offense of violating the pledge given by every inhabitant of a tithing to keep the peace; breach of the peace

burghmote.d: A court or meeting of a burgh or borough; a borough court held three times yearly

burion.d: The red-breasted house sparrow of California (Carpodacus frontalis); -- called also crimson-fronted bullfinch

burkism.d: The practice of killing persons for the purpose of selling their bodies for dissection

burrel fly.d: The botfly or gadfly of cattle (Hypoderma bovis). See Gadfly

burrel shot.d: A mixture of shot, nails, stones, pieces of old iron, etc., fired from a cannon at short range, in an emergency

burring machine.d: A machine for cleansing wool of burs, seeds, and other substances

bursch.d: A youth; especially, a student in a german university

burschenschaft.d: In Germany, any of various associations of university students formed (the original one at Jena in 1815) to support liberal ideas, or the organization formed by the affiliation of the local bodies. The organization was suppressed by the government in 1819, but was secretly revived, and is now openly maintained as a social organization, the restrictive laws having been repealed prior to 1849

bursten.d: p. p. of Burst, v. i

burstwort.d: A plant (Herniaria glabra) supposed to be valuable for the cure of hernia or rupture

buscon.d: One who searches for ores; a prospector

bushelman.d: A tailor's assistant for repairing garments; -- called also busheler

bushment.d: A thicket; a cluster of bushes

busket.d: A small bush; also, a sprig or bouquet

butcher bird.d: any species of shrike of the genus Lanius, so called because they impale their prey on thorns

butlerage.d: A duty of two shillings on every tun of wine imported into England by merchant strangers; -- so called because paid to the king's butler for the king

butter and eggs.d: a name given to several perennial plants having showy flowers of two shades of yellow, or of yellow and orange, such as Narcissus incomparabilis in Europe, and the toadflax (Linaria vulgaris) in the United States; the latter is a naturalized weed in North America

butter-scotch.d: A kind of candy, mainly composed of sugar and butter

butterbird.d: The rice bunting or bobolink; -- so called in the island of Jamaica

butting joint.d: A joint between two pieces of timber or wood, at the end of one or both, and either at right angles or oblique to the grain, as the joints which the struts and braces form with the truss posts; -- sometimes called abutting joint

buttonweed.d: The name of several plants of the genera Spermacoce and Diodia, of the Madder family

butyl mercaptan.d: A volatile liquid, C4H9.SH, having a strong odor like that of a skunk; also called butanethiol.  All three isomers, normal, sec-, and tert-butanethiol possess the skunk odor

buzzardet.d: A hawk resembling the buzzard, but with legs relatively longer

by-dependence.d: An appendage; that which depends on something else, or is distinct from the main dependence; an accessory

by-speech.d: An incidental or casual speech, not directly relating to the point

by-street.d: A separate, private, or obscure street; an out of the way or cross street

by-stroke.d: An accidental or a slyly given stroke

by-turning.d: An obscure road; a way turning from the main road

by-view.d: A private or selfish view; self-interested aim or purpose

by-wash.d: The outlet from a dam or reservoir; also, a cut to divert the flow of water

by-wipe.d: A secret or side stroke, as of raillery or sarcasm

c q d.d: In radiotelegraphy, the letters signified by the code call formerly used (cf. S O S) by ships in distress, formed by combining the code call C Q (formerly used as a general call for all stations) with D for distress

c. g. t..d: An abbreviation for Confédération Générale du Travail (the French syndicalist labor union)

ca ira.d: The refrain of a famous song of the French Revolution

caballeria.d: An ancient Spanish land tenure similar to the English knight's fee; hence, in Spain and countries settled by the Spanish, a land measure of varying size.  In Cuba it is about 33 acres; in Puerto Rico, about 194 acres; in the Southwestern United States, about 108 acres

cabassou.d: A species of armadillo of the genus Xenurus (Xenurus unicinctus and Xenurus hispidus); the tatouay

cabiri.d: Certain deities originally worshiped with mystical rites by the Pelasgians in Lemnos and Samothrace and afterwards throughout Greece; -- also called sons of Hephæstus (or Vulcan), as being masters of the art of working metals

cabiric.d: Of or pertaining to the Cabiri, or to their mystical worship

caboched.d: Showing the full face, but nothing of the neck; -- said of the head of a beast in armorial bearing

caburn.d: A small line made of spun yarn, to bind or worm cables, seize tackles, etc

cachaemia.d: A degenerated or poisoned condition of the blood

cachiri.d: A fermented liquor made in Cayenne from the grated root of the manioc, and resembling perry

cachunde.d: A pastil or troche, composed of various aromatic and other ingredients, highly celebrated in India as an antidote, and as a stomachic and antispasmodic

cackerel.d: The mendole; a small worthless Mediterranean fish considered poisonous by the ancients. See Mendole

cacochymic.d: Having the fluids of the body vitiated, especially the blood

cacoon.d: One of the seeds or large beans of a tropical vine (Entada scandens) used for making purses, scent bottles, etc

cacotechny.d: A corruption or corrupt state of art

cacoxene.d: A hydrous phosphate of iron occurring in yellow radiated tufts. The phosphorus seriously injures it as an iron ore

cadene.d: A species of inferior carpet imported from the Levant

cadie.d: A Scotch errand boy, porter, or messenger

cadilesker.d: A chief judge in the Turkish empire, so named originally because his jurisdiction extended to the cases of soldiers, who are now tried only by their own officers

cadrans.d: An instrument with a graduated disk by means of which the angles of gems are measured in the process of cutting and polishing

caducibranchiate.d: With temporary gills: -- applied to those Amphibia in which the gills do not remain in adult life

caen stone.d: A cream-colored limestone for building, found near Caen, France

cafe latte.d: A type of espresso coffee topped with foamy steamed milk, and usually served in a tall glass or mug; also called latte

cafenet.d: A humble inn or house of rest for travelers, where coffee is sold

caffetannic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, the tannin of coffee

cafila.d: A caravan of travelers; a military supply train or government caravan; a string of pack horses

cagit.d: A kind of parrot, of a beautiful green color, found in the Philippine Islands

cahenslyism.d: A plan proposed to the Pope in 1891 by P. P. Cahensly, a member of the German parliament, to divide the foreign-born population of the United States, for ecclesiastical purposes, according to European nationalities, and to appoint bishops and priests of like race and speaking the same language as the majority of the members of a diocese or congregation. This plan was successfully opposed by the American party in the Church

cahinca root.d: The root of an American shrub (Chiococca racemosa), found as far north as Florida Keys, from which cahincic acid is obtained; also, the root of the South American Chiococca anguifuga, a celebrated antidote for snake poison

cahincic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, cahinca, the native name of a species of Brazilian Chiococca, perhaps Chiococca racemosa; as, cahincic acid

caimacam.d: The governor of a sanjak or district in Turkey

cajanus.d: a genus of erect densely branched shrubby perennials of Old World tropics; naturalized in other warm regions

calabura.d: a fast-growing tropical American evergreen (Muntingia calabura) having white flowers and white fleshy edible fruit; bark yields a silky fiber used in cordage and wood is valuable for staves

calade.d: A slope or declivity in a manege ground down which a horse is made to gallop, to give suppleness to his haunches

caladenia.d: any of various orchids of the genus Caladenia

calamander wood.d: A valuable furniture wood from India and Ceylon, of a hazel-brown color, with black stripes, very hard in texture. It is a species of ebony, and is obtained from the Diospyros quæsita. Called also Coromandel wood

calambour.d: A species of agalloch, or aloes wood, of a dusky or mottled color, of a light, friable texture, and less fragrant than calambac; -- used by cabinetmakers

calamist.d: One who plays upon a reed or pipe

calamistrate.d: To curl or friz, as the hair

calamistration.d: The act or process of curling the hair

calandrinia.d: a large genus of low-growing herbs; widespread throughout tropical and warm temperate regions having usually basal leaves and panicles of purplish ephemeral flowers

calaveras skull.d: A human skull reported, by Prof. J. D. Whitney, as found in 1886 in a Tertiary auriferous gravel deposit, lying below a bed of black lava, in Calaveras County, California. It is regarded as very doubtful whether the skull really belonged to the deposit in which it was found. If it did, it indicates an unprecedented antiquity for human beings of an advanced type

calcareo-argillaceous.d: consisting of, or containing, calcareous and argillaceous earths

calcareo-bituminous.d: Consisting of, or containing, lime and bitumen

calcareo-siliceous.d: Consisting of, or containing, calcareous and siliceous earths

calcavella.d: A sweet wine from Portugal; -- so called from the district of Carcavelhos

calcedon.d: A foul vein, like chalcedony, in some precious stones

calcigenous.d: Tending to form, or to become, a calx or earthlike substance on being oxidized or burnt; as magnesium, calcium. etc

calcispongiae.d: An order of marine sponges, containing calcareous spicules. See Porifera

calcographic.d: Relating to, or in the style of, calcography

calendrer.d: A person who calenders cloth; a calender

caliche-topped.d: covered with caliche{2}, a hard calcium-carbonate encrusted soil

california jack.d: A game at cards, a modification of seven-up, or all fours

calippic.d: Of or pertaining to Calippus, an Athenian astronomer

calistheneum.d: A gymnasium; esp. one for light physical exercise by women and children

callid.d: Characterized by cunning or shrewdness; crafty

callimorpha.d: a genus of insects comprising the cinnabar moths

callisaurus.d: a genus of lizards including the the zebra-tailed lizard

callophis.d: a genus of Asian coral snakes

calmucks.d: A branch of the Mongolian race inhabiting parts of the Russian and Chinese empires; also (sing.), the language of the Calmucks

calopogon.d: a genus of terrestrial orchids of North America

caloriduct.d: A tube or duct for conducting heat; a caliduct

calorificient.d: Having, or relating to the power of producing heat; -- applied to foods which, being rich in carbon, as the fats, are supposed to give rise to heat in the animal body by oxidation

calorimotor.d: A voltaic battery, having a large surface of plate, and producing powerful heating effects

calycifloral.d: Having the petals and stamens adnate to the calyx; -- applied to a subclass of dicotyledonous plants in the system of the French botanist Candolle

calycozoa.d: A group of acalephs of which Lucernaria is the type. The body is cup-shaped with eight marginal lobes bearing clavate tentacles. An aboral sucker serves for attachment. The interior is divided into four large compartments. See Lucernarida

calystegia.d: a genus of climbing or scrambling herbs; bindweed

camachile.d: a common thorny tropical American tree (Pithecellobium dulce) having terminal racemes of yellow flowers followed by sickle-shaped or circinate edible pods and yielding good timber and a yellow dye and mucilaginous gum

camberkeeled.d: Having the keel arched upwards, but not actually hogged; -- said of a ship

cambrasine.d: A kind of linen cloth made in Egypt, and so named from its resemblance to cambric

camel-backed.d: Having a back like a camel; humpbacked

camisated.d: Dressed with a shirt over the other garments

camonflet.d: A small mine, sometimes formed in the wall or side of an enemy's gallery, to blow in the earth and cut off the retreat of the miners

campagnol.d: A mouse (Arvicala agrestis), called also meadow mouse, which often does great damage in fields and gardens, by feeding on roots and seeds

campaned.d: Furnished with, or bearing, campanes, or bells

campanularian.d: A hydroid of the family Campanularidæ, characterized by having the polyps or zooids inclosed in bell-shaped calicles or hydrothecæ

campfight.d: A duel; the decision of a case by a duel

camphretic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from camphor

campyloneurum.d: a genus of epiphytic ferns of tropical America

can hook.d: A device consisting of a short rope with flat hooks at each end, for hoisting casks or barrels by the ends of the staves

canafistola.d: a deciduous or semi-evergreen tree (Cassia fistula) having scented sepia to yellow flowers in drooping racemes and pods whose pulp is used medicinally; it grows in tropical Asia, Central and South America, and Australia

canape confident.d: A sofa having a seat at each end at right angles to the main seats

cancelier.d: To turn in flight; -- said of a hawk

cancerite.d: Like a cancer; having the qualities or virulence of a cancer; affected with cancer

candellila.d: either of two Mexican shrubs Pedilanthus bracteatus or Pedilanthus pavonis

canderos.d: An East Indian resin, of a pellucid white color, from which small ornaments and toys are sometimes made

candify.d: To make or become white, or candied

candle foot.d: The illumination produced by a British standard candle at a distance of one foot; -- used as a unit of illumination

candle meter.d: The illumination given by a standard candle at a distance of one meter; -- used as a unit of illumination, except in Great Britain

candleberry tree.d: A shrub (the Myrica cerifera, or wax-bearing myrtle), common in North America, the little nuts of which are covered with a greenish white wax, which was formerly, used for hardening candles; -- also called bayberry tree, bayberry, or candleberry

candlebomb.d: A small glass bubble, filled with water, which, if placed in the flame of a candle, bursts by expansion of steam

candlewaster.d: One who consumes candles by being up late for study or dissipation

candroy.d: A machine for spreading out cotton cloths to prepare them for printing

canker bloom.d: The bloom or blossom of the wild rose or dog-rose

canker blossom.d: That which blasts a blossom as a canker does

canker fly.d: A fly that preys on fruit

canker-bit.d: Eaten out by canker, or as by canker

cannele.d: A style of interweaving giving to fabrics a channeled or fluted effect; also, a fabric woven so as to have this effect; a rep

canon bit.d: That part of a bit which is put in a horse's mouth

canon bone.d: The shank bone, or great bone above the fetlock, in the fore and hind legs of the horse and allied animals, corresponding to the middle metacarpal or metatarsal bone of most mammals. See Horse

cantatory.d: Containing cant or affectation; whining; singing

canticoy.d: A social gathering; usually, one for dancing

cantiniere.d: A woman who carries a canteen for soldiers; a vivandière

canton crape.d: A soft, white or colored silk fabric, of a gauzy texture and wavy appearance, used for ladies' scarfs, shawls, bonnet trimmings, etc.; -- called also Oriental crape

cantrap.d: A charm; an incantation; a shell; a trick; adroit mischief

cantred.d: A district comprising a hundred villages, as in Wales

canyada.d: A small cañon; a narrow valley or glen; also, but less frequently, an open valley

caoutchin.d: An inflammable, volatile, oily, liquid hydrocarbon, obtained by the destructive distillation of caoutchouc

capaciate.d: to become active so as to be able to penetrate an ovum; -- of sperm, in the female reproduction system

caparro.d: A large South American monkey (Lagothrix Humboldtii), with prehensile tail

capcase.d: A small traveling case or bandbox; formerly, a chest

capellane.d: The curate of a chapel; a chaplain

capellet.d: A swelling, like a wen, on the point of the elbow (or the heel of the hock) of a horse, caused probably by bruises in lying down

caperberry.d: The small olive-shaped berry of the European and Oriental caper, said to be used in pickles and as a condiment

caperclaw.d: To treat with cruel playfulness, as a cat treats a mouse; to abuse

capillature.d: A bush of hair; frizzing of the hair

capitan pasha.d: The chief admiral of the Turkish fleet

capitibranchiata.d: A division of annelids in which the gills arise from or near the head. See Tubicola

capitolian.d: Of or pertaining to the Capitol in Rome

capivi.d: A balsam of the Spanish West Indies.  See Copaiba

capnomor.d: A limpid, colorless oil with a peculiar odor, obtained from beech tar

capo tasto.d: A sort of bar or movable nut, attached to the finger board of a guitar or other  fretted instrument for the purpose of raising uniformly the pitch of all the strings

capoc.d: A sort of cotton so short and fine that it can not be spun, used in the East Indies to line palanquins, to make mattresses, etc

capoch.d: A hood; especially, the hood attached to the gown of a monk

caponiere.d: A work made across or in the ditch, to protect it from the enemy, or to serve as a covered passageway

cappadine.d: A floss or waste obtained from the cocoon after the silk has been reeled off, used for shag

cappeak.d: The front piece of a cap; -- now more commonly called visor

capping plane.d: A plane used for working the upper surface of staircase rails

capreoline.d: Of or pertaining to the roebuck

capriped.d: Having feet like those of a goat

capsquare.d: A metal covering plate which passes over the trunnions of a cannon, and holds it in place

captainry.d: Power, or command, over a certain district; chieftainship

car mile.d: A mile traveled by a single car, taken as a unit of computation, as in computing the average travel of each car of a system during a given period

carabus.d: A genus of ground beetles, including numerous species. They devour many injurious insects

caracoly.d: An alloy of gold, silver, and copper, of which an inferior quality of jewelry is made

caracore.d: A light vessel or proa used by the people of Borneo, etc., and by the Dutch in the East Indies

carapato.d: A south American tick of the genus Amblyomma. There are several species, very troublesome to man and beast

carbazol.d: A white crystallized substance, C12H8NH, derived from aniline and other amines

carbazotic.d: Containing, or derived from, carbon and nitrogen

carbon transmitter.d: A telephone transmitter in which a carbon contact is used

carbonaro.d: A member of a secret political association in Italy, organized in the early part of the nineteenth centry for the purpose of changing the government into a republic

carborundum cloth.d: Cloth or paper covered with powdered carborundum; -- a foprm of sandpaper

carbunculation.d: The blasting of the young buds of trees or plants, by excessive heat or cold

carcel lamp.d: A French mechanical lamp, for lighthouses, in which a superabundance of oil is pumped to the wick tube by clockwork

carcinosys.d: The affection of the system with cancer

cardialgla.d: A burning or gnawing pain, or feeling of distress, referred to the region of the heart, accompanied with cardiac palpitation; heartburn. It is usually a symptom of indigestion

cardinalize.d: To exalt to the office of a cardinal

cardiolgy.d: The science which treats of the heart and its functions

carduelinae.d: a subfamily of birds consisting of the old world finches, many of which have taken up residence in the Americas; -- it is a subgroup of finches used in some classifications, in which the Fringillidae are divided into two subfamilies, the Carduelinae (including the goldfinches, siskins, redpolls, crossbills, and linnets) and Fringillinae (the brambling and the chaffinches).  The siskins and goldfinches have migrated as far south as the southern end of South America

cargoose.d: A species of grebe (Podiceps crisratus); the crested grebe

carinaria.d: A genus of oceanic heteropod Mollusca, having a thin, glassy, bonnet-shaped shell, which covers only the nucleus and gills

carinatae.d: A grand division of birds, including all existing flying birds; -- So called from the carina or keel on the breastbone

carminic.d: Of or pertaining to, or derived from, carmine

carnary.d: A vault or crypt in connection with a church, used as a repository for human bones disintered from their original burial places; a charnel house

carnate.d: Invested with, or embodied in, flesh

carnin.d: A white crystalline nitrogenous substance, found in extract of meat, and related to xanthin

carnot's cycle.d: An ideal heat-engine cycle in which the working fluid goes through the following four successive operations: (1) Isothermal expansion to a desired point; (2) adiabatic expansion to a desired point; (3) isothermal compression to such a point that (4) adiabatic compression brings it back to its initial state

carolin.d: A former gold coin of Germany worth nearly five dollars; also, a gold coin of Sweden worth nearly five dollars

carolitic.d: Adorned with sculptured leaves and branches

caroteel.d: A tierce or cask for dried fruits, etc., usually about 700 lbs

carpetmonger.d: One who deals in carpets; a buyer and seller of carpets

carpetway.d: A border of greensward left round the margin of a plowed field

carpintero.d: A california woodpecker (Melanerpes formicivorus), noted for its habit of inserting acorns in holes which it drills in trees. The acorns become infested by insect larvæ, which, when grown, are extracted for food by the bird

carrancha.d: The Brazilian kite (Polyborus Brasiliensis); -- so called in imitation of its notes

cartbote.d: Wood to which a tenant is entitled for making and repairing carts and other instruments of husbandry

cartist.d: In Spain and Portugal, one who supports the constitution

carvelbuilt.d: Having the planks meet flush at the seams, instead of lapping as in a clinker-built vessel

carvist.d: A hawk which is of proper age and training to be carried on the hand; a hawk in its first year

cascade method.d: A method of attaining successively lower temperatures by utilizing the cooling effect of the expansion of one gas in condensing another less easily liquefiable, and so on

cascaron.d: Lit., an eggshell; hence, an eggshell filled with confetti to be thrown during balls, carnivals, etc

case-bay.d: The space between two principals or girders

cash railway.d: A form of cash carrier in which a small carrier or car travels upon a kind of track

cassava wood.d: A West Indian tree (Turpinia occidentalis) of the family Staphyleaceæ

casse paper.d: Broken paper; the outside quires of a ream

casse-tete.d: A small war club, esp. of savages; -- so called because of its supposed use in crushing the skull

cassel brown.d: A brown pigment of varying permanence, consisting of impure lignite. It was found originally near Cassel (now Kassel), Germany

cassican.d: An American bird of the genus Cassicus, allied to the starlings and orioles, remarkable for its skillfully constructed and suspended nest; the crested oriole. The name is also sometimes given to the piping crow, an Australian bird

cassioberry.d: The fruit of the Viburnum obovatum, a shrub which grows from Virginia to Florida

castillan.d: Of or pertaining to Castile, in Spain

castlebuilder.d: Fig.: one who builds castles in the air or forms visionary schemes

cat o' nine tails.d: a whip used as an instrument of punishment consisting of nine pieces of knotted line or cord fastened to a handle; -- formerly used to flog offenders on the bare back; -- called also the cat.  It was used in the British Navy to maintain discipline on board sailing ships

cat-harping.d: One of the short ropes or iron cramps used to brace in the shrouds toward the masts so a to give freer sweep to the yards

cat-hole.d: One of two small holes astern, above the gunroom ports, through which hawsers may be passed

cat-salt.d: A sort of salt, finely granulated, formed out of the bittern or leach brine

catabasion.d: A vault under altar of a Greek church

cataclysmist.d: One who believes that the most important geological phenomena have been produced by cataclysms

catacoustic.d: That part of acoustics which treats of reflected sounds or echoes See Acoustics

cataian.d: A native of Cathay or China; a foreigner; -- formerly a term of reproach

catallacta.d: A division of Protozoa, of which Magosphæra is the type. They exist both in a myxopod state, with branched pseudopodia, and in the form of ciliated bodies united in free, spherical colonies

catalogize.d: To insert in a catalogue; to register; to catalogue

catanadromous.d: Ascending and descending fresh streams from and to the sea, as the salmon; anadromous

catapeltic.d: Of or pertaining to a catapult

cataphractic.d: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a cataphract

catasterism.d: A placing among the stars; a catalogue of stars

catch title.d: A short expressive title used for abbreviated book lists, etc

catch-basin.d: A cistern or vault at the point where a street gutter discharges into a sewer, to catch bulky matters which would not pass readily through the sewer

catch-meadow.d: A meadow irrigated by water from a spring or rivulet on the side of hill

catechuic.d: Of or pertaining to catechu or its derivatives. See catechin

catechumenate.d: The state or condition of a catechumen or the time during which one is a catechumen

catechumenical.d: Of or pertaining to catechumens; as, catechumenical instructions

catel.d: Property; -- often used by Chaucer in contrast with rent, or income

catelectrotonic.d: Relating to, or characterized by, catelectrotonus

catery.d: The place where provisions are deposited

catharist.d: One aiming at or pretending to a greater purity of like than others about him; -- applied to persons of various sects. See Albigenses

cathedrated.d: Relating to the chair or office of a teacher

cato-cathartic.d: A remedy that purges by alvine discharges

catskill period.d: The closing subdivision of the Devonian age in America. The rocks of this period are well developed in the Catskill mountains, and extend south and west under the Carboniferous formation. See the Diagram under Geology

catso.d: A base fellow; a rogue; a cheat

catstick.d: A stick or club employed in the game of ball called cat or tipcat

catstitch.d: To fold and sew down the edge of with a coarse zigzag stitch

cauda galli.d: A plume-shaped fossil, supposed to be a seaweed, characteristic of the lower Devonian rocks; as, the cauda galli grit

caufle.d: A gang of slaves. Same as Coffle

causidical.d: Pertaining to an advocate, or to the maintenance and defense of suits

causticily.d: The quality of being caustic; corrosiveness; as, the causticity of potash

cauterism.d: The use or application of a caustic; cautery

cautionary block.d: A block in which two or more trains are permitted to travel, under restrictions imposed by a caution card or the like

cavalero.d: A cavalier; a gallant; a libertine

cavalry-sword.d: a stout sword with a curved blade and thick back

cavicornia.d: A group of ruminants whose horns are hollow, and planted on a bony process of the front, as the ox

cavilous.d: Characterized by caviling, or disposed to cavil; quibbing

cavo-rilievo.d: Hollow relief; sculpture in relief within a sinking made for the purpose, so no part of it projects beyond the plain surface around

cawky.d: Of or pertaining to cawk; like cawk

cecidomyia.d: A genus of small dipterous files, including several very injurious species, as the Hessian fly. See Hessian fly

cedule.d: A scroll; a writing; a schedule

celidography.d: A description of apparent spots on the disk of the sun, or on planets

cellepore.d: A genus of delicate branching corals, made up of minute cells, belonging to the Bryozoa

cenatory.d: Of or pertaining to dinner or supper

centiloquy.d: A work divided into a hundred parts

cerealia.d: Public festivals in honor of Ceres

cetylic.d: Of, pertaining to, or derived from, spermaceti

chandlerly.d: Like a chandler; in a petty way

chanfrin.d: The fore part of a horse's head

change key.d: A key adapted to open only one of a set of locks; -- distinguished from a master key

chanuka.d: same as Hanukka; -- a variant spelling

chaomancy.d: Divination by means of appearances in the air

chaped.d: Furnished with a chape or chapes

chapellany.d: A chapel within the jurisdiction of a church; a subordinate ecclesiastical foundation

char-a-bancs.d: A long, light, open vehicle, with benches or seats running lengthwise

characid.d: any freshwater fish of the family Characinidae; -- also called characin

characterism.d: A distinction of character; a characteristic

chargeship.d: The office of a chargé d'affaires

charism.d: A miraculously given power, as of healing, speaking foreign languages without instruction, etc., attributed to some of the early Christians

chasselas.d: A white grape, esteemed for the table

chatteration.d: The act or habit of chattering

chiococca.d: a genus of shrubs of tropical and subtropical New World

chlorura.d: one of the genera of birds which comprise the towhees

chopchurch.d: An exchanger or an exchange of benefices

chouka.d: The Indian four-horned antelope; the chikara

chreotechnics.d: The science of the useful arts, esp. agriculture, manufactures, and commerce

cierge.d: A wax candle used in religous rites

cimbal.d: A kind of confectionery or cake

cinchonaceous.d: Allied or pertaining to cinchona, or to the plants that produce it

cinura.d: The group of Thysanura which includes Lepisma and allied forms; the bristletails. See Bristletail, and Lepisma

circensial.d: Of or pertaining to, or held in, the Circus, In Rome

cosmographically.d: In a cosmographic manner; in accordance with cosmography

cosmolabe.d: An instrument resembling the astrolabe, formerly used for measuring the angles between heavenly bodies; -- called also pantacosm

cosmometry.d: The art of measuring the world or the universe

cosmoramic.d: Of or pertaining to a cosmorama

cosmothetic.d: Assuming or positing the actual existence or reality of the physical or external world

cossack post.d: An outpost consisting of four men, forming one of a single line of posts substituted for the more formal line of sentinels and line of pickets

cossic.d: Of or relating to algebra; as, cossic numbers, or the cossic art

costal-nerved.d: Having the nerves spring from the midrib

coston lights.d: Signals made by burning lights of different colors and used by vessels at sea, and in the life-saving service; -- named after their inventor

cosupreme.d: A partaker of supremacy; one jointly supreme

coticular.d: Pertaining to whetstones; like or suitable for whetstones

cotland.d: Land appendant to a cot or cottage, or held by a cottager or cotter

cotqueanity.d: The condition, character, or conduct of a cotquean

cottagely.d: Cottagelike; suitable for a cottage; rustic

cottise.d: A diminutive of the bendlet, containing one half its area or one quarter the area of the bend. When a single cottise is used alone it is often called a cost. See also Couple-close

cottised.d: Set between two cottises, -- said of a bend; or between two barrulets, -- said of a bar or fess

cottoid.d: Like a fish of the genus Cottus

cottolene.d: A product from cotton-seed, used as lard

cotton batting.d: Cotton prepared in sheets or rolls for quilting, upholstering, and similar purposes

cottonary.d: Relating to, or composed of, cotton; cottony

couchancy.d: State of lying down for repose

coudee.d: A measure of length; the distance from the elbow to the end of the middle finger; a cubit

couleur.d: Color; -- chiefly used in a few French phrases, as couler de rose, color of rose; and hence, adjectively, rose-colored; roseate

coulomb meter.d: Any instrument by which electricity can be measured in coulombs

coulure.d: A disease affecting grapes, esp. in California, manifested by the premature dropping of the fruit

coumaric.d: Relating to, derived from, or like, the Dipterix odorata, a tree of Guiana

coumarou.d: The tree (Dipteryx odorata) which bears the tonka bean; also, the bean itself

councilist.d: One who belongs to a council; one who gives an opinion

count-wheel.d: The wheel in a clock which regulates the number of strokes

counter tenor.d: One of the middle parts in music, between the tenor and the treble; high tenor

counter-couchant.d: Lying down, with their heads in opposite directions; -- said of animals borne in a coat of arms

counter-courant.d: Running in opposite directions; -- said of animals borne in a coast of arms

counter-roll.d: A duplicate roll (record or account) kept by an officer as a check upon another officer's roll

counter-salient.d: Leaping from each other; -- said of two figures on a coat of arms

counter-subversion.d: the aspect of counterintelligence designed to detect and prevent subversive activities

countercaster.d: A caster of accounts; a reckoner; a bookkeeper; -- used contemptuously

countercharm.d: To destroy the effect of a charm upon

counterflory.d: Adorned with flowers (usually fleurs-de-lis) so divided that the tops appear on one side and the bottoms on the others; -- said of any ordinary

countergage.d: An adjustable gage, with double points for transferring measurements from one timber to another, as the breadth of a mortise to the place where the tenon is to be made

counterpassant.d: Passant in opposite directions; -- said of two animals

counterponderate.d: To equal in weight; to counterpoise; to equiponderate

counterprove.d: To take a counter proof of, or a copy in reverse, by taking an impression directly from the face of an original.  See Counter proof, under Counter

counterscale.d: Counterbalance; balance, as of one scale against another

countersecure.d: To give additional security to or for

counterstep.d: A contrary method of procedure; opposite course of action

countersway.d: A swaying in a contrary direction; an opposing influence

counterterm.d: A term or word which is the opposite of, or antithesis to, another; an antonym; -- the opposite of synonym; as, “foe” is the counterterm of “friend”

countertime.d: The resistance of a horse, that interrupts his cadence and the measure of his manege, occasioned by a bad horseman, or the bad temper of the horse

countertrippant.d: Trippant in opposite directions. See Trippant

countervote.d: To vote in opposition to; to balance or overcome by voting; to outvote

counterwait.d: To wait or watch for; to be on guard against

counterwheel.d: To cause to wheel or turn in an opposite direction

countor.d: An advocate or professional pleader; one who counted for his client, that is, orally pleaded his cause

coupe-gorge.d: Any position giving the enemy such advantage that the troops occupying it must either surrender or be cut to pieces

coupee.d: A motion in dancing, when one leg is a little bent, and raised from the floor, and with the other a forward motion is made

couple-beggar.d: One who makes it his business to marry beggars to each other

couple-close.d: A diminutive of the chevron, containing one fourth of its surface. Couple-closes are generally borne one on each side of a chevron, and the  blazoning may then be either a chevron between two couple-closes or chevron cottised

coupstick.d: A stick or switch used among some American Indians in making or counting a coup

couranto.d: A sprightly dance; a coranto; a courant

courche.d: A square piece of linen used formerly by women instead of a cap; a kerchief

court-baron.d: An inferior court of civil jurisdiction, attached to a manor, and held by the steward; a baron's court; -- now fallen into disuse

court-craft.d: The artifices, intrigues, and plottings, at courts

court-cupboard.d: A movable sideboard or buffet, on which plate and other articles of luxury were displayed on special ocasions

court-leet.d: A court of record held once a year, in a particular hundred, lordship, or manor, before the steward of the leet

courtbred.d: Bred, or educated, at court; polished; courtly

courtiery.d: The manners of a courtier; courtliness

couscousou.d: A favorite dish in Barbary. See Couscous

cover-point.d: The fielder in the games of cricket and lacrosse who supports “point.”

coversed sine.d: The versed sine of the complement of an arc or angle. See Illust. of Functions

coverside.d: A region of country having covers; a hunting country

covert baron.d: Under the protection of a husband; married

cow tree.d: A tree (Galactodendron utile or Brosimum Galactodendron) of South America, which yields, on incision, a nourishing fluid, resembling milk

cow-pilot.d: A handsomely banded, coral-reef fish, of Florida and the West Indies (Pomacentrus saxatilis); -- called also mojarra

cowalker.d: A phantasmic or “astral” body deemed to be separable from the physical body and capable of acting independently; a doppelgänger

cowblakes.d: Dried cow dung used as fuel

cowleech.d: One who heals diseases of cows; a cow doctor

cowquake.d: A genus of plants (Briza); quaking grass

cowwheat.d: A weed of the genus Melampyrum, with black seeds, found on European wheatfields

coyol.d: a tropical American palm (Acrocomia vinifera) having edible nuts and yielding a useful fiber

crab-yaws.d: A disease in the West Indies. It is a kind of ulcer on the soles of the feet, with very hard edges. See Yaws

crack-loo.d: A kind of gambling game consisting in pitching coins to or towards the ceiling of a room so that they shall fall as near as possible to a certain crack in the floor

cracker state.d: Georgia; -- a nickname. See Cracker, n. 5

cracovian.d: Of or pertaining to Cracow in Poland

cracowes.d: Long-toed boots or shoes formerly worn in many parts of Europe; -- so called from Cracow, in Poland, where they were first worn in the fourteenth century

cradleland.d: Land or region where one was cradled; hence, land of origin

craftsmaster.d: One skilled in his craft or trade; one of superior cunning

cramponee.d: Having a cramp or square piece at the end; -- said of a cross so furnished

crane's-bill.d: The geranium; -- so named from the long axis of the fruit, which resembles the beak of a crane

cranioclasm.d: The crushing of a child's head, as with the cranioclast or craniotomy forceps in cases of very difficult delivery

crantara.d: The fiery cross, used as a rallying signal in the Highlands of Scotland

crants.d: A garland carried before the bier of a maiden

crapnel.d: A hook or drag; a grapnel

crase.d: To break in pieces; to crack

craspedota.d: The hydroid or naked-eyed medusæ. See Hydroidea

crassament.d: A semisolid mass or clot, especially that formed in coagulation of the blood

crastination.d: Procrastination; a putting off till to-morrow

crawl stroke.d: A racing stroke, in which the swimmer, lying flat on the water with face submerged, takes alternate overhand arm strokes while moving his legs up and down alternately from the knee

craze-mill.d: A mill for grinding tin ore

crazedness.d: A broken state; decrepitude; an impaired state of the intellect

cream-faced.d: White or pale, as the effect of fear, or as the natural complexion

cream-fruit.d: A plant of Sierra Leone which yields a wholesome, creamy juice

cream-slice.d: A wooden knife with a long thin blade, used in handling cream or ice cream

creatic.d: Relating to, or produced by, flesh or animal food; as, creatic nausea

creatinin.d: A white, crystalline, nitrogenous body closely related to creatin but more basic in its properties, formed from the latter by the action of acids, and occurring naturally in muscle tissue and in urine

creatureship.d: The condition of being a creature

creaturize.d: To make like a creature; to degrade

creaze.d: The tin ore which collects in the central part of the washing pit or buddle

crebricostate.d: Marked with closely set ribs or ridges

crebrisulcate.d: Marked with closely set transverse furrows

credit foncier.d: A company licensed for the purpose of carrying out improvements, by means of loans and advances upon real securities

credit mobilier.d: A joint stock company, formed for general banking business, or for the construction of public works, by means of loans on personal estate, after the manner of the crédit foncier on real estate. In practice, however, this distinction has not been strictly observed

creeky.d: Containing, or abounding in, creeks; characterized by creeks; like a creek; winding

cremaillere.d: An indented or zigzaged line of intrenchment

creole state.d: Louisiana; -- a nickname. See Creole, n. & a

creolean.d: Pertaining to, or characteristic of, the Creoles

crescentwise.d: In the form of a crescent; like a crescent

cresselle.d: A wooden rattle sometimes used as a substitute for a bell, in the Roman Catholic church, during the latter part of Holy Week, or the last week of Lent

cretism.d: A Cretan practice; lying; a falsehood

creux.d: Used in English only in the expression en creux. Thus, engraving en creux is engraving in intaglio, or by sinking or hollowing out the design

crimpage.d: The act or practice of crimping; money paid to a crimp for shipping or enlisting men

crincum.d: A twist or bend; a turn; a whimsey

crincum-crancum.d: A twist; a whimsey or whim

cringeling.d: One who cringes meanly; a fawner

crinicultural.d: Relating to the growth of hair

crinitory.d: Of or relating to hair; as, a crinitory covering

cripply.d: Lame; disabled; in a crippled condition

crithomancy.d: A kind of divination by means of the dough of the cakes offered in the ancient sacrifices, and the meal strewed over the victims

crizzel.d: A kind of roughness on the surface of glass, which clouds its transparency

crociary.d: One who carries the cross before an archbishop

crocodility.d: A caption or sophistical mode of arguing

croconate.d: A salt formed by the union of croconic acid with a base

croconic.d: Of, pertaining to, or resembling saffron; having the color of saffron; as, croconic acid

croftland.d: Land of superior quality, on which successive crops are raised

crofton system.d: A system of prison discipline employing for consecutive periods cellular confinement, associated imprisonment under the mark system, restraint intermediate between imprisonment and freedom, and liberation on ticket of leave

croissante.d: Terminated with crescents; -- said of a cross the ends of which are so terminated

cronel.d: The iron head of a tilting spear

cronian.d: Saturnian; -- applied to the North Polar Sea

croodle.d: To cower or cuddle together, as from fear or cold; to lie close and snug together, as pigs in straw

crookbill.d: A New Zealand plover (Anarhynchus frontalis), remarkable for having the end of the beak abruptly bent to the right

cropsick.d: Sick from excess in eating or drinking

croquante.d: A brittle cake or other crisp pastry

cross-bearer.d: A subdeacon who bears a cross before an archbishop or primate on solemn occasions

cross-birth.d: Any preternatural labor, in which the body of the child lies across the pelvis of the mother, so that the shoulder, arm, or trunk is the part first presented at the mouth of the uterus

cross-bun.d: A bun or cake marked with a cross  of icing, and intended to be eaten on Good Friday; also, called hot cross bun, even when not hot

cross-crosslet.d: A cross having the three upper ends crossed, so as to from three small crosses

cross-days.d: The three days preceding the Feast of the Ascension

cross-modality.d: ability to integrate information from different sense modalities

cross-reading.d: The reading of the lines of a newspaper directly across the page, instead of down the columns, thus producing a ludicrous combination of ideas

cross-spale.d: One of the temporary wooden braces, placed horizontally across a frame to hold it in position until the deck beams are in; a cross-pawl

cross-tie.d: A sleeper supporting and connecting the rails, and holding them in place

cross-vaulting.d: Vaulting formed by the intersection of two or more simple vaults

cross-week.d: Rogation week, when the cross was borne in processions

crotaphite.d: The temple or temporal fossa. Also used adjectively

crotonic.d: Of or pertaining to, or derived from, a plant of the genus Croton, or from croton oil

crottles.d: A name given to various lichens gathered for dyeing.  See crottal

crow's-nest.d: A box or platform near the top of a mast, esp. in whalers, to shelter the man on the lookout

crow-quill.d: A quill of the crow, or a very fine pen made from such a quill

crow-silk.d: A filamentous fresh-water alga (Conferva rivularis of Linnaeus, Rhizoclonium rivulare of Kutzing)

crow-trodden.d: Marked with crow's-feet, or wrinkles, about the eyes

crown office.d: The criminal branch of the Court of King's or Queen's Bench, commonly called the crown side of the court, which takes cognizance of all criminal cases

crown-imperial.d: A spring-blooming plant (Fritillaria imperialis) of the Lily family, having at the top of the stalk a cluster of pendent bell-shaped flowers surmounted with a tuft of green leaves

crown-saw.d: A saw in the form of a hollow cylinder, with teeth on the end or edge, and operated by a rotative motion

crowstone.d: The top stone of the gable end of a house

crowth.d: An ancient musical instrument. See 4th Crowd

cruciation.d: The act of torturing; torture; torment

crucigerous.d: Bearing the cross; marked with the figure of a cross

crummable.d: Capable of being crumbed or broken into small pieces

crustaceologist.d: One versed in crustaceology; a crustalogist

crustaceousness.d: The state or quality of being crustaceous or having a crustlike shell

crustated.d: Covered with a crust; as, crustated basalt

crustific.d: Producing or forming a crust or skin

crux ansata.d: A cross in the shape of the ankh

cryptidine.d: One of the quinoline bases, obtained from coal tar as an oily liquid, C11H11N; also, any one of several substances metameric with, and resembling, cryptidine proper

cryptobranchiata.d: A division of the Amphibia; the Derotremata

cryptocoryne.d: any plant of the genus Cryptocoryne; evergreen perennials growing in fresh or brackish water; tropical Asia

crypturi.d: An order of flying, dromæognathous birds, including the tinamous of South America. See Tinamou

crystallogenic.d: Pertaining to the production of crystals; crystal-producing; as, crystallogenic attraction

crystallomancy.d: Divination by means of a crystal or other transparent body, especially a beryl

ctenoidei.d: A group of fishes, established by Agassiz, characterized by having scales with a pectinated margin, as in the perch. The group is now generally regarded as artificial

ctenophoric.d: Of or pertaining to the Ctenophora

cubation.d: The act of lying down; a reclining

cubbridge-head.d: A bulkhead on the forecastle and half deck of a ship

cubebic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, cubebs; as, cubebic acid (a soft olive-green resin extracted from cubebs)

cubicular.d: Belonging to a chamber or bedroom

cubile.d: The lowest course of stones in a building

cubo-octahedral.d: Presenting a combination of a cube and an octahedron

cubo-octahedron.d: A combination of a cube and octahedron, esp. one in which the octahedral faces meet at the middle of the cubic edges

cuckold's knot.d: A hitch or knot, by which a rope is secured to a spar, the two parts of the rope being crossed and seized together; -- called also cuckold's neck
