cuckoobud.d: A species of Ranunculus (Ranunculus bulbosus); -- called also butterflower, buttercup, kingcup, goldcup

cucquean.d: A woman whose husband is unfaithful to her

cucujo.d: The fire beetle of Mexico and the West Indies

cuculoid.d: Like or belonging to the cuckoos (Cuculidæ)

cucurbitive.d: Having the shape of a gourd seed; -- said of certain small worms

cudden.d: A clown; a low rustic; a dolt

cuinage.d: The stamping of pigs of tin, by the proper officer, with the arms of the duchy of Cornwall

cuir bouilli.d: In decorative art, boiled leather, fitted by the process to receive impressed patterns, like those produced by chasing metal, and to retain the impression permanently

culasse.d: The lower faceted portion of a brilliant-cut diamond

culcita.d: a genus that includes some plants usually placed in e.g. genus Dicksonia; terrestrial brackenlike ferns of tropical America, Malasia to Australia and Polynesia; also native in southwestern Europe and Atlantic islands

culdee.d: One of a class of anchorites who lived in various parts of Scotland, Ireland, and Wales

cullyism.d: The state of being a cully

culpon.d: A shred; a fragment; a strip of wood

cultirostral.d: Having a bill shaped like the colter of a plow, or like a knife, as the heron, stork, etc

cultirostres.d: A tribe of wading birds including the stork, heron, crane, etc

cultrivorous.d: Devouring knives; swallowing, or pretending to swallow, knives; -- applied to persons who have swallowed, or have seemed to swallow, knives with impunity

culture features.d: The artificial features of a district as distinguished from the natural

culture myth.d: A myth accounting for the discovery of arts and sciences or the advent of a higher civilization, as in the Prometheus myth

culverkey.d: A bunch of the keys or samaras of the ash tree

culvertailed.d: United or fastened by a dovetailed joint

cuminic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, cumin, or from oil of caraway; as, cuminic acid

cumu-cirro-stratus.d: Nimbus, or rain cloud. See Nimbus, and Cloud

cumulatist.d: One who accumulates; one who collects

cundurango.d: The bark of a South American vine (Gonolobus Condurango) of the Milkweed family. It has been supposed, but erroneously, to be a cure for cancer

cunningman.d: A fortune teller; one who pretends to reveal mysteries

cup shake.d: A shake or fissure between the annual rings of a tree, found oftenest near the roots

cup-gall.d: A kind of oak-leaf gall. See Gall

cup-moss.d: A kind of lichen, of the genus Cladonia

cuproid.d: A solid related to a tetrahedron, and contained under twelve equal triangles

curaçao.d: A liqueur, or cordial, flavored with the peel from the sour orange, and sometimes with cinnamon and mace; -- first made at the island of Curaçcao in the Netherlands Antilles near Venezuela

curculionidous.d: Pertaining to the Curculionideæ, or weevil tribe

cureall.d: A remedy for all diseases, or for all ills; a panacea

curialism.d: The view or doctrine of the ultramontane party in the Latin Church

curialist.d: One who belongs to the ultramontane party in the Latin Church

curiality.d: The privileges, prerogatives, or retinue of a court

curiologic.d: Pertaining to a rude kind of hieroglyphics, in which a thing is represented by its picture instead of by a symbol

curmurring.d: Murmuring; grumbling; -- sometimes applied to the rumbling produced by a slight attack of the gripes

curship.d: The state of being a cur; one who is currish

curtail dog.d: A dog with a docked tail; formerly, the dog of a person not qualified to course, which, by the forest laws, must have its tail cut short, partly as a mark, and partly from a notion that the tail is necessary to a dog in running; hence, a dog not fit for sporting

curtal friar.d: A friar who acted as porter at the gate of a monastery

curtation.d: The interval by which the curtate distance of a planet is less than the true distance

cururo.d: A Chilian burrowing rodent of the genus Spalacopus

curvation.d: The act of bending or crooking

curvative.d: Having the margins only a little curved; -- said of leaves

curvilinead.d: An instrument for drawing curved lines

curvilinearity.d: The state of being curvilinear or of being bounded by curved lines

curvirostres.d: A group of passerine birds, including the creepers and nuthatches

cushion tire.d: A thick solid-rubber tire, as for a bicycle, with a hollow groove running lengthwise on the inside

cutgrass.d: A grass with leaves having edges furnished with very minute hooked prickles, which form a cutting edge; one or more species of Leersia

cutlass fish.d: a peculiar, long, thin, marine fish (Trichiurus lepturus) of the southern United States and West Indies, having a long whiplike scaleless body and sharp daggerlike teeth; -- called also frostfish, saber fish, silver eel, and, improperly, swordfish; also, several related members of the genus Trichiurus.  It is closely related to snake mackerel

cutling.d: The art of making edged tools or cutlery

cutose.d: A variety of cellulose, occuring as a fine transparent membrane covering the aerial organs of plants, and forming an essential ingredient of cork; by oxidation it passes to suberic acid

cuttoo plate.d: A hood over the end of a wagon wheel hub to keep dirt away from the axle

cutwal.d: The chief police officer of a large city

cyamellone.d: A complex derivative of cyanogen, regarded as an acid, and known chiefly in its salts; -- called also hydromellonic acid

cyanuric.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, cyanic and uric acids

cyatholith.d: A kind of coccolith, which in shape resembles a minute cup widened at the top, and varies in size from 1/6000 to 1/8000 of an inch

cyathophylloid.d: Like, or pertaining to, the family Cyathophyllidæ

cyclas.d: A long gown or surcoat (cut off in front), worn in the Middle Ages. It was sometimes embroidered or interwoven with gold. Also, a rich stuff from which the gown was made

cyclobranchiate.d: Having the gills around the margin of the body, as certain limpets

cycloganoid.d: Of or pertaining to the Cycloganoidei

cycloganoidei.d: An order of ganoid fishes, having cycloid scales. The bowfin (Amia calva) is a living example

cycloidei.d: An order of fishes, formerly proposed by Agassiz, for those with thin, smooth scales, destitute of marginal spines, as the herring and salmon. The group is now regarded as artificial

cyclostomi.d: A glass of fishes having a suckerlike mouth, without jaws, as the lamprey; the Marsipobranchii

cylindrometric.d: Belonging to a scale used in measuring cylinders

cymophanous.d: Having a wavy, floating light; opalescent; chatoyant

cynarrhodium.d: A fruit like that of the rose, consisting of a cup formed of the calyx tube and receptacle, and containing achenes

cynoidea.d: A division of Carnivora, including the dogs, wolves, and foxes

cyphonism.d: A punishment sometimes used by the ancients, consisting in the besmearing of the criminal with honey, and exposing him to insects. It is still in use among some Oriental nations

cypress-pine.d: any of several evergreen trees or shrubs of Australia and N Caledonia

cypseliform.d: Like or belonging to the swifts (Cypselidæ.)

cyrenian.d: Pertaining to Cyrene, in Africa; Cyrenaic

cysticerce.d: The larval form of a tapeworm, having the head and neck of a tapeworm attached to a saclike body filled with fluid; -- called also bladder worm, hydatid, and measle (as, pork measle)

cysticule.d: An appendage of the vestibular ear sac of fishes

cystidea.d: An order of Crinoidea, mostly fossils of the Paleozoic rocks. They were usually roundish or egg-shaped, and often unsymmetrical; some were sessile, others had short stems

cystoplast.d: A nucleated cell having an envelope or cell wall, as a red blood corpuscle or an epithelial cell; a cell concerned in growth

czarinian.d: Of or pertaining to the czar or the czarina; czarish

czarish.d: Of or pertaining to the czar

czarowitz.d: The title of the eldest son of the czar of Russia

cæsarean.d: Of or pertaining to Cæsar or the Cæsars; imperial

d valve.d: A kind of slide valve. See Slide valve, under Slide

dabb.d: A large, spine-tailed lizard (Uromastix spinipes), found in Egypt, Arabia, and Palestine; -- called also dhobb, and dhubb

dactyliology.d: That branch of archæology which has to do with gem engraving

dactylonomy.d: The art of numbering or counting by the fingers

daddle.d: To toddle; to walk unsteadily, like a child or an old man; hence, to do anything slowly or feebly

daedalous.d: Having a variously cut or incised margin; -- said of leaves

dag-tailed.d: Daggle-tailed; having the tail clogged with daglocks

dagges.d: An ornamental cutting of the edges of garments, introduced about a. d. 1346, according to the Chronicles of St Albans

daggle-tail.d: Having the lower ends of garments defiled by trailing in mire or filth; draggle-tailed

dagswain.d: A coarse woolen fabric made of daglocks, or the refuse of wool

daguerrean.d: Pertaining to Daguerre, or to his invention of the daguerreotype

hippocrepian.d: One of an order of fresh-water Bryozoa, in which the tentacles are on a lophophore, shaped like a horseshoe. See Phylactolæma

hircic.d: Of, pertaining to, or derived from, mutton suet; -- applied by Chevreul to an oily acid which was obtained from mutton suet, and to which he attributed the peculiar taste and smell of that substance. The substance has also been called hircin

histophyly.d: The tribal history of cells, a division of morphophyly

historionomer.d: One versed in the phenomena of history and the laws controlling them

historize.d: To relate as history; to chronicle; to historicize

histrionize.d: To act; to represent on the stage, or theatrically

hit..d: Having become very popular or acclaimed; -- said of entertainment performances; as, a hit song, a hit movie

hittorf rays.d: Rays (chiefly cathode rays) developed by the electric discharge in Hittorf tubes

hoazin.d: A remarkable South American bird (Opisthocomus cristatus); the crested touraco. By some Zoologists it is made the type of a distinct order (Opisthocomi)

hobbly.d: Rough; uneven; causing one to hobble; as a hobbly road

hobbyhorsical.d: Pertaining to, or having, a hobby or whim; eccentric; whimsical

hocco.d: The crested curassow; -- called also royal pheasant. See Curassow

hockday.d: A holiday commemorating the expulsion of the Danes, formerly observed on the second Tuesday after Easter; -- called also hocktide

hockle.d: To hamstring; to hock; to hough

hoddengray.d: Applied to coarse cloth made of undyed wool, formerly worn by Scotch peasants

hodiern.d: Of this day; belonging to the present day

hoemother.d: The basking or liver shark; -- called also homer. See Liver shark, under Liver

hogchain.d: A chain or tie rod, in a boat or barge, to prevent the vessel from hogging

hogframe.d: A trussed frame extending fore and aft, usually above deck, and intended to increase the longitudinal strength and stiffness. Used chiefly in American river and lake steamers. Called also hogging frame, and hogback

hogger-pipe.d: The upper terminal pipe of a mining pump

hogger-pump.d: The top pump in the pit

hognosesnake.d: A harmless North American snake of the genus Heterodon, esp. Heterodon platyrhynos; -- called also puffing adder, blowing adder, and sand viper

hogreeve.d: A civil officer charged with the duty of impounding hogs running at large

hogringer.d: One who puts rings into the snouts of hogs

hogscore.d: A distance line drawn across the rink or course between the middle line and the tee

holcad.d: A large ship of burden, in ancient Greece

holder-forth.d: One who speaks in public; an haranguer; a preacher.  See hold forth (b) under hold

hole in the air.d: same as Air hole, above; an air pocket

holethnic.d: Of or pertaining to a holethnos or parent race

holethnos.d: A parent stock or race of people, not yet divided into separate branches or tribes

holluschickie.d: A young male fur seal, esp. one from three to six years old; -- called also bachelor, because prevented from breeding by the older full-grown males

holmos.d: A name given to a vase having a rounded body

holocentrus.d: The type genus of the family Holocentridae, comprising some of the squirrelfishes

holostraca.d: A division of phyllopod Crustacea, including those that are entirely covered by a bivalve shell

holy cross.d: The cross as the symbol of Christ's crucifixion

homacanth.d: Having the dorsal fin spines symmetrical, and in the same line; -- said of certain fishes

homaloid.d: Flat; even; -- a term applied to surfaces and to spaces, whether real or imagined, in which the definitions, axioms, and postulates of Euclid respecting parallel straight lines are assumed to hold true

homaxonial.d: Relating to that kind of homology or symmetry, the mathematical conception of organic form, in which all axes are equal. See under Promorphology

home-bred.d: Bred at home; domestic; not foreign

home-driven.d: Driven to the end, as a nail; driven close

home-felt.d: Felt in one's own breast; inward; private

home-schooled.d: Receiving or having received formal education, especially primary or secondary education, at home rather than in a school. homefield.d: A field adjacent to its owner's home

homeling.d: A person or thing belonging to a home or to a particular country; a native; as, a word which is a homeling

homelyn.d: The European sand ray (Raia maculata); -- called also home, mirror ray, and rough ray

homeothermism.d: The process or state of being homoiothermal

hommocky.d: Filled with hommocks; piled in the form of hommocks; -- said of ice

homocategoric.d: Belonging to the same category of individuality; -- a morphological term applied to organisms so related

homodemic.d: A morphological term signifying development, in the case of multicellular organisms, from the same unit deme or unit of the inferior orders of individuality

homodynamy.d: The homology of metameres. See Metamere

homoeomeria.d: The state or quality of being homogeneous in elements or first principles; likeness or identity of parts

homoeozoic.d: Pertaining to, or including, similar forms or kinds of life; as, homœozoic belts on the earth's surface

homoioptoton.d: A figure in which the several parts of a sentence end with the same case, or inflection generally

homologinic.d: Pertaining to, or characterized by, homology; as, homologinic qualities, or differences

homologoumena.d: Those books of the New Testament which were acknowledged as canonical by the early church; -- distinguished from antilegomena

homoplast.d: One of the plastids composing the idorgan of Haeckel; -- also called homoörgan

homopolic.d: In promorphology, pertaining to or exhibiting that kind of organic form, in which the stereometric ground form is a pyramid, with similar poles. See Promorphology

homotonous.d: Of the same tenor or tone; equable; without variation

homotropal.d: Turned in the same direction with something else

homotypal.d: Of the same type of structure; pertaining to a homotype; as, homotypal parts

honestation.d: The act of honesting; grace; adornment

honey-bag.d: The receptacle for honey in a honeybee

honey-mouthed.d: Soft to sweet in speech; persuasive

honeyberry.d: The fruit of either of two trees having sweetish berries: (a) An Old World hackberry (Celtis australis). (b) In the West Indies, the genip (Melicocca bijuga)

honiton lace.d: A kind of pillow lace, remarkable for the beauty of its figures; -- so called because chiefly made in Honiton, England

honved.d: The Hungarian army in the revolutionary war of 1848-49

hood molding.d: A projecting molding over the head of an arch, forming the outermost member of the archivolt; -- called also hood mold

hoofmark.d: a visible impression on a surface made by the hoof of an animal

hook-and-ladder truck.d: A firefighting truck equipped with a ladder extendable to great length, for access to the upper stories of buildings; it also carries other firefighting equipment; called also ladder truck

hooke's gearing.d: Spur gearing having teeth slanting across the face of the wheel, sometimes slanting in opposite directions from the middle

hooke's joint.d: A universal joint. See under Universal

hoot down.d: To shout down; to cause (a speaker) to cease trying to speak by loud derisive shouts

hop, skip, and a jump.d: a short distance; as, it's just a hop, skip and a jump away

hopperings.d: Gravel retaining in the hopper of a cradle

hoppo.d: A collector of customs, as at Canton; an overseer of commerce

hopyard.d: A field where hops are raised

hordeic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, barley; as, hordeic acid, an acid identical or isomeric with lauric acid

hordock.d: An unidentified plant mentioned by Shakespeare, perhaps equivalent to burdock

hornotine.d: A yearling; a bird of the year

hornwrack.d: A bryozoan of the genus Flustra

horologiographer.d: A maker of clocks, watches, or dials

horologiography.d: An account of instruments that show the hour

horometry.d: The art, practice, or method of measuring time by hours and subordinate divisions

horrisonous.d: Sounding dreadfully; uttering a terrible sound

horse guards.d: A body of cavalry so called; esp., a British regiment, called the Royal Horse Guards, which furnishes guards of state for the sovereign

horse-drench.d: A dose of physic for a horse

horse-jockey.d: A professional rider and trainer of race horses

horse-leechery.d: The business of a farrier; especially, the art of curing the diseases of horses

horse-litter.d: A carriage hung on poles, and borne by and between two horses

horsecart.d: A heavycart drawn by a horse, used for farm work

horsenail.d: A thin, pointed nail, with a heavy flaring head, for securing a horsehoe to the hoof; a horsehoe nail

horsewood.d: A West Indian tree (Calliandra latifolia) with showy, crimson blossoms

hospitate.d: To receive hospitality; to be a guest

host plant.d: A plant which aids, shelters, or protects another plant in its growth, as those which are used for nurse crops

hostess-ship.d: The character, personality, or office of a hostess

hostilize.d: To make hostile; to cause to become an enemy

hostry.d: A hostelry; an inn or lodging house

hot-brained.d: Ardent in temper; violent; rash; impetuous; as, hot-brained youth

hot-livered.d: Of an excitable or irritable temperament; irascible

hotchkiss gun.d: A built-up, rifled, rapid-fire gun of oil-tempered steel, having a rectangular breechblock which moves horizontally or vertically in a mortise cut completely through the jacket. It is made in France

hotcockles.d: A childish play, in which one covers his eyes, and guesses who strikes him or his hand placed behind him

hotei-chiku.d: A small bamboo (Phyllostachys aurea) of Southeast China having slender culms flexuous when young

houve.d: A head covering of various kinds; a hood; a coif; a cap

The telescope was launched into orbit on April 24, 1990.  Since then the telescope has taken thousands of images, many of them unique, recording never before seen astronomical phenomena.  Service missions were performed

hucksterage.d: The business of a huckster; small dealing; peddling

hulver.d: Holly, an evergreen shrub or tree

humanify.d: To make human; to invest with a human personality; to incarnate

humicubation.d: The act or practice of lying on the ground

humiri.d: A fragrant balsam obtained from Brazilian trees of the genus Humirium

humoralist.d: One who favors the humoral pathology or believes in humoralism

humstrum.d: An instrument out of tune or rudely constructed; music badly played

hunger-starve.d: To starve with hunger; to famish

hungerer.d: One who hungers; one who longs

hurden.d: A coarse kind of linen; -- called also harden

hurkaru.d: In India, a running footman; a messenger

huswifery.d: The business of a housewife; female domestic economy and skill

huttoning.d: Forcible manipulation of a dislocated, stiff, or painful joint

hyalea.d: A pteropod of the genus Cavolina. See Pteropoda, and Illustration in Appendix

hyblaean.d: Pertaining to Hybla, an ancient town of Sicily, famous for its bees

hybodus.d: An extinct genus of sharks having conical, compressed teeth

hydantoic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, hydantoin. See Glycoluric

hydriform.d: Having the form or structure of a hydra

hydrina.d: The group of hydroids to which the fresh-water hydras belong

hydrobiplane.d: A hydro-aëroplane having two supporting planes

hydroferrocyanic.d: Pertaining to, or containing, or obtained from, hydrogen, ferrous iron, and cyanogen; as, hydroferrocyanic acid. See Ferrocyanic

hydrofluate.d: A supposed compound of hydrofluoris acid and a base; a fluoride

hydrofluosilicic.d: Pertaining to, or denoting, a compound consisting of a double fluoride of hydrogen and silicon; silicofluoric. See Silicofluoric

hydroidea.d: An extensive order of Hydrozoa or Acalephæ

hydrophlorone.d: A white, crystalline benzene derivative, C8H10O2, obtained by the reduction of phlorone

hydrostatician.d: One who is versed or skilled in hydrostatics

hydrosulphurous.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained by the reduction of sulphurous acid. See Hyposulphurous acid, under Hyposulphurous

hydrotellurate.d: A salt formed by the union of hydrotelluric acid and the base

hydrotelluric.d: Formed by hydrogen and tellurium; as, hydrotelluric acid, or hydrogen telluride

hydrotic.d: Causing a discharge of water or phlegm

hyemal.d: Belonging to winter; done in winter

hyemation.d: The passing of a winter in a particular place; a wintering

hygeist.d: One skilled in hygiena; a hygienist

hygrophthalmic.d: Serving to moisten the eye; -- sometimes applied to the lachrymal ducts

hylaeosaur.d: A large Wealden dinosaur from the Tilgate Forest, England. It was about twenty feet long, protected by bony plates in the skin, and armed with spines

hylism.d: A theory which regards matter as the original principle of evil

hylobate.d: Any species of the genus Hylobates; a gibbon, or long-armed ape. See Gibbon

hylodes.d: The piping frog (Hyla Pickeringii), a small American tree frog, which in early spring, while breeding in swamps and ditches, sings with high, shrill, but musical, notes

hyoganoidei.d: A division of ganoid fishes, including the gar pikes and bowfins

hyopastron.d: The second lateral plate in the plastron of turtles; -- called also hyosternum

hyperaspist.d: One who holds a shield over another; hence, a defender

hyperboliform.d: Having the form, or nearly the form, of an hyperbola

hypercarbureted.d: Having an excessive proportion of carbonic acid; -- said of bicarbonates or acid carbonates

hyperegol.d: A substance which can form one of a pair of hypergolic substances.  See hypergolic

hypermyriorama.d: A show or exhibition having a great number of scenes or views

hyperorganic.d: Higher than, or beyond the sphere of, the organic

hyperthyrion.d: That part of the architrave which is over a door or window

hyphenated american.d: An American who is referred to by a hyphenated term with the first word indicating an origin in a foreign country, and the second term being “American”, as Irish-American, Italian-American, African-American, Asian-American

hypnum.d: The largest genus of true mosses; feather moss

hypoarian.d: Of or pertaining to a hypoarion

hypoarion.d: An oval lobe beneath each of the optic lobes in many fishes; one of the inferior lobes

hypobole.d: A figure in which several things are mentioned that seem to make against the argument, or in favor of the opposite side, each of them being refuted in order

hypodactylum.d: The under side of the toes

hypodicrotic.d: Exhibiting retarded dicrotism; as, a hypodicrotic pulse curve

hypognatous.d: Having the maxilla, or lower jaw, longer than the upper, as in the skimmer

hyporadius.d: One of the barbs of the hypoptilum, or aftershaft of a feather. See Feather

hyposkeletal.d: Beneath the endoskeleton; hypaxial; as, the hyposkeletal muscles; -- opposed to episkeletal

hypostrophe.d: The act of a patient turning himself

hyposulphuric.d: Pertaining to, or containing, sulphur in a lower state of oxidation than in the sulphuric compounds; as, hyposulphuric acid

hypothenal.d: Of or pertaining to the prominent part of the palm of the hand above the base of the little finger, or a corresponding part in the forefoot of an animal; as, the hypothenar eminence

hypothetist.d: One who proposes or supports an hypothesis

hysterophyte.d: A plant, like the fungus, which lives on dead or living organic matter

hystricine.d: Like or pertaining to the porcupines

hystricomorphous.d: Like, or allied to, the porcupines; -- said of a group (Hystricomorpha) of rodents

i o u.d: A paper having on it these letters, with a sum named, and duly signed; -- in use in England as an acknowledgment of a debt, and taken as evidence thereof, but not amounting to a promissory note; a due bill

i' ll.d: Contraction for I will or I shall

i. w. w..d: Industrial Workers of the World (the name of two American labor organizations, one of which advocates syndicalism)

iambize.d: To satirize in iambics; to lampoon

ianthina.d: Any gastropod of the genus Ianthina, of which various species are found living in mid ocean; -- called also purple shell, and violet snail

iatromathematician.d: One of a school of physicians in Italy, about the middle of the 17th century, who tried to apply the laws of mechanics and mathematics to the human body, and hence were eager student of anatomy; -- opposed to the iatrochemists

icebird.d: An Arctic sea bird, as the Arctic fulmar

ichneumonidan.d: Of or pertaining to the Ichneumonidæ, or ichneumon flies

ichnoscopy.d: The search for the traces of anything

ichorhaemia.d: Infection of the blood with ichorous or putrid substances

ichthidin.d: A substance from the egg yolk of osseous fishes

ichthin.d: A nitrogenous substance resembling vitellin, present in the egg yolk of cartilaginous fishes

ichthus.d: In early Christian and ecclesiastical art, an emblematic fish, or the Greek word for fish, which combined the initials of the Greek words Ihsoy^s, Christo`s, Qeoy^ Gio`s Swth`r, Jesus, Christ, Son of God, Savior

ichthyodorulite.d: One of the spiny plates found on the back and tail of certain skates

ichthyomancy.d: Divination by the heads or the entrails of fishes

ichthyophthira.d: A division of copepod crustaceans, including numerous species parasitic on fishes

ichthyotomy.d: The anatomy or dissection of fishes

iconism.d: The formation of a figure, representation, or semblance; a delineation or description

iconomical.d: Opposed to pictures or images as objects of worship

iconophilist.d: A student, or lover of the study, of iconography

icosandria.d: A Linnæan class of plants, having twenty or more stamens inserted in the calyx

icosandrian.d: Pertaining to the class Icosandria; having twenty or more stamens inserted in the calyx

ictic.d: Pertaining to, or caused by, a blow; sudden; abrupt

ictodosaur.d: An extinct reptile intermediate in form between the therapsids and most primitive true mammals

ictodosauria.d: An order of extinct reptiles of the Upper Triassic

idalian.d: Of or pertaining to Idalium, a mountain city in Cyprus, or to Venus, to whom it was sacred

idealogic.d: Of or pertaining to an idealogue, or to idealization

ideat.d: The actual existence supposed to correspond with an idea; the correlate in real existence to the idea as a thought or existence

identism.d: The doctrine taught by Schelling, that matter and mind, and subject and object, are identical in the Absolute; -- called also the system of identity or doctrine of identity

idiorepulsive.d: Repulsive by itself; as, the idiorepulsive power of heat

idiothermic.d: Self-heating; warmed, as the body of animal, by process going on within itself

idioticon.d: A dictionary of a peculiar dialect, or of the words and phrases peculiar to one part of a country; a glossary

idoloclast.d: A breaker of idols; an iconoclast

igasuric.d: Pertaining to, or obtained from, nux vomica or St. Ignatius's bean; as, igasuric acid

igasurine.d: An alkaloid found in nux vomica, and extracted as a white crystalline substance

ignigenous.d: Produced by the action of fire, as lava

ignorantism.d: The spirit of those who extol the advantage of ignorance; obscurantism

ignorantist.d: One opposed to the diffusion of knowledge; an obscurantist

iguanian.d: Resembling, or pertaining to, the iguana

ihlang-ihlang.d: A rich, powerful, perfume, obtained from the volatile oil of the flowers of Canada odorata, an East Indian tree

ihvh.d: A transliteration of the four constants forming the Hebrew tetragrammaton or “incommunicable name” of the Supreme Being, which in latter Jewish tradition is not pronounced save with the vowels of adonai or elohim, so that the true pronunciation is lost

ileocaecal.d: Pertaining to the ileum and cæcum

ilicic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, the holly (Ilex), and allied plants; as, ilicic acid

ilixanthin.d: A yellow dye obtained from the leaves of the holly

intertex.d: To intertwine; to weave or bind together

intervary.d: To alter or vary between; to change

interventor.d: One who intervenes; a mediator; especially (Eccles. Hist.), a person designated by a church to reconcile parties, and unite them in the choice of officers

intervert.d: To turn to another course or use

interwish.d: To wish mutually in regarded to each other

intinctivity.d: The lack of the quality of coloring or tingeing other bodies

intoxicatedness.d: The state of being intoxicated; intoxication; drunkenness

intraaxillary.d: Situated below the point where a leaf joins the stem

intractile.d: Not tractile; incapable of being drawn out or extended

intrafusion.d: The act of pouring into a vessel; specif. (Med.), the operation of introducing a substance into a blood vessel; as, intrafusion of blood

intramercurial.d: Between the planet Mercury and the sun; -- as, the hypothetical Vulcan is intramercurial

intransgressible.d: Incapable of being transgressed; not to be passed over or crossed

intransigentes.d: The extreme radicals; the party of the irreconcilables

intransmissible.d: Not capable of being transmitted; as, an intransmissable illness

intransmutable.d: Not capable of being transmuted or changed into another substance

intraterritorial.d: Within the territory or a territory

intreasure.d: To lay up, as in a treasury; to hoard

intrenchant.d: Not to be gashed or marked with furrows

introreception.d: The act of admitting into or within

intrunk.d: To inclose as in a trunk; to incase

intrusionist.d: One who intrudes; especially, one who favors the appointment of a clergyman to a parish, by a patron, against the wishes of the parishioners

inturbidate.d: To render turbid; to darken; to confuse

inturgescence.d: A swelling; the act of swelling, or state of being swelled

inunctuosity.d: The lack of unctuosity; freedom from greasiness or oiliness; as, the inunctuosity of porcelain clay

inveil.d: To cover, as with a veil

invendibility.d: The quality of being invendible; invendibleness; unsalableness

inverisimilitude.d: Lack of verisimilitude or likelihood; improbability

inverted rectifier.d: A device which converts direct current to alternating current

invigilance.d: Lack of vigilance; neglect of watching; carelessness

invillaged.d: Turned into, or reduced to, a village

invisible ink.d: A fluid that has no color in the visible spectrum, but may be detected under certain conditions, as under ultraviolet light.  It may be used to write notes not readable under normal light

invision.d: Lack of vision or of the power of seeing

invitrifiable.d: Not admitting of being vitrified, or converted into glass

invulgar.d: To cause to become or appear vulgar

iodal.d: An oily liquid, CI3.CHO, analogous to chloral and bromal

iodhydrin.d: One of a series of compounds containing iodine, and analogous to the chlorhydrins

iodized salt.d: Table salt to which an inorganic iodide compound has been added as a nutritional supplement to prevent goiter

iodoquinine.d: A iodide of quinine obtained as a brown substance,. It is the base of herapathite. See Herapathite

iodothyrin.d: A peculiar substance obtained from the thyroid gland, containing from nine to ten per cent of iodine

ionidium.d: A genus of violaceous plants, chiefly found in tropical America, some species of which are used as substitutes for ipecacuanha

ioqua shell.d: The shell of a large Dentalium (Dentalium pretiosum), formerly used as shell money, and for ornaments, by the Indians of the west coast of North America

ipomoeic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained by the oxidation of convolvulin (obtained from jalap, the tubers of Ipomœa purga), and identical in most of its properties with sebacic acid

irenarch.d: An officer in the Greek empire having functions corresponding to those of a justice of the peace

iridious.d: Of or pertaining to iridium; -- applied specifically to compounds in which iridium has a low valence

iridoline.d: A nitrogenous base C10H9N, extracted from coal-tar naphtha, as an oily liquid. It is a member of the quinoline series, and is probably identical with lepidine

iriscope.d: A philosophical toy for exhibiting the prismatic tints by means of thin films

irish american.d: A native of Ireland who has become an American citizen; also, a child or descendant of such a person

iron sickness.d: The the process of deterioration afflicting a ship that is iron-sick

iron-cased.d: Cased or covered with iron, as a vessel; ironclad

iron-hearted.d: Hard-hearted; unfeeling; cruel; as, an iron-hearted master

iron-sick.d: Having the ironwork loose or corroded; -- said of a ship when her bolts and nails are so eaten with rust that she has become leaky

iron-sided.d: Having iron sides, or very firm sides

ironheads.d: A European composite herb (Centaurea nigra); -- so called from the resemblance of its knobbed head to an iron ball fixed on a long handle

ironwort.d: An herb of the Mint family (Sideritis), supposed to heal sword cuts; also, a species of Galeopsis

irrecognition.d: A failure to recognize; absence of recognition

irreconcile.d: To prevent from being reconciled; to alienate or disaffect

irreconcilement.d: The state or quality of being unreconciled; disagreement

irrecordable.d: Not fit or possible to be recorded

irrejectable.d: That can not be rejected; irresistible

irrelation.d: The quality or state of being irrelative; lack of connection or relation

irrelavancy.d: The quality or state of being irrelevant; as, the irrelevancy of an argument

irrelavant.d: Not relevant; not applicable or pertinent; not bearing upon or serving to support; foreign; extraneous; as, testimony or arguments irrelevant to a case

irremittable.d: Not capable of being remitted; irremissible

irremunerable.d: Not remunerable; not capable of remuneration

irrepealability.d: The quality or state of being irrepealable

irrepresentable.d: Not capable of being represented or portrayed

irreprovable.d: Incapable of being justly reproved; irreproachable; blameless; upright

irresilient.d: Not resilient; not recoiling or rebounding; inelastic

irresolubleness.d: The state or quality of being irresoluble; insolubility

irresolvedly.d: Without settled determination; in a hesitating manner; doubtfully

irreversible steering gear.d: A steering gear, esp. for an automobile, not affected by the road wheels, as when they strike an obstacle side ways, but easily controlled by the hand wheel or steering lever

irrevoluble.d: That has no finite period of revolution; not revolving

irrision.d: The act of laughing at another; derision

irrubrical.d: Contrary to the rubric; not rubrical

isabella grape.d: A favorite sweet American grape of a purple color. See Fox grape, under Fox

isabella moth.d: A common American moth (Pyrrharctia isabella), of an isabella color.  The larva, called woolly bear and hedgehog caterpillar, is densely covered with hairs, which are black at each end of the body, and red in the middle part

isagelous.d: Containing the same information; as, isagelous sentences

isagon.d: A figure or polygon whose angles are equal

isapostolic.d: Having equal, or almost equal, authority with the apostles of their teachings

isatic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, isatin; as, isatic acid, which is also called trioxindol

isatogen.d: A complex nitrogenous radical, C8H4NO2, regarded as the essential residue of a series of compounds, related to isatin, which easily pass by reduction to indigo blue

isatropic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained from atropine, and isomeric with cinnamic acid

ischiocerite.d: The third joint or the antennæ of the Crustacea

ischury.d: A retention or suppression of urine

isethionic.d: Pertaining to, derived from, or designating, an acid, HO.C2H4.SO3H, obtained as an oily or crystalline substance, by the action of sulphur trioxide on alcohol or ether. It is derivative of sulphuric acid

islandy.d: Of or pertaining to islands; full of islands

isobarism.d: The quality or state of being equal in weight, especially in atmospheric pressure. Also, the theory, method, or application of isobaric science

isocephalism.d: A peculiarity in the design of bas-relief by which the heads of human figures are kept at the same height from the ground, whether the personages are seated, standing, or mounted on horseback; -- called also isokephaleia

isochor.d: A line upon a thermodynamic diagram so drawn as to represent the pressures corresponding to changes of temperature when the volume of the gas operated on is constant

isochronon.d: A clock that is designed to keep very accurate time

isocrymal.d: Pertaining to, having the nature of, or illustrating, an isocryme; as, an isocrymal line; an isocrymal chart

isocryme.d: A line connecting points on the earth's surface having the same mean temperature in the coldest month of the year

isocyanic.d: Designating an acid isomeric with cyanic acid

isocyanuric.d: Designating, or pertaining to, an acid isomeric with cyanuric acid, and called also fulminuric acid. See under Fulminuric

isodiabatic.d: Pertaining to the reception or the giving out of equal quantities of heat by a substance

isonandra.d: A genus of sapotaceous trees of India. Isonandra Gutta is the principal source of gutta-percha

isonitroso-.d: A combining form (also used adjectively), signifying: Pertaining to, or designating, the characteristic, nitrogenous radical, NOH, called the isonitroso group

isopleura.d: A subclass of Gastropoda, in which the body is symmetrical, the right and left sides being equal

isopodiform.d: Having the shape of an isopod; -- said of the larvæ of certain insects

isorcin.d: A crystalline hydrocarbon derivative, metameric with orcin, but produced artificially; -- called also cresorcin

isosporic.d: Producing but one kind of spore, as the ferns and Equiseta.  Cf. Heterosporic

isosulphocyanic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid, HNCS, isomeric with sulphocyanic acid

isotherombrose.d: A line connecting or marking points on the earth's surface, which have the same mean summer rainfall

isouric.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a complex nitrogenous acid, isomeric with uric acid

isuret.d: An artificial nitrogenous base, isomeric with urea, and forming a white crystalline substance; -- called also isuretine

ita palm.d: A magnificent species of palm (Mauritia flexuosa), growing near the Orinoco. The natives eat its fruit and buds, drink its sap, and make thread and cord from its fiber

itacism.d: Pronunciation of η (eta) as the modern Greeks pronounce it, that is, like e in the English word be. This was the pronunciation advocated by Reuchlin and his followers, in opposition to the etacism of Erasmus. See Etacism

itacist.d: One who is in favor of itacism

itaconic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid, C5H6O4, which is obtained as a white crystalline substance by decomposing aconitic and other organic acids

itelmen.d: An aboriginal tribe inhabiting the southern part of the Kamchatka peninsula; called also Kamchadal and Kamtschadal

iterable.d: Capable of being iterated or repeated

itzibu.d: A silver coin of Japan, worth about thirty-four cents

iulidan.d: One of the Iulidæ, a family of myriapods, of which the genus Iulus is the type. See Iulus

ivan ivanovitch.d: An ideal personification of the typical Russian or of the Russian people; -- used as “John Bull” is used for the typical Englishman

ivoride.d: A composition resembling ivory in appearance and used as a substitute for it

ixodian.d: A tick of the genus Ixodes, or the family Ixodidæ

izedi.d: One of an Oriental religious sect which worships Satan or the Devil

jaal goat.d: A species of wild goat (Capra Nubiana) found in the mountains of Abyssinia, Upper Egypt, and Arabia; -- called also beden, and jaela

jacchus.d: The common marmoset (Hapale vulgaris). Formerly, the name was also applied to other species of the same genus

jackboot tactics.d: Harsh strongarm tactics; repressive, bullying and militaristic tactics like those used in authoritarian or totalitarian countries; --  used opprobriously, and often in hyperbolic exaggeration of police tactics in democratic countries

jackslave.d: A low servant; a mean fellow

jacksmith.d: A smith who makes jacks. See 2d Jack, 4, c

jackwood.d: Wood of the jack (Artocarpus integrifolia), used in cabinetwork

jacobaean lily.d: A bulbous plant  (Amaryllis formosissima syn. Sprekelia formosissima) from Mexico. It bears a single, large, deep, red, lilylike flower

jaghir.d: A village or district the government and revenues of which are assigned to some person, usually in consideration of some service to be rendered, esp. the maintenance of troops

jagua palm.d: A great Brazilian palm (Maximiliana regia), having immense spathes which are used for baskets and tubs

jahvism.d: The religion or worship of Yahweh (Jehovah), or the system of doctrines, etc., connected with it

jahvist.d: The author of the passages of the Old Testament, esp. those of the Hexateuch, in which God is styled Yahweh, or Jehovah; the author of the Yahwistic, or Jehovistic, Prophetic Document (J); also, the document itself

jakie.d: A South American striped frog (Pseudis paradoxa), remarkable for having a tadpole larger than the adult, and hence called also paradoxical frog

jalons.d: Long poles, topped with wisps of straw, used as landmarks and signals

jambolana.d: A myrtaceous tree of the West Indies and tropical America (Calyptranthes Jambolana), with astringent bark, used for dyeing. It bears an edible fruit

jambool.d: The Java plum; also, a drug obtained from its bark and seeds, formerly used as a remedy for diabetes

jamdani.d: A silk fabric, with a woven pattern of sprigs of flowers

jane-of-apes.d: A silly, pert girl; -- corresponding to jackanapes

janizarian.d: Of or pertaining to the janizaries, or their government

jantu.d: A machine of great antiquity, used in Bengal for raising water to irrigate land

jards.d: A callous tumor on the leg of a horse, below the hock

jargle.d: To emit a harsh or discordant sound

jasperated.d: mixed with jasper; containing particles of jasper; as, jasperated agate

jasperize.d: To convert into, or make to resemble, jasper

jaspidean.d: Consisting of jasper, or containing jasper; jaspery; jasperlike

jasponyx.d: An onyx, part or all of whose layers consist of jasper

jatrophic.d: Of or pertaining to physic nuts, the seeds of plants of the genus Jatropha

javelinier.d: A soldier armed with a javelin

jaw-fall.d: Depression of the jaw; hence, depression of spirits

jazel.d: A gem of an azure color

jazerant.d: A coat of defense made of small plates of metal sewed upon linen or the like; also, this kind of armor taken generally; as, a coat of jazerant

jedding ax.d: A stone mason's tool, having a flat face and a pointed part

jeffersonian simplicity.d: The absence of pomp or display which Jefferson aimed at in his administration as President (1801-1809), eschewing display or ceremony tending to distinguish the President from the people, as in going to the capital on horseback and with no escort, the abolition of court etiquette and the weekly levee, refusal to recognize titles of honor, etc

jemidar.d: The chief or leader of a band or body of persons; esp., in the native army of India, an officer of a rank corresponding to that of lieutenant in the English army

jeniquen.d: A Mexican name for the Sisal hemp (Agave rigida, var. Sisalana); also, its fiber

jentling.d: A fish of the genus Leuciscus; the blue chub of the Danube

jeofail.d: An oversight in pleading, or the acknowledgment of a mistake or oversight

jerkoff.d: A lazy, foolish, stupid, or otherwise contemptible person; -- an offensive and disparaging term

jeronymite.d: One belonging of the mediæval religious orders called Hermits of St. Jerome

jerquing.d: The searching of a ship for unentered goods

jessant.d: Springing up or emerging; -- said of a plant or animal

jesuitess.d: One of an order of nuns established on the principles of the Jesuits, but suppressed by Pope Urban in 1633

jesuitocracy.d: Government by Jesuits; also, the whole body of Jesuits in a country

jet d'eau.d: A stream of water spouting, esp. upward, from a fountain or pipe for ornament; also, the fountain or pipe from which it issues

jeterus.d: A yellowness of the parts of plants which are normally green; yellows

jeunesse doree.d: Lit., gilded youth; young people of wealth and fashion, esp. if given to prodigal living; -- in the French Revolution, applied to young men of the upper classes who aided in suppressing the Jacobins after the Reign of Terror

jew's-harp.d: An instrument of music, which, when placed between the teeth, gives, by means of a bent metal tongue struck by the finger, a sound which is modulated by the breath; -- called also Jew's-trump

jew's-stone.d: A large clavate spine of a fossil sea urchin

jharal.d: A wild goat (Capra Jemlaica) which inhabits the loftiest mountains of India. It has long, coarse hair, forming a thick mane on its head and neck

jigjog.d: A jolting motion; a jogging pace

jill-flirt.d: A light, giddy, or wanton girl or woman. See Gill-flirt

jingal.d: A small portable piece of ordnance, mounted on a swivel

jinny road.d: An inclined road in a coal mine, on which loaded cars descend by gravity, drawing up empty ones

jnr..d: Abbreviation for Junior, used after a name by a son who has the same first and last name as his father; -- less commonly used than Jr

jocantry.d: The act or practice of jesting

jocote.d: A common tropical American shrub or small tree (Spondias purpurea) with purplish fruit

joe miller.d: A jest book; a stale jest; a worn-out joke

johannean.d: Of or pertaining to John, esp. to the Apostle John or his writings

joinhand.d: Writing in which letters are joined in words; -- distinguished from writing in single letters

joint-fir.d: A genus (Ephedra) of leafless shrubs, with the stems conspicuously jointed; -- called also shrubby horsetail. There are about thirty species, of which two or three are found from Texas to California

jolly-boat.d: A boat of medium size belonging to a ship

joseph's flower.d: A composite herb (Tragopogon pratensis), of the same genus as the salsify

joss paper.d: Gold and silver paper burned by the Chinese, in the form of coins or ingots, in worship and at funerals

jossa.d: A command to a horse, probably meaning “stand still.”

joule's cycle.d: The cycle for the air engine proposed by Joule. In it air is taken by a pump from a cold chamber and compressed adiabatically until its pressure is eqal to that of the air in a hot chamber, into which it is then delivered, thereby displacing an equal amount of hot air into the engine cylinder. Here it expands adiabatically to the temperature of the cold chamber into which it is finally exhausted. This cycle, reversed, is used in refrigerating machines

jovialist.d: One who lives a jovial life

jovicentric.d: Revolving around the planet Jupiter; appearing as viewed from Jupiter

jovinianist.d: An adherent to the doctrines of Jovinian, a monk of the fourth century, who denied the virginity of Mary, and opposed the asceticism of his time

jowter.d: A mounted peddler of fish; -- called also jouster

jubilar.d: Pertaining to, or having the character of, a jubilee

judas-colored.d: Red; -- from a tradition that Judas Iscariot had red hair and beard

jugata.d: The figures of two heads on a medal or coin, either side by side or joined

juglandine.d: An alkaloid found in the leaves of the walnut (Juglans regia)

jukes, the.d: A pseudonym used to designate the descendants of two sisters, the “Jukes” sisters, whose husbands were sons of a backwoodsman of Dutch descent. They lived in the State of New York, and their history was investigated by R. L. Dugdale as an example of the inheritance of criminal and immoral tendencies, disease, and pauperism.  Sixty per cent of those traced showed, degeneracy, and they are estimated to have cost society $1,308,000 in 75 years

julus.d: A catkin or ament. See Ament

jumart.d: The fabled offspring of a bull and a mare

jumelle.d: Twin; paired; -- said of various objects made or formed in pairs, as a binocular opera glass, a pair of gimmal rings, etc

jump spark.d: A spark produced by the jumping of electricity across a permanent gap

jumpered.d: having a jumper{2} connecting two contacts in (a circuit)

juncous.d: Full of rushes: resembling rushes; juncaceous

jungermannia.d: A genus of hepatic mosses, now much circumscribed, but formerly comprising most plants of the family, which is sometimes therefore called Jungermanniaceæ

juniperite.d: One of the fossil Coniferæ, evidently allied to the juniper

jura-trias.d: A term applied to many American Mesozoic strata, in which the characteristics of the Jurassic and Triassic periods appear to be blended

justiceable.d: Liable to trial in a court of justice

justicement.d: Administration of justice; procedure in courts of justice

justico.d: Formerly, a close coat or waistcoat with sleeves

juvia.d: A Brazilian name for the lofty myrtaceous tree (Bertholetia excelsa) which produces the large seeds known as Brazil nuts

juwansa.d: The camel's thorn. See under Camel

juxtaposit.d: To place in close connection or contiguity; to juxtapose

kabook.d: A clay ironstone found in Ceylon

kafal.d: The Arabian name of two trees of the genus Balsamodendron, which yield a gum resin and a red aromatic wood

kahani.d: A kind of notary public, or attorney, in the Levant

kahau.d: A long-nosed monkey (Nasalis larvatus, formerly Semnopithecus nasalis), native of Borneo. The general color of the body is bright chestnut, with the under parts, shoulders, and sides of the head, golden yellow, and the top of the head and upper part of the back brown. Called also proboscis monkey.  It is now an endangered species

kakaralli.d: A kind of wood common in Demerara, durable in salt water, because not subject to the depredations of the sea worm and barnacle

kalasie.d: A long-tailed monkey of Borneo (Semnopithecus rubicundus). It has a tuft of long hair on the head

kaleege.d: One of several species of large, crested, Asiatic pheasants, belonging to the genus Euplocamus, and allied to the firebacks

kamichi.d: A curious South American bird (Anhima  or Palamedea cornuta), often domesticated by the natives and kept with poultry, which it defends against birds of prey. It has a long, slender, hornlike ornament on its head, and two sharp spurs on each wing. Although its beak, feet, and legs resemble those of gallinaceous birds, it is related in anatomical characters to the ducks and geese (Anseres). Called also horned screamer. The name is sometimes applied also to the chaja. See Chaja, and Screamer

kamtschadales.d: An aboriginal tribe inhabiting the southern part of the Kamchatka peninsula; called also Kamchadals and Itelmen

kanacka.d: A native of the Sandwich Islands

kapia.d: The fossil resin of the kauri tree of New Zealand

karagane.d: A species of gray fox found in Russia

karmathian.d: One of an Islamic sect founded in the ninth century by Karmat

karob.d: The twenty-fourth part of a grain; -- a weight used by goldsmiths

karyomiton.d: The reticular network of fine fibers, of which the nucleus of a cell is in part composed; -- in opposition to kytomiton, or the network in the body of the cell

karyostenotic.d: Pertaining to, or connected with, karyostenosis; as, the karyostenotic mode of nuclear division

katastate.d: A substance formed by a catabolic process; -- opposed to anastate. See catabolic

kathetal.d: Making a right angle; perpendicular, as two lines or two sides of a triangle, which include a right angle

kattimundoo.d: A caoutchouc-like substance obtained from the milky juice of the East Indian Euphorbia Kattimundoo. It is used as a cement

kecksy.d: The hollow stalk of an umbelliferous plant, such as the cow parsnip or the hemlock

keelfat.d: A cooler; a vat for cooling wort, etc

kefir grains.d: Small hard yellowish aggregations found in the Caucasus region, and containing various yeasts and bacteria. They are used as a ferment in preparing kefir

kenogenetic.d: Of or pertaining to kenogenesis; as, kenogenetic processes

kent bugle.d: A curved bugle, having six finger keys or stops, by means of which the performer can play upon every key in the musical scale; -- called also keyed bugle, and key bugle

keramographic.d: Suitable to be written upon; capable of being written upon, as a slate; -- said especially of a certain kind of globe

kerana.d: A kind of long trumpet, used among the Persians

keratophyte.d: A gorgonian coral having a horny axis

keratosa.d: An order of sponges having a skeleton composed of hornlike fibers. It includes the commercial sponges

kerchered.d: Covered, or bound round, with a kercher

kern baby.d: A doll or image decorated with corn (grain) flowers, etc., carried in the festivals of a kern, or harvest-home. Called also harvest queen

keslop.d: The stomach of a calf, prepared for rennet

ketmie.d: The name of certain African species of Hibiscus, cultivated for the acid of their mucilage

key-cold.d: Cold as a metallic key; lifeless

khutbah.d: An address or public prayer read from the steps of the pulpit in Muslim mosques, offering glory to God, praising Mohammed and his descendants, and the ruling princes

kibblings.d: Portions of small fish used for bait on the banks of Newfoundland

kicksy-wicksy.d: That which is restless and uneasy

kidney-form.d: Having the form or shape of a kidney; reniform; as, a kidney-shaped leaf; a kidney-shaped swimming pool

kiggelaria.d: A small genus of South African shrubs or small trees

kilkenny cats.d: Two cats fabled, in an Irish story, to have fought till nothing was left but their tails. It is probably a parable of a local contest between Kilkenny and Irishtown, which impoverished both towns

killow.d: An earth of a blackish or deep blue color

kilnhole.d: The mouth or opening of an oven or kiln

king's bench.d: Formerly, the highest court of common law in England; -- so called because the king used to sit there in person. It consisted of a chief justice and four puisne, or junior, justices. During the reign of a queen it was called the Queen's Bench. Its jurisdiction was transferred by the judicature acts of 1873 and 1875 to the high court of justice created by that legislation

king-post.d: A member of a common form of truss, as a roof truss. It is strictly a tie, intended to prevent the sagging of the tiebeam in the middle. If there are struts, supporting the main rafters, they often bear upon the foot of the king-post. Called also crown-post

kingston metal.d: An alloy of tin, copper, and mercury, sometimes used for the bearings and packings of machinery

kingston valve.d: A conical valve, opening outward, to close the mouth of a pipe which passes through the side of a vessel below the water line

kingtruss.d: A truss, framed with a king-post; -- used in roofs, bridges, etc

kinit.d: A unit of force equal to the force which, acting for one second, will give a pound a velocity of one foot per second; -- proposed by J. D. Everett, an English physicist

kioways.d: A tribe of Indians distantly related to the Shoshones.  They formerly inhabited the region about the head waters of the North Platte

kipe.d: An osier basket used for catching fish

kippernut.d: A name given to earthnuts of several kinds

kipskin.d: Leather prepared from the skin of young or small cattle, intermediate in grade between calfskin and cowhide

kirumbo.d: A bird of Madagascar (Leptosomus discolor), the only living type of a family allied to the rollers. It has a pair of loral plumes. The male is glossy green above, with metallic reflections; the female is spotted with brown and black

kissing strings.d: Cap or bonnet strings made long to tie under the chin

kissingcrust.d: The portion of the upper crust of a loaf which has touched another loaf in baking

kitambilla.d: A small shrubby spiny tree (Dovyalis hebecarpa) cultivated for its maroon-purple fruit with sweet purple pulp tasking like gooseberries; it is native to Sri Lanka and India

kitchen middens.d: Relics of neolithic man found on the coast of Denmark, consisting of shell mounds, some of which are ten feet high, one thousand feet long, and two hundred feet wide. The name is applied also to similar mounds found on the American coast from Canada to Florida, made by the North American Indians

kitchenry.d: The body of servants employed in the kitchen; the staff of a kitchen

kitish.d: Like or relating to a kite

kivikivi.d: Any species of Apteryx, esp. Apteryx australis; -- so called in imitation of its notes.  More commonly called kiwi. See Apteryx

kleeneboc.d: An antelope (Cerphalopus pygmæus), found in South Africa. It is of very small size, being but one foot high at the shoulder. It is remarkable for its activity, and for its mild and timid disposition. Called also guevi, and pygmy antelope

klicket.d: A small postern or gate in a palisade, for the passage of sallying parties

knab.d: To seize with the teeth; to gnaw

knapple.d: To break off with an abrupt, sharp noise; to bite; to nibble

knappy.d: Having knaps; full of protuberances or humps; knobby

knaveship.d: A small due, in meal, established by usage, which is paid to the under miller

kneadingly.d: In the manner of one kneading

knee jerk liberal.d: a person of strong liberal convictions who reacts predictably and emotionally to certain events

knee jerk reaction.d: an immediate unthinking emotional reaction produced by an event or statement to which the reacting person is highly sensitive; -- in persons with strong feelings on a topic, it may be very predictable

knight marshal.d: An officer in the household of the British sovereign, who has cognizance of transgressions within the royal household and verge, and of contracts made there, a member of the household being one of the parties

knight service.d: The military service by rendering which a knight held his lands

knight's fee.d: The fee of a knight; specif., the amount of land the holding of which imposed the obligation of knight service, being sometimes a hide{1}(b) or less, sometimes six or more hides

knight-er-ratic.d: Pertaining to a knight-errant or to knight-errantry

knitch.d: A number of things tied or knit together; a bundle; a fagot

knittle.d: A string that draws together a purse or bag

knockstone.d: A block upon which ore is broken up

knotberry.d: The cloudberry (Rudus Chamæmorus); -- so called from its knotted stems

knowa bleness.d: The state or quality of being knowable

knowledge worker.d: A person whose occupation is predominantly concerned with generating or interpreting information, as contrasted with manual labor

koellia.d: The genus comprising the American mountain mint, synonymous with Pycnanthemum

koftgari.d: Ornamental work produced by inlaying steel with gold, -- a variety of damascening much used in the arts of India

kohl-rabi.d: A variety of cabbage, in which the edible part is a large, turnip-shaped swelling of the stem, above the surface of the ground

kolarian.d: An individual of one of the races of aboriginal inhabitants which survive in Hindustan

koluschan.d: Designating, or pertaining to, a linguistic stock of North American Indians comprising the Tlinkit tribes of the Alexander Archipelago of southeastern Alaska and adjacent coast lands. Their language bears some affinity to Mexican tongues

komenic.d: Of or pertaining to, or designating, an acid derived from meconic acid

komtok.d: An African freshwater fish (Protopterus annectens), belonging to the Dipnoi. It can breathe air by means of its lungs, and when waters dry up, it encases itself in a nest of hard mud, where it remains till the rainy season. It is used as food

konseal.d: A form of capsule for inclosing a dose of medicine that is offensive, caustic, or the like

kosteletzya.d: A small genus of herbs of the Southeastern U. S. and tropical America and Africa

koulan.d: A wild horse (Equus onager or Asinus onager) inhabiting the plains of Central Asia; -- called also gour, khur, and onager

krakowiak.d: A lively Polish dance. See Cracovienne

krameric.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, Krameria (rhatany); as, krameric acid, usually called ratanhia-tannic acid

kranging hook.d: A hook for holding the blubber while cutting it away

kriegsspiel.d: A game of war, played for practice, on maps

kritarchy.d: The rule of the judges over Israel

krupp gun.d: A breech-loading steel cannon manufactured at the works of Friedrich Krupp, at Essen in Prussia.  Guns of over eight-inch bore are made up of several concentric cylinders; those of a smaller size are forged solid

krupp process.d: A process practiced by Friedrich Krupp, Essen, Germany, for washing pig iron, differing from the Bell process in using manganese as well as iron oxide, and performed in a Pernot furnace.  Called also the Bell-Krupp process

kruppize.d: To treat by, or subject to, the Krupp process

kuklux.d: The name adopted in the southern part of the United States by a secret political organization, active for several years after the close of the Civil War, and having for its aim the repression of the political power of the freed negroes; -- called also Kuklux Klan and the Klan.  It exerienced a revival in the 1920's, in the north as well as the south, and persists as a weak organization into the 1990's.  Its goals were primarily anti-negro and anti-Catholic, and its tactics included terrorist att

kurakkan.d: An East Indian cereal grass (Eleusine coracana) whose seed yield a somewhat bitter flour, a staple in the Orient

kurilian.d: Of or pertaining to the Kurile Islands, a chain of islands in the Pacific ocean, extending from the southern extremity of Kamchatka to Yesso

kussier.d: A Turkish instrument of music, with a hollow body covered with skin, over which five strings are stretched

kwan yin.d: A female Bodhisattva; often called Goddess of Mercy and considered an aspect of the Bodisattva Avalokitesvara; identified with Japanese Kwannon

kyar.d: Cocoanut fiber, or the cordage made from it. See Coir

kyloes.d: The cattle of the Hebrides, or of the Highlands

kynurenic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained from the urine of dogs. By decomposition the acid yields a nitrogenous base (called kynurin) and carbonic acid

kyrielle.d: A litany beginning with the words, “Kyrie eleison.”

kyriolexy.d: The use of literal or simple expressions, as distinguished from the use of figurative or obscure ones

kyriological.d: Serving to denote objects by conventional signs or alphabetical characters; as, the original Greek alphabet of sixteen letters was called kyriologic, because it represented the pure elementary sounds. See Curiologic

labadist.d: A follower of Jean de Labadie, a religious teacher of the 17th century, who left the Roman Catholic Church and taught a kind of mysticism, and the obligation of community of property among Christians

labrus.d: A genus of marine fishes, including the wrasses of Europe. See Wrasse

laburnic.d: Of, pertaining to, or derived from, the laburnum

labyrinthal.d: Pertaining to, or resembling, a labyrinth; intricate; labyrinthian

labyrinthibranch.d: Of or pertaining to the Labyrinthici

labyrinthici.d: An order of teleostean fishes, including the Anabas, or climbing perch, and other allied fishes

labyrinthiform.d: Having the form of a labyrinth; intricate

labyrinthodon.d: A genus of very large fossil amphibians, of the Triassic period, having bony plates on the under side of the body. It is the type of the order Labyrinthodonta. Called also Mastodonsaurus

laccic.d: Pertaining to lac, or produced from it; as, laccic acid

laccin.d: A yellow amorphous substance obtained from lac

lace-bark.d: A shrub in the West Indies (Lagetta Iintearia); -- so called from the lacelike layers of its inner bark

lace-winged.d: Having thin, transparent, reticulated wings; as, the lace-winged flies

laceman.d: A man who deals in lace

lacert.d: A muscle of the human body

lacertiloid.d: Like or belonging to the Lacertilia

lachrymae christi.d: A rich, sweet, red Neapolitan wine

lachrymals.d: Tears; also, lachrymal feelings or organs

lachrymary.d: Containing, or intended to contain, tears; lachrymal

lackbrain.d: One who is deficient in understanding; a witless person

laconize.d: To imitate the manner of the Laconians, especially in brief, pithy speech, or in frugality and austerity

lacrimoso.d: Plaintive; -- a term applied to a mournful or pathetic movement or style

lactage.d: The produce of animals yielding milk; milk and that which is made from it

lactamic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an amido acid related to lactic acid, and called also amido-propionic acid

lactarene.d: A preparation of casein from milk, used in printing calico

lacteously.d: In a lacteous manner; after the manner of milk

lactimide.d: A white, crystalline substance obtained as an anhydride of alanine, and regarded as an imido derivative of lactic acid

lactoabumin.d: The albumin present in milk, apparently identical with ordinary serum albumin. It is distinct from the casein of milk

lactucic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, the juice of the Lactuca virosa; -- said of certain acids

lactucone.d: A white, crystalline, tasteless substance, found in the milky sap of species of Lactuca, and constituting an essential ingredient of lactucarium

lacturamic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an organic amido acid, which is regarded as a derivative of lactic acid and urea

lacustral.d: Found in, or pertaining to, lakes or ponds, or growing in them; as, lacustrine flowers

lacwork.d: Ornamentation by means of lacquer painted or carved, or simply colored, sprinkled with gold or the like; -- said especially of Oriental work of this kind

ladder-backed.d: Having horizontal stripes on the back, reminiscent of a ladder; -- used of birds; as, a ladder-backed woodpecker

lademan.d: One who leads a pack horse; a miller's servant

ladies' eardrops.d: The small-flowered Fuchsia (Fuchsia coccinea), and other closely related species

lady's bedstraw.d: The common bedstraw (Galium verum); also, a slender-leaved East Indian shrub (Pharnaceum Mollugo), with white flowers in umbels

lady's bower.d: A climbing plant with fragrant blossoms (Clematis vitalba)

lady's cloth.d: A kind of broadcloth of light weight, used for women's dresses, cloaks, etc

lady's comb.d: An umbelliferous plant (Scandix Pecten-Veneris), its clusters of long slender fruits remotely resembling a comb

lady's cushion.d: An herb growing in dense tufts; the thrift (Armeria vulgaris)

lady's finger.d: The kidney vetch, Anthyllis vulneraria; called also lady's fingers

lady's hair.d: A plant of the genus Briza (Briza media); a variety of quaking grass

lady's mantle.d: A genus of rosaceous herbs (Alchemilla), esp. the European Alchemilla vulgaris, which has leaves with rounded and finely serrated lobes

lady's thumb.d: An annual weed (Polygonum Persicaria), having a lanceolate leaf with a dark spot in the middle

lady's traces.d: A name given to several species of the orchidaceous genus Spiranthes, in which the white flowers are set in spirals about a slender axis and remotely resemble braided hair

lady-killing.d: The art or practice of captivating the hearts of women

laemodipoda.d: A division of amphipod Crustacea, in which the abdomen is small or rudimentary and the legs are often reduced to five pairs.  The whale louse, or Cyamus, and Caprella are examples

laemodipodous.d: Of or pertaining to the Laemodipoda

laetere sunday.d: The fourth Sunday of Lent; -- so named from the Latin word Lætare (rejoice), the first word in the antiphone of the introit sung that day in the Roman Catholic service

lagenian.d: Like, or pertaining to, Lagena, a genus of Foraminifera having a straight, chambered shell

lagenophera.d: A small genus of herbs of Australia and South America having small solidary white or purple flowers similar to true daisies of genus Bellis

lager wine.d: Wine which has been kept for some time in the cellar

lagophthalmia.d: A morbid condition in which the eye stands wide open, giving a peculiar staring appearance

lagopous.d: Having a dense covering of long hair, like the foot of a hare

laicality.d: The state or quality of being laic; the state or condition of a layman

lakeweed.d: The water pepper (Polygonum Hydropiper), an aquatic plant of Europe and North America

lambale.d: A feast at the time of shearing lambs

lambative.d: Taken by licking with the tongue

lambert pine.d: The gigantic sugar pine of California and Oregon (Pinus Lambertiana). It has the leaves in fives, and cones a foot long. The timber is soft, and like that of the white pine of the Eastern States

lamellary.d: Of or pertaining to lamella or to lamellae; lamellar

lamelliferous.d: Bearing, or composed of, lamellae, or thin layers, plates, or scales; foliated

laminaa.d: A thin plate or scale; a layer or coat lying over another; -- said of thin plates or platelike substances, as of bone or minerals

laminability.d: The quality or state of being laminable

lampadist.d: One who gained the prize in the lampadrome

lampadrome.d: A race run by young men with lighted torches in their hands.  He who reached the goal first, with his torch unextinguished, gained the prize

lampate.d: A supposed salt of lampic acid

lampic.d: Pertaining to, or produced by, a lamp; -- formerly said of a supposed acid

lampoonry.d: The act of lampooning; a lampoon, or lampoons

lampyrine.d: An insect of the genus Lampyris, or family Lampyridæ. See Lampyris

lancasterian.d: Of or pertaining to the monitorial system of instruction followed by Joseph Lancaster, of England, in which advanced pupils in a school teach pupils below them

lance fish.d: A slender marine fish of the genus Ammodytes, especially Ammodytes tobianus of the English coast; -- called also sand lance

lancegay.d: A kind of spear anciently used. Its use was prohibited by a statute of Richard II

lancepesade.d: An assistant to a corporal; a private performing the duties of a corporal; -- called also lance corporal

lanch.d: To throw, as a lance; to let fly; to launch

land league.d: In Ireland, a combination of tenant farmers and other, organized, with Charles Stewart Parnell as president, in 1879 with a view to the reduction of farm rents and a reconstruction of the land laws

land of steady habits.d: Connecticut; -- a nickname alluding to the moral character of its inhabitants, implied by the rigid laws (see Blue laws) of the early period

landamman.d: A chief magistrate in some of the Swiss cantons

landflood.d: An overflowing of land by river; an inundation; a freshet

landreeve.d: A subordinate officer on an extensive estate, who acts as an assistant to the steward

langarey.d: One of numerous species of long-winged, shrikelike birds of Australia and the East Indies, of the genus Artamus, and allied genera; called also wood swallow

langate.d: A linen roller used in dressing wounds

langdak.d: A wolf (Canis pallipes), found in India, allied to the jackal

langteraloo.d: An old game at cards. See Loo (a)

languageless.d: Lacking or wanting language; speechless; silent

langya.d: One of several species of East Indian and Asiatic fresh-water fishes of the genus Ophiocephalus, remarkable for their power of living out of water, and for their tenacity of life; -- called also walking fishes

laniariform.d: Shaped like a laniary, or canine, tooth

lanioid.d: Of or pertaining to the shrikes (family Laniidæ)

lantanuric.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a nitrogenous organic acid of the uric acid group, obtained by the decomposition of allantoin, and usually called allanturic acid

lanternfly.d: any one of several species of large, handsome, brightly marked, tropical hemipterous insects of the genera Laternaria, Fulgora, and allies, of the family Fulgoridæ. The largest species is Laternaria phosphorea of Brazil. The head has a snoutlike process in some species which was formerly thought to emit a phosphorescent light

lap-welded.d: Having edges or ends united by a lap weld; as, a lap-welded pipe

lapidescence.d: The state or quality of being lapidescent

lapillation.d: The state of being, or the act of making, stony

lapling.d: One who has been fondled to excess; one fond of ease and sensual delights; -- a term of contempt

laqueary.d: Using a noose, as a gladiator

laramie group.d: An extensive series of strata, principally developed in the Rocky Mountain region, as in the Laramie Mountains, and formerly supposed to be of the Tertiary age, but now generally regarded as Cretaceous, or of intermediate and transitional character. It contains beds of lignite, often valuable for coal, and is hence also called the lignitic group. See Chart of Geology

larget.d: A short piece of bar iron for rolling into a sheet; a small billet

largition.d: The bestowment of a largess or gift

larixinic.d: Of, or derived from, the larch (Larix); as, larixinic acid

lark-colored.d: Having the sandy brown color of the European larks

laroid.d: Like or belonging to the Gull family (Laridæ)

larvalia.d: An order of Tunicata, including Appendicularia, and allied genera; -- so called because certain larval features are retained by them through life. Called also Copelata. See Appendicularia

laser disk.d: A digital data storage medium consisting of a thin disk onto which the data is impressed by a laser, in the form of a linear sequence of dots; same as optical disk.  The data is subsequently read back by the use of a laser beam.  See also compact disk

laserwort.d: Any plant of the umbelliferous genus Laserpitium, of several species (as Laserpitium glabrum, and Laserpitium siler), the root of which yields a resinous substance of a bitter taste. The genus is mostly European

lath-shaped.d: Having a slender elongated form, like a lath; -- said of the feldspar of certain igneous rocks, as diabase, as seen in microscopic sections

lathereeve.d: Formerly, the head officer of a lathe. See 1st Lathe

latian.d: Belonging, or relating, to Latium, a country of ancient Italy. See Latin

latibulize.d: To retire into a den, or hole, and lie dormant in winter; to retreat and lie hid

laticlave.d: A broad stripe of purple on the fore part of the tunic, worn by senators in ancient Rome as an emblem of office

latigo halter.d: A kind of halter usually made of raw hide

latinistic.d: Of, pertaining to, or derived from, Latin; in the Latin style or idiom

latinitaster.d: One who has but a smattering of Latin

latinly.d: In the manner of the Latin language; in correct Latin

latirostres.d: The broad-billed singing birds, such as the swallows, and their allies

latisternal.d: Having a broad breastbone, or sternum; -- said of anthropoid apes

latitancy.d: Act or state of lying hid, or lurking

latitat.d: A writ based upon the presumption that the person summoned was hiding

latreutical.d: Acting as a hired servant; serving; ministering; assisting

latterday.d: Belonging to present times or those recent by comparison

laughsome.d: Exciting laughter; also, addicted to laughter; merry

laurestine.d: The Viburnum Tinus, an evergreen shrub or tree of the south of Europe, which flowers during the winter months

lautverschiebung.d: The regular changes which the primitive Indo-European stops, or mute consonants, underwent in the Teutonic languages, probably as early as the 3d century b. c. , often called the first Lautverschiebung, sound shifting, or consonant shifting

lavatic.d: Like lava, or composed of lava; lavic

lavoesium.d: A supposed new metallic element, which was said to have been discovered in pyrites, and some other minerals, and to be of a silver-white color, and malleable.  It is not currently (1998) a recognized element

lavolt.d: An old dance, for two persons, being a kind of waltz, in which the woman made a high spring or bound

lay shaft.d: A secondary shaft, as in a sliding change gear for an automobile; a cam shaft operated by a two-to-one gear in an internal-combustion engine. It is generally a shaft moving more or less independently of the other parts of a machine, as, in some marine engines, a shaft, driven by a small auxiliary engine, for independently operating the valves of the main engine to insure uniform motion

layship.d: The condition of being a layman

leaf cutter.d: Any one of various species of wild bees of the genus Megachile, which cut rounded pieces from the edges of leaves, or the petals of flowers, to be used in the construction of their nests, which are made in holes and crevices, or in a leaf rolled up for the purpose. Among the common American species are Megachile brevis and Megachile centuncularis. Called also rose-cutting bee

leaf-footed.d: Having leaflike expansions on the legs; -- said of certain insects; as, the leaf-footed bug (Leptoglossus phyllopus)

leaf-hopper.d: A small leaping insect that sucks the juices of plants

leaf-nosed.d: Having a leaflike membrane on the nose; -- said of certain bats, esp. of the genera Phyllostoma and Rhinonycteris. See Vampire

leafroller.d: The larva of any tortricid moth which makes a nest by rolling up the leaves of plants and tying the leaves with spun silk; aalso, the moth itself.  See Tortrix

lean-witted.d: Having but little sense or shrewdness

lecanomancy.d: Divination practiced with water in a basin, by throwing three stones into it, and invoking the demon whose aid was sought

lecanoric.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an organic acid which is obtained from several varieties of lichen (Lecanora, Roccella, etc.), as a white, crystalline substance, and is called also orsellic acid, diorsellinic acid, lecanorin, etc

lechanorales.d: A category used in some classification systems for all lichens that produce apothecia

lectica.d: A kind of litter or portable couch

lecythis.d: A genus of gigantic trees, chiefly Brazilian, of the order Myrtaceæ, having woody capsules opening by an apical lid. Lecythis Zabucajo yields the delicious sapucaia nuts. Lecythis Ollaria produces the monkey-pots, its capsules. Its bark separates into thin sheets, like paper, used by the natives for cigarette wrappers

ledgment.d: A string-course or horizontal suit of moldings, such as the base moldings of a building

leetman.d: One subject to the jurisdiction of a court-leet

left-brain.d: Of or pertaining to the left cerebral hemisphere of the brain

leg bridge.d: A type of bridge for small spans in which  the floor girders are rigidly secured at their extremities to supporting steel legs, driven into the ground as piling, or resting on mudsills

legatura.d: A tie or brace; a syncopation

leggiadro.d: Light or graceful; in a light, delicate, and brisk style

legific.d: Of or pertaining to making laws
