legionry.d: A body of legions; legions, collectively

lego-literary.d: Pertaining to the literature of law

leiotrichan.d: Of or pertaining to the Leiotrichi

leitneria.d: A genus of trees or shrubs coextensive with the family Leitneriaceae, and including the corkwood (Leitneria floridana)

lemmatization.d: The act or process of lemmatizing; conversion into a lemma{2}

lemniscata.d: A curve in the form of the figure 8, with both parts symmetrical, generated by the point in which a tangent to an equilateral hyperbola meets the perpendicular on it drawn from the center

lenger.d: Longer; longest; -- obsolete compar. and superl. of long

lenitude.d: The quality or habit of being lenient; lenity

lenni-lenape.d: A general name for a group of Algonquin tribes which formerly occupied the coast region of North America from Connecticut to Virginia. They included the Mohicans, Delawares, Shawnees, and several other tribes

leonese.d: Of or pertaining to Leon, in Spain

lepadoid.d: A stalked barnacle of the genus Lepas, or family Lepadidæ; a goose barnacle. Also used adjectively

lepidodendrid.d: One of an extinct family of trees allied to the modern club mosses, and including Lepidodendron and its allies

lepidoganoid.d: Any one of a division (Lepidoganoidei) of ganoid fishes, including those that have scales forming a coat of mail. Also used adjectively

lepismoid.d: Like or pertaining to the Lepisma

leptiform.d: Having a form somewhat like leptus; -- said of active insect larvae having three pairs of legs. See Larva

leptocardia.d: The lowest class of Vertebrata, including only the Amphioxus. The heart is represented only by a simple pulsating vessel. The blood is colorless; the brain, renal organs, and limbs are wanting, and the backbone is represented only by a simple, unsegmented notochord. See Amphioxus

leptocardian.d: Of or pertaining to the Leptocardia

leptoptilus.d: A genus of birds including the adjutant bird (Leptoptilus dubius, also called adjutant stork) and marabous

lernaea.d: A Linnæan genus of parasitic Entomostraca, -- the same as the family Lernæidæ

lernaeacea.d: A suborder of copepod Crustacea, including a large number of remarkable forms, mostly parasitic on fishes. The young, however, are active and swim freely. See Illustration in Appendix

lernean.d: One of a family (Lernæidæ) of parasitic Crustacea found attached to fishes and other marine animals. Some species penetrate the skin and flesh with the elongated head, and feed on the viscera. See Illust. in Appendix

lesquerella.d: A genus of low-growing hairy herbs, comprising some of the bladderpods

lessener.d: One who, or that which, lessens

letheon.d: Sulphuric ether used as an anæsthetic agent

letheonize.d: To subject to the influence of letheon

leucaniline.d: A colorless, crystalline, organic base, obtained from rosaniline by reduction, and also from other sources. It forms colorless salts

leucitoid.d: The trapezohedron or tetragonal trisoctahedron; -- so called as being the form of the mineral leucite

leucoethiopic.d: White and black; -- said of a white animal of a black species, or the albino of the negro race

leuconic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a complex organic acid, obtained as a yellowish white gum by the oxidation of croconic acid

leucopathy.d: The state of an albino, or of a white child of black parents

leucophlegmacy.d: A dropsical habit of body, or the commencement of anasarca; paleness, with viscid juices and cold sweats

leucophlegmatic.d: Having a dropsical habit of body, with a white bloated skin

leucosoid.d: Like or pertaining to the Leucosoidea, a tribe of marine crabs including the box crab or Calappa

leucoturic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a nitrogenous organic substance of the uric acid group, called leucoturic acid or oxalantin. See Oxalantin

leucous.d: White; -- applied to albinos, from the whiteness of their skin and hair

levana.d: A goddess who protected newborn infants

levation.d: The act of raising; elevation; upward motion, as that produced by the action of a levator muscle

levelism.d: The disposition or endeavor to level all distinctions of rank in society

leverwood.d: The American hop hornbeam (Ostrya Virginica), a small tree with very tough wood

levesel.d: A leafy shelter; a place covered with foliage

levir.d: A husband's brother; -- used in reference to levirate marriages

levirostres.d: A group of birds, including the hornbills, kingfishers, and related forms

lexiphanic.d: Using, or interlarded with, pretentious words; bombastic; as, a lexiphanic writer or speaker; lexiphanic writing

lexiphanicism.d: The use of pretentious words, language, or style

libellulid.d: A dragon fly; -- from Libellula, the name of the typical genus

libelluloid.d: Like or pertaining to the dragon flies

libidinosity.d: The state or quality of being libidinous; libidinousness

lichanura.d: A genus of boas of western North America

lichenic.d: Of, pertaining to, or obtained from, lichens

lichenographist.d: One who describes lichens; one versed in lichenography

lichenography.d: A description of lichens; the science which illustrates the natural history of lichens

lichwort.d: An herb, the wall pellitory. See Pellitory

licitation.d: The act of offering for sale to the highest bidder

lickpenny.d: A devourer or absorber of money

lieberkuehn's glands.d: The simple tubular glands of the small intestines; -- called also crypts of Lieberkuehn

lieberkuhn.d: A concave metallic mirror attached to the object-glass end of a microscope, to throw down light on opaque objects; a reflector

liedertafel.d: A popular name for any society or club which meets for the practice of male part songs

lierne rib.d: In Gothic vaulting, any rib which does not spring from the impost and is not a ridge rib, but passes from one boss or intersection of the principal ribs to another

lifestring.d: A nerve, or string, that is imagined to be essential to life

light-winged.d: Having light and active wings; volatile; fleeting

lightroom.d: A small room from which the magazine of a naval vessel is lighted, being separated from the magazine by heavy glass windows

lign-aloes.d: Aloes wood, or agallochum. See     Agallochum

lignoceric.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid of the formic acid series, found in the tar, wax, or paraffine obtained by distilling certain kinds of wood, as the beech

lignum rhodium.d: The fragrant wood of several shrubs and trees, especially of species of Rhodorhiza from the Canary Islands, and of the West Indian Amyris balsamifera

lignum-vitae.d: A tree (Guaiacum officinale) found in the warm latitudes of America, from which the guaiacum of medicine is procured. Its wood is very hard and heavy, and is used for various mechanical purposes, as for the wheels of ships' blocks, cogs, bearings, and the like. See Guaiacum

lilly-pilly.d: An Australian myrtaceous tree (Eugenia Smithii), having smooth ovate leaves, and panicles of small white flowers. The wood is hard and fine-grained

lilywort.d: Any plant of the Lily family or order

limacina.d: A genus of small spiral pteropods, common in the Arctic and Antarctic seas. It contributes to the food of the right whales

limbat.d: A cooling periodical wind in the Isle of Cyprus, blowing from the northwest from eight o'clock, A. M., to the middle of the day or later

limbous.d: With slightly overlapping borders; -- said of a suture

limburg cheese.d: A soft cheese made in the Belgian province of Limburg (Limbourg), and usually not eaten until the curing has developed a peculiar and, to most people, unpleasant odor

lime-twigged.d: Beset with snares; insnared, as with birdlime

limehound.d: A dog used in hunting the wild boar; a leamer

limenean.d: Of or pertaining to Lima, or to the inhabitants of Lima, in Peru

limitaneous.d: Of or pertaining to a limit

limitive.d: Involving a limit; as, a limitive law, one designed to limit existing powers

limoniad.d: A nymph of the meadows; -- called also Limniad

limu.d: The Hawaiian name for seaweeds. Over sixty kinds are used as food, and have species names, as Limu Lipoa, Limu palawai, etc

limuloidea.d: An order of Merostomata, including among living animals the genus Limulus, with various allied fossil genera, mostly of the Carboniferous period. Called also Xiphosura

linament.d: Lint; esp., lint made into a tent for insertion into wounds or ulcers

lindheimera.d: A genus having only one species, the Texas star

lindia.d: A peculiar genus of rotifers, remarkable for the absence of ciliated disks. By some Zoologists it is thought to be like the ancestral form of the Arthropoda

lindiform.d: Resembling the genus Lindia; -- said of certain apodous insect larvæ

linearensate.d: Having the form of a sword, but very long and narrow

ling-bird.d: The European meadow pipit; -- called also titling

lingism.d: A mode of treating certain diseases, as obesity, by gymnastics; -- proposed by Pehr Henrik Ling, a Swede. See Kinesiatrics

lingot.d: A linget or ingot; also, a mold for casting metals. See Linget

linguacious.d: Given to the use of the tongue; loquacious

linguadental.d: Formed or uttered by the joint use of the tongue and teeth, or rather that part of the gum just above the front teeth; dentolingual, as the letters d and t

linguatulina.d: An order of wormlike, degraded, parasitic arachnids. They have two pairs of retractile hooks, near the mouth. Called also Pentastomida

linoxin.d: A resinous substance obtained as an oxidation product of linoleic acid

lion's ear.d: A name given in Western South America to certain plants with shaggy tomentose leaves, as species of Culcitium, and Espeletia

lion's leaf.d: A South European plant of the genus Leontice (Leontice leontopetalum), the tuberous roots of which contain so much alkali that they are sometimes used as a substitute for soap

lion's tail.d: A genus of labiate plants (Leonurus); -- so called from a fancied resemblance of its flower spikes to the tuft of a lion's tail. Leonurus Cardiaca is the common motherwort

lionced.d: Adorned with lions' heads; having arms terminating in lions' heads; -- said of a cross

lipans.d: A tribe of North American Indians, inhabiting the northern part of Mexico. They belong to the Tinneh stock, and are closely related to the Apaches

liparian.d: Any species of a family (Liparidæ) of destructive bombycid moths, as the tussock moths

lipic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, fat. The word was formerly used specifically to designate a supposed acid obtained by the oxidation of oleic acid, tallow, wax, etc

lipid-lowering.d: Serving to reduce the concentration of lipid, such as cholesterol, in the blood; -- of medications, such as Mevinolin, that are used especially to reduce blood cholesterol, as a preventive measure against heart disease

lipothymous.d: Pertaining, or given, to swooning; fainting

litherly.d: Crafty; cunning; mischievous; wicked; treacherous; lazy

lithobilic.d: Pertaining to or designating an organic acid of the tartaric acid series, distinct from lithofellic acid, but, like it, obtained from certain bile products, as bezoar stones

lithochromics.d: The art of printing colored pictures on canvas from oil paintings on stone

lithodome.d: Any one of several species of bivalves, which form holes in limestone, in which they live; esp., any species of the genus Lithodomus

lithodomus.d: A genus of elongated bivalve shells, allied to the mussels, and remarkable for their ability to bore holes for shelter, in solid limestone, shells, etc. Called also Lithophagus

lithofracteur.d: An explosive compound of nitroglycerin. See Nitroglycerin

lithoglypher.d: One who curs or engraves precious stones

lithoglyphic.d: Of or pertaining to the art of cutting and engraving precious stones

litholatry.d: The worship of a stone or stones

lithologist.d: One who is skilled in lithology

lithophosphor.d: A stone that becomes phosphoric by heat

lithophosphoric.d: Pertaining to lithophosphor; becoming phosphoric by heat

lithophyse.d: A spherulitic cavity often with concentric chambers, observed in some volcanic rocks, as in rhyolitic lavas. It is supposed to be produced by expanding gas, whence the name

lithosian.d: Any one of various species of moths belonging to the family Lithosidæ. Many of them are beautifully colored

lithotriptist.d: One skilled in breaking and extracting stone in the bladder

lithotypic.d: Of, pertaining to, or produced by, lithotypy

lithotypy.d: The art or process of making a kind of hard, stereotype plate, by pressing into a mold, taken from a page of type or other matter, a composition of gum shellac and sand of a fine quality, together with a little tar and linseed oil, all in a heated state

litraneter.d: An instrument for ascertaining the specific gravity of liquids

little-ease.d: An old slang name for the pillory, stocks, etc., of a prison

littress.d: A smooth kind of cartridge paper used for making cards

lituiform.d: Having the form of a lituus; like a lituite

livelode.d: Course of life; means of support; livelihood

living picture.d: A tableau in which persons take part; also, specif., such a tableau as imitating a work of art

lixt.d: 2d pers. sing. pres. of Lige, to lie, to tell lies, -- contracted for ligest

lizard's tail.d: A perennial plant of the genus Saururus (Saururus cernuus), growing in marshes, and having white flowers crowded in a slender terminal spike, somewhat resembling in form a lizard's tail; whence the name

llandeilo group.d: A series of strata in the lower Silurian formations of Great Britain; -- so named from Llandeilo in Southern Wales. See Chart of Geology

loadmanage.d: Pilotage; skill of a pilot or loadsman

loanin.d: An open space between cultivated fields through which cattle are driven, and where the cows are sometimes milked; also, a lane

loanmonger.d: A dealer in, or negotiator of, loans

lobbish.d: Like a lob; consisting of lobs

lobcock.d: A dull, sluggish person; a lubber; a lob

lobefoot.d: A bird having lobate toes; esp., a phalarope

lobiped.d: Having lobate toes, as a coot

lock hospital.d: A hospital for the treatment of venereal diseases

lock step.d: A mode of marching by a body of men going one after another as closely as possible, in which the leg of each moves at the same time with the corresponding leg of the person before him

lock stitch.d: A peculiar sort of stitch formed by the locking of two threads together, as in the work done by some sewing machines. See Stitch

lock-down.d: A contrivance to fasten logs together in rafting; -- used by lumbermen

lock-weir.d: A waste weir for a canal, discharging into a lock chamber

locustic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, the locust; -- formerly used to designate a supposed acid

lode-ship.d: An old name for a pilot boat

loeven's larva.d: The peculiar larva of Polygordius. See Polygordius

log-chip.d: A thin, flat piece of board in the form of a quadrant of a circle attached to the log line; -- called also log-ship. See 2d Log, n., 2

log-ship.d: A part of the log. See Log-chip, and 2d Log, n., 2

loggat.d: A small log or piece of wood

logometric.d: Serving to measure or ascertain chemical equivalents; stoichiometric

loiseleuria.d: A genus of plants having only one species, the alpine azalea

lokao.d: A green vegetable dye imported from China

lombard-house.d: A bank or a pawnbroker's shop

london smoke.d: A neutral tint given to spectacles, shade glasses for optical instruments, etc., which reduces the intensity without materially changing the color of the transmitted light

long primer.d: A kind of type, in size between small pica and bourgeois

long-breathed.d: Having the power of retaining the breath for a long time; long-winded

long-horned.d: Having a long horn or horns; as, a long-horned goat, or cow; having long antennæ, as certain beetles (Longicornia)

long-stop.d: One who is set to stop balls which pass the wicket keeper

longbeak.d: The American redbellied snipe (Macrorhamphus scolopaceus); -- called also long-billed dowitcher

longicornia.d: A division of beetles, including a large number of species, in which the antennæ are very long.  Most of them, while in the larval state, bore into the wood or beneath the bark of trees, and some species are very destructive to fruit and shade trees. See Apple borer, under Apple, and Locust beetle, under Locust

longilateral.d: Having long sides; especially, having the form of a long parallelogram

longimetry.d: The art or practice of measuring distances or lengths

longipalp.d: One of a tribe of beetles, having long maxillary palpi

longipennes.d: A group of longwinged sea birds, including the gulls, petrels, etc

longipennine.d: Of or pertaining to the Longipennes; longipennate

longirostres.d: A group of birds characterized by having long slender bills, as the sandpipers, curlews, and ibises. It is now regarded as an artificial division

longmynd rocks.d: The sparingly fossiliferous conglomerates, grits, schists, and slates of Great Britain, which lie at the base of the Cambrian system; -- so called, because typically developed in the Longmynd Hills, Shropshire

longspun.d: Spun out, or extended, to great length; hence, long-winded; tedious

longtail.d: An animal, particularly a log, having an uncut tail.  Cf. Curtail. Dog

looked-for.d: same as anticipated, 2; as, his looked-for advancement

lool.d: A vessel used to receive the washings of ores of metals

looplight.d: A small narrow opening or window in a tower or fortified wall; a loophole

loord.d: A dull, stupid fellow; a drone

looseleaf binder.d: A type of notebook with hard covers attached to metal rings which open, allowing sheets of writing paper to be conveniently inserted into it and removed from it

looseleaf paper.d: Sheets of writing paper having holes at the edge permitting insertion into and removal from a looseleaf binder

lopeared.d: Having ears which droop or hang down; as, a lop-eared hound

lophiomys.d: A very singular rodent (Lophiomys Imhausi) of Northeastern Africa. It is the only known representative of a special family (Lophiomyidæ), remarkable for the structure of the skull. It has handlike feet, and the hair is peculiar in structure and arrangement

lophobranchii.d: An order of teleostean fishes, having the gills arranged in tufts on the branchial arches, as the Hippocampus and pipefishes

lophosteon.d: The central keel-bearing part of the sternum in birds

loppard.d: A tree, the top of which has been lopped off

lopseed.d: A perennial herb (Phryma Leptostachya), having slender seedlike fruits

lopsided victory.d: A victory in a contest in which one side defeats the other overwhelmingly; -- in sports, meaning one side scores much more than the other; in war, meaning one side has many more casualties than the other

lordolatry.d: Worship of, or reverence for, a lord as such

lords and ladies.d: The European wake-robin (Arum maculatum), -- those with purplish spadix the lords, and those with pale spadix the ladies

lorel.d: A good for nothing fellow; a vagabond

loreto nuns.d: Members of a congregation of nuns founded by Mrs. Mary Teresa Ball, near Dublin, Ireland, in 1822, and now spread over Ireland, India, Canada, and the United States.  The nuns are called also Ladies of Loreto.  They are engaged in teaching girls

lorettine.d: One of an order of nuns founded in 1812 at Loretto, in Kentucky. The members of the order (called also Sisters of Loretto, or Friends of Mary at the Foot of the Cross) devote themselves to the cause of education and the care of destitute orphans, their labors being chiefly confined to the western United States

losenger.d: A flatterer; a deceiver; a cozener

lotophagi.d: A people visited by Ulysses in his wanderings. They subsisted on the lotus. See Lotus (b), and Lotus-eater

loutou.d: A crested black monkey (Semnopithecus maurus) of Java

louvered door.d: A door having louvers in place of a solid panel, in part or all of the surface of the door

lovemonger.d: One who deals in affairs of love

low-churchism.d: The principles of the low-church party

low-churchmanship.d: The state of being a low-churchman

low-lived.d: Characteristic of, or like, one bred in a low and vulgar condition of life; mean; dishonorable; contemptible; as, low-lived dishonesty

low-polluting.d: producing little pollution, especially air pollution; as, a low-polluting electric car

low-studded.d: Furnished or built with short studs; as, a low-studded house or room

low-thoughted.d: Having one's thoughts directed toward mean or insignificant subjects

low-warp loom.d: a hand loom in which the warp is carried horizontally; for weaving tapestry

loxodromism.d: The act or process of tracing a loxodromic curve; the act of moving as if in a loxodromic curve

lucernal.d: Of or pertaining to a lamp

lucernaria.d: A genus of acalephs, having a bell-shaped body with eight groups of short tentacles around the margin.  It attaches itself by a sucker at the base of the pedicel

lucernarian.d: Of or pertaining to the Lucernarida

lucernarida.d: A division of acalephs, including Lucernaria and allied genera; -- called also Calycozoa

luciferian.d: Of or pertaining to Lucifer; having the pride of Lucifer; satanic; devilish

luciform.d: Having, in some respects, the nature of light; resembling light

luctation.d: Effort to overcome in contest; struggle; endeavor

lucule.d: A spot or fleck on the sun brighter than the surrounding surface

ludificatory.d: Making sport; tending to excite derision

ludlow group.d: A subdivision of the British Upper Silurian lying below the Old Red Sandstone; -- so named from the Ludlow, in Western England. See the Chart of Geology

lugmark.d: A mark cut into the ear of an animal to identify it; an earmark

lumachel.d: A grayish brown limestone, containing fossil shells, which reflect a beautiful play of colors. It is also called fire marble, from its fiery reflections

lumbric.d: An earthworm, or a worm resembling an earthworm

lump together.d: To combine (various items) and treat them as a unit.  See lump, v. i

lung-grown.d: Having lungs that adhere to the pleura

lunicurrent.d: Having relation to changes in currents that depend on the moon's phases

lunistice.d: The farthest point of the moon's northing and southing, in its monthly revolution

lunulite.d: Any bryozoan of the genus Lunulites, having a more or less circular form

lupulinic.d: Pertaining to, or obtained from, hops; specifically, designating an acid obtained by the decomposition of lupulin

lurchline.d: The line by which a fowling net was pulled over so as to inclose the birds

lurg.d: A large marine annelid (Nephthys cæca), inhabiting the sandy shores of Europe and America. It is whitish, with a pearly luster, and grows to the length of eight or ten inches

lusern.d: A lynx. See 1st Lucern and Loup-cervier

lussheburgh.d: A spurious coin of light weight imported into England from Luxemburg, or Lussheburgh, as it was formerly called

lustrical.d: Pertaining to, or used for, purification

lutarious.d: Of, pertaining to, or like, mud; living in mud

luteic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, weld (Reseda luteola)

luteocobaltic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, certain compounds of cobalt having a yellow color.  Cf. Cobaltic

lutulence.d: The state or quality of being lutulent

lycanthropist.d: One affected by the disease lycanthropy

lychnobite.d: One who labors at night and sleeps in the day

lychnoscope.d: Same as Low side window, under Low, a

lycopodiaceous.d: Belonging, or relating, to the Lycopodiaceæ, an order of cryptogamous plants (called also club mosses) with branching stems, and small, crowded, one-nerved, and usually pointed leaves

lycopodite.d: An old name for a fossil club moss

lydine.d: A violet dye derived from aniline

lyencephala.d: A group of Mammalia, including the marsupials and monotremes; -- so called because the corpus callosum is rudimentary

lyencephalous.d: Pertaining to, or characteristic of, the Lyencephala

lyopomata.d: An order of brachiopods, in which the valves of shell are not articulated by a hinge.  It includes the Lingula, Discina, and allied forms

lyre bird.d: Any one of two or three species of Australian birds of the genus Menura. The male is remarkable for having the sixteen tail feathers very long and, when spread, arranged in the form of a lyre. The common lyre bird (Menura superba), inhabiting New South Wales, is about the size of a grouse. Its general color is brown, with rufous color on the throat, wings, tail coverts and tail. Called also lyre pheasant and lyre-tail

lyrid.d: One of the group of shooting stars which come into the air in certain years on or about the 19th of April; -- so called because the apparent path among the stars if traced backwards crosses the constellation Lyra

lyrie.d: A European fish (Peristethus cataphractum), having the body covered with bony plates, and having three spines projecting in front of the nose; -- called also noble, pluck, pogge, sea poacher, and armed bullhead

lyriferous.d: Having a lyre-shaped shoulder girdle, as certain fishes

lysiloma.d: A small genus of tropical American trees and shrubs with pinnate leaves and flat straight pods

m'-naught.d: To increase the power of (a single-cylinder beam engine) by adding a small high-pressure cylinder with a piston acting on the beam between the center and the flywheel end, using high-pressure steam and working as a compound engine, -- a plan introduced by M'Naught, a Scottish engineer, in 1845

m-1.d: A semiautomatic rifle which was standard issue to infantrymen in the United States Army in the mid-20th century

maara shell.d: A large, pearly, spiral, marine shell (Turbo margaritaceus), from the Pacific Islands. It is used as an ornament

maasha.d: An East Indian coin, of about one tenth of the weight of a rupee

mabby.d: A spirituous liquor or drink distilled from potatoes; -- used in the Barbadoes

mabolo.d: A kind of persimmon tree (Diospyros discolor) from the Philippine Islands, now introduced into the East and West Indies. It bears an edible fruit as large as a quince

macaranga gum.d: A gum of a crimson color, obtained from a tree (Macaranga Indica) that grows in the East Indies.  It is used in taking impressions of coins, medallions, etc., and sometimes as a medicine

macaronian.d: Pertaining to, or like, macaroni (originally a dish of mixed food); hence, mixed; confused; jumbled

macassar oil.d: A kind of oil formerly used in dressing the hair; -- so called because originally obtained from Macassar, a district of the Island of Celebes. Also, an imitation of the same, of perfumed castor oil and olive oil.  Cf. antimacassar

macauco.d: Any one of several species of small lemurs, as Lemur murinus, which resembles a rat in size

macavahu.d: A small Brazilian monkey (Callithrix torquatus), -- called also collared teetee

maccaroni wheat.d: A type of wheat (Triticum durum) with hard dark-colored kernels high in gluten and used for bread and pasta; grown especially in South Russia, North Africa, and North central North America

macco.d: A gambling game in vogue in the eighteenth century

machaeranthera.d: A genus of wildflowers of Western North America

machaerodus.d: A genus of extinct mammals allied to the cats, and having in the upper jaw canine teeth of remarkable size and strength; -- hence called saber-toothed tigers

machiavelian.d: Of or pertaining to Machiavelli, or to his supposed principles for conduct of government, as enunciated in his tract The Prince; politically cunning; characterized by duplicity, political expediency, unscrupulous cunning, or bad faith; crafty

machiavelism.d: The supposed principles of Machiavelli, or practice in conformity to them; political artifice, intended to favor arbitrary power

maclurea.d: A genus of spiral gastropod shells, often of large size, characteristic of the lower Silurian rocks

macrame lace.d: A coarse lace made of twine, used especially in decorating furniture

macro-chemistry.d: The science which treats of the chemical properties, actions or relations of substances in quantity; -- distinguished from micro-chemistry

macrochires.d: A division of birds including the swifts and humming birds. So called from the length of the distal part of the wing

macrodactyl.d: One of a group of wading birds (Macrodactyli) having very long toes

macrodiagonal.d: The longer of two diagonals, as of a rhombic prism. See Crystallization

macropod.d: Any one of a group of maioid crabs remarkable for the length of their legs; -- called also spider crab

macropteres.d: A division of birds; the Longipennes

macruroid.d: Like or pertaining to the Macrura

mad-apple.d: The eggplant bush (Solanum melongena).  See Eggplant

madecass.d: A native or inhabitant of Madagascar, or Madecassee. See Malagasy

madeira vine.d: A herbaceous climbing vine (Boussingaultia baselloides) very popular in cultivation, having shining entire leaves and racemes of small fragrant white flowers

madjoun.d: An intoxicating confection from the hemp plant; -- used by the Turks and Hindus

madrepora.d: A genus of reef corals abundant in tropical seas. It includes than one hundred and fifty species, most of which are elegantly branched

madreporiform.d: Resembling a madreporian coral in form or structure

madrina.d: An animal (usually an old mare), wearing a bell and acting as the leader of a troop of pack mules

maegbote.d: Compensation for the injury done by slaying a kinsman

magazine camera.d: A camera in which a number of plates can be exposed without reloading

magdaleon.d: A medicine in the form of a roll, a esp. a roll of plaster

maggotish.d: Full of whims or fancies; maggoty

maghet.d: A name for daisies and camomiles of several kinds

magistratic.d: Of, pertaining to, or proceeding from, a magistrate; having the authority of a magistrate

magnality.d: A great act or event; a great attainment

magnase black.d: A black pigment which dries rapidly when mixed with oil, and is of intense body

magnetician.d: One versed in the science of magnetism; a magnetist

magnetizee.d: A person subjected to the influence of animal magnetism

magneto-electric.d: Pertaining to, or characterized by, electricity by the action of magnets; as, magneto-electric induction

magnetomotor.d: A voltaic series of two or more large plates, producing a great quantity of electricity of low tension, and hence adapted to the exhibition of electro-magnetic phenomena

mahabarata.d: A celebrated sacred epic poem of the Hindus, written in Sanskrit.  It is of great length, and is chiefly devoted to a history, in many episodes, of a civil war between two dynasties of ancient India

mahaled.d: A cherry tree (Prunus Mahaleb) of Southern Europe.  The wood is prized by cabinetmakers, the twigs are used for pipe stems, the flowers and leaves yield a perfume, and from the fruit a violet dye and a fermented liquor (like kirschwasser) are prepared

maharif.d: An African antelope (Hippotragus Bakeri). Its face is striped with black and white

maharmah.d: A muslin wrapper for the head and the lower part of the face, worn by Turkish and Armenian women when they go abroad

mahometanize.d: To convert to Islam, the religion of Mohammed; to Mohammedanize

mahon stock.d: An annual cruciferous plant with reddish purple or white flowers (Malcolmia maritima).  It is called in England Virginia stock, but the plant comes from the Mediterranean

mahoohoo.d: The African white two-horned rhinoceros (Atelodus simus)

mahori.d: One of the dark race inhabiting principally the islands of Eastern Polynesia. Also used adjectively

mahovo.d: A device for saving power in stopping and starting a railroad car, by means of a heavy fly wheel

mahrati.d: The language of the Mahrattas; the language spoken in the Deccan and Concan

mahwa tree.d: An East Indian sapotaceous tree (Bassia latifolia, and also Bassia butyracea), whose timber is used for wagon wheels, and the flowers for food and in preparing an intoxicating drink. It is one of the butter trees. The oil, known as mahwa and yallah, is obtained from the kernels of the fruit

maidmarian.d: The lady of the May games; one of the characters in a morris dance; a May queen. Afterward, a grotesque character personated in sports and buffoonery by a man in woman's clothes

maikel.d: A South American carnivore of the genus Conepatus, allied to the skunk, but larger, and having a longer snout. The tail is not bushy

maikong.d: A South American wild dog (Canis cancrivorus); the crab-eating dog

main-gauche.d: The dagger held in the left hand, while the rapier is held in the right; -- used to parry thrusts of the adversary's rapier

main-hamper.d: A hamper to be carried in the hand; a hand basket used in carrying grapes to the press

mainor.d: A thing stolen found on the person of the thief

mainpernable.d: Capable of being admitted to give surety by mainpernors; able to be mainprised

mainpernor.d: A surety, under the old writ of mainprise, for a prisoner's appearance in court at a day

maioid.d: Of or pertaining to the genus Maia, or family Maiadeae

majorat.d: The right of succession to property according to age; -- so termed in some of the countries of continental Europe

majorate.d: The office or rank of a major

majusculae.d: Capital letters, as found in manuscripts of the sixth century and earlier

make-belief.d: A feigning to believe; make believe

make-game.d: An object of ridicule; a butt

making-iron.d: A tool somewhat like a chisel with a groove in it, used by calkers of ships to finish the seams after the oakum has been driven in

malacissation.d: The act of making soft or supple

malacobdella.d: A genus of nemertean worms, parasitic in the gill cavity of clams and other bivalves. They have a large posterior sucker, like that of a leech. See Illust. of Bdellomorpha

malacostomous.d: Having soft jaws without teeth, as certain fishes

malacostracology.d: That branch of Zoological science which relates to the crustaceans; -- called also carcinology

malacozoa.d: An extensive group of Invertebrata, including the Mollusca, Brachiopoda, and Bryozoa. Called also Malacozoaria

malacozoic.d: Of or pertaining to the Malacozoa

malambo.d: A yellowish aromatic bark, used in medicine and perfumery, said to be from the South American shrub Croton Malambo

malamethane.d: A white crystalline substance forming the ethyl salt of malamic acid

malamic.d: Of or designating an acid intermediate between malic acid and malamide, and known only by its salts

malapterurus.d: A genus of African siluroid fishes, including the electric catfishes. See Electric cat, under Electric

malapterurus electricus.d: The species name of the electric catfish, a freshwater catfish of the Nile and tropical central Africa having an electric organ

maldanian.d: Any species of marine annelids of the genus Maldane, or family Maldanidae.  They have a slender, round body, and make tubes in the sand or mud

male-spirited.d: Having the spirit of a male; vigorous; courageous

malebranchism.d: The philosophical system of Malebranche, an eminent French metaphysician.  The fundamental doctrine of his system is that the mind can not have knowledge of anything external to itself except in its relation to God

maleficience.d: The doing of evil, harm, or mischief

mallee bird.d: The leipoa, or Australian moundbird; it incubates eggs naturally in sandy mounds.  See Leipoa

mallowwort.d: Any plant of the order Malvaceae

malma.d: A spotted trout (Salvelinus malma), inhabiting Northern America, west of the Rocky Mountains; -- called also Dolly Varden trout, bull trout, red-spotted trout, and golet

maltonic.d: Of, pertaining to, or derived from, maltose; specif., designating an acid called also gluconic or dextronic acid. See Gluconic

mameluco.d: A child born of a white father and Indian mother

mammonization.d: The process of making mammonish; the state of being under the influence of mammonism

mammothrept.d: A child brought up by its grandmother; a spoiled child

managery.d: Management; manner of using; conduct; direction

manation.d: The act of issuing or flowing out

mancipate.d: To enslave; to bind; to restrict

maniglion.d: Either one of two handles on the back of a piece of ordnance

manovery.d: A contrivance or maneuvering to catch game illegally

manqueller.d: A killer of men; a manslayer

manred.d: Homage or service rendered to a superior, as to a lord; vassalage

mansionry.d: The state of dwelling or residing; occupancy as a dwelling place

manubial.d: Belonging to spoils; taken in war

manuducent.d: One who leads by the hand; a manuductor

matrisib.d: One related on the mother's side
