miliolitic.d: Of or pertaining to the genus Miliola; containing miliolites

militate against.d: To argue against; to cast doubt on; -- used in reference to facts which tend to disprove a hypothesis; as, the absence of a correlation of budget deficits with inflation militates against any causal relation between the two.  Opposite of support

militiate.d: To carry on, or prepare for, war

milkful.d: Full of milk; abounding with food

mill-cake.d: The incorporated materials for gunpowder, in the form of a dense mass or cake, ready to be subjected to the process of granulation

mill-sixpence.d: A milled sixpence; -- the sixpence being one of the first English coins milled (1561)

millefiore glass.d: Slender rods or tubes of colored glass fused together and embedded in clear glass; -- used for paperweights and other small articles

millennianism.d: Belief in, or expectation of, the millennium{2}; millenarianism

millennist.d: One who believes in the millennium{2}

millennium bug.d: An error in the coding of certain computer programs which store the year component of the date as two digits, assuming that the first two digits are 19, rather than as a complete number of four digits; when such programs are used after January 1, 2000, the date may be misinterpreted, causing serious errors or total failure of the program; -- called also year 2000 bug, year 2000 problem and Y2K bug

millepora.d: A genus of Hydrocorallia, which includes the millipores

millinet.d: A stiff cotton fabric used by milliners for lining bonnets

millionary.d: Of or pertaining to millions; consisting of millions; as, the millionary chronology of the pundits

milliweber.d: The thousandth part of one weber

millrind.d: A figure supposed to represent the iron which holds a millstone by being set into its center

miltwaste.d: A small European fern (Asplenium Ceterach) formerly used in medicine

mimotannic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a variety of tannin or tannic acid found in Acacia, Mimosa, etc

minaceous.d: Of the color of minium or red lead; miniate

mince-meat.d: Minced meat; meat chopped very fine; a mixture of boiled meat, suet, apples, etc., chopped very fine, to which spices and raisins are added; -- used in making mince pie

mineralogize.d: To study mineralogy by collecting and examining minerals

minie ball.d: A conical rifle bullet, with a cavity in its base plugged with a piece of iron, which, by the explosion of the charge, is driven farther in, expanding the sides to fit closely the grooves of the barrel

minie rifle.d: A rifle adapted to minie balls

miniment.d: A trifle; a trinket; a token

minious.d: Of the color of red or vermilion

minishment.d: The act of diminishing, or the state of being diminished; diminution

minniebush.d: A low shrub (Menziesia pilosa) of the eastern U. S. with downy twigs

mino bird.d: An Asiatic bird (Gracula musica), allied to the starlings.  It is black, with a white spot on the wings, and a pair of flat yellow wattles on the head.  It is often tamed and taught to pronounce words.  It is one of the birds called mynah bird

minorat.d: A custom or right, analogous to borough-English in England, formerly existing in various parts of Europe, and surviving in parts of Germany and Austria, by which certain entailed estates, as a homestead and adjacent land, descend to the youngest male heir

mint state.d: A numerical grade indicating the degree of perfection of the condition of a coin which is classified as uncirculated, ranging from 70 for a coin in perfect condition to 60 for a coin which is uncirculated but may have a weak strike, or numerous small scratches from being handled in mint bags; usually used as the abbreviation MS; as, an MS-67 Morgan Dollar

mint-master.d: The master or superintendent of a mint. Also used figuratively

mintman.d: One skilled in coining, or in coins; a coiner

minutary.d: Pertaining to, or consisting of, minutes

minute-jack.d: A figure which strikes the hour on the bell of some fanciful clocks; -- called also jack of the clock house

mirabilary.d: One who, or a work which, narrates wonderful things; one who writes of wonders

miraculize.d: To cause to seem to be a miracle

misacceptation.d: Wrong acceptation; understanding in a wrong sense

misaffection.d: An evil or wrong affection; the state of being ill affected

misalter.d: To alter wrongly; esp., to alter for the worse

misassay.d: To assay, or attempt, improperly or unsuccessfully

misbear.d: To carry improperly; to carry (one's self) wrongly; to misbehave

misbede.d: To wrong; to do injury to

miscarriageable.d: Capable of miscarrying; liable to fail

miscellane.d: A mixture of two or more sorts of grain; -- now called maslin and meslin

mischaracterize.d: To characterize falsely or erroneously; to give a wrong character to

miscognize.d: To fail to apprehend; to misunderstand

misconfident.d: Having a mistaken confidence; wrongly trusting

misconsequence.d: A wrong consequence; a false deduction

misconstruable.d: Such as can be misconstrued, as language or conduct

misconstruct.d: To construct wrongly; to construe or interpret erroneously

miscontinuance.d: Discontinuance; also, continuance by undue process

miscredent.d: A miscreant, or believer in a false religious doctrine

misdistinguish.d: To make wrong distinctions in or concerning

misenter.d: To enter or insert wrongly, as a charge in an account

misfall.d: To befall, as ill luck; to happen to unluckily

misfeign.d: To feign with an evil design

misimprove.d: To use for a bad purpose; to abuse; to misuse; as, to misimprove time, talents, advantages, etc

misimprovement.d: Ill use or employment; use for a bad purpose

misincline.d: To cause to have a wrong inclination or tendency; to affect wrongly

misinterpretable.d: Capable of being misinterpreted; liable to be misunderstood

miskindle.d: To kindle amiss; to inflame to a bad purpose; to excite wrongly

mislactation.d: Defective flow or vitiated condition of the milk

misle.d: To rain in very fine drops, like a thick mist; to mizzle; to drizzle

mislight.d: To deceive or lead astray with a false light

misly.d: Raining in very small drops; drizzling

mismake.d: To make or form amiss; to spoil in making

mismeter.d: To give the wrong meter to, as to a line of verse

misobserve.d: To observe inaccurately; to mistake in observing

misobserver.d: One who misobserves; one who fails to observe properly

mispersuasion.d: A false persuasion; wrong notion or opinion

mispoint.d: To point improperly; to punctuate wrongly

misprofess.d: To make a false profession; to make pretensions to skill which is not possessed

misrecollect.d: To have an erroneous remembrance of; to suppose erroneously that one recollects

misregulate.d: To regulate wrongly or imperfectly; to fail to regulate

misrender.d: To render wrongly; to translate or recite wrongly

misrepeat.d: To repeat wrongly; to give a wrong version of

misrepute.d: To have in wrong estimation; to repute or estimate erroneously

missheathed.d: Sheathed by mistake; wrongly sheathed; sheathed in a wrong place

missit.d: To sit badly or imperfectly upon; to misbecome

missound.d: To sound wrongly; to utter or pronounce incorrectly

misstayed.d: Having missed stays; -- said of a ship

mistemper.d: To temper ill; to disorder; as, to mistemper one's head

misterm.d: To call by a wrong name; to miscall

misthrive.d: To thrive poorly; to be not thrifty or prosperous

mistide.d: To happen or come to pass unfortunately; also, to suffer evil fortune

mistransport.d: To carry away or mislead wrongfully, as by passion

misurato.d: Measured; -- a direction to perform a passage in strict or measured time

miswander.d: To wander in a wrong path; to stray; to go astray

misween.d: To ween amiss; to misjudge; to distrust; to be mistaken

miswend.d: To go wrong; to go astray

misworship.d: Wrong or false worship; mistaken practices in religion

misy.d: An impure yellow sulphate of iron; yellow copperas or copiapite

mitis casting.d: A process, invented by P. Ostberg, for producing malleable iron castings by melting wrought iron, to which from 0.05 to 0.1 per cent of aluminum is added to lower the melting point, usually in a petroleum furnace, keeping the molten metal at the bubbling point until it becomes quiet, and then pouring the molten metal into a mold lined with a special mixture consisting essentially of molasses and ground burnt fire clay; also, a casting made by this process; -- called also wrought-iron casting

mitis metal.d: The malleable iron produced by mitis casting; -- called also simply mitis

mittler's green.d: A pigment of a green color, the chief constituent of which is oxide of chromium

mixogamous.d: Pairing with several males; -- said of certain fishes of which several males accompany each female during spawning

mixolydian mode.d: The seventh ecclesiastical mode, whose scale commences on G

mixtilineal.d: Containing, or consisting of, lines of different kinds, as straight, curved, and the like; as, a mixtilinear angle, that is, an angle contained by a straight line and a curve

mixtly.d: With mixture; in a mixed manner; mixedly

mmolendinaceous.d: Resembling the sails of a windmill

mnemonician.d: One who instructs in the art of improving or using the memory

moabite stone.d: A block of black basalt, found at Dibon in Moab by Rev. F. A. Klein, Aug. 19, 1868, which bears an inscription of thirty-four lines, dating from the 9th century b. c., and written in the Moabite alphabet, the oldest Phoenician type of the Semitic alphabet.  It records the victories of Mesha, king of Moab, esp. those over Israel (2 Kings iii. 4, 5, 27)

moble.d: To wrap the head of in a hood

mockado.d: A stuff made in imitation of velvet; -- probably the same as mock velvet

modalist.d: One who regards Father, Son, and Spirit as modes of being, and not as persons, thus denying personal distinction in the Trinity

modius.d: A dry measure, containing about a peck

moebles.d: Movables; furniture; -- also used in the singular (moeble)

moggan.d: A closely fitting knit sleeve; also, a legging of knitted material

moghul empire.d: The empire created in India by invading Mongolians (Tatars), established under Baber, who conquered Hindustan in 1526.  The established religion of the empire was Islam.  After the death of the Great Mogul Aurung-Zeb in 1707, power passed to the Mahrattas and the British.  The empire existed only nominally in the early 1800's, and was finally abolished in 1857 by the deposing of the last emperor

mohammedan era.d: The era in use in Moslem countries. See Mohammedan year, below

mohammedan year.d: The year used by Muslims, consisting of twelve lunar months without intercalation, so that they retrograde through all the seasons in about 321/2 years.  The Mohammedan era begins with the year 622 a. d., the first day of the Mohammedan year 1332 being Nov. 30, 1913, according to the Gregorian calendar

mohurrum.d: The first month of the Mohammedan year

moile.d: A kind of high shoe anciently worn

moineau.d: A small flat bastion, raised in the middle of an overlong curtain

moire metallique.d: A crystalline or frosted appearance produced by some acids on tin plate; also, the tin plate thus treated

mole-eyed.d: Having eyes like those of the mole; having imperfect sight

moliminous.d: Of great bulk or consequence; very important

mollebart.d: An agricultural implement used in Flanders, consisting of a kind of large shovel drawn by a horse and guided by a man

mollemoke.d: Any one of several species of large pelagic petrels and fulmars, as Fulmarus glacialis, of the North Atlantic, and several species of Aestrelata, of the Southern Ocean. See Fulmar

molossine.d: A bat of the genus Molossus, as the monk bat

moltable.d: Capable of assuming a molten state; meltable; fusible

momier.d: A name given in contempt to strict Calvinists in Switzerland, France, and some parts of Germany, in the early part of the 19th century

monadelphia.d: A Linnaean class of plants having the stamens united into a tube, or ring, by the filaments, as in the Mallow family

monadiform.d: Having the form of a monad; resembling a monad in having one or more filaments of vibratile protoplasm; as, monadiform young

monandria.d: A Linnaean class of plants embracing those having but a single stamen

monandric.d: Of or pertaining to monandry; practicing monandry as a system of marriage

monarcho.d: The nickname of a crackbrained Italian who fancied himself an emperor

monasticon.d: A book giving an account of monasteries

monday's child.d: A child who is fair of face; -- a reference to a nineteenth century poem.  See below

monembryony.d: The condition of an ovule having but a single embryo

moneral.d: Of or pertaining to the Monera

moneran.d: Of or pertaining to the Monera

moneyage.d: A tax paid to the first two Norman kings of England to prevent them from debashing the coin

moniment.d: Something to preserve memory; a reminder; a monument; hence, a mark; an image; a superscription; a record

monitor nozzle.d: A nozzle capable of turning completely round in a horizontal plane and having a limited play in a vertical plane, used in hydraulic mining, fire-extinguishing apparatus, etc

monk's seam.d: An extra middle seam made at the junction of two breadths of canvas, ordinarily joined by only two rows of stitches

monkey's puzzle.d: A lofty coniferous Chilian tree (Araucaria araucana, formerly Araucaria imbricata), the branches of which are so crowded and intertwisted “as to puzzle a monkey to climb.”  It is also called monkey puzzle and monkey puzzle tree.  The edible nuts are over an inch long, and are called piñon by the Chilians

monkey-bread.d: The fruit of the Adansonia digitata; also, the tree. See Adansonia

monkey-pot.d: The fruit of two South American trees (Lecythis Ollaria, and Lecythis Zabucajo), which have for their fruit large, pot-shaped, woody capsules containing delicious nuts, and opening almost explosively by a circular lid at the top.  Vases and pots are made of this capsule

monkeywrench.d: A wrench or spanner which has one fixed and one adjustable jaw

monkflower.d: A name of certain curious orchids which bear three kinds of flowers formerly referred to three genera, but now ascertained to be sexually different forms of the same genus (Catasetum tridentatum, etc.)

monocarbonic.d: Containing one carboxyl group; as, acetic acid is a monocarbonic acid.  The more common term is monocarboxylic.  Contrasted with dicarboxylic, tricarboxylic, etc

monocondyla.d: A group of vertebrates, including the birds and reptiles, or those that have only one occipital condyle; the Sauropsida

monodelphia.d: The group that includes all ordinary or placental mammals; the Placentalia. See Mammalia

monodynamic.d: Possessing but one capacity or power

monoecian.d: Of or pertaining to the Monoecia; monoecious

monogamia.d: A Linnaean order of plants, having solitary flowers with united anthers, as in the genus Lobelia

monogoneutic.d: Having but one brood in a season

monogynia.d: A Linnaean order of plants, including those which have only one style or stigma

monomachist.d: One who fights in single combat; a duelist

monomya.d: An order of lamellibranchs having but one muscle for closing the shell, as the oyster

monoousian.d: Having but one and the same nature or essence

monopersonal.d: Having but one person, or form of existence

monophanous.d: Having one and the same appearance; having a mutual resemblance

monophysitical.d: Of or pertaining to Monophysites, or their doctrines

monoplastic.d: That has one form, or retains its primary form, as, a monoplastic element

monopneumona.d: A suborder of Dipnoi, including the Ceratodus

monopody.d: A measure of but a single foot

monoptote.d: A noun having only one case

monorganic.d: Belonging to, or affecting, a single organ, or set of organs

monotessaron.d: A single narrative framed from the statements of the four evangelists; a gospel harmony

monothalama.d: A division of Foraminifera including those that have only one chamber

monothalaman.d: A foraminifer having but one chamber

monothalmic.d: Formed from one pistil; -- said of fruits

monothelitic.d: Of or pertaining to the Monothelites, or their doctrine

monotomous.d: Having a distinct cleavage in a single direction only

monoxylous.d: Made of one piece of wood

monsignore.d: My lord; -- an ecclesiastical dignity bestowed by the pope, entitling the bearer to social and domestic rank at the papal court. (Abbrev. Mgr.)

mont de piete.d: One of certain public pawnbroking establishments which originated in Italy in the 15th century, the object of which was to lend money at a low rate of interest to poor people in need; -- called also mount of piety.  The institution has been adopted in other countries, as in Spain and France. See Lombard-house

monte-acid.d: An acid elevator, as a tube through which acid is forced to some height in a sulphuric acid manufactory

montem.d: A custom, formerly practiced by the scholars at Eton school, England, of going every third year, on Whittuesday, to a hillock near the Bath road, and exacting money from all passers-by, to support at the university the senior scholar of the school

montessori method.d: A system of training and instruction, primarily for use with normal children aged from three to six years, devised by Dr. Maria Montessori while teaching in the “Houses of Childhood” (schools in the poorest tenement districts of Rome, Italy), and first fully described by her in 1909.  The fundamental aim is to create self-motivation for education, and the leading features are freedom for physical activity (no stationary desks and chairs), informal and individual instruction, the very early devel

monteth.d: A vessel in which glasses are washed; -- so called from the name of the inventor

monthling.d: That which is a month old, or which lives for a month

montrue.d: That on which anything is mounted; a setting; hence, a saddle horse

monureid.d: Any one of a series of complex nitrogenous substances regarded as derived from one molecule of urea; as, alloxan is a monureid

moodir.d: The governor of a province in Egypt, etc

moon-culminating.d: Culminating, or coming to the meredian, at or about the same time with the moon; -- said of a star or stars, esp. of certain stars selected beforehand, and named in an ephemeris (as the Nautical Almanac), as suitable to be observed in connection with the moon at culmination, for determining terrestrial longitude

moon-eye.d: A eye affected by the moon; also, a disease in the eye of a horse

moonglade.d: The bright reflection of the moon's light on an expanse of water

moorball.d: A fresh-water alga (Cladophora Aegagropila) which forms a globular mass

mooress.d: A female Moor; a Moorish woman

moorpan.d: A clayey layer or pan underlying some moors, etc

mooruk.d: A species of cassowary (Casuarius Bennetti) found in New Britain, and noted for its agility in running and leaping.  It is smaller and has stouter legs than the common cassowary.  Its crest is bilobed; the neck and breast are black; the back, rufous mixed with black; and the naked skin of the neck, blue

moot-hall.d: A hall for public meetings; a hall of judgment

moot-hill.d: A hill of meeting or council; an elevated place in the open air where public assemblies or courts were held by the Saxons; -- called, in Scotland, mute-hill

mootman.d: One who argued moot cases in the inns of court

moplah.d: One of a class of Muslims in Malabar

mordicant.d: Biting; acrid; as, the mordicant quality of a body

mordication.d: The act of biting or corroding; corrosion

morgay.d: The European small-spotted dogfish, or houndfish. See the Note under Houndfish

moric.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, fustic (see Morin); as, moric acid

moril.d: An edible fungus. Same as 1st Morel

morinda.d: A genus of rubiaceous trees and shrubs, mostly East Indian, many species of which yield valuable red and yellow dyes. The wood is hard and beautiful, and used for gunstocks

moringic.d: Designating an organic acid obtained from oil of ben. See Moringa

morintannic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a variety of tannic acid extracted from fustic (Chlorophora tinctoria,  formerly Maclura tinctoria and Morus tinctoria) as a yellow crystalline substance; -- called also maclurin

morosaurus.d: An extinct genus of large herbivorous dinosaurs, found in Jurassic strata in America

moroxylic.d: Of, pertaining to, or derived from, the mulberry; moric

morris-chair.d: A kind of easy-chair with a back which may be lowered or raised

morsing horn.d: A horn or flask for holding powder, as for priming

morsitation.d: The act of biting or gnawing

mortifiedness.d: The state of being mortified; humiliation; subjection of the passions

mortpay.d: Dead pay; the crime of taking pay for the service of dead soldiers, or for services not actually rendered by soldiers

mortress.d: A dish of meats and other ingredients, cooked together; an ollapodrida

mosaism.d: Attachment to the system or doctrines of Moses; that which is peculiar to the Mosaic system or doctrines

mosasauria.d: An order of large, extinct, marine reptiles, found in the Cretaceous rocks, especially in America.  They were serpentlike in form and in having loosely articulated and dilatable jaws, with large recurved teeth, but they had paddlelike feet. Some of them were over fifty feet long. They are, essentially, fossil sea serpents with paddles. Called also Pythonomarpha, and Mosasauria

moschine.d: Of or pertaining to Moschus, a genus including the musk deer

moslings.d: Thin shreds of leather shaved off in dressing skins

motacil.d: Any singing bird of the genus Motacilla; a wagtail

moth-eat.d: To eat or prey upon, as a moth eats a garment

mother-of-thyme.d: An aromatic plant (Thymus Serphyllum); -- called also wild thyme

motley collection.d: A collection of objects of various kinds; a hodgepodge; a medley; a confused mixture; an omnium gatherum

motley-minded.d: Having a mind of a jester; foolish

motograph.d: A device utilized in the making of a loud-speaking telephone, depending on the fact that the friction between a metallic point and a moving cylinder of moistened chalk, or a moving slip of paper, on which it rests is diminished by the passage of a current between the point and the moving surface

mouillation.d: The act of uttering the sound of a mouillé letter

moundbird.d: Any of several large-footed short-winged birds of Australasia, which build mounds of decaying vegetation to incubate eggs.  Called also mound builder, mound maker, megapode, brush turkey, and scrub fowl

mountain specter.d: An optical phenomenon sometimes seen on the summit of mountains (as on the Brocken) when the observer is between the sun and a mass of cloud.  The figures of the observer and surrounding objects are seen projected on the cloud, greatly enlarged and often encircled by rainbow colors

mousle.d: To sport with roughly; to rumple

mousquetaire glove.d: A woman's glove with a long, loosely fitting wrist

mouth-footed.d: Having the basal joints of the legs converted into jaws

mowburn.d: To heat and ferment in the mow, as hay when housed too green

mucamide.d: The acid amide of mucic acid, obtained as a white crystalline substance

mucivore.d: An insect which feeds on mucus, or the sap of plants, as certain Diptera, of the tribe Mucivora

muck pile.d: The broken material at the face of a tunnel being bored, after being crushed by blasting

muck rake.d: A rake for scraping up muck or dung. See Muckrake, v. i., below

mucksy.d: Somewhat mucky; soft, sticky, and dirty; muxy

mucousness.d: The quality or state of being mucous; sliminess

mud-crab.d: A crab of the genus Panopœus (also written Panopeus)

mud-dauber.d: A wasp of the family Sphegidae (Sphecidae) which builds a nest of mud and stores insects and spiders in it; a digger-wasp

mugiloid.d: Like or pertaining to the genus Mugil, or family Mugilidae

mugweed.d: A slender European weed (Galium Cruciata); -- called also crossweed

mulberry-faced.d: Having a face of a mulberry color, or blotched as if with mulberry stains

mulctary.d: Imposing a pecuniary penalty; consisting of, or paid as, a fine

mule killer.d: Any of several arthropods erroneously supposed to kill live stock, in the southern United States, by stinging or by being swallowed

mulewort.d: A fern of the genus Hemionitis

mulierly.d: In the manner or condition of a mulier; in wedlock; legitimately

mullar.d: A die, cut in intaglio, for stamping an ornament in relief, as upon metal

mulloid.d: Like or pertaining to the genus Mullus, which includes the surmullet, or red mullet

multicentral.d: Having many, or several, centers; as, a multicentral cell

multiferous.d: Bearing or producing much or many

multiflue.d: Having many flues; as, a multiflue boiler. See Boiler

multigranulate.d: Having, or consisting of, many grains

multipresence.d: The state or power of being multipresent

multipresent.d: Being, or having the power to be, present in two or more places at once

multisect.d: Divided into many similar segments; -- said of an insect or myriapod

multisiliquous.d: Having many pods or seed vessels

multisonous.d: Having many sounds, or sounding much

multiversant.d: Turning into many shapes; assuming many forms; protean

multivious.d: Having many ways or roads; by many ways

multum.d: An extract of quassia licorice, fraudulently used by brewers in order to economize malt and hops

mum-chance.d: A game of hazard played with cards in silence

mumbledy peg.d: A game played with a pocketknife, the object of which is to throw the knife in any of a vairety of ways (such as over the back), or from various positions, and have it stick in the ground or another surface.  Also called mumble-the-peg and mumble peg

mundification.d: The act or operation of cleansing

mundil.d: A turban ornamented with an imitation of gold or silver embroidery

munerary.d: Having the nature of a gift

munify.d: To prepare for defense; to fortify

muraenoid.d: Like or pertaining to the genus Muraena, or family Muraenidae

murdress.d: A battlement in ancient fortifications with interstices for firing through

murenger.d: One who had charge of the wall of a town, or its repairs

murexoin.d: A complex nitrogenous compound obtained as a scarlet crystalline substance, and regarded as related to murexide

muricoid.d: Like, or pertaining to, the genus Murex, or family Muricidae

muride.d: Bromine; -- formerly so called from its being obtained from sea water

murnival.d: In the game of gleek, four cards of the same value, as four aces or four kings; hence, four of anything

murrion.d: Infected with or killed by murrain

murza.d: One of the hereditary nobility among the Tatars, esp. one of the second class

musar.d: An itinerant player on the musette, an instrument formerly common in Europe

muscales.d: An old name for mosses in the widest sense, including the true mosses and also hepaticae and sphagna

muscardin.d: The common European dormouse; -- so named from its odor

muscariform.d: Having the form of a brush

muscarin.d: A solid crystalline substance, C5H13NO2, found in the toadstool (Agaricus muscarius), and in putrid fish. It is a typical ptomaine, and a violent poison

muscicapine.d: Of or pertaining to the Muscicapidae, a family of birds that includes the true flycatchers

muscivora-forficata.d: A gray flycatcher of Southwestern U. S. and Mexico and Central America having a long forked tail and white breast and salmon and scarlet markings; the scissortailed flycatcher

muscle reading.d: The art of making discriminations between objects of choice, of discovering the whereabouts of hidden objects, etc., by inference from the involuntary movements of one whose hand the reader holds or with whom he is otherwise in muscular contact

muscule.d: A long movable shed used by besiegers in ancient times in attacking the walls of a fortified town

musculosity.d: The quality or state of being musculous; muscularity

museless.d: Unregardful of the Muses; disregarding the power of poetry; unpoetical

muset.d: A small hole or gap through which a wild animal passes; a muse

mushroom-headed.d: Having a cylindrical body with a convex head of larger diameter; having a head like that of a mushroom

muslinet.d: A sort of coarse or light cotton cloth

musquaw.d: The American black bear. See Bear

musrole.d: The nose band of a horse's bridle

mussulmanic.d: Of, pertaining to, or like, the Muslims (Mussulmans), or their customs: Islamic

mustaiba.d: A close-grained, heavy wood of a brownish color, brought from Brazil, and used in turning, for making the handles of tools, and the like

mutandum.d: A thing which is to be changed; something which must be altered; -- used chiefly in the plural

mutessarif.d: In Turkey prior to the revolution, an administrative authority of any of certain sanjaks.  They were appointed directly by the Sultan

mutessarifat.d: In Turkey, a sanjak whose head is a mutessarif

mutuary.d: One who borrows personal chattels which are to be consumed by him, and which he is to return or repay in kind

mutuation.d: The act of borrowing or exchanging

muzarab.d: One of a denomination of Christians formerly living under the government of the Moors in Spain, and having a liturgy and ritual of their own

muzarabic.d: Of or pertaining to Muzarabs; as, the Muzarabic liturgy

myadestes.d: A genus of birds including  the solitaires, thrushes noted for their beautiful songs

myall wood.d: A durable, fragrant, and dark-colored Australian wood, used by the natives for spears. It is obtained from the small tree Acacia homolophylla

myaria.d: A division of bivalve mollusks of which the common clam (Mya) is the type

mycomelic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a complex nitrogenous acid of the alloxan group, obtained as a honey-yellow powder.  Its solutions have a gelatinous consistency

mycothrix.d: The chain of micrococci formed by the division of the micrococci in multiplication

myelonal.d: Of or pertaining to the myelon; as, the myelonal, or spinal, nerves

mygale.d: A genus of very large hairy spiders of the family Ctenizidae, having four lungs and only four spinnerets.  They do not spin webs, but usually construct tubes in the earth, which are often furnished with a trapdoor.  The South American bird spider (Mygale avicularia), and the crab spider, or matoutou (Mygale cancerides) are among the largest species.  They are also called trapdoor spiders.  Some of the species are erroneously called tarantulas, as the Texas tarantula (Mygale Hentzii)

mykiss.d: A salmon (Salmo mykiss, syn. Salmo purpuratus) marked with black spots and a red throat, found in most of the rivers from Alaska to the Colorado River, and in Siberia; -- called also black-spotted trout, cutthroat trout, and redthroat trout

mynchery.d: A nunnery; -- a term still applied to the ruins of certain nunneries in England

myogalid.d: One of the Myogalodae, a family of Insectivora, including the desman, and allied species

myomancy.d: Divination by the movements of mice

myophan.d: A contractile striated layer found in the bodies and stems of certain Infusoria

myriacanthous.d: Having numerous spines, as certain fishes

myriarch.d: A captain or commander of ten thousand men

myriological.d: Of or relating to a myriologue

myriologist.d: One who composes or sings a myriologue

myriologue.d: An extemporaneous funeral song, composed and sung by a woman on the death of a friend

myriophyllous.d: Having an indefinitely great or countless number of leaves

myrmicine.d: Of or pertaining to Myrmica, a genus of ants including the small house ant (Myrmica molesta), and many others

myrmotherine.d: Feeding upon ants; -- said of certain birds

myronic.d: Pertaining to, or obtained from, mustard; -- used specifically to designate a glucoside called myronic acid, found in mustard seed

myropolist.d: One who sells unguents or perfumery

mystacal.d: Of or pertaining to the upper lip, or mustache

mysterize.d: To make mysterious; to make a mystery of

mytiloid.d: Like, or pertaining to, the genus Mytilus, or family Mytilidae

mytilotoxine.d: A poisonous base (leucomaine) found in the common mussel.  It either causes paralysis of the muscles, or gives rise to convulsions, including death by an accumulation of carbonic acid in the blood

myxinoid.d: Like, or pertaining to, the genus Myxine

myxocystodea.d: A division of Infusoria including the Noctiluca.  See Noctiluca

myxophyta.d: A phylum of the vegetable kingdom consisting of the class Myxomycetes.  By some botanists it is not separated from the Thallophyta

myzostomata.d: An order of curious parasitic worms found on crinoids. The body is short and disklike, with four pairs of suckers and five pairs of hook-bearing parapodia on the under side

nabk.d: The edible berries of the Zizyphys Lotus, a tree of Northern Africa, and Southwestern Europe

naid.d: Any one of numerous species of small, fresh-water, chaetopod annelids of the tribe Naidina.  They belong to the Oligochaeta

namation.d: A distraining or levying of a distress; an impounding

namedropper.d: Someone who pretends that famous people are his/her friends.  Someone who namedrops

nandine.d: An African carnivore (Nandinia binotata), allied to the civets.  It is spotted with black

nandou.d: Any one of three species of South American ostriches of the genera Rhea and Pterocnemia, especially the smallest, Pterocnemia pennata (formerly Rhea Americana), called also the common rhea.  They are tall fast-running flightless birds similar to ostriches but three-toed, found from Peru to the Straits of Magellan.  See Rhea

nap-taking.d: A taking by surprise; an unexpected onset or attack

nape-crest.d: An African bird of the genus Schizorhis, related to the plantain eaters

napha water.d: A perfume distilled from orange flowers

naphthalate.d: A salt of naphthalic acid; a phthalate

naphthide.d: A compound of naphthalene or its radical with a metallic element; as, mercuric naphthide

narine.d: Of or belonging to the nostrils

narrable.d: Capable of being narrated or told

narratory.d: Giving an account of events; narrative; as, narratory letters

nascal.d: A kind of pessary of medicated wool or cotton, formerly used

nasicornous.d: Bearing a horn, or horns, on the nose, as the rhinoceros

nasiform.d: Having the shape of a nose

nasolachrymal.d: Connected with the lachrymal apparatus and the nose; as, the nasolachrymal, or lachrymal duct

nasopalatal.d: Connected with both the nose and the palate; as, the nasopalatine or incisor, canal connecting the mouth and the nasal chamber in some animals; the nasopalatine nerve

nasutness.d: Quickness of scent; hence, nice discernment; acuteness

natalitial.d: Of or pertaining to one's birth or birthday, or one's nativity

natals.d: One's birth, or the circumstances attending it

natatorious.d: Adapted for swimming; -- said of the legs of certain insects

natchnee.d: An annual grass (Eleusine coracona), cultivated in India as a food plant

nathmore.d: Not the more; never the more

naticoid.d: Like or belonging to Natica, or the family Naticidae

nationalness.d: The quality or state of being national; nationality

native steel.d: A sort of steel which has been found where a burning coal seam had reduced and carbonized adjacent iron ore

natural family.d: a group of living organisms classed as a family in a toxonomic classification

natural product chemistry.d: That branch of chemistry which deals with the isolation, identification, structure elucidation, and study of the chemical characteristics of chemical substances produced by living organisms

natural steel.d: Steel made by the direct refining of cast iron in a finery, or, as wootz, by a direct process from the ore

natureless.d: Not in accordance with nature; unnatural

naturity.d: The quality or state of being produced by nature

naturize.d: To endow with a nature or qualities; to refer to nature

nauropometer.d: An instrument for measuring the amount which a ship heels at sea

nauscopy.d: The power or act of discovering ships or land at considerable distances

navigerous.d: Bearing ships; capable of floating vessels

nayaur.d: A specied of wild sheep (Ovis Hodgsonii), native of Nepal and Tibet.  It has a dorsal mane and a white ruff beneath the neck

nayword.d: A byword; a proverb; also, a watchword

neapolitan ice.d: An ice or ice cream containing eggs as well as cream

near-legged.d: Having the feet so near together that they interfere in traveling

neatress.d: A woman who takes care of cattle

nebalia.d: A genus of small marine Crustacea, considered the type of a distinct order (Nebaloidea, or Phyllocarida.)

nebulation.d: The condition of being nebulated; also, a clouded, or ill-defined, color mark

necessitattion.d: The act of making necessary, or the state of being made necessary; compulsion

neckmold.d: A small convex molding surrounding a column at the junction of the shaft and capital

necronite.d: Fetid feldspar, a mineral which, when struck, exhales a fetid odor

necroscopic.d: Or or relating to post-mortem examinations

nectostem.d: That portion of the axis which bears the nectocalyces in the Siphonophora

nefand.d: Unfit to speak of; unmentionable; impious; execrable

nefasch.d: Any fish of the genus Distichodus.  Several large species inhabit the Nile

neglection.d: The state of being negligent; negligence

negotiosity.d: The state of being busy; multitude of business

negotious.d: Very busy; attentive to business; active

negotiousness.d: The state of being busily occupied; activity

negrita.d: A blackish fish (Hypoplectrus nigricans), of the Sea-bass family.  It is a native of the West Indies and Florida

nehiloth.d: A term supposed to mean, perforated wind instruments of music, as pipes or flutes

neif.d: A woman born in the state of villeinage; a female serf

neishout.d: The mahogany-like wood of the South African tree Pteroxylon utile, the sawdust of which causes violent sneezing (whence the name).  Also called sneezewood

nematogene.d: One of the dimorphic forms of the species of Dicyemata, which produced vermiform embryos; -- opposed to rhombogene

nemophilist.d: One who is fond of forest or forest scenery; a haunter of the woods

nemophily.d: Fondness for forest scenery; love of the woods

neo-greek.d: A member of a body of French painters (F. les néo-Grecs) of the middle 19th century.  The term is rather one applied by outsiders to certain artists of grave and refined style, such as Hamon and Aubert, than a name adopted by the artists themselves

neo-hebraic.d: Of, pert. to, or designating, modern Hebrew, or Hebrew of later date than the Biblical

neo-hegelianism.d: The philosophy of a school of British and American idealists who follow Hegel in dialectical or logical method and in the general outcome of their doctrine.  The founders and leaders of Neo-Hegelianism include: in England, T. H. Green (1836-1882); in Scotland, J. Caird (1820-98) and E. Caird (1835-1908); in the United States, W. T. Harris (1835-1909) and Josiah Royce (1855- -)

neo-kantianism.d: The philosophy of modern thinkers who follow Kant in his general theory of knowledge, esp. of a group of German philosophers including F. A. Lange, H. Cohen, Paul Natorp, and others

neocarida.d: The modern, or true, Crustacea, as distinguished from the Merostomata

neoclassic architecture.d: All that architecture which, since the beginning of the Italian Renaissance, about 1420, has been designed with deliberate imitation of Greco-Roman buildings

neocracy.d: Government by new or inexperienced hands; upstart rule; raw or untried officials

neocriticism.d: The form of Neo-Kantianism developed by French idealists, following C. Renouvier.  It rejects the noumena of Kant, restricting knowledge to phenomena as constituted by a priori categories

neodamode.d: In ancient Sparta, one of those Helots who were freed by the state in reward for military service

neogaean.d: Of or pertaining to the New World, or Western Hemisphere

neography.d: A new method or system of writing

neologic.d: Of or pertaining to neology; employing new words; of the nature of, or containing, new words or new doctrines

neologization.d: The act or process of neologizing

neomenia.d: The time of the new moon; the beginning of the month in the lunar calendar

neomenoidea.d: A division of vermiform gastropod mollusks, without a shell, belonging to the Isopleura

neonomian.d: One who advocates adheres to new laws; esp. one who holds or believes that the gospel is a new law

neonomianism.d: The doctrines or belief of the neonomians

neorama.d: A panorama of the interior of a building, seen from within

neossine.d: The substance constituting the edible bird's nest

nephelodometer.d: An instrument for reckoning the distances or velocities of clouds

nepotal.d: Of or relating to a nephew

neptunicentric.d: As seen from Neptune, or having Neptune as a center; as, Neptunicentric longitude or force

nereidian.d: Any annelid resembling Nereis, or of the family Lycoridae or allied families

nero-antico.d: A beautiful black marble found in fragments among Roman ruins, and usually thought to have come from ancient Laconia

nerve-shaken.d: Affected by a tremor, or by a nervous disease; weakened; overcome by some violent influence or sensation; shocked

netify.d: To render neat; to clean; to put in order

neurapophysial.d: Of or pertaining to a neurapophysis

neurism.d: Nerve force. See Vital force, under Vital

neuro-central.d: Between the neural arch and the centrum of a vertebra; as, the neurocentral suture

neuro-epidermal.d: Pertaining to, or giving rise to, the central nervous system and epidermis; as, the neuroepidermal, or epiblastic, layer of the blastoderm

neurocord.d: A cordlike organ composed of elastic fibers situated above the ventral nervous cord of annelids, like the earthworm

neuropharmacologic.d: acting upon or influencing nervous functions; -- of chemical substances

neuropodous.d: Having the limbs on, or directed toward, the neural side, as in most invertebrates; -- opposed to haemapodous

neuropteral.d: Of or pertaining to the Neuroptera

neuropteris.d: An extensive genus of fossil ferns, of which species have been found from the Devonian to the Triassic formation

neurosensiferous.d: Pertaining to, or forming, both nerves and sense organs

neutrosophy.d: A branch of philosophy, introduced by Florentin Smarandache in 1980, which studies the origin, nature, and scope of neutralities, as well as their interactions with different ideational spectra.  Neutrosophy considers a proposition, theory, event, concept, or entity, “A” in relation to its opposite, “Anti-A” and that which is not A, “Non-A”, and that which is neither “A” nor “Anti-A”, denoted by “Neut-A”.  Neutrosophy is the basis of neutrosophic logic, neutrosophic probability, neutrosophic set

neuvaines.d: Prayers offered up for nine successive days

new thought.d: Any form of belief in mental healing, other than (1) Christian Science and (2) hypnotism or psychotherapy.  It was practised in the 19th century, and its central principle was affirmative thought, or suggestion, employed with the conviction that man produces changes in his health, his finances, and his life by the adoption of a favorable mental attitude.  As a therapeutic doctrine it stands for silent and absent mental treatment, and the theory that all diseases are mental in origin.  As a cult

newfanglist.d: One who is eager for novelties or desirous of change

newfangly.d: In a newfangled manner; with eagerness for novelty

news-writer.d: One who gathers news for, and writes, news-letters, articles in news periodicals, or items for broadcast on news programs

nez perces.d: A tribe of Indians, in the late 1800's mostly inhabiting Idaho.  They were involved under Chief Joseph, in the last major battle of the Indian wars, attempting to resist being moved to a reservation

niagara period.d: A subdivision or the American Upper Silurian system, embracing the Medina, Clinton, and Niagara epoch. The rocks of the Niagara epoch, mostly limestones, are extensively distributed, and at Niagara Falls consist of about eighty feet of shale supporting a greater thickness of limestone, which is gradually undermined by the removal of the shale. See Chart of Geology

nibelungs.d: In German mythology, the children of the mist, a race of dwarfs or demonic beings, the original possessors of the famous hoard and ring won by Siegfrid; also, the Burgundian kings in the Nibelungenlied

nicagua.d: The laughing falcon. See under laughing

nichts.d: A quantity of no importance; nothing

nicolaitan.d: One of certain corrupt persons in the early church at Ephesus, who are censured in Rev. ii. 6, 15

nicotidine.d: A complex, oily, nitrogenous base, isomeric with nicotine, and obtained by the reduction of certain derivatives of the pyridine group

nidgery.d: A trifle; a piece of foolery

nidulation.d: The time of remaining in the nest

nidulite.d: A Silurian fossil, formerly supposed to consist of eggs

niepce's process.d: A process, now no longer used, invented by J. N. Niepce, a French chemist, in 1829.  It depends upon the action of light in rendering a thin layer of bitumen, with which the plate is coated, insoluble

nighly.d: In a near relation in place, time, degree, etc.; within a little; almost

nighness.d: The quality or state of being nigh

night before christmas.d: The popular name for a poem by Clement Clarke Moore titled A Visit from St. Nicholas, a popular poem with the theme of St. Nicholas (Santa Claus) coming to bring gifts to children on Christmans eve

night-eyed.d: Capable of seeing at night; sharp-eyed

night-faring.d: Going or traveling in the night

nightrobe.d: A loose dress designed to be worn in bed by women; a nightgown

nigritic.d: Pertaining to, or having the characteristics of, negroes, or of the Negritos, Papuans, and the Melanesian races; negritic

nimbiferous.d: Serving to bring clouds or stormy weather

nine-bark.d: A white-flowered rosaceous shrub (Neillia opulifolia, or  Spiraea opulifolia), common in the Northern United States.  The bark separates into many thin layers, whence the name

ninescore.d: Nine times twenty, or one hundred and eighty

niopo.d: A kind of snuff prepared by the natives of Venezuela from the roasted seeds of a leguminous tree (Piptadenia peregrina), thence called niopo tree

nitranilic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a complex organic acid produced as a white crystalline substance by the action of nitrous acid on hydroquinone

nitrohydrochloric.d: Of, pertaining to, or containing, nitric and hydrochloric acids

nitromuriatic.d: Of, pertaining to, or composed of, nitric acid and muriatic acid; nitrohydrochloric. See Nitrohydrochloric

nitrophnol.d: Any one of a series of nitro derivatives of phenol.  They are yellow oily or crystalline substances and have well-defined acid properties, as picric acid

nitroprussic.d: Pertaining to, derived from, or designating, a complex acid called nitroprussic acid, obtained indirectly by the action of nitric acid on potassium ferrocyanide (yellow prussiate), as a red crystalline unstable substance.  It forms salts called nitroprussides, which give a rich purple color with alkaline sulphides

nitroquinol.d: A hypothetical nitro derivative of quinol or hydroquinone, not known in the free state, but forming a well defined series of derivatives

nitrosaccharin.d: An explosive nitro derivative of certain sugars, analogous to nitroglycerin, gun cotton, etc

nitrosalicylic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a nitro derivative of salicylic acid, called also anilic acid

nitrosylic.d: Of, pertaining to, or containing, nitrosyl; as, nitrosylic acid

nixie clerk.d: A post-office clerk in charge of the nixies

no-man's land.d: A space amidships used to keep blocks, ropes, etc.; a space on a ship belonging to no one in particular to care for

nobert's lines.d: Fine lines ruled on glass in a series of groups of different closeness of line, and used to test the power of a microscope

nobili's rings.d: Colored rings formed upon a metal plate by the electrolytic disposition of copper, lead peroxide, etc. They may be produced by touching with a pointed zinc rod a silver plate on which is a solution of copper sulphate

nobilitate.d: To make noble; to ennoble; to exalt

nobless.d: Dignity; greatness; noble birth or condition

nobley.d: The body of nobles; the nobility

noctidial.d: Comprising a night and a day; as, a noctidial day

noctilionid.d: A South American bat of the genus Noctilio, having cheek pouches and large incisor teeth

noctilucin.d: A fatlike substance in certain marine animals, to which they owe their phosphorescent properties

noctuary.d: A record of what passes in the night; a nightly journal; -- distinguished from diary

nodation.d: Act of making a knot, or state of being knotted

nodosarine.d: Resembling in form or structure a foraminiferous shell of the genus Nodosaria

noemics.d: The science of the understanding; intellectual science

noetian.d: One of the followers of Noetus, who lived in the third century.  He denied the distinct personality of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost

noggen.d: Made of hemp; hence, hard; rough; harsh

nogoodnik.d: A worthless, disreputable, or malicious person

nolition.d: Adverse action of will; unwillingness; -- opposed to volition

nolleity.d: The state of being unwilling; nolition

nomancy.d: The art or practice of divining the destiny of persons by the letters which form their names

nomopelmous.d: Having a separate and simple tendon to flex the first toe, or hallux, as do passerine birds

non compos.d: Not of sound mind; not having the regular use of reason; hence, also, as a noun, an idiot; a lunatic; one devoid of reason, either by nature or from accident

non-ego.d: The union of being and relation as distinguished from, and contrasted with, the ego. See Ego

non-episcopal.d: Not Episcopal; not pertaining to the Episcopal church or system

non-feasance.d: An omission or neglect to do something, esp. that which ought to have been done.  Cf. Malfeasance

non-pros.d: To decline or fail to prosecute; to allow to be dropped (said of a suit); to enter judgment against (a plaintiff who fails to prosecute); as, the plaintiff was non-prossed

nonacquiescence.d: Refusal of acquiescence; failure to yield or comply

nonaerobiotic.d: Capable of living without atmospheric oxygen; anaerobic

nonagrian.d: Any moth of the genus Nonagria and allied genera, as the spindleworm and stalk borer

nonalienation.d: Failure to alienate; also, the state of not being alienated

nonappointment.d: Neglect of making appointment; failure to receive an appointment

noncommital.d: Not expressing a preference; as, although favoring European unity he was noncommittal about the form it should take

noncondensible.d: Not condensible; incapable of being liquefied; -- said of gases

nonconduction.d: The quality of not being able to conduct or transmit; failure to conduct

nonconstat.d: It does not appear; it is not plain or clear; it does not follow

nondecane.d: A hydrocarbon of the paraffin series, a white waxy substance, C19H40; -- so called from the number of carbon atoms in the molecule

nondeciduate.d: Characterized by the absence of a decidua; indeciduate

nondecisive.d: not crucial; not comprising a decisive factor in a result.  Opposite of crucial and decisive

nondo.d: A coarse umbelliferous plant (Ligusticum actaeifolium) with a large aromatic root.  It is found chiefly in the Alleghany region.  Also called Angelico

nonelect.d: A person or persons not elected, or chosen, to salvation

nonimporting.d: Not importing; not bringing from foreign countries

noninflectional.d: Not admitting of, or characterized by, inflection

noninhabitant.d: One who is not an inhabitant; a stranger; a foreigner; a nonresident

nonjurorism.d: The doctrines, or action, of the Nonjurors

nonlimitation.d: Want of limitation; failure to limit

nonnecessity.d: Absence of necessity; the quality or state of being unnecessary

nonoic.d: Pertaining to, derived from, or resembling, nonane; as, nonoic acid, which is also called pelargonic acid.  Cf. Pelargonic

nonone.d: Any one of several metameric unsaturated hydrocarbons (C9H14) of the valylene series

nonoxygenous.d: Without oxygen; characterized by the absence of oxygen; as, a nonoxygenous alkaloid

nonphotobiotic.d: Capable of living without light; as, nonphotobiotic plant cells, or cells which habitually live in darkness

nonplane.d: Not lying in one plane; not planar; -- said of certain curves

nonpreparation.d: Neglect or failure to prepare; want of preparation

nonpresentation.d: Neglect or failure to present; state of not being presented

nonproduction.d: A failure to produce or exhibit

nonregardance.d: Want of due regard; disregard; slight

nonrendition.d: Neglect of rendition; the not rendering what is due

nonsane.d: Unsound; not perfect; as, a person of nonsane memory

nonslaveholding.d: Not possessing or holding slaves; as, a nonslaveholding State

nonsubmission.d: Want of submission; failure or refusal to submit

nonterm.d: A vacation between two terms of a court

nonthematic.d: having no theme.  Opposite of thematic

nonuniformist.d: One who believes that past changes in the structure of the earth have proceeded from cataclysms or causes more violent than are now operating; -- called also nonuniformitarian

nonusance.d: Neglect of using; failure to use

nonvocalic.d: not vocalic; not having vowel character; -- used of liquids and nasals.  Opposite of vocalic

nonylenic.d: Of, pertaining to, related to, or designating, nonylene or its compounds; as, nonylenic acid

nonylic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, nonyl or its compounds; as, nonylic acid

nook-shotten.d: Full of nooks, angles, or corners

noon-flower.d: The goat's beard, whose flowers close at midday

norfolk dumpling.d: A kind of boiled dumpling made in Norfolk

norfolk spaniel.d: One of a breed of field spaniels similar to the clumbers, but shorter in body and of a liver-and-white or black-and-white color

norimon.d: A Japanese covered litter, carried by men

noropianic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid of the aromatic series obtained from opianic acid

north-american.d: of or pertaining to or characteristic of the continent or countries of North America and their peoples

northness.d: A tendency in the end of a magnetic needle to point to the north

norwegium.d: A rare metallic element, of doubtful identification, said to occur in the copper-nickel of Norway.  Not recognized as an element (1999)

nose around.d: to look around or search, especially where one has no authority to do so; to pry; to be nosy.  Same as nose{2}, v. i

nosel.d: To nurse; to lead or teach; to foster; to nuzzle

nosesmart.d: A kind of cress, a pungent cruciferous plant, including several species of the genus Nasturtium

notaeum.d: The back or upper surface, as of a bird

notchweed.d: A foul-smelling weed, the stinking goosefoot (Chenopodium Vulvaria)

note paper.d: Writing paper, not exceeding in size, when folded once, five by eight inches

notidanian.d: Any one of several species of sharks of the family Notidanidae, or Hexanchidae. Called also cow sharks. See Shark

notobranchiata.d: A division of nudibranchiate mollusks having gills upon the back

notobranchiate.d: Of or pertaining to the Notobranchiata

notodontian.d: Any one of several species of bombycid moths belonging to Notodonta, Nerice, and allied genera. The caterpillar of these moths has a hump, or spine, on its back

notorhizal.d: Having the radicle of the embryo lying against the back of one of the cotyledons; incumbent

nototherium.d: An extinct genus of gigantic herbivorous marsupials, found in the Pliocene formation of Australia

nototrema.d: The pouched, or marsupial, frog of South America

noule.d: The top of the head; the head or noll

nounize.d: To change (an adjective, verb, etc.) into a noun; to nominalize

noursle.d: To nurse; to rear; to bring up

novatianism.d: The doctrines or principles of the Novatians

novene.d: Relating to, or dependent on, the number nine; novenary

novilunar.d: Of or pertaining to the new moon

nubigenous.d: Born of, or produced from, clouds

nucament.d: A catkin or ament; the flower cluster of the hazel, pine, willow, and the like

nuclear device.d: an explosive device, whether used as a weapon or for other purposes, which depends for most of its explosive power on the release of energy from within atomic nuclei.  A fission device or a fusion device

nuclear war.d: A war in which nuclear weapons are used by both sides.  As generally used, the term assumes major use of nuclear weapons by at least two opposing warring states.  As of 1999, no nuclear war has occurred

nucleoidioplasma.d: Hyaline plasma contained in the nucleus of vegetable cells

nuddle.d: To walk quickly with the head bent forward; -- often with along

nudibranchiata.d: A division of opisthobranchiate mollusks, having no shell except while very young.  The gills are naked and situated upon the back or sides. See Ceratobranchia

nugation.d: The act or practice of trifling

nugify.d: To render trifling or futile; to make silly

nullibiety.d: The state or condition of being nowhere

numerally.d: According to number; in number; numerically

numismatography.d: A treatise on, or description of, coins and medals

nunchion.d: A portion of food taken at or after noon, usually between full meals; a luncheon

nunciate.d: One who announces; a messenger; a nuncio

nundinate.d: To buy and sell at fairs or markets

nundination.d: Traffic at fairs; marketing; buying and selling

nunnish.d: Of, pertaining to, or resembling a nun; characteristic of a nun

nurl.d: To cut with reeding or fluting on the edge of, as coins, the heads of screws, etc.; to knurl

nursepond.d: A pond where fish are fed

nutrication.d: The act or manner of feeding

nutritial.d: Pertaining to, or connected with, nutrition; nutritious

nyctaginia.d: A genus consisting of only one species

nyctibune.d: A South American bird of the genus Nyctibius, allied to the goatsuckers

nyctophile.d: Any Australian bat of the genus Nyctophilus, having a very simple nasal appendage

pieceless.d: Not made of pieces; whole; entire

piecener.d: One who supplies rolls of wool to the slubbing machine in woolen mills

piepoudre.d: An ancient court of record in England, formerly incident to every fair and market, of which the steward of him who owned or had the toll was the judge

piercel.d: A kind of gimlet for making vents in casks; -- called also piercer

pierre-perdu.d: Blocks of stone or concrete heaped loosely in the water to make a foundation (as for a sea wall), a breakwater, a mole, etc

pietra dura.d: Hard and fine stones in general, such as are used for inlay and the like, as distinguished from the softer stones used in building; thus, a Florentine mosaic is a familiar instance of work in pietra dura, though the ground may be soft marble

piffero.d: A fife; also, a rude kind of oboe or a bagpipe with an inflated skin for reservoir

pig-jawed.d: Having the upper jaw projecting beyond the lower, with the upper incisors in advance of the lower; -- said of dogs

pig-sticking.d: Boar hunting; -- so called by Anglo-Indians

pignoration.d: The act of pledging or pawning

pigwidgeon.d: A cant word for anything petty or small. It is used by Drayton as the name of a fairy

pile-worn.d: Having the pile worn off; threadbare

pileiform.d: Having the form of a pileus or cap; pileate

pilentum.d: An easy chariot or carriage, used by Roman ladies, and in which the vessels, etc., for sacred rites were carried

pillorize.d: To set in, or punish with, the pillory; to pillory

pilot wheel.d: A wheel, usually with radial handles projecting from the rim, for traversing the saddle of a machine tool, esp. an automatic machine tool, by hand

pilotism.d: Pilotage; skill in the duties of a pilot

pilpul.d: Among the Jews, penetrating investigation, disputation, and drawing of conclusions, esp. in Talmudic study

pilser.d: An insect that flies into a flame

pimaric.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid found in galipot, and isomeric with abietic acid

pimpillo.d: A West Indian name for the prickly pear (Opuntia); -- called also pimploes

pimpinel.d: The burnet saxifrage. See under Saxifrage

pimpship.d: The office, occupation, or persom of a pimp

pin-eyed.d: Having the stigma visible at the throad of a gamopetalous corolla, while the stamens are concealed in the tube; -- said of dimorphous flowers. The opposite of thrum-eyed

pin-fire.d: Having a firing pin to explode the cartridge; as, a pin-fire rifle

pin-tailed.d: Having a tapered tail, with the middle feathers longest; -- said of birds

pinacate bug.d: Any of several clumsy, wingless beetles of the genus Eleodes, found in the Pacific States

pincoffin.d: A commercial preparation of garancin, yielding fine violet tints

pindal.d: The peanut (Arachis hypogæa); -- so called in the West Indies

pine-clad.d: Clad or crowned with pine trees; as, pine-clad hills

pine-tree state.d: Maine; -- a nickname alluding to the pine tree in its coat of arms

pinefinch.d: A small American bird (Spinus spinus syn. Chrysomitris spinus); -- called also pine siskin, and American siskin

pinguefaction.d: A making of, or turning into, fat

pink-sterned.d: Having a very narrow stern; -- said of a vessel

pinnothere.d: A crab of the genus pinnotheres. See Oyster crab, under Oyster

pinnywinkles.d: An instrument of torture, consisting of a board with holes into which the fingers were pressed, and fastened with pegs

pioneers' day.d: In Utah, a legal holiday, July 24, commemorated the arrival, in 1847, of Brigham Young and his followers at the present site of Salt Lake City

pipemouth.d: Any fish of the genus Fistularia; -- called also tobacco pipefish. See Fistularia

pipevine.d: Any climbing species of Aristolochia; esp., the Dutchman's pipe (Aristolochia sipho). See under Dutchman

pipewood.d: An ericaceous shrub (Leucothoë acuminata) of the southern United States, from the wood of which pipe bowls are made

piprine.d: Of or pertaining to the pipras, or the family Pipridæ

pirameter.d: A dynamometer for ascertaining the power required to draw carriages over roads

piririgua.d: A South American bird (Guira guira) allied to the cuckoos

piscicapture.d: Capture of fishes, as by angling

piscinal.d: Belonging to a fishpond or a piscina

pissabed.d: A name locally applied to various wild plants, as dandelion, bluet, oxeye daisy, etc

pistachio green.d: A light yellowish green color resembling that of the pistachio nut

pistillaceous.d: Growing on, or having nature of, the pistil; of or pertaining to a pistil

pistillation.d: The act of pounding or breaking in a mortar; pestillation

pitch-faced.d: Having the arris defined by a line beyond which the rock is cut away, so as to give nearly true edges; -- said of squared stones that are otherwise quarry-faced

pitheci.d: A division of mammals including the apes and monkeys.  Sometimes used in the sense of Primates

pittacal.d: A dark blue substance obtained from wood tar. It consists of hydrocarbons which when oxidized form the orange-yellow eupittonic compounds, the salts of which are dark blue

pittle-pattle.d: To talk unmeaningly; to chatter or prattle

piédouche.d: A pedestal of small size, used to support small objects, as busts, vases, and the like

piña cloth.d: A fine fabric for scarfs, handkerchiefs, embroidery, etc., woven from the fiber obtained from the leaf of the sterile pineapple plant. It is delicate, soft, and transparent, with a tinge of pale yellow

piñon.d: The edible seed of several species of pine; also, the tree producing such seeds, as Pinus Pinea of Southern Europe, and Pinus Parryana, cembroides, edulis, and monophylla, the nut pines of Western North America

placit.d: A decree or determination; a dictum

placitory.d: Of or pertaining to pleas or pleading, in courts of law

placitum.d: A public court or assembly in the Middle Ages, over which the sovereign president when a consultation was held upon affairs of state

placodermal.d: Of or pertaining to the placoderms; like the placoderms

placoganoidei.d: A division of ganoid fishes including those that have large external bony plates and a cartilaginous skeleton

placoides.d: A group of fishes including the sharks and rays; the Elasmobranchii; -- called also Placoidei

placophora.d: A division of gastropod Mollusca, including the chitons.  The back is covered by eight shelly plates.  Called also Polyplacophora. See Illust. under Chiton, and Isopleura

plagihedral.d: Having an oblique spiral arrangement of planes, as levogyrate and dextrogyrate crystals

plagiostomi.d: An order of fishes including the sharks and rays; -- called also Plagiostomata

plagiostomous.d: Of or pertaining to the Plagiostomi

plagueful.d: Abounding, or infecting, with plagues; pestilential; as, plagueful exhalations

plagueless.d: Free from plagues or the plague

plain-dealing.d: Practicing plain dealing; artless. See Plain dealing, under Dealing

plainant.d: One who makes complaint; the plaintiff

plains wanderer.d: A bird of the genus Pedionomus (Pedionomus torquatus) of New South Wales, the only species in the genus.  Pedionomus is the only genus of the family Pedionomidae of the order Passeriformes and the plains wanderer is thus the only species in the family.  The total world population (ca. 2000) is estimated to be 5 to 10 thousand

planarida.d: A division of Turbellaria; the Dendrocœla

planary.d: Of or pertaining to a plane

plancher.d: A floor of wood; also, a plank

plane-parallel.d: Having opposite surfaces exactly plane and parallel, as a piece of glass

plani-.d: Combining forms signifying flat, level, plane; as planifolious, planimetry, plano-concave

plank-sheer.d: The course of plank laid horizontally over the timberheads of a vessel's frame

plano-conical.d: Plane or flat on one side, and conical on the other

plano-horizontal.d: Having a level horizontal surface or position

plano-orbicular.d: Plane or flat on one side, and spherical on the other

plant-cane.d: A stalk or shoot of sugar cane of the first growth from the cutting. The growth of the second and following years is of inferior quality, and is called rattoon

plantership.d: The occupation or position of a planter, or the management of a plantation, as in the United States or the West Indies

plantigrada.d: A subdivision of Carnivora having plantigrade feet. It includes the bears, raccoons, and allied species

plashet.d: A small pond or pool; a puddle

plashoot.d: A hedge or fence formed of branches of trees interlaced, or plashed

plasmation.d: The act of forming or molding

plastography.d: The art of forming figures in any plastic material

plate-gilled.d: Having flat, or leaflike, gills, as the bivalve mollusks

platetrope.d: One of a pair of a paired organs

platinichloric.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid consisting of platinic chloride and hydrochloric acid, and obtained as a brownish red crystalline substance, called platinichloric, or chloroplatinic, acid

platinochloric.d: Pertaining to, derived from, or designating, an acid consisting of platinous chloride and hydrochloric acid, called platinochloric acid, or chloroplatinous, acid

platycoelian.d: Flat at the anterior and concave at the posterior end; -- said of the centra of the vertebræ of some extinct dinouaurs

platymeter.d: An apparatus for measuring the capacity of condensers, or the inductive capacity of dielectrics

platypod.d: An animal having broad feet, or a broad foot

platyptera.d: A division of Pseudoneuroptera including the species which have four broad, flat wings, as the termites, or white-ants, and the stone flies (Perla)

platyrhini.d: A division of monkeys, including the American species, which have a broad nasal septum, thirty-six teeth, and usually a prehensile tail. See Monkey

pleaseman.d: An officious person who courts favor servilely; a pickthank

pleasurist.d: A person devoted to worldly pleasure

plebicolist.d: One who flatters, or courts the favor of, the common people; a demagogue

plectognathi.d: An order of fishes generally having the maxillary bone united with the premaxillary, and the articular united with the dentary

plectospondyli.d: An extensive suborder of fresh-water physostomous fishes having the anterior vertebræ united and much modified; the Eventognathi

plectospondylous.d: Of or pertaining to the Plectospondyli

plenal.d: Full; complete; as, a plenal view or act

plenariness.d: Quality or state of being plenary

plenarty.d: The state of a benefice when occupied

plenicorn.d: A ruminant having solid horns or antlers, as the deer

plenist.d: One who holds that all space is full of matter

plesimorphism.d: The property possessed by some substances of crystallizing in closely similar forms while unlike in chemical composition

plethron.d: A long measure of 100 Greek, or 101 English, feet; also, a square measure of 10,000 Greek feet

pleurenchyma.d: A tissue consisting of long and slender tubular cells, of which wood is mainly composed

pleurocarpic.d: Side-fruited; -- said of those true mosses in which the pedicels or the capsules are from lateral archegonia; -- opposed to acrocarpous

pleuroderes.d: A group of fresh-water turtles in which the neck can not be retracted, but is bent to one side, for protection. The matamata is an example

pleuronectoid.d: Pertaining to the Pleuronectidæ, or Flounder family

pleuroptera.d: A group of Isectivora, including the colugo

pleurosigma.d: A genus of diatoms of elongated elliptical shape, but having the sides slightly curved in the form of a letter S.  Pleurosigma angulatum has very fine striations, and is a favorite object for testing the high powers of microscopes

pleurotoma.d: Any marine gastropod belonging to Pleurotoma, and ether allied genera of the family Pleurotmidæ. The species are very numerous, especially in tropical seas. The outer lip has usually a posterior notch or slit

pleyt.d: An old term for a river boat

plicidentine.d: A form of dentine which shows sinuous lines of structure in a transverse section of the tooth

pliform.d: In the form of a ply, fold, or doubling

plimsoll's mark.d: A mark conspicuously painted on the port side of all British sea-going merchant vessels, to indicate the limit of submergence allowed by law; -- so called from Samuel Plimsoll, by whose efforts the act of Parliament to prevent overloading was procured

pliosaurus.d: An extinct genus of marine reptiles allied to Plesiosaurus, but having a much shorter neck

plonge.d: To cleanse, as open drains which are entered by the tide, by stirring up the sediment when the tide ebbs

plongee.d: A slope or sloping toward the front; as, the plongée of a parapet; the plongée of a shell in its course

plotinian.d: Of pertaining to the Plotinists or their doctrines

plouter.d: To wade or move about with splashing; to dabble; also, to potter; trifle; idle

plowbote.d: Wood or timber allowed to a tenant for the repair of instruments of husbandry. See Bote

plowfoot.d: An adjustable staff formerly attached to the plow beam to determine the depth of the furrow

plowgate.d: The Scotch equivalent of the English word plowland

plowpoint.d: A detachable share at the extreme front end of the plow body

pluecker tube.d: A vacuum tube, used in spectrum analysis, in which the part through which the discharge takes place is a capillary tube, thus producing intense incandescence of the contained gases

plumassary.d: A plume or collection of ornamental feathers

plumbagineous.d: Pertaining to natural order (Plumbagineæ) of gamopetalous herbs, of which Plumbago is the type. The order includes also the marsh rosemary, the thrift, and a few other genera

plumularia.d: Any hydroid belonging to Plumularia and other genera of the family Plumularidæ. They generally grow in plumelike forms

pluries.d: A writ issued in the third place, after two former writs have been disregarded

plurifarious.d: Of many kinds or fashions; multifarious

pluriparous.d: Producing several young at a birth; as, a pluriparous animal

pneumatogarm.d: A tracing of the respiratory movements, obtained by a pneumatograph or stethograph

pneumometry.d: Measurement of the capacity of the lungs for air

pneumonophora.d: The division of Siphonophora which includes the Physalia and allied genera; -- called also Pneumatophoræ

pneumophora.d: A division of holothurians having an internal gill, or respiratory tree

pneumoskeleton.d: A chitinous structure which supports the gill in some invertebrates

pnyx.d: The place at Athens where the meetings of the people were held for making decrees, etc

poachard.d: A common European duck (Aythya ferina); -- called also goldhead, poker, and fresh-water widgeon, or red-headed widgeon

poak.d: Waste matter from the preparation of skins, consisting of hair, lime, oil, etc

pocan.d: The poke (Phytolacca decandra); -- called also pocan bush

pock-broken.d: Broken out, or marked, with smallpox; pock-fretten

pock-pudding.d: A bag pudding; a name of reproach or ridicule formerly applied by the Scotch to the English

pocoson.d: Low, wooded grounds or swamps in Eastern Maryland and Virginia

podical.d: Anal; -- applied to certain organs of insects

podocephalous.d: Having a head of flowers on a long peduncle, or footstalk

podophthalmic.d: Having the eyes on movable footstalks, or pedicels

podoscaph.d: A canoe-shaped float attached to the foot, for walking on water

podostomata.d: An order of Bryozoa of which Rhabdopleura is the type. See Rhabdopleura

podrida.d: A miscellaneous dish of meats. See Olla-podrida

podurid.d: Any species of Podura or allied genera

poecilopod.d: One of the Pœcilopoda. Also used adjectively

poecilopoda.d: Originally, an artificial group including many parasitic Entomostraca, together with the horseshoe crabs (Limuloidea)

poenamu.d: A variety of jade or nephrite, -- used in New Zealand for the manufacture of axes and weapons

poephaga.d: A group of herbivorous marsupials including the kangaroos and their allies

poets' corner.d: An angle in the south transept of Westminster Abbey, London; -- so called because it contains the tombs of Chaucer, Spenser, Dryden, Ben Jonson, Gray, Tennyson, Browning, and other English poets, and memorials to many buried elsewhere

poetship.d: The state or personality of a poet

poicile.d: The frescoed porch or gallery in Athens where Zeno taught

point alphabet.d: An alphabet for the blind with a system of raised points corresponding to letters

point applique.d: Lace having a needle-made design applied to a net ground, this ground often being machine-made

point switch.d: A switch made up of a rail from each track, both rails being tapered far back and connected to throw alongside the through rail of either track

pointingstock.d: An object of ridicule or scorn; a laughingstock

pointleted.d: Having a small, distinct point; apiculate

pokebag.d: The European long-tailed titmouse; -- called also poke-pudding

poking-stick.d: A small stick or rod of steel, formerly used in adjusting the plaits of ruffs

polarily.d: In a polary manner; with polarity

polaristic.d: Pertaining to, or exhibiting, poles; having a polar arrangement or disposition; arising from, or dependent upon, the possession of poles or polar characteristics; as, polaristic antagonism

polary.d: Tending to a pole; having a direction toward a pole

poldway.d: A kind of coarse bagging, -- used for coal sacks

poledavy.d: A sort of coarse canvas; poldway

polewig.d: The European spotted goby (Gobius minutus); -- called also pollybait

politicalism.d: Zeal or party spirit in politics

politize.d: To play the politician; to dispute as politicians do

pollage.d: A head or poll tax; hence, extortion

polliwig.d: A tadpole; -- called also purwiggy and porwigle

polt-foot.d: Having a distorted foot, or a clubfoot or clubfeet

polverine.d: Glassmaker's ashes; a kind of potash or pearlash, brought from the Levant and Syria, -- used in the manufacture of fine glass

polyacoustics.d: The art of multiplying or magnifying sounds

polyacron.d: A solid having many summits or angular points; a polyhedron

polyactinia.d: An old name for those Anthozoa which, like the actinias, have numerous simple tentacles

polyadelphia.d: A Linnæan class of plants having stamens united in three or more bodies or bundles by the filaments

polyadelphian.d: Belonging to the class Polyadelphia; having stamens united in three or more bundles

polyarchist.d: One who advocates polyarchy; -- opposed to monarchist

polybranchia.d: A division of Nudibranchiata including those which have numerous branchiæ on the back

polychoerany.d: A government by many chiefs, princes, or rules

polychronious.d: Enduring through a long time; chronic

polycosmic.d: Representing multiple possible worlds; -- used of a computational ontology that includes logically inconsistent assertions (theories), structured as different possible worlds; as, the only way to accommodate different theories of physics in one ontology is for that ontology to be polycosmic

polycotyledonary.d: Having the villi of the placenta collected into definite patches, or cotyledons

polycystidea.d: A division of Gregarinæ including those that have two or more internal divisions of the body

polycystina.d: A division of Radiolaria including numerous minute marine species. The skeleton is composed of silica, and is often very elegant in form and sculpture. Many have been found in the fossil state

polycyttaria.d: A division of Radiolaria. It includes those having one more central capsules

polyeidism.d: The quality or state of being polyeidic

polygalic.d: Of, pertaining to, or obtained from, Polygala; specifically, designating an acrid glucoside (called polygalic acid, senegin, etc.), resembling, or possibly identical with, saponin

polygoneutic.d: Having two or more broods in a season

polygony.d: Any plant of the genus Polygonum

polygordius.d: A genus of marine annelids, believed to be an ancient or ancestral type. It is remarkable for its simplicity of structure and want of parapodia. It is the type of the order Archiannelida, or Gymnotoma. See Loeven's larva

polygrooved.d: Having many grooves; as, a polygrooved rifle or gun (referring to the rifling)

polygyn.d: A plant of the order Polygynia

polygynia.d: A Linnæan order of plants having many styles

polygynian.d: Having many styles; belonging to the order Polygynia

polymastism.d: The condition of having more than two mammæ, or breasts

polymathist.d: One versed in many sciences; a person of various learning

polymeniscous.d: Having numerous facets; -- said of the compound eyes of insects and crustaceans

polymorphosis.d: The assumption of several structural forms without a corresponding difference in function; -- said of sponges, etc

polymyoid.d: Having numerous vocal muscles; of or pertaining to the Polymyodæ

polyonomous.d: Having many names or titles; polyonymous

polyonomy.d: The use of a variety of names for the same object

polyonym.d: An object which has a variety of names

polyoptron.d: A glass through which objects appear multiplied, but diminished in size

polyorama.d: A view of many objects; also, a sort of panorama with dissolving views

polyparous.d: Producing or bearing a great number; bringing forth many

polypean.d: Of or pertaining to a polyp, or polyps

polyperythrin.d: A coloring matter found in many simple Anthozoa and some hydroids

polyphaser.d: A machine generating more than one pressure wave; a multiphaser

polyphotal.d: Pertaining to or designating arc lamps so constructed that more than one can be used on a single circuit
