polypode.d: A plant of the genus Polypodium; polypody

polyprotodonta.d: A division of marsupials in which there are more fore incisor teeth in each jaw

polypteroidei.d: A suborder of existing ganoid fishes having numerous fins along the back. The bichir, or Polypterus, is the type. See Illust. under Crossopterygian

polypterus.d: An African genus of ganoid fishes including the bichir

polyschematist.d: Having, or existing in, many different forms or fashions; multiform

polysilicic.d: Of or pertaining to compounds formed by the condensation of two or more molecules of silicic acid

polystomata.d: A division of trematode worms having more two suckers. Called also Polystomea and Polystoma

polysyndetic.d: Characterized by polysyndeton, or the multiplication of conjunctions

polytheize.d: To adhere to, advocate, or inculcate, the doctrine of polytheism

polytungstic.d: Containing several tungsten atoms or radicals; as, polytungstic acid

polyzoary.d: The compound organism of a polyzoan

polyzoon.d: One of the individual zooids forming the compound organism of a polyzoan

pomacentroid.d: Pertaining to the Pomacentridæ, a family of bright-colored tropical fishes having spiny opercula; -- often called coral fishes

pomewater.d: A kind of sweet, juicy apple

pommelion.d: The cascabel, or hindmost knob, of a cannon

pommette.d: Having two balls or protuberances at each end; -- said of a cross

pompeian red.d: A brownish red approaching maroon, supposed to be imitated from the color of the wall panels of houses in Pompeii, which were decorated during the last age of the Republic

pompet.d: The ball formerly used to ink the type

pompillion.d: An ointment or pomatum made of black poplar buds

pompom girl.d: a female cheerleader, especially one who waves a pompon{5} while performing a cheering routine

ponderary.d: Of or pertaining to weight; as, a ponderary system

ponghee.d: A Buddhist priest of the higher orders in Burmah

ponibility.d: The capability of being placed or located

pontee.d: An iron rod used by glass makers for manipulating the hot glass; -- called also, puntil, puntel, punty, and ponty. See Fascet

pontificality.d: The state and government of the pope; the papacy

pontifice.d: Bridgework; structure or edifice of a bridge

pontifician.d: Of or pertaining to the pontiff or pope

pontvolant.d: A kind of light bridge, used in sieges, for surprising a post or outwork which has but a narrow moat; a flying bridge

poonac.d: A kind of oil cake prepared from the cocoanut. See Oil cake, under Cake

poonah painting.d: A style of painting, popular in England in the 19th century, in which a thick opaque color is applied without background and with scarcely any shading, to thin paper, producing flowers, birds, etc., in imitation of Oriental work

poonga oil.d: A kind of oil used in India for lamps, and for boiling with dammar for pitching vessels. It is pressed from the seeds of a leguminous tree (Pongamia glabra)

poopoo.d: Excrement; feces; -- informal baby talk sometimes used as a euphemism

poor-john.d: A small European fish, similar to the cod, but of inferior quality

poor-will.d: A bird of the Western United States (Phalænoptilus Nutalli) allied to the whip-poor-will

poorbox.d: A receptacle in which money given for the poor is placed

poorliness.d: The quality or state of being poorly; ill health

pope's head.d: A long-handled brush for dusting ceilings, etc., also for washing windows

popelote.d: A word variously explained as “a little puppet,” “a little doll,” or “a young butterfly.”  Cf. Popet

poppit.d: a small plastic bead  with opposed holes and protuberant knobs, so shaped that the beads may be fastened to each other in chains and detached easily, and can be used to form variable-length chains for use as necklaces, bracelets, or other ornamental objects.  Also called poppet and poppit bead

porime.d: A theorem or proposition so easy of demonstration as to be almost self-evident

porite.d: Any coral of the genus Porites, or family Poritidæ

porkwood.d: The coarse-grained brownish yellow wood of a small tree (Pisonia obtusata) of Florida and the West Indies. Also called pigeon wood, beefwood, and corkwood

porotype.d: A copy of a print, writing, etc., made by placing it upon a chemically prepared paper which is acted upon by a gas which permeates the paper of the print, writing, etc

porphyrogenitism.d: The principle of succession in royal families, especially among the Eastern Roman emperors, by which a younger son, if born after the accession of his father to the throne, was preferred to an elder son who was not so born

porpita.d: A genus of bright-colored Siphonophora found floating in the warmer parts of the ocean. The individuals are round and disk-shaped, with a large zooid in the center of the under side, surrounded by smaller nutritive and reproductive zooids, and by slender dactylozooids near the margin. The disk contains a central float, or pneumatocyst

port-royalist.d: One of the dwellers in the Cistercian convent of Port Royal des Champs, near Paris, when it was the home of the Jansenists in the 17th century, among them being Arnauld, Pascal, and other famous scholars.  Cf. Jansenist

portage group.d: A subdivision of the Chemung period in American geology. See Chart of Geology

portague.d: A Portuguese gold coin formerly current, and variously estimated to be worth from three and one half to four and one half pounds sterling

portate.d: Borne not erect, but diagonally athwart an escutcheon; as, a cross portate

portemonnaie.d: A small pocketbook or wallet for carrying money

portgreve.d: In old English law, the chief magistrate of a port or maritime town.; a portreeve

porthook.d: One of the iron hooks to which the port hinges are attached

portingal.d: Of or pertaining to Portugal; Portuguese

portland stone.d: A yellowish-white calcareous freestone from the Isle of Portland in England, much used in building

portland vase.d: A celebrated cinerary urn or vase found in the tomb of the Emperor Alexander Severus. It is owned by the Duke of Portland, and kept in the British Museum

portoir.d: One who, or that which, bears; hence, one who, or that which, produces

portpane.d: A cloth for carrying bread, so as not to touch it with the hands

pospolite.d: A kind of militia in Poland, consisting of the gentry, which, in case of invasion, was summoned to the defense of the country

possessival.d: Of or pertaining to the possessive case; as, a possessival termination

post note.d: A note issued by a bank, payable at some future specified time, as distinguished from a note payable on demand

post-abdomen.d: That part of a crustacean behind the cephalothorax; -- more commonly called abdomen

post-captain.d: A captain of a war vessel whose name appeared, or was “posted,” in the seniority list of the British navy, as distinguished from a commander whose name was not so posted. The term was also used in the United States navy; but no such commission as post-captain was ever recognized in either service, and the term has fallen into disuse

post-disseizin.d: A subsequent disseizin committed by one of lands which the disseizee had before recovered of the same disseizor; a writ founded on such subsequent disseizin, now abolished

post-disseizor.d: A person who disseizes another of lands which the disseizee had before recovered of the same disseizor

post-fine.d: A duty paid to the king by the cognizee in a fine of lands, when the same was fully passed; -- called also the king's silver

post-it note.d: A small sheet of paper having the back part partly covered with a non-permanent gum which allows the note to be attached temporarily to another object, and easily removed without leaving any trace of glue on the object to which it was affixed.  Such note papers are sold in pads of varying sizes

post-temporal.d: Situated back of the temporal bone or the temporal region of the skull; -- applied especially to a bone which usually connects the supraclavicle with the skull in the pectoral arch of fishes

post-tragus.d: A ridge within and behind the tragus in the ear of some animals

post-tympanic.d: Situated behind the tympanum, or in the skull, behind the auditory meatus

postable.d: Capable of being carried by, or as by, post

postero.d: - (&unr_;). A combining form meaning posterior, back; as, postero-inferior, situated back and below; postero-lateral, situated back and at the side

postexist.d: To exist after; to live subsequently

postfact.d: Relating to a fact that occurs after another

postgeniture.d: The condition of being born after another in the same family; -- distinguished from primogeniture

postillate.d: To explain by marginal notes; to postil

postillation.d: The act of postillating; exposition of Scripture in preaching

postillator.d: One who postillates; one who expounds the Scriptures verse by verse

postliminiary.d: Pertaining to, or involving, the right of postliminium

postmaster-general.d: The chief officer of the post-office department of a government. In the United States the postmaster-general is a member of the cabinet

postpliocene.d: Of or pertaining to the period immediately following the Pliocene; Pleistocene. Also used as a noun. See Quaternary

postponence.d: The act of postponing, in sense 2

postremote.d: More remote in subsequent time or order

postscapula.d: The part of the scapula behind or below the spine, or mesoscapula

posttertiary.d: Following, or more recent than, the Tertiary; Quaternary

postulatory.d: Of the nature of a postulate

pot lace.d: Lace whose pattern includes one or more representations of baskets or bowls from which flowers spring

pot shot.d: Lit., a shot fired simply to fill the pot; hence, a shot fired at an animal or person when at rest or within easy range, or fired simply to kill, without reference to the rules of sport; a shot needling no special skill

pot-walloper.d: A voter in certain boroughs of England, where, before the passage of the reform bill of 1832, the qualification for suffrage was to have boiled (walloped) his own pot in the parish for six months

potamian.d: A river tortoise; one of a group of tortoises (Potamites, or Trionychoidea) having a soft shell, webbed feet, and a sharp beak. See Trionyx

potance.d: The stud in which the bearing for the lower pivot of the verge is made

potargo.d: A kind of sauce or pickle

potassoxyl.d: The radical KO, derived from, and supposed to exist in, potassium hydroxide and other compounds

potestate.d: A chief ruler; a potentate. [Obs.] Wyclif

potlid.d: The lid or cover of a pot

potsdam group.d: A subdivision of the Primordial or Cambrian period in American geology; -- so named from the sandstone of Potsdam, New York. See Chart of Geology

pouch-shell.d: A small British and American pond snail (Bulinus hypnorum)

pouchong.d: A superior kind of souchong tea

pouncet box.d: A box with a perforated lid, for sprinkling pounce, or for holding perfumes

pound-breach.d: The breaking of a public pound for releasing impounded animals

poundrate.d: A rate or proportion estimated at a certain amount for each pound; poundage

powder-posted.d: Affected with dry rot; reduced to dust by rot. See Dry rot, under Dry

powderflask.d: A flask in which gunpowder is carried, having a charging tube at the end

powderhorn.d: A horn in which gunpowder is carried

powdermill.d: A mill in which gunpowder is made

powdike.d: A dike a marsh or fen

powerable.d: Capable of being effected or accomplished by the application of power; possible

practisant.d: An agent or confederate in treachery

praecognita.d: This previously known, or which should be known in order to understand something else

praecommissure.d: A transverse commissure in the anterior part of the third ventricle of the brain; the anterior cerebral commissure

praecornu.d: The anterior horn of each lateral ventricle of the brain

praenominical.d: Of or pertaining to a prænomen

praetexta.d: A white robe with a purple border, worn by a Roman boy before he was entitled to wear the toga virilis, or until about the completion of his fourteenth year, and by girls until their marriage. It was also worn by magistrates and priests

praetores.d: A division of butterflies including the satyrs

praise-meeting.d: A religious service mainly in song

prangos.d: A genus of umbelliferous plants, one species of which (Prangos pabularia), found in Tibet, Cashmere, Afghanistan, etc., has been used as fodder for cattle.  It has decompound leaves with very long narrow divisions, and a highly fragrant smell resembling that of new clover hay

praseo-.d: A combining form signifying green; as, praseocobalt, a green variety of cobalt

preachman.d: A preacher; -- so called in contempt

preadamitic.d: Existing or occurring before Adam; preadamic; as, preadamitic periods

preadvertise.d: To advertise beforehand; to preannounce publicly

preambulary.d: Of or pertaining to a preamble; introductory; contained or provided for in a preamble

preantenultimate.d: Being or indicating the fourth syllable from the end of a word, or that before the antepenult

preapprehension.d: An apprehension or opinion formed before examination or knowledge

prebendate.d: To invest with the office of prebendary; to present to a prebend

prebronchial.d: Situated in front of the bronchus; -- applied especially to an air sac on either side of the esophagus of birds

precalculate.d: To calculate or determine beforehand; to prearrange

precation.d: The act of praying; supplication; entreaty

precel.d: To surpass; to excel; to exceed

precieuse.d: An affected woman of polite society, esp. one of the literary women of the French salons of the 17th century.  See aslo preciosity

precipitantness.d: The quality or state of being precipitant; precipitation

precoetanean.d: One contemporary with, but older than, another

precognosce.d: To examine beforehand, as witnesses or evidence

preconceit.d: An opinion or notion formed beforehand; a preconception

preconizate.d: To proclaim; to publish; also, to summon; to call

preconsign.d: To consign beforehand; to make a previous consignment of

precursorship.d: The position or condition of a precursor

predeclare.d: To declare or announce beforehand; to preannounce

prededication.d: A dedication made previously or beforehand

predisponency.d: The state of being predisposed; predisposition

predy.d: Cleared and ready for engagement, as a ship

preexistentism.d: The theory of a preëxistence of souls before their association with human bodies

prefidence.d: The quality or state of being prefident

pregravitate.d: To descend by gravity; to sink

pregustation.d: The act of tasting beforehand; foretaste

prehnitic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a tetrabasic acid of benzene obtained as a white crystalline substance; -- probably so called from the resemblance of the wartlike crystals to the mammillæ on the surface of prehnite

preindesignate.d: Having no sign expressive of quantity; indefinite. See Predesignate

prejudical.d: Of or pertaining to the determination of some matter not previously decided; as, a prejudical inquiry or action at law

prejudicative.d: Forming a judgment without due examination; prejudging

prelal.d: Of or pertaining to printing; typographical

prelatically.d: In a prelatical manner; with reference to prelates

prelation.d: The setting of one above another; preference

prelumbar.d: Situated immediately in front of the loins; -- applied to the dorsal part of the abdomen

premonstrator.d: One who, or that which, premonstrates

premosaic.d: Relating to the time before Moses; as, premosaic history

premunite.d: To fortify beforehand; to guard against objection

prender.d: The power or right of taking a thing before it is offered

prensation.d: The act of seizing with violence

preopercular.d: Situated in front of the operculum; pertaining to the preoperculum

prepollence.d: The quality or state of being prepollent; superiority of power; predominance; prevalence

prepollent.d: Having superior influence or power; prevailing; predominant

prepositure.d: The office or dignity of a provost; a provostship

prepossessor.d: One who possesses, or occupies, previously

preraphaelism.d: The doctrine or practice of a school of modern painters who profess to be followers of the painters before Raphael. Its adherents advocate careful study from nature, delicacy and minuteness of workmanship, and an exalted and delicate conception of the subject

preraphaelite.d: Of or pertaining to the style called preraphaelitism; as, a preraphaelite figure; a preraphaelite landscape

preregnant.d: One who reigns before another; a sovereign predecessor

preremote.d: More remote in previous time or prior order

prescious.d: Foreknowing; having foreknowledge; as, prescious of ills

presentaneous.d: Ready; quick; immediate in effect; as, presentaneous poison

presentoir.d: An ornamental tray, dish, or the like, used as a salver

presignification.d: The act of signifying or showing beforehand

presphenoidal.d: Of or pertaining to the presphenoid bone; presphenoid

pressiroster.d: One of a tribe of wading birds (Pressirostres) including those which have a compressed beak, as the plovers

pressirostral.d: Of or pertaining to the pressirosters

pressive.d: Pressing; urgent; also, oppressive; as, pressive taxation

presspack.d: To pack, or prepare for packing, by means of a press

pressure wires.d: Wires leading from various points of an electric system to a central station, where a voltmeter indicates the potential of the system at those points

prestidigital.d: Nimble-fingered; having fingers fit for prestidigitation, or juggling

prestimony.d: A fund for the support of a priest, without the title of a benefice. The patron in the collator

prestriction.d: Obstruction, dimness, or defect of sight

pretemporal.d: Situated in front of the temporal bone

preterient.d: Passed through; antecedent; previous; as, preterient states

preterimperfect.d: Old name of the tense also called imperfect

preteritness.d: The quality or state of being past

preternaturalness.d: The quality or state of being preternatural

preterperfect.d: Old name of the tense also called preterit

preterpluperfect.d: Old name of the tense also called pluperfect

pretervection.d: The act of carrying past or beyond

pretex.d: To frame; to devise; to disguise or excuse; hence, to pretend; to declare falsely

prevenancy.d: The act of anticipating another's wishes, desires, etc., in the way of favor or courtesy; hence, civility; obligingness

prevene.d: To come before; to anticipate; hence, to hinder; to prevent

preventingly.d: So as to prevent or hinder

prian.d: A fine, white, somewhat friable clay; also, the ore contained in a mixture of clay and pebbles

priapean.d: A species of hexameter verse so constructed as to be divisible into two portions of three feet each, having generally a trochee in the first and the fourth foot, and an amphimacer in the third; -- applied also to a regular hexameter verse when so constructed as to be divisible into two portions of three feet each

priapulacea.d: A suborder of Gephyræa, having a cylindrical body with a terminal anal opening, and usually with one or two caudal gills

pricking-up.d: The first coating of plaster in work of three coats upon laths. Its surface is scratched once to form a better key for the next coat. In the United States called scratch coat

pricklouse.d: A tailor; -- so called in contempt

prickpunch.d: A pointed steel punch, to prick a mark on metal

pricksong.d: Music written, or noted, with dots or points; -- so called from the points or dots with which it is noted down

prickwood.d: A shrub (Euonymus Europæus); -- so named from the use of its wood for goads, skewers, and shoe pegs. Called also spindle tree

priestcap.d: A form of redan, so named from its shape; -- called also swallowtail

priestery.d: Priests, collectively; the priesthood; -- so called in contempt

priestism.d: The influence, doctrines, principles, etc., of priests or the priesthood

primigenious.d: First formed or generated; original; primigenial

primipilar.d: Of or pertaining to the captain of the vanguard of a Roman army

primitia.d: The first fruit; the first year's whole profit of an ecclesiastical preferment

primitial.d: Being of the first production; primitive; original

primordian.d: A name given to several kinds of plums; as, red primordian, amber primordian, etc

primrose league.d: A league of both sexes among the Conservatives, founded in 1883. So called because primrose was (erroneously, it is said) taken to be the favorite flower of the Conservative statesman Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield

principiation.d: Analysis into primary or elemental parts

printing in.d: A process by which cloud effects or other features not in the original negative are introduced into a photograph. Portions, such as the sky, are covered while printing and the blank space thus reserved is filled in by printing from another negative

printing out.d: A method of printing, in which the image is fully brought out by the direct actinic action of light without subsequent development by means of chemicals

priscillianist.d: A follower of Priscillian, bishop of Avila in Spain, in the fourth century, who mixed various elements of Gnosticism and Manicheism with Christianity

prism glass.d: Glass with one side smooth and the other side formed into sharp-edged ridges so as to reflect the light that passes through, used at windows to throw the light into the interior

privado.d: A private friend; a confidential friend; a confidant

pro thyalosoma.d: The investing portion, or spherical envelope, surrounding the eccentric germinal spot of the germinal vesicle

probe-pointed.d: Having a blunt or button-shaped extremity; -- said of cutting instruments

proboscidifera.d: An extensive division of pectinibranchiate gastropods, including those that have a long retractile proboscis, with the mouth at the end, as the cones, whelks, tritons, and cowries. See Illust. of Gastropoda, and of Winkle

procellarian.d: One of a family of oceanic birds (Procellaridæ) including the petrels, fulmars, and shearwaters.  They are often seen in great abundance in stormy weather

proceres.d: An order of large birds; the Ratitæ; -- called also Proceri

proces verbal.d: An authentic minute of an official act, or statement of facts

processionalist.d: One who goes or marches in a procession

procinct.d: A state of complete readiness for action

proclive.d: Having a tendency by nature; prone; proclivous

procoele.d: A lateral cavity of the prosencephalon; a lateral ventricle of the brain

procris.d: Any species of small moths of the genus Procris. The larvæ of some species injure the grapevine by feeding in groups upon the leaves

procrusteanize.d: To stretch or contract according to some rule or standard

proctorage.d: Management by a proctor, or as by a proctor; hence, control; superintendence; -- in contempt

proctucha.d: A division of Turbellaria including those that have an intestine terminating posteriorly

produce race.d: A race to be run by the produce of horses named or described at the time of entry

producer's surplus.d: Any profit above the normal rate of interest and wages accruing to a producer on account of some monopoly (temporary or permanent) of the means or materials of production; -- called also Producer's rent

proeguminal.d: Serving to predispose; predisposing; as, a proeguminal cause of disease

proemptosis.d: The addition of a day to the lunar calendar

proface.d: Much good may it do you! -- a familiar salutation or welcome

profaner.d: One who treats sacred things with irreverence, or defiles what is holy; one who uses profane language

profection.d: A setting out; a going forward; advance; progression

profectitious.d: Proceeding from, as from a parent; derived, as from an ancestor

profert.d: The exhibition or production of a record or paper in open court, or an allegation that it is in court

professorialism.d: The character, manners, or habits of a professor

professory.d: Of or pertaining to a professor; professorial

progenerate.d: To beget; to generate; to produce; to procreate; as, to progenerate a race

prognathi.d: A comprehensive group of mankind, including those that have prognathous jaws

proin.d: To lop; to trim; to prune; to adorn

prolation.d: The act of prolating or pronouncing; utterance; pronunciation

prolatum.d: A prolate spheroid. See Ellipsoid of revolution, under Ellipsoid

prolegate.d: The deputy or substitute for a legate

prolifical.d: Producing young or fruit abundantly; fruitful; prolific

prolificate.d: To make prolific; to fertilize; to impregnate

promanation.d: The act of flowing forth; emanation; efflux

promerit.d: To oblige; to confer a favor on

promerops.d: Any one of several species of very brilliant birds belonging to Promerops, Epimarchus, and allied genera, closely related to the paradise birds, and mostly native of New Guinea. They have a long curved beak and a long graduated tail

promethea.d: A large American bombycid moth (Callosamia promethea). Its larva feeds on the sassafras, wild cherry, and other trees, and suspends its cocoon from a branch by a silken band

promissive.d: Making a promise; implying a promise; promising

promorphological.d: Relating to promorphology; as, a promorphological conception

promorphologist.d: One versed in the science of promorphology

promove.d: To move forward; to advance; to promote

prompt-book.d: The book used by a prompter of a theater

prompt-note.d: A memorandum of a sale, and time when payment is due, given to the purchaser at a sale of goods

prong-hoe.d: A hoe with prongs to break the earth

pronuncial.d: Of or pertaining to pronunciation; pronunciative

proof-arm.d: To arm with proof armor; to arm securely; as, to proof-arm herself

proof-proof.d: Proof against proofs; obstinate in the wrong

propension.d: The quality or state of being propense; propensity

prophetize.d: To give predictions; to foreshow events; to prophesy

propidene.d: The unsymmetrical hypothetical hydrocarbon radical, CH3.CH2.CH, analogous to ethylidene, and regarded as the type of certain derivatives of propane; -- called also propylidene

propination.d: The act of pledging, or drinking first, and then offering the cup to another

propiolic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an organic acid (called also propargylic acid) of the acetylene or tetrolic series, analogous to propionic acid, and obtained as a white crystalline substance

propithecus.d: A genus including the long-tailed, or diadem, indris. See Indris

proplastics.d: The art of making molds for castings

propodial.d: Of or pertaining to the propodialia, or the parts of the limbs to which they belong

propugn.d: To contend for; to defend; to vindicate

propulsation.d: The act of driving away or repelling; a keeping at a distance

propulse.d: To repel; to drive off or away

prorector.d: An officer who presides over the academic senate of a German university

prosaicism.d: The quality or state of being prosaic; a prosaic manner or style

prosal.d: Of or pertaining to prose; prosaic

proseminary.d: A seminary which prepares pupils for a higher institution

prosiliency.d: The act of leaping forth or forward; projection

prosimetrical.d: Consisting both of prose and verse

prosopulmonata.d: A division of pulmonate mollusks having the breathing organ situated on the neck, as in the common snail

prosphysis.d: A growing together of parts; specifically, a morbid adhesion of the eyelids to each other or to the eyeball

prostibulous.d: Of or pertaining to prostitutes or prostitution; meretricious

prosylogism.d: A syllogism preliminary or logically essential to another syllogism; the conclusion of such a syllogism, which becomes a premise of the following syllogism

protactic.d: Giving a previous narrative or explanation, as of the plot or personages of a play; introductory

protatic.d: Of or pertaining to the protasis of an ancient play; introductory

proteidea.d: An order of aquatic amphibians having prominent external gills and four legs. It includes Proteus and Menobranchus (Necturus).  Called also Proteoidea, and Proteida

proterosaurus.d: An extinct genus of reptiles of the Permian period.  Called also Protosaurus

protestantly.d: Like a Protestant; in conformity with Protestantism

protestator.d: One who makes protestation; a protester

proto-doric.d: Pertaining to, or designating, architecture, in which the beginnings of the Doric style are supposed to be found

protocanonical.d: Of or pertaining to the first canon, or that which contains the authorized collection of the books of Scripture; -- opposed to deutero-canonical

protocatechuic.d: Pertaining to, derived from, or designating, an organic acid which is obtained as a white crystalline substance from catechin, asafetida, oil of cloves, etc., and by distillation itself yields pyrocatechin

protometals.d: A finer form of metals, indicated by enhanced lines in their spark spectra (which are also observed in the spectra of some stars), obtained at the highest available laboratory temperatures (Lockyer); as protocalcium, protochromium, protocopper, protonickel, protosilicon, protostrontium, prototitanium, protovanadium

protoorganism.d: An organism whose nature is so difficult to determine that it might be referred to either the animal or the vegetable kingdom

protoplasta.d: A division of fresh-water rhizopods including those that have a soft body and delicate branched pseudopodia. The genus Gromia is one of the best-known

protosilicate.d: A silicate formed with the lowest proportion of silicic acid, or having but one atom of silicon in the molecule

protosomite.d: One of the primitive segments, or metameres, of an animal

protoxidize.d: To combine with oxygen, as any elementary substance, in such proportion as to form a protoxide

protozoonite.d: One of the primary, or first-formed, segments of an embryonic arthropod

protractive.d: Drawing out or lengthening in time; prolonging; continuing; delaying

protuberancy.d: The quality or state of being protuberant; protuberance; prominence

provant.d: To supply with provender or provisions; to provide for

provection.d: A carrying forward, as of a final letter, to a following word; as, for example, a nickname for an ekename

proveditor.d: One employed to procure supplies, as for an army, a steamer, etc.; a purveyor; one who provides for another

provencial.d: Of or pertaining to Provence in France

proventriulus.d: The glandular stomach of birds, situated just above the crop

proverbialize.d: To turn into a proverb; to speak in proverbs

providore.d: One who makes provision; a purveyor

provisorship.d: The office or position of a provisor

provokement.d: The act that which, provokes; one who excites anger or other passion, or incites to action; as, a provoker of sedition

proxene.d: An officer who had the charge of showing hospitality to those who came from a friendly city or state

proxenetism.d: The action of a go-between or broker in negotiating immoral bargains between the sexes; procuring

prutenic.d: Prussian; -- applied to certain astronomical tables published in the sixteenth century, founded on the principles of Copernicus, a Prussian

prytanis.d: A member of one of the ten sections into which the Athenian senate of five hundred was divided, and to each of which belonged the presidency of the senate for about one tenth of the year

prytany.d: The period during which the presidency of the senate belonged to the prytanes of the section

psalmistry.d: The use of psalms in devotion; psalmody

psalmograph.d: A writer of psalms; a psalmographer

psalmographer.d: A writer of psalms, or sacred songs and hymns

psalmography.d: The act or practice of writing psalms, or sacred songs

psarolite.d: A silicified stem of tree fern, found in abundance in the Triassic sandstone

psephism.d: A proposition adopted by a majority of votes; especially, one adopted by vote of the Athenian people; a statute

pseudo-bulb.d: An aërial corm, or thickened stem, as of some epiphytic orchidaceous plants

pseudo-china.d: The false china root, a plant of the genus Smilax (Smilax Pseudo-china), found in America

pseudo-cone.d: One of the soft gelatinous cones found in the compound eyes of certain insects, taking the place of the crystalline cones of others

pseudo-cumene.d: A hydrocarbon of the aromatic series, metameric with mesitylene and cumene, found in coal tar, and obtained as a colorless liquid

pseudo-dipteral.d: Falsely or imperfectly dipteral, as a temple with the inner range of columns surrounding the cella omitted, so that the space between the cella wall and the columns is very great, being equal to two intercolumns and one column

pseudo-galena.d: False galena, or blende. See Blende (a)

pseudo-heart.d: Any contractile vessel of invertebrates which is not of the nature of a real heart, especially one of those pertaining to the excretory system

pseudo-hyperthophic.d: Falsely hypertrophic; as, pseudo-hypertrophic paralysis, a variety of paralysis in which the muscles are apparently enlarged, but are really degenerated and replaced by fat

pseudo-metallic.d: Falsely or imperfectly metallic; -- said of a kind of luster, as in minerals

pseudo-monocotyledonous.d: Having two coalescent cotyledons, as the live oak and the horse-chestnut

pseudo-peripteral.d: Falsely or imperfectly peripteral, as a temple having the columns at the sides attached to the walls, and an ambulatory only at the ends or only at one end

pseudobacteria.d: Microscopic organic particles, molecular granules, powdered inorganic substances, etc., which in form, size, and grouping resemble bacteria

pseudocoelia.d: The fifth ventricle in the mammalian brain. See Ventricle

pseudofilaria.d: One of the two elongated vibratile young formed by fission of the embryo during the development of certain Gregarinæ

pseudonavicula.d: One of the minute spindle-shaped embryos of Gregarinæ and some other Protozoa

pseudoneuroptera.d: division of insects (Zool.) reticulated wings, as in the Neuroptera, but having an active pupa state. It includes the dragon flies, May flies, white ants, etc. By some Zoologists they are classed with the Orthoptera; by others, with the Neuroptera

pseudoneuropterous.d: Of or pertaining to the Pseudoneuroptera

pseudorhabdite.d: One of the peculiar rodlike corpuscles found in the integument of certain Turbellaria. They are filled with a soft granular substance

pseudotinea.d: The bee moth, or wax moth (Galleria)

psilology.d: Love of empty of empty talk or noise

psilopaedes.d: birds whose young at first have down on the pterylæ only; -- called also Gymnopædes

psilopaedic.d: Having down upon the pterylæ only; -- said of the young of certain birds

psilosopher.d: A superficial or narrow pretender to philosophy; a sham philosopher

psitta-co-fulvine.d: A yellow pigment found in the feathers of certain parrots

psittaci.d: The order of birds which comprises the parrots

psychian.d: Any small moth of the genus Psyche and allied genera (family Psychidæ). The larvæ are called basket worms. See Basket worm, under Basket

psycho-motor.d: Of or pertaining to movement produced by action of the mind or will

psychomachy.d: A conflict of the soul with the body

psychopannychism.d: The doctrine that the soul falls asleep at death, and does not wake until the resurrection of the body

ptenoglossa.d: A division of gastropod mollusks having the teeth of the radula arranged in long transverse rows, somewhat like the barbs of a feather

ptenoglossate.d: Of or pertaining to the Ptenoglossa

pteranodontia.d: A group of pterodactyls destitute of teeth, as in the genus Pteranodon

pterichthys.d: A genus of Devonian fossil fishes with winglike appendages. The head and most of the body were covered with large bony plates. See Placodermi

pteridomania.d: A madness, craze, or strong fancy, for ferns

pteroceras.d: A genus of large marine gastropods having the outer border of the lip divided into lobes; -- called also scorpion shell

pterocletes.d: A division of birds including the sand grouse.  They are in some respects intermediate between the pigeons and true grouse.  Called also Pteroclomorphæ

pteroglossal.d: Having the tongue finely notched along the sides, so as to have a featherlike appearance, as the toucans

pteron.d: The region of the skull, in the temporal fossa back of the orbit, where the great wing of the sphenoid, the temporal, the parietal, and the frontal hones approach each other

pterophore.d: Any moth of the genus Pterophorus and allied genera; a plume moth. See Plume moth, under Plume

ptilopaedic.d: Having nearly the whole surface of the skin covered with down; dasypædic; -- said of the young of certain birds

ptilopteri.d: An order of birds including only the penguins

publicity pamphlet.d: A pamphlet which, in some States of the United States having the initiative or referendum, is mailed to the voters to inform them as to the nature of a measure submitted by the initiative or referendum. The pamphlet contains a copy of the proposed law and arguments for and against it by those favoring and opposing it, respectively

pudding fish.d: A large, handsomely colored, blue and bronze, labroid fish (Iridio radiatus, syn. Platyglossus radiatus) of Florida, Bermuda, and the West Indies. Called also pudiano, doncella, and, at Bermuda, bluefish

puddle-ball.d: The lump of pasty wrought iron as taken from the puddling furnace to be hammered or rolled

puddle-bar.d: An iron bar made at a single heat from a puddle-ball hammering and rolling

puff-leg.d: Any one of numerous species of beautiful humming birds of the genus Eriocnemis having large tufts of downy feathers on the legs

puff-legged.d: Having a conspicuous tuft of feathers on the legs

puggry.d: A light scarf wound around a hat or helmet to protect the head from the sun

puit.d: A well; a small stream; a fountain; a spring

pulicene.d: Pertaining to, or abounding in, fleas; pulicose

pulkha.d: A Laplander's traveling sledge. See Sledge

pulmograde.d: Swimming by the expansion and contraction, or lunglike movement, of the body, or of the disk, as do the medusæ

pulmonarian.d: Any arachnid that breathes by lunglike organs, as the spiders and scorpions. Also used adjectively

pulpatoon.d: A kind of delicate confectionery or cake, perhaps made from the pulp of fruit

pulpitical.d: Of or pertaining to the pulpit; suited to the pulpit

pulpitish.d: Of or pertaining to the pulpit; like preaching

pulu.d: A vegetable substance consisting of soft, elastic, yellowish brown chaff, gathered in the Hawaiian Islands from the young fronds of free ferns of the genus Cibotium, chiefly Cibotium Menziesii; -- used for stuffing mattresses, cushions, etc., and as an absorbent

pulverate.d: To beat or reduce to powder or dust; to pulverize

pulvillio.d: A kind of perfume in the form of a powder, formerly much used, -- often in little bags

pulvinic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained by the decomposition of vulpinic acid, as a white crystalline substance

pumiciform.d: Resembling, or having the structure of, pumice

punctator.d: One who marks with points. specifically, one who writes Hebrew with points; -- applied to a Masorite

puncticular.d: Comprised in, or like, a point; exact

punction.d: A puncturing, or pricking; a puncture

puncto.d: A nice point of form or ceremony

punctualist.d: One who is very exact in observing forms and ceremonies

pundle.d: A short and fat woman; a squab

pungy.d: A small sloop or shallop, or a large boat with sails

punnology.d: The art or practice of punning; paronomasia

puntello.d: One of the points sometimes drilled as guides for cutting away superfluous stone

pupivora.d: A group of parasitic Hymenoptera, including the ichneumon flies, which destroy the larvæ and pupæ of insects

puppetish.d: Resembling a puppet in appearance or action; of the nature of a puppet

puppetman.d: A master of a puppet show

purbeck beds.d: The strata of the Purbeck stone, or Purbeck limestone, belonging to the Oolitic group. See the Chart of Geology

purbeck stone.d: A limestone from the Isle of Purbeck in England

purfile.d: A sort of ancient trimming of tinsel and thread for women's gowns; -- called also bobbinwork

purificative.d: Having power to purify; tending to cleanse

purparty.d: A share, part, or portion of an estate allotted to a coparcener

purprise.d: A close or inclosure; the compass of a manor

purpureo-.d: A combining form signifying of a purple or purple-red color. Specif. (Chem.), used in designating certain brilliant purple-red compounds of cobaltic chloride and ammonia, similar to the roseocobaltic compounds. See Cobaltic.

pusane.d: A piece of armor for the breast; often, an addition to, or reënforcement of. the breastplate; -- called also pesane

putage.d: Prostitution or fornication on the part of a woman

putanism.d: Habitual lewdness or prostitution of a woman; harlotry

putidity.d: The quality or state of being putrid

putour.d: A keeper of a brothel; a procurer

putredinous.d: Proceeding from putrefaction, or partaking of the putrefactive process; having an offensive smell; stinking; rotten

putrescin.d: A nontoxic diamine, C4H12N2, formed in the putrefaction of the flesh of mammals and some other animals

puzzel.d: A harlot; a drab; a hussy

puzzle-headed.d: Having the head full of confused notions; given to getting perplexed over simple matters; also, characteristic of persons that are so

pycnaspidean.d: Having the posterior side of the tarsus covered with small irregular scales; -- said of certain birds

pycnodont.d: Any fossil fish belonging to the Pycnodontini. They have numerous round, flat teeth, adapted for crushing

pycnodontini.d: An extinct order of ganoid fishes. They had a compressed body, covered with dermal ribs (pleurolepida) and with enameled rhomboidal scales

pygarg.d: A quadruped, probably the addax, an antelope having a white rump

pygobranchia.d: A division of opisthobranchiate mollusks having the branchiæ in a wreath or group around the anal opening, as in the genus Doris

pygopodes.d: A division of swimming birds which includes the grebes, divers, auks, etc., in which the legs are placed far back

pygopodous.d: Of or pertaining to the Pygopodes

pylagore.d: a deputy of a State at the Amphictyonic council

pyral.d: Of or pertaining to a pyre

pyramidoid.d: A solid resembling a pyramid; -- called also pyramoid

pyrethrine.d: An alkaloid extracted from the root of the pellitory of Spain (Anacyclus pyrethrum)

pyritaceous.d: Of or pertaining to pyrites. See Pyritic

pyroacetic.d: Pertaining to, and designating, a substance (acetone) obtained by the distillation of the acetates. It is now called also pyroacetic ether, and formerly was called pyroacetic spirit

pyroantimonic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid of antimony analogous to pyrophosphoric acid

pyroarsenic.d: Pertaining to or designating, an acid of arsenic analogous to pyrophosphoric acid

pyroboric.d: Pertaining to derived from, or designating, an acid, H2B4O7 (called also tetraboric acid), which is the acid ingredient of ordinary borax, and is obtained by heating boric acid

pyrocitric.d: Pertaining to, or designating, any one of three acids obtained by the distillation of citric acid, and called respectively citraconic, itaconic, and mesaconic acid

pyrognostic.d: Of or pertaining to characters developed by the use of heat; pertaining to the characters of minerals when examined before the blowpipe; as, the pyrognostic characters of galena

pyrolignite.d: A crude acetate produced by treating pyroligneous acid with a metal or basic compound; as, pyrolignite of iron (iron liquor)

pyrologist.d: One who is versed in, or makes a study of, pyrology

pyromalic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid now called maleic acid

pyromucic.d: Pertaining to, derived from, or designating, an acid obtained as a white crystalline substance by the distillation of mucic acid, or by the oxidation of furfurol

pyrophone.d: A musical instrument in which the tones are produced by flames of hydrogen, or illuminating gas, burning in tubes of different sizes and lengths

pyrosulphuric.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid called also disulphuric acid) obtained by distillation of certain sulphates, as a colorless, thick, oily liquid, H2S2O7 resembling sulphuric acid. It is used in the solution of indigo, in the manufacture of alizarin, and in dehydration

pyrotartaric.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained as a white crystalline substance by the distillation of tartaric acid

pyrothonide.d: A kind of empyreumatic oil produced by the combustion of textures of hemp, linen, or cotton in a copper vessel, -- formerly used as a remedial agent

pyrotritartaric.d: Designating an acid which is more commonly called uric acid

pyrouric.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid now called cyanuric acid. See Cyanuric

pyrovanadic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid of vanadium, analogous to pyrophosphoric acid

pyroxanthin.d: A yellow crystalline hydrocardon extracted from crude wood spirit; -- called also eblanin

pyroxylic.d: Derived from wood by distillation; -- formerly used in designating crude wood spirit

pyrula.d: A genus of large marine gastropods having a pear-shaped shell.  It includes the fig-shells. See Illust. in Appendix

pyruvil.d: A complex nitrogenous compound obtained by heating together pyruvic acid and urea

pythagorize.d: To speculate after the manner of Pythagoras

pythocenic.d: Producing decomposition, as diseases which are supposed to be accompanied or caused by decomposition

pythonism.d: The art of predicting events after the manner of the priestess of Apollo at Delphi; equivocal prophesying

q.e.d.d: Which was demonstrated; -- a phrase used after the conclusion of some line of reasoning, especially in mathematical or logical proofs

qua-bird.d: The American night heron. See under Night

quadragenarious.d: Consisting of forty; forty years old

quadragene.d: An indulgence of forty days, corresponding to the forty days of ancient canonical penance

quadrin.d: A small piece of money, in value about a farthing, or a half cent

quadrinodal.d: Possessing four nodes; as, quadrinodal curves

quadripennate.d: Having four wings; -- said of insects

quadrisulcate.d: Having four hoofs; as, a quadrisulcate foot; a quadrisulcate animal

quamoclit.d: Formerly, a genus of plants including the cypress vine (Quamoclit vulgaris, now called Ipomœa Quamoclit). The genus is now merged in Ipomœa

quannet.d: A flat file having the handle at one side, so as to be used like a plane

quarry-man.d: A man who is engaged in quarrying stones; a quarrier

quartane.d: Butane, each molecule of which has four carbon atoms

quartenylic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid of the acrylic acid series, metameric with crotonic acid, and obtained as a colorless liquid; -- so called from having four carbon atoms in the molecule. Called also isocrotonic acid

quarter-saw.d: To saw (a log) into quarters; specif., to saw into quarters and then into boards, as by cutting alternately from each face of a quarter, to secure lumber that will warp relatively little or show the grain advantageously

quarterhung.d: Having trunnions the axes of which lie below the bore; -- said of a cannon

quarteron.d: A quarter; esp., a quarter of a pound, or a quarter of a hundred

quartine.d: A supposed fourth integument of an ovule, counting from the outside

quashee.d: A negro of the West Indies

quasi corporation.d: A corporation consisting of a person or body of persons invested with some of the qualities of an artificial person, though not expressly incorporated, esp. the official of certain municipal divisions such as counties, schools districts, and the towns of some States of the United States, certain church officials, as a churchwarden, etc

quater-cousin.d: A cousin within the first four degrees of kindred

queach.d: A thick, bushy plot; a thicket

queachy.d: Yielding or trembling under the feet, as moist or boggy ground; shaking; moving

quebec group.d: The middle of the three groups into which the rocks of the Canadian period have been divided in the American Lower Silurian system. See the Chart of Geology

quech.d: A word occurring in a corrupt passage of Bacon's Essays, and probably meaning, to stir, to move

queen olive.d: Properly, a kind of superior olive grown in the region of Seville, Spain. It is large size and oblong shape with a small but long pit; it is cured when green, keeps well, and has a delicate flavor. Loosely, any olive of similar character

queen truss.d: A truss framed with queen-posts; a queen-post truss

queen-post.d: One of two suspending posts in a roof truss, or other framed truss of similar form. See King-post

queencraft.d: Craft or skill in policy on the part of a queen

quenouille training.d: A method of training trees or shrubs in the shape of a cone or distaff by tying down the branches and pruning

quercitannic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a tannic acid found in oak bark and extracted as a yellowish brown amorphous substance

querele.d: A complaint to a court. See Audita Querela

querl.d: To twirl; to turn or wind round; to coil; as, to querl a cord, thread, or rope

querpo.d: The inner or body garments taken together. See Cuerpo

quesal.d: The long-tailed, or resplendent, trogon (Pharomachus mocinno, formerly Trogon resplendens), native of Southern Mexico and Central America. Called also quetzal, and golden trogon

questant.d: One who undertakes a quest; a seeker

questman.d: One legally empowered to make quest of certain matters, esp. of abuses of weights and measures

questmonger.d: One who lays informations, and encourages petty lawsuits

questorship.d: The office, or the term of office, of a questor

quica.d: A small South American opossum (Didelphys quica), native of Guiana and Brazil. It feeds upon insects, small birds, and fruit

quichuan.d: Designating, or pertaining to, a linguistic stock of South American Indians, including the majority of the civilized tribes of the ancient Peruvian Empire with some wild tribes never subjugated by the Incas. Most of these Indians are short, but heavy and strong. They are brachycephalic and of remarkably low cranial capacity. Nevertheless, they represent one of the highest of native American civilizations, characterized by agricultural, military, and administrative skill rather than by science or

quicken tree.d: The European rowan tree; -- called also quickbeam, and quickenbeam. See Rowan tree

quiddany.d: A confection of quinces, in consistency between a sirup and marmalade

quiddative.d: Constituting, or containing, the essence of a thing; quidditative

quillaia bark.d: The bark of a rosaceous tree (Quillaja Saponaria), native of Chile.  The bark is finely laminated, and very heavy with alkaline substances, and is used commonly by the Chileans instead of soap.  Also called soap bark

quinazol.d: A complex nitrogenous base related to cinnoline

quindecemvirate.d: The body or office of the quindecemviri

quindecone.d: An unsaturated hydrocarbon, C15H26, of the valylene series, produced artificially as an oily liquid

quindecylic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid of the fatty acid series, containing fifteen atoms of carbon; called also pentadecylic acid

quinible.d: An interval of a fifth; also, a part sung with such intervals

quininic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a nitrogenous acid obtained as a yellow crystalline substance by the oxidation of quinine

quinologist.d: One who is versed in quinology

quinovic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a crystalline acid obtained from some varieties of cinchona bark

quinoyl.d: A radical of which quinone is the hydride, analogous to phenyl

quinquarticular.d: Relating to the five articles or points; as, the quinquarticular controversy between Arminians and Calvinists

quinque-.d: A combining form meaning five, five times, fivefold; as, quinquefid, five-cleft; quinquedentate, five-toothed

quinquennalia.d: Public games celebrated every five years

quinquevir.d: One of five commissioners appointed for some special object

quintilllion.d: According to the French notation, which is used on the Continent and in America, the cube of a million, or a unit with eighteen ciphers annexed; according to the English notation, a number produced by involving a million to the fifth power, or a unit with thirty ciphers annexed. See the Note under Numeration

quintine.d: The embryonic sac of an ovule, sometimes regarded as an innermost fifth integument.  Cf. Quartine, and Tercine

quintole.d: A group of five notes to be played or sung in the time of four of the same species

quinzaine.d: The fifteenth day after a feast day, including both in the reckoning

quirboilly.d: Leather softened by boiling so as to take any required shape. Upon drying, it becomes exceedingly hard, and hence was formerly used for armor

quitch grass.d: A perennial grass (Agropyrum repens) having long running rootstalks, by which it spreads rapidly and pertinaciously, and so becomes a troublesome weed. Also called couch grass, quack grass, quick grass, twitch grass. See Illustration in Appendix

quizzism.d: The act or habit of quizzing

quodlibetarian.d: One who discusses any subject at pleasure

quoll.d: A marsupial of Australia (Dasyurus macrurus), about the size of a cat

quotationist.d: One who makes, or is given to making, quotations

r and d.d: research and development; -- used mostly to refer to the division of a corporation responsible for performing research and developing new products; -- a commonly used abbreviation

ra-.d: A prefix, from the Latin re and ad combined, coming to us through the French and Italian. See Re-, and Ad-

rabate.d: To recover to the fist, as a hawk

rabble-rout.d: A tumultuous crowd; a rabble; a noisy throng

rabdology.d: The method or art of performing arithmetical operations by means of Napier's bones. See Napier's bones

rabdomancy.d: Divination by means of rods or wands

rabinet.d: A kind of small ordnance formerly in use

racahout.d: A preparation from acorns used by the Arabs as a substitute for chocolate, and also as a beverage for invalids

racket-tail.d: Any one of several species of humming birds of the genus Steganura, having two of the tail feathers very long and racket-shaped

racket-tailed.d: Having long and spatulate, or racket-shaped, tail feathers

racktail.d: An arm attached to a swinging notched arc or rack, to let off the striking mechanism of a repeating clock

racovian.d: One of a sect of Socinians or Unitarians in Poland

radiant engine.d: A semiradial engine. See Radial engine, above

radiate-veined.d: Having the principal veins radiating, or diverging, from the apex of the petiole; -- said of such leaves as those of the grapevine, most maples, and the castor-oil plant

radio-flagellata.d: A group of Protozoa having both flagella and pseudopodia

radioconductor.d: A substance or device that has its conductivity altered in some way by electric waves, as a coherer

radioli.d: The barbs of the radii of a feather; barbules

raghuvansa.d: A celebrated Sanskrit poem having for its subject the Raghu dynasty

ragman's roll.d: The rolls of deeds on parchment in which the Scottish nobility and gentry subscribed allegiance to Edward I. of England, A. D. 1296

raguled.d: Notched in regular diagonal breaks; -- said of a line, or a bearing having such an edge

raiae.d: The order of elasmobranch fishes which includes the sawfishes, skates, and rays; -- called also Rajae, and Rajii

raiffeisen.d: Designating, or pertaining to, a form of cooperative bank founded among the German agrarian population by Friedrich Wilhelm Raiffeisen (1818-88); as, Raiffeisen banks, the Raiffeisen system, etc. The banks are unlimited-liability institutions making small loans at a low rate of interest, for a designated purpose, to worthy members only

railleur.d: A banterer; a jester; a mocker

rain-tight.d: So tight as to exclude rain; as, a rain-tight roof

raip.d: A rope; also, a measure equal to a rod

raku ware.d: A kind of earthenware made in Japan, resembling Satsuma ware, but having a paler color

ramberge.d: Formerly, a kind of large war galley

rambooze.d: A beverage made of wine, ale (or milk), sugar, etc

ramist.d: A follower of Pierre Ramé, better known as Ramus, a celebrated French scholar, who was professor of rhetoric and philosophy at Paris in the reign of Henry II., and opposed the Aristotelians

ramline.d: A line used to get a straight middle line, as on a spar, or from stem to stern in building a vessel

ramoon.d: A small West Indian tree (Trophis Americana) of the Mulberry family, whose leaves and twigs are used as fodder for cattle

ramsted.d: A yellow-flowered weed; -- so named from a Mr. Ramsted who introduced it into Pennsylvania. See Toad flax. Called also Ramsted weed

ranal.d: Having a general affinity to ranunculaceous plants

randall grass.d: The meadow fescue (Festuca elatior). See under Grass

ransomless.d: Incapable of being ransomed; without ransom

ranterism.d: The practice or tenets of the Ranters

ranz des vaches.d: The name for numerous simple, but very irregular, melodies of the Swiss mountaineers, blown on a long tube called the Alpine horn, and sometimes sung

raphaelism.d: The principles of painting introduced by Raphael, the Italian painter

raphaelite.d: One who advocates or adopts the principles of Raphaelism

raphany.d: A convulsive disease, attended with ravenous hunger, not uncommon in Sweden and Germany. It was so called because supposed to be caused by eating corn with which seeds of jointed charlock (Raphanus raphanistrum) had been mixed, but the condition is now known to be a form of ergotism

rapid-fire mount.d: A mount permitting easy and quick elevation or depression and training of the gun, and fitted with a device for taking up the recoil

raptores.d: An order of birds, same as Accipitres. Called also Raptatores

rapturize.d: To put, or be put, in a state of rapture

rasante.d: Sweeping; grazing; -- applied to a style of fortification in which the command of the works over each other, and over the country, is kept very low, in order that the shot may more effectually sweep or graze the ground before them

raskolnik.d: The name applied by the Russian government to any subject of the Greek faith who dissents from the established church. The Raskolniki embrace many sects, whose common characteristic is a clinging to antique traditions, habits, and customs. The schism originated in 1667 in an ecclesiastical dispute as to the correctness of the translation of the religious books. rasores.d: An order of birds; the Gallinae

rat-tailed.d: Having a long, tapering tail like that of a rat

ratihabition.d: Confirmation or approbation, as of an act or contract

ratitate.d: Of or pertaining to the Ratitae

rattinet.d: A woolen stuff thinner than ratteen

rattleweed.d: Any plant of the genus Astragalus. See Milk vetch

ray grass.d: A perennial European grass (Lolium perenne); -- called also rye grass, and red darnel. See Darnel, and Grass

razor-edged.d: having an edge as sharp as that of a razor; very sharp

razure.d: The act of erasing or effacing, or the state of being effaced; obliteration. See Rasure

re-ally.d: To bring together again; to compose or form anew

re-assail.d: To assail again; as, Her old fears reassailed her.  Usually used without the hyphen

re-attribute.d: To attribute to another source or cause.  Usually used without the hyphen

re-bind.d: To provide with a new binding, as of books.  Usually used without the hyphen

re-ferment.d: To ferment, or cause to ferment, again

re-ignite.d: To ignite anew, as of a fire

re-install.d: To install again; as, She reinstalled the the washer after it had been repaired

re-search.d: To search again; to examine anew

re-store.d: To store again; as, the goods taken out were re-stored

readeption.d: A regaining; recovery of something lost

readvertency.d: The act of adverting to again, or of reviewing

reaggravation.d: The last monitory, published after three admonitions and before the last excommunication

reanswer.d: To answer in return; to repay; to compensate; to make amends for

reassemblage.d: Assemblage a second time or again

reasty.d: Rusty and rancid; -- applied to salt meat

rebiting.d: The act or process of deepening worn lines in an etched plate by submitting it again to the action of acid

rebullition.d: The act of boiling up or effervescing

recadency.d: A falling back or descending a second time; a relapse

recapacitate.d: To qualify again; to confer capacity on again

recaptor.d: One who recaptures; one who takes a prize which had been previously taken

receiptment.d: The receiving or harboring a felon knowingly, after the commission of a felony

receivedness.d: The state or quality of being received, accepted, or current; as, the receivedness of an opinion

receptary.d: Generally or popularly admitted or received

rechase.d: To chase again; to chase or drive back

rechauffé.d: A dish of food that has been warmed again, hence, fig., something made up from old material; a rehash

recipiangle.d: An instrument with two arms that are pivoted together at one end, and a graduated arc, -- used by military engineers for measuring and laying off angles of fortifications

reciprocornous.d: Having horns turning backward and then forward, like those of a ram

reclusory.d: The habitation of a recluse; a hermitage

recoct.d: To boil or cook again; hence, to make over; to vamp up; to reconstruct

recognitor.d: One of a jury impaneled on an assize

recomforture.d: The act of recomforting; restoration of comfort

recompensive.d: Of the nature of recompense; serving to recompense

recompilement.d: The act of recompiling; new compilation or digest; as, a recompilement of the laws

reconcentrado.d: Lit., one who has been reconcentrated; specif., in Cuba, the Philippines, etc., during the revolution of 1895-98, one of the rural noncombatants who were concentrated by the military authorities in areas surrounding the fortified towns, and later were reconcentrated in the smaller limits of the towns themselves

recontinuance.d: The act or state of recontinuing

recorporification.d: The act of investing again with a body; the state of being furnished anew with a body

recouch.d: To retire again to a couch; to lie down again

recourseful.d: Having recurring flow and ebb; moving alternately

recoveror.d: The demandant in a common recovery after judgment

recrementitial.d: Of the nature of a recrement. See Recrement, 2 (b)

rectificator.d: That which rectifies or refines; esp., a part of a distilling apparatus in which the more volatile portions are separated from the less volatile by the process of evaporation and condensation; a rectifier

recto-vesical.d: Of or pertaining to both the rectum and the bladder

rectoral.d: Pertaining to a rector or governor

recumbence.d: The act of leaning, resting, or reclining; the state of being recumbent

recursant.d: Displayed with the back toward the spectator; -- said especially of an eagle

recurviroster.d: A bird whose beak bends upward, as the avocet

recussion.d: The act of beating or striking back

red-gum.d: An eruption of red pimples upon the face, neck, and arms, in early infancy; tooth rash; strophulus

red-hand.d: Having hands red with blood; in the very act, as if with red or bloody hands; -- said of a person taken in the act of homicide; hence, fresh from the commission of crime; as, he was taken red-hand or red-handed

red-riband.d: The European red band fish, or fireflame. See Rend fish

redargutory.d: Pertaining to, or containing, redargution; refutatory

redde.d: obs. imp. of Read, or Rede

redditive.d: Answering to an interrogative or inquiry; conveying a reply; as, redditive words

redemptionary.d: One who is, or may be, redeemed

redemptionist.d: A monk of an order founded in 1197; -- so called because the order was especially devoted to the redemption of Christians held in captivity by the Mohammedans. Called also Trinitarian

redhibitory.d: Of or pertaining to redhibition; as, a redhibitory action or fault

redhoop.d: The male of the European bullfinch

redhorn.d: Any species of a tribe of butterflies (Fugacia) including the common yellow species and the cabbage butterflies. The antennae are usually red

redisburse.d: To disburse anew; to give, or pay, back

redisseize.d: To disseize anew, or a second time

redisseizin.d: A disseizin by one who once before was adjudged to have dassezed the same person of the same lands, etc.; also, a writ which lay in such a case

redressless.d: Not having redress; such as can not be redressed; irremediable

redstreak.d: A kind of apple having the skin streaked with red and yellow, -- a favorite English cider apple

redub.d: To refit; to repair, or make reparation for; hence, to repay or requite

reduit.d: A central or retired work within any other work

reduvid.d: Any hemipterous insect of the genus Redivius, or family Reduvidae. They live by sucking the blood of other insects, and some species also attack man

redwithe.d: A west Indian climbing shrub (Combretum Jacquini) with slender reddish branchlets

reeden.d: Consisting of a reed or reeds

reedification.d: The act reedifying; the state of being reedified

reedless.d: Destitute of reeds; as, reedless banks

reedwork.d: A collective name for the reed stops of an organ

reef-band.d: A piece of canvas sewed across a sail to strengthen it in the part where the eyelet holes for reefing are made

reenforced concrete.d: Concrete having within its mass a system of iron or steel supports, such as bars, rods, or a heavy mesh, to provide increased tensile strength and shear resistance.  Same as Ferro-concrete

reenthrone.d: To enthrone again; to replace on a throne

refar.d: To go over again; to repeat

refel.d: To refute; to disprove; as, to refel the tricks of a sophister

reflexity.d: The state or condition of being reflected

reforestization.d: The act or process of reforestizing

reforestize.d: To convert again into a forest; to plant again with trees

reformado.d: A monk of a reformed order

reformalize.d: To affect reformation; to pretend to correctness

reformly.d: In the manner of a reform; for the purpose of reform

refortification.d: A fortifying anew, or a second time

refossion.d: The act of digging up again

refrication.d: A rubbing up afresh; a brightening

regalian.d: Pertaining to regalia; pertaining to the royal insignia or prerogatives

regardable.d: Worthy of regard or notice; to be regarded; observable

regeneratory.d: Having power to renew; tending to reproduce; regenerating

regent diamond.d: A famous diamond of fine quality, which weighs about 137 carats and is among the state jewels of France. It is so called from the Duke of Orleans, Regent of France, to whom it was sold in 1717 by Pitt the English Governor of Madras (whence also called the Pitt diamond), who bought it of an Indian merchant in 1701

regian.d: An upholder of kingly authority; a royalist

regidor.d: One of a body of officers charged with the government of Spanish municipalities, corresponding to the English alderman

regiminal.d: Of or relating to regimen; as, regiminal rules

regive.d: To give again; to give back

regratery.d: The act or practice of regrating

regratiatory.d: A returning or giving of thanks

regrede.d: To go back; to retrograde, as the apsis of a planet's orbit

regredience.d: A going back; a retrogression; a return

regulize.d: To reduce to regulus; to separate, as a metal from extraneous matter; as, to regulize antimony

rehibition.d: The returning of a thing purchased to the seller, on the ground of defect or frand

rehibitory.d: Of or relating to rehibition; as, a rehibitory action

reichsrath.d: The parliament of Austria (exclusive of Hungary, which has its own diet, or parliament). It consists of an Upper and a Lower House, or a House of Lords and a House of Representatives

reichsstand.d: A free city of the former German empire

reigle.d: A hollow cut or channel for quiding anything; as, the reigle of a side post for a flood gate

relativistic mass equation.d:
an equation expressing the mass of an object as a function of its velocity: as the velocity v of an object increases, its mass m increases from its rest mass m0 according to the equation:
   m = m0/1 - v2/c2

where c is the speed of light in a vacuum.  If the speed of an object were to become equal to that of light, it can be seen that the mass would be infinite, from which it follows that nothing can accelerate up to or beyond the speed of light

relay cylinder.d: In a variable expansion central-valve engine, a small auxiliary engine for automatically adjusting the steam distribution to the load on the main engine

relay governor.d: A speed regulator, as a water-wheel governor, embodying the relay principle

relbun.d: The roots of the Chilian plant Calceolaria arachnoidea, -- used for dyeing crimson

relentment.d: The act or process of relenting; the state of having relented

relievement.d: The act of relieving, or the state of being relieved; relief; release

reliquian.d: Of or pertaining to a relic or relics; of the nature of a relic

remainder-man.d: One who has an estate after a particular estate is determined. See Remainder, n., 3

remblai.d: Earth or materials made into a bank after having been excavated

remean.d: To give meaning to; to explain the meaning of; to interpret

rememorate.d: To recall something by means of memory; to remember

rememoration.d: A recalling by the faculty of memory; remembrance

remissful.d: Inclined to remit punishment; lenient; clement

remord.d: To excite to remorse; to rebuke

renal-portal.d: Both renal and portal. See Portal

renascible.d: Capable of being reproduced; ablle to spring again into being

rendible.d: Capable of being rent or torn

reneye.d: To deny; to reject; to renounce

renidification.d: The act of rebuilding a nest

reordain.d: To ordain again, as when the first ordination is considered defective

reperception.d: The act of perceiving again; a repeated perception of the same object

repudiable.d: Admitting of repudiation; fit or proper to be put away

repugnable.d: Capable of being repugned or resisted

reputeless.d: Not having good repute; disreputable; disgraceful; inglorius

requin.d: The man-eater, or white shark (Carcharodon carcharias); -- so called on account of its causing requiems to be sung

requisitor.d: One who makes reqisition; esp., one authorized by a requisition to investigate facts

rerefief.d: A fief held of a superior feudatory; a fief held by an under tenant

rescat.d: To ransom; to release; to rescue

rescribe.d: To write back; to write in reply

rescription.d: A writing back; the answering of a letter

rescriptive.d: Pertaining to, or answering the purpose of, a rescript; hence, deciding; settling; determining

rescussee.d: The party in whose favor a rescue is made

reseminate.d: To produce again by means of seed

reserve city.d: In the national banking system of the United States, any of certain cities in which the national banks are required (U. S. Rev. Stat. sec. 5191) to keep a larger reserve (25 per cent) than the minimum (15 per cent) required of all other banks. The banks in certain of the reserve cities (specifically called central reserve cities) are required to keep their reserve on hand in cash; banks in other reserve cities may keep half of their reserve as deposits in these banks (U. S. Rev. Stat. sec. 5195)

resinaceous.d: Having the quality of resin; resinous

resorcylic.d: Of, or pertaining to, or producing, resorcin; as, resorcylic acid

respection.d: The act of respecting; respect; regard

respectless.d: Having no respect; without regard; regardless

respersion.d: The act of sprinkling or scattering

respirative.d: Of or pertaining to respiration; as, respirative organs

ressaldar.d: In the Anglo-Indian army, a native commander of a ressala

restagnate.d: To stagnate; to cease to flow

restem.d: To force back against the current; as, to restem their backward course

restiness.d: The quality or state of being resty; sluggishness

restringe.d: To confine; to contract; to stringe

restringency.d: Quality or state of being restringent; astringency

resty.d: Disposed to rest; indisposed toexercton; sluggish; also, restive

resultance.d: The act of resulting; that which results; a result

resuscitant.d: One who, or that which resuscitates. Also used adjectively

retection.d: Act of disclosing or uncovering something concealed

revendicate.d: To reclaim; to demand the restoration of

revengeable.d: Capable of being revenged; as, revengeable wrong

rewel bone.d: An obsolete phrase of disputed meaning, -- perhaps, smooth or polished bone

rhabdocoelous.d: Of or pertaining to the Rhabdocoela

rhodammonium.d: Pertaining to, derived from, or containing, rhodium and ammonia; -- said of certain complex compounds

ricinic.d: Pertaining to, or derived from, castor oil; formerly, designating an acid now called ricinoleic acid

riden.d: imp. pl. & p. p. of Ride

right-lined.d: Formed by right lines; rectilineal; as, a right-lined angle

rigoll.d: A musical instrument formerly in use, consisting of several sticks bound together, but separated by beads, and played with a stick with a ball at its end

ringlestone.d: The ringed dotterel, or ring plover

riotry.d: The act or practice of rioting; riot

ritornelle.d: A short return or repetition; a concluding symphony to an air, often consisting of the burden of the song

riverhood.d: The quality or state of being a river

rivose.d: Marked with sinuate and irregular furrows

rixatrix.d: A scolding or quarrelsome woman; a scold

rixdaler.d: A Dutch silver coin, worth about $1.00

ro-setta stone.d: A stone found at Rosetta, in Egypt, bearing a trilingual inscription, by aid of which, with other inscriptions, a key was obtained to the hieroglyphics of ancient Egypt

rochelime.d: Lime in the lump after it is burned; quicklime

roching cask.d: A tank in which alum is crystallized from a solution

rolly-poly.d: A kind of pudding made of paste spread with fruit, rolled into a cylindrical form, and boiled or steamed

rolly-pooly.d: A game in which a ball, rolling into a certain place, wins

romajikai.d: An association, including both Japanese and Europeans, having for its object the changing of the Japanese method of writing by substituting Roman letters for Japanese characters.  Laso known as Hyojun Romajikai

romansch.d: The language of the Grisons in Switzerland, a corruption of the Latin

rombowline.d: Old, condemned canvas, rope, etc., unfit for use except in chafing gear

romeine.d: A mineral of a hyacinth or honey-yellow color, occuring in square octahedrons. It is an antimonate of calcium

rompu.d: Broken, as an ordinary; cut off, or broken at the top, as a chevron, a bend, or the like

ronchil.d: An American marine food fish (Bathymaster signatus) of the North Pacific coast, allied to the tilefish

rondache.d: A circular shield carried by foot soldiers

rondeletia.d: A tropical genus of rubiaceous shrubs which often have brilliant flowers

roosa oil.d: The East Indian name for grass oil. See under Grass

roostcock.d: The male of the domestic fowl; a cock

rootcap.d: A mass of parenchymatous cells which covers and protects the growing cells at the end of a root; a pileorhiza

rose-rial.d: A name of several English gold coins struck in different reigns and having having different values; a rose noble

rosemaloes.d: The liquid storax of the East Indian Liquidambar orientalis

roseo-.d: A prefix (also used adjectively) signifying rose-red; specifically used to designate certain rose-red compounds (called roseo-cobaltic compounds) of cobalt with ammonia.  Cf. Luteo-

roseworm.d: The larva of any one of several species of lepidopterous insects which feed upon the leaves, buds, or blossoms of the rose, especially Cacaecia rosaceana, which rolls up the leaves for a nest, and devours both the leaves and buds

rosland.d: heathy land; land full of heather; moorish or watery land

rosmarine.d: Dew from the sea; sea dew

rostelliform.d: Having the form of a rostellum, or small beak

rostrifera.d: A division of pectinibranchiate gastropods, having the head prolonged into a snout which is not retractile

rotal.d: Relating to wheels or to rotary motion; rotary

rotalite.d: Any fossil foraminifer of the genus Rotalia, abundant in the chalk formation. See Illust. under Rhizopod

roture.d: The condition of being a roturier

rouet.d: A small wheel formerly fixed to the pan of firelocks for discharging them

rouge dragon.d: One of the four pursuivants of the English college of arms

rougecroix.d: One of the four pursuivants of the English college of arms

rough-grained.d: Having a rough grain or fiber; hence, figuratively, having coarse traits of character; not polished; brisque

roughing-in.d: The first coat of plaster laid on brick; also, the process of applying it

roughsetter.d: A mason who builds rough stonework

roughstrings.d: Pieces of undressed timber put under the steps of a wooden stair for their support

roughwork.d: To work over coarsely, without regard to nicety, smoothness, or finish

roundaboutness.d: The quality of being roundabout; circuitousness

roundridge.d: To form into round ridges by plowing

routinary.d: Involving, or pertaining to, routine; ordinary; customary

routously.d: With that violation of law called a rout. See 5th Rout, 4
