roynish.d: Mangy; scabby; hence, mean; paltry; troublesome

ruba-dub.d: The sound of a drum when continuously beaten; hence, a clamorous, repeated sound; a clatter

rubelle.d: A red color used in enameling

ruberythrinic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid extracted from madder root. It is a yellow crystalline substance from which alizarin is obtained

rubiacin.d: A substance found in madder root, and probably identical with ruberythrinic acid

rubianic.d: pertaining to, or derived from, rubian; specifically, designating an acid called also ruberythrinic acid

rubiform.d: Having the nature or quality of red; as, the rubiform rays of the sun

rubiretin.d: One of the red dye products extracted from madder root, and probably identical with ruberythrinic acid

ruby-tailed.d: Having the tail, or lower part of the body, bright red

rucervine.d: Of, like, or pertaining to, a deer of the genus Rucervus, which includes the swamp deer of India

rudderhole.d: The hole in the deck through which the rudderpost passes

rudmasday.d: Either of the feasts of the Holy Cross, occuring on May 3 and September 14, annually

rudolphine.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a set of astronomical tables computed by Kepler, and founded on the observations of Tycho Brahe; -- so named from Rudolph II., emperor of Germany

ruedesheimer.d: A German wine made near Rüdesheim, on the Rhine

ruffianage.d: Ruffians, collectively; a body of ruffians

rufigallic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid which is obtained from gallic acid as a brown or red crystalline substance, and is related to rufiopin and anthracene

rufterhood.d: A kind of hood for a hawk

rug-gowned.d: Wearing a coarse gown or shaggy garment made of rug

ruiniform.d: Having the appearance of ruins, or of the ruins of houses; -- said of certain minerals

rule-monger.d: A stickler for rules; a slave of rules

rullichies.d: Chopped meat stuffed into small bags of tripe. They are cut in slices and fried

rumkin.d: A popular or jocular name for a drinking vessel

rump-fed.d: A Shakespearean word of uncertain meaning.  Perhaps “fattened in the rump, pampered.”

rumseller.d: One who sells rum; one who deals in intoxicating liquors; especially, one who sells spirituous beverages at retail

rundel.d: A moat with water in it; also, a small stream; a runlet

runghead.d: The upper end of a floor timber in a ship

running load.d: The air pressure supported by each longitudinal foot segment of a wing

rupert's drop.d: A kind of glass drop with a long tail, made by dropping melted glass into water. It is remarkable for bursting into fragments when the surface is scratched or the tail broken; -- so called from Prince Rupert, nephew of Charles I., by whom they were first brought to England. Called also Rupert's ball, and glass tear

ruption.d: A breaking or bursting open; breach; rupture

ruptuary.d: One not of noble blood; a plebeian; a roturier

rush-bearing.d: A kind of rural festival at the dedication of a church, when the parishioners brought rushes to strew the church

rushbuckler.d: A bullying and violent person; a braggart; a swashbuckler

rushiness.d: The quality or state of abounding with rushes

rusma.d: A depilatory made of orpiment and quicklime, and used by the Turks. See Rhusma

russian church.d: The established church of the Russian empire up to the revolution of 1917, at which time the ruling Communist party tried to suppress all religious worship.  The czar was the nominal head of the church, but he never claimed the right of deciding questions of theology and dogma. It still forms a portion, by far the largest, of the Orthodox (Eastern) Church and is governed by the Patriarch and the Holy Synod. In 1988 the church, with official approval, celebrated the 1000 year anniversary of the b

rustful.d: Full of rust; resembling rust; causing rust; rusty

ruta-baga.d: A kind of turnip commonly with a large and long or ovoid yellowish root; a Swedish turnip. See Turnip

rutic.d: Pertaining to, or obtained from, rue (Ruta); as, rutic acid, now commonly called capric acid

rutilate.d: To shine; to emit rays of light

rutilian.d: Any species of lamellicorn beetles belonging to Rutila and allied genera, as the spotted grapevine beetle (Pelidnota punctata)

rutterkin.d: An old crafty fox or beguiler -- a word of contempt

rutylene.d: A liquid hydrocarbon, C10H18, of the acetylene series.  It is produced artificially

sabbaton.d: A round-toed, armed covering for the feet, worn during a part of the sixteenth century in both military and civil dress

sabelloid.d: Like, or related to, the genus Sabella

sabotiere.d: A kind of freezer for ices

sabretasche.d: A leather case or pocket worn by cavalry at the left side, suspended from the sword belt

sabrina work.d: A variety of appliqué work for quilts, table covers, etc

saccharimetrical.d: Of or pertaining to saccharimetry; obtained by saccharimetry

saccharinic.d: Of, pertaining to, or derived from, saccharin; specifically, designating a complex acid not known in the free state but well known in its salts, which are obtained by boiling dextrose and levulose (invert sugar) with milk of lime

saccharone.d: A white crystalline substance, C6H8O6, obtained by the oxidation of saccharin, and regarded as the lactone of saccharonic acid

saccharonic.d: Of, pertaining to, or derived from, saccharone; specifically, designating an unstable acid which is obtained from saccharone (a) by hydration, and forms a well-known series of salts

saccholactate.d: A salt of saccholactic acid; -- formerly called also saccholate

saccholactic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid now called mucic acid; saccholic

sacchulmic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained as a dark amorphous substance by the long-continued boiling of sucrose with very dilute sulphuric acid. It resembles humic acid

sacchulmin.d: An amorphous huminlike substance resembling sacchulmic acid, and produced together with it

sacculo-cochlear.d: Pertaining to the sacculus and cochlea of the ear

sacculo-utricular.d: Pertaining to the sacculus and utriculus of the ear

sack-winged.d: Having a peculiar pouch developed near the front edge of the wing; -- said of certain bats of the genus Saccopteryx

sacrificable.d: Capable of being offered in sacrifice

sacrificator.d: A sacrificer; one who offers a sacrifice

sadducaic.d: Pertaining to, or like, the Sadducees; as, Sadducaic reasonings

sadducize.d: To adopt the principles of the Sadducees

saengerbund.d: A singers' union; an association of singers or singing clubs, esp. German

saengerfest.d: A festival of singers; a German singing festival

safe-keeping.d: The act of keeping or preserving in safety from injury or from escape; care; custody

safe-pledge.d: A surety for the appearance of a person at a given time

safety chain.d: A normally slack chain for preventing excessive movement between a truck and a car body in sluing

sagination.d: The act of fattening or pampering

sagus.d: A genus of palms from which sago is obtained

saint-simonism.d: A system of socialism in which the state owns all the property and the laborer is entitled to share according to the quality and  amount of his work, founded by Saint Simon (1760-1825); -- called also Saint- Simonianism

saintism.d: The character or quality of saints; also, hypocritical pretense of holiness

saintologist.d: One who writes the lives of saints

sakieh.d: A kind of water wheel used in Egypt for raising water, from wells or pits, in buckets attached to its periphery or to an endless rope

salagane.d: The esculent swallow. See under Esculent

salal-berry.d: The edible fruit of the Gaultheria Shallon, an ericaceous shrub found from California northwards. The berries are about the size of a common grape and of a dark purple color

salamandrina.d: A suborder of Urodela, comprising salamanders

salamstone.d: A kind of blue sapphire brought from Ceylon

salicylite.d: A compound of salicylal; -- named after the analogy of a salt

salicylous.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a substance formerly called salicylous acid, and now salicylal

salina period.d: The period in which the American Upper Silurian system, containing the brine-producing rocks of central New York, was formed. See the Chart of Geology

saliniform.d: Having the form or the qualities of a salt, especially of common salt

salisburia.d: The ginkgo tree (Ginkgo biloba, or Salisburia adiantifolia)

salmonet.d: A salmon of small size; a samlet

salso-acid.d: Having a taste compounded of saltness and acidity; both salt and acid

saltatorious.d: Capable of leaping; formed for leaping; saltatory; as, a saltatorious insect or leg

saltfoot.d: A large saltcellar formerly placed near the center of the table. The superior guests were seated above the saltfoot

saltigradae.d: A tribe of spiders including those which lie in wait and leap upon their prey; the leaping spiders; called also Salticidae

salvatory.d: A place where things are preserved; a repository

salver-shaped.d: Tubular, with a spreading border. See Hypocraterimorphous

samoyedes.d: An ignorant and degraded Turanian tribe which occupies a portion of Northern Russia and a part of Siberia

samshoo.d: A spirituous liquor distilled by the Chinese from the yeasty liquor in which boiled rice has fermented under pressure

sanability.d: The quality or state of being sanable; sanableness; curableness

sanable.d: Capable of being healed or cured; susceptible of remedy

sanation.d: The act of healing or curing

sancho pedro.d: A variety of auction pitch in which the nine (sancho) and five (pedro) of trumps are added as counting cards at their pip value, and the ten of trumps counts game

sanctifyingly.d: In a manner or degree tending to sanctify or make holy

sanctiloquent.d: Discoursing on heavenly or holy things, or in a holy manner

sandaliform.d: Shaped like a sandal or slipper

sandemanian.d: A follower of Robert Sandeman, a Scotch sectary of the eighteenth century. See Glassite

sandemanianism.d: The faith or system of the Sandemanians

sandnecker.d: A European flounder (Hippoglossoides limandoides); -- called also rough dab, long fluke, sand fluke, and sand sucker

sanhita.d: A collection of vedic hymns, songs, or verses, forming the first part of each Veda

sankha.d: A chank shell (Turbinella pyrum); also, a shell bracelet or necklace made in India from the chank shell

sans-culotte.d: A fellow without breeches; a ragged fellow; -- a name of reproach given in the first French revolution to the extreme republican party, who rejected breeches as an emblem peculiar to the upper classes or aristocracy, and adopted pantaloons

sans-culottic.d: Pertaining to, or involving, sans-culottism; radical; revolutionary; Jacobinical

sans-culottism.d: Extreme republican principles; the principles or practice of the sans-culottes

santalic.d: Of, pertaining to, or obtained from, sandalwood (Santalum); -- used specifically to designate an acid obtained as a resinous or red crystalline dyestuff, which is called also santalin

santonic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid (distinct from santoninic acid) obtained from santonin as a white crystalline substance

santoninic.d: Of or pertaining to santonin; -- used specifically to designate an acid not known in the free state, but obtained in its salts

sapan wood.d: A dyewood yielded by Caesalpinia Sappan, a thorny leguminous tree of Southern Asia and the neighboring islands. It is the original Brazil wood

saponacity.d: The quality or state of being saponaceous

saponul.d: A soapy mixture obtained by treating an essential oil with an alkali; hence, any similar compound of an essential oil

saporific.d: Having the power to produce the sensation of taste; producing taste, flavor, or relish

saporosity.d: The quality of a body by which it excites the sensation of taste

saprophagan.d: One of a tribe of beetles which feed upon decaying animal and vegetable substances; a carrion beetle

sarabaite.d: One of certain vagrant or heretical Oriental monks in the early church

sarcel.d: One of the outer pinions or feathers of the wing of a bird, esp. of a hawk

sarcolactic.d: Relating to muscle and milk; as, sarcolactic acid. See Lactic acid, under Lactic

sarcophagan.d: Any animal which eats flesh, especially any carnivorous marsupial

sarcorhamphi.d: A division of raptorial birds comprising the vultures

sarcoseptum.d: One of the mesenteries of an anthozoan

sarcosin.d: A crystalline nitrogenous substance, formed in the decomposition of creatin (one of the constituents of muscle tissue). Chemically, it is methyl glycocoll

sarculation.d: A weeding, as with a hoe or a rake

sarigue.d: A small South American opossum (Didelphys opossum), having four white spots on the face

sarpo.d: A large toadfish of the Southern United States and the Gulf of Mexico (Batrachus tau, var. pardus)

sarum use.d: A liturgy, or use, put forth about 1087 by St. Osmund, bishop of Sarum, based on Anglo-Saxon and Norman customs

sashery.d: A collection of sashes; ornamentation by means of sashes

sassarara.d: A word used to emphasize a statement

sassorol.d: The rock pigeon. See under Pigeon

satellitious.d: Pertaining to, or consisting of, satellites

satrapal.d: Of or pertaining to a satrap, or a satrapy

satsuma ware.d: A kind of ornamental hard-glazed pottery made at Satsuma in Kiushu, one of the Japanese islands

saturity.d: The state of being saturated; fullness of supply

saturnicentric.d: Appearing as if seen from the center of the planet Saturn; relating or referred to Saturn as a center

saturnist.d: A person of a dull, grave, gloomy temperament

satyrion.d: Any one of several kinds of orchids

sauba ant.d: A South American ant (Oecodoma cephalotes) remarkable for having two large kinds of workers besides the ordinary ones, and for the immense size of its formicaries. The sauba ant cuts off leaves of plants and carries them into its subterranean nests, and thus often does great damage by defoliating trees and cultivated plants

saulie.d: A hired mourner at a funeral

saunders-blue.d: A kind of color prepared from calcined lapis lazuli; ultramarine; also, a blue prepared from carbonate of copper

saurognathous.d: Having the bones of the palate arranged as in saurians, the vomer consisting of two lateral halves, as in the woodpeckers (Pici)

sauroidichnite.d: The fossil track of a saurian

saururae.d: An extinct order of birds having a long vertebrated tail with quills along each side of it. Archaeopteryx is the type. See Archaeopteryx, and Odontornithes

saw-set.d: An instrument used to set or turn the teeth of a saw a little sidewise, that they may make a kerf somewhat wider than the thickness of the blade, to prevent friction; -- called also saw-wrest

saw-whet.d: A small North American owl (Nyctale Acadica), destitute of ear tufts and having feathered toes; -- called also Acadian owl

saw-wort.d: Any plant of the composite genus Serratula; -- so named from the serrated leaves of most of the species

sax-tuba.d: A powerful instrument of brass, curved somewhat like the Roman buccina, or tuba

saxicava.d: Any species of marine bivalve shells of the genus Saxicava. Some of the species are noted for their power of boring holes in limestone and similar rocks

saxicavid.d: Of or pertaining to the saxicavas

saxifragous.d: Dissolving stone, especially dissolving stone in the bladder

saxonic.d: Relating to the Saxons or Anglo- Saxons

saxony yarn.d: A fine grade of woolen yarn twisted somewhat harder and smoother than zephyr yarn

sayette.d: A mixed stuff, called also sagathy. See Sagathy

saymaster.d: A master of assay; one who tries or proves

saynd.d: p. p. of Senge, to singe

scalaria.d: Any one of numerous species of marine gastropods of the genus Scalaria, or family Scalaridae, having elongated spiral turreted shells, with rounded whorls, usually crossed by ribs or varices. The color is generally white or pale. Called also ladder shell, and wentletrap. See Ptenoglossa, and Wentletrap

scalary.d: Resembling a ladder; formed with steps

scale-winged.d: Having the wings covered with small scalelike structures, as the Lepidoptera; scaly-winged

scaleback.d: Any one of numerous species of marine annelids of the family Polynoidae, and allies, which have two rows of scales, or elytra, along the back. See Illust. under Chaetopoda

scalebeam.d: The lever or beam of a balance; the lever of a platform scale, to which the poise for weighing is applied

scamblingly.d: In a scambling manner; with turbulence and noise; with bold intrusiveness

scampavia.d: A long, low war galley used by the Neapolitans and Sicilians in the early part of the nineteenth century

scansores.d: An artifical group of birds formerly regarded as an order. They are distributed among several orders by modern ornithologists

scantlet.d: A small pattern; a small quantity

scape-wheel.d: The wheel in an escapement (as of a clock or a watch) into the teeth of which the pallets play

scapegallows.d: One who has narrowly escaped the gallows for his crimes

scaphism.d: An ancient mode of punishing criminals among the Persians, by confining the victim in a trough, with his head and limbs smeared with honey or the like, and exposed to the sun and to insects until he died

scarmage.d: A slight contest; a skirmish. See Skirmish

scatch.d: A kind of bit for the bridle of a horse; -- called also scatchmouth

scatter-brain.d: A giddy or thoughtless person; one incapable of concentration or attention

scatterling.d: One who has no fixed habitation or residence; a vagabond

scavage.d: A toll or duty formerly exacted of merchant strangers by mayors, sheriffs, etc., for goods shown or offered for sale within their precincts

scepterellate.d: Having a straight shaft with whorls of spines; -- said of certain sponge spicules. See Illust. under Spicule

schediasm.d: Cursory writing on a loose sheet

schematist.d: One given to forming schemes; a projector; a schemer

schene.d: An Egyptian or Persian measure of length, varying from thirty-two to sixty stadia

schetic.d: Of or pertaining to the habit of the body; constitutional

schisma.d: An interval equal to half a comma

schizocoelous.d: Pertaining to, or of the nature of, a schizocoele

schizognath.d: Any bird with a schizognathous palate

schlich.d: The finer portion of a crushed ore, as of gold, lead, or tin, separated by the water in certain wet processes

schmelze.d: A kind of glass of a red or ruby color, made in Bohemia

schneiderian.d: Discovered or described by C. V. Schneider, a German anatomist of the seventeenth century

schoharie grit.d: The formation belonging to the middle of the three subdivisions of the Corniferous period in the American Devonian system; -- so called from Schoharie, in New York, where it occurs. See the Chart of Geology

schorly.d: Pertaining to, or containing, schorl; as, schorly granite

schwenkfelder.d: A member of a religious sect founded by Kaspar von Schwenkfeld, a Silesian reformer who disagreed with Luther, especially on the deification of the body of Christ

scincoidea.d: A tribe of lizards including the skinks. See Skink

scincoidian.d: Any one of numerous species of lizards of the family Scincidae or tribe Scincoidea. The tongue is not extensile. The body and tail are covered with overlapping scales, and the toes are margined. See Illust. under Skink

sciot.d: Of or pertaining to the island Scio (Chio or Chios)

sciotheric.d: Of or pertaining to a sundial

sciscitation.d: The act of inquiring; inquiry; demand

scissible.d: Capable of being cut or divided by a sharp instrument

scissors-tailed.d: Having the outer feathers much the longest, the others decreasing regularly to the median ones

scitamineous.d: Of or pertaining to a natural order of plants (Scitamineae), mostly tropical herbs, including the ginger, Indian shot, banana, and the plants producing turmeric and arrowroot

sclerodermic.d: Having the integument, or skin, hard, or covered with hard plates

scoffery.d: The act of scoffing; scoffing conduct; mockery

scoley.d: To go to school; to study

scolithus.d: A tubular structure found in Potsdam sandstone, and believed to be the fossil burrow of a marine worm

scombriformes.d: A division of fishes including the mackerels, tunnies, and allied fishes

scomfish.d: To suffocate or stifle; to smother

scopeloid.d: Like or pertaining to fishes of the genus Scopelus, or family Scopelodae, which includes many small oceanic fishes, most of which are phosphorescent

scopiferous.d: Bearing a tuft of brushlike hairs

scopuliped.d: Any species of bee which has on the hind legs a brush of hairs used for collecting pollen, as the hive bees and bumblebees

scorpene.d: A marine food fish of the genus Scorpaena, as the European hogfish (Scorpaena scrofa), and the California species (Scorpaena guttata)

scorpionwort.d: A leguminous plant (Ornithopus scorpioides) of Southern Europe, having slender curved pods

scortatory.d: Pertaining to lewdness or fornication; lewd

scotal.d: The keeping of an alehouse by an officer of a forest, and drawing people to spend their money for liquor, for fear of his displeasure

scotch rite.d: The ceremonial observed by one of the Masonic systems, called in full the Ancient and Accepted Scotch Rite; also, the system itself, which confers thirty-three degrees, of which the first three are nearly identical with those of the York rite

scottering.d: The burning of a wad of pease straw at the end of harvest

scovel.d: A mop for sweeping ovens; a malkin

scrabbed eggs.d: A Lenten dish, composed of eggs boiled hard, chopped, and seasoned with butter, salt, and pepper

scraffle.d: To scramble or struggle; to wrangle; also, to be industrious

scraggedness.d: Quality or state of being scragged

scrapepenny.d: One who gathers and hoards money in trifling sums; a miser

scratch coat.d: The first coat in plastering; -- called also scratchwork. See Pricking-up

scratch player.d: One that starts from the scratch; hence, one of first-rate ability

screw-cutting.d: Adapted for forming a screw by cutting; as, a screw-cutting lathe

scribable.d: Capable of being written, or of being written upon

scribatious.d: Skillful in, or fond of, writing

scribism.d: The character and opinions of a Jewish scribe in the time of Christ

scrine.d: A chest, bookcase, or other place, where writings or curiosities are deposited; a shrine

scrippage.d: The contents of a scrip, or wallet

scriptory.d: Of or pertaining to writing; expressed in writing; used in writing; as, scriptory wills; a scriptory reed

scripturalism.d: The quality or state of being scriptural; literal adherence to the Scriptures

scripturalist.d: One who adheres literally to the Scriptures

scripturist.d: One who is strongly attached to, or versed in, the Scriptures, or who endeavors to regulate his life by them

scrobicular.d: Pertaining to, or surrounding, scrobiculae; as, scrobicular tubercles

scroddled ware.d: Mottled pottery made from scraps of differently colored clays

scrupulize.d: To perplex with scruples; to regard with scruples

scruze.d: To squeeze, compress, crush, or bruise

scuddle.d: To run hastily; to hurry; to scuttle

sculptile.d: Formed by carving; graven; as, sculptile images

scutelliplantar.d: Having broad scutella on the front, and small scales on the posterior side, of the tarsus; -- said of certain birds

scutibranchiata.d: An order of gastropod Mollusca having a heart with two auricles and one ventricle. The shell may be either spiral or shieldlike

scutibranchiate.d: Having the gills protected by a shieldlike shell; of or pertaining to the Scutibranchiata

scutiped.d: Having the anterior surface of the tarsus covered with scutella, or transverse scales, in the form of incomplete bands terminating at a groove on each side; -- said of certain birds

scyle.d: To hide; to secrete; to conceal

scyllaea.d: A genus of oceanic nudibranchiate mollusks having the small branched gills situated on the upper side of four fleshy lateral lobes, and on the median caudal crest

scyphobranchii.d: An order of fishes including the blennioid and gobioid fishes, and other related families

scyphophori.d: An order of fresh-water fishes inhabiting tropical Africa. They have rudimentary electrical organs on each side of the tail

scythewhet.d: Wilson's thrush; -- so called from its note

sea adder.d: The European fifteen-spined stickleback (Gasterosteus spinachia); -- called also bismore

sea apple.d: The fruit of a West Indian palm (Manicaria Plukenetii), often found floating in the sea

sea arrow.d: A squid of the genus Ommastrephes. See Squid

sea bear.d: Any fur seal. See under Fur

sea beast.d: Any large marine mammal, as a seal, walrus, or cetacean

sea blite.d: A plant (Suaeda maritima) of the Goosefoot family, growing in salt marshes

sea breach.d: A breaking or overflow of a bank or a dike by the sea

sea chart.d: A chart or map on which the lines of the shore, islands, shoals, harbors, etc., are delineated

sea chickweed.d: A fleshy plant (Arenaria peploides) growing in large tufts in the sands of the northern Atlantic seacoast; -- called also sea sandwort, and sea purslane

sea clam.d: Any one of the large bivalve mollusks found on the open seacoast, especially those of the family Mactridae, as the common American species. (Mactra solidissima or Spisula solidissima); -- called also beach clam, and surf clam

sea cock.d: In a steamship, a cock or valve close to the vessel's side, for closing a pipe which communicates with the sea

sea cocoa.d: A magnificent palm (Lodoicea Sechellarum) found only in the Seychelles Islands. The fruit is an immense two-lobed nut. It was found floating in the Indian Ocean before the tree was known, and called sea cocoanut, and double cocoanut

sea colander.d: A large blackfish seaweed (Agarum Turneri), the frond of which is punctured with many little holes

sea compass.d: The mariner's compass. See under Compass

sea corn.d: A yellow cylindrical mass of egg capsules of certain species of whelks (Buccinum), which resembles an ear of maize

sea dove.d: The little auk, or rotche. See Illust. of Rotche

sea fern.d: Any gorgonian which branches like a fern

sea fir.d: A sertularian hydroid, especially Sertularia abietina, which branches like a miniature fir tree

sea flower.d: A sea anemone, or any related anthozoan

sea fowl.d: Any bird which habitually frequents the sea, as an auk, gannet, gull, tern, or petrel; also, all such birds, collectively

sea gherkin.d: Any small holothurian resembling in form a gherkin

sea ginger.d: A hydroid coral of the genus Millepora, especially Millepora alcicornis, of the West Indies and Florida.  So called because it stings the tongue like ginger. See Illust. under Millepore

sea girdles.d: A kind of kelp (Laminaria digitata) with palmately cleft fronds; -- called also sea wand, seaware, and tangle

sea goddess.d: A goddess supposed to live in or reign over the sea, or some part of the sea

sea gown.d: A gown or frock with short sleeves, formerly worn by mariners

sea heath.d: A low perennial plant (Frankenia laevis) resembling heath, growing along the seashore in Europe

sea hen.d: The common guillemot; -- applied also to various other sea birds

sea laces.d: A kind of seaweed (Chorda Filum) having blackish cordlike fronds, often many feet long

sea lemon.d: Any one of several species of nudibranchiate mollusks of the genus Doris and allied genera, having a smooth, thick, convex yellow body

sea leopard.d: Any one of several species of spotted seals, especially Ogmorhinus leptonyx, and Leptonychotes Weddelli, of the Antarctic Ocean. The North Pacific sea leopard is the harbor seal

sea marge.d: Land which borders on the sea; the seashore

sea mud.d: A rich slimy deposit in salt marshes and along the seashore, sometimes used as a manure; -- called also sea ooze

sea orange.d: A large American holothurian (Lophothuria Fabricii) having a bright orange convex body covered with finely granulated scales.  Its expanded tentacles are bright red

sea partridge.d: The gilthead (Crenilabrus melops), a fish of the British coasts

sea pass.d: A document carried by neutral merchant vessels in time of war, to show their nationality; a sea letter or passport. See Passport

sea peach.d: A beautiful American ascidian (Cynthia pyriformis syn. Halocynthia pyriformis) having the size, form, velvety surface, and color of a ripe peach

sea pear.d: A pedunculated ascidian of the genus Boltonia

sea perch.d: The European bass (Roccus lupus syn. Labrax lupus); -- called also sea dace

sea pie.d: The oyster catcher, a limicoline bird of the genus Haematopus

sea porcupine.d: Any fish of the genus Diodon, and allied genera, whose body is covered with spines. See Illust. under Diodon

sea pork.d: An American compound ascidian (Amoroecium stellatum) which forms large whitish masses resembling salt pork

sea reed.d: The sea-sand reed. See under Reed

sea saurian.d: Any marine saurian; esp. (Paleon.), the large extinct species of Mosasaurus, Ichthyosaurus, Plesiosaurus, and related genera

sea scurf.d: Any bryozoan which forms rounded or irregular patches of coral on stones, seaweeds, etc

sea snipe.d: A sandpiper, as the knot and dunlin

sea term.d: A term used specifically by seamen; a nautical word or phrase

sea thongs.d: A kind of blackish seaweed (Himanthalia lorea) found on the northern coasts of the Atlantic. It has a thonglike forking process rising from a top-shaped base

sea trumpet.d: A great blackish seaweed of the Southern Ocean, having a hollow and expanding stem and a pinnate frond, sometimes twenty feet long

sea turn.d: A breeze, gale, or mist from the sea

sea willow.d: A gorgonian coral with long flexible branches

sea withwind.d: A kind of bindweed (Convolvulus Soldanella) growing on the seacoast of Europe

sea-bordering.d: Bordering on the sea; situated beside the sea

sea-built.d: Built at, in, or by the sea

sea-gate.d: A long, rolling swell of the sea

sea-island.d: Of or pertaining to certain islands along the coast of South Carolina and Georgia; as, sea-island cotton, a superior cotton of long fiber produced on those islands

sea-roving.d: Cruising at random on the ocean

sea-walled.d: Surrounded, bounded, or protected by the sea, as if by a wall

seabeard.d: A green seaweed (Cladophora rupestris) growing in dense tufts

seaboat.d: A boat or vessel adapted to the open sea; hence, a vessel considered with reference to her power of resisting a storm, or maintaining herself in a heavy sea; as, a good sea boat

seah.d: A Jewish dry measure containing one third of an ephah

seal-brown.d: Of a rich dark brown color, like the fur of the fur seal after it is dyed

seannachie.d: A bard among the Highlanders of Scotland, who preserved and repeated the traditions of the tribes; also, a genealogist

searedness.d: The state of being seared or callous; insensibility

starmonger.d: A fortune teller; an astrologer; -- used in contempt

starost.d: A nobleman who possessed a starosty

starosty.d: A castle and domain conferred on a nobleman for life

starproof.d: Impervious to the light of the stars; as, a starproof elm

starthroat.d: Any humming bird of the genus Heliomaster.  The feathers of the throat have a brilliant metallic luster

startingly.d: By sudden fits or starts; spasmodically

startish.d: Apt to start; skittish; shy; -- said especially of a horse

startlish.d: Easily startled; apt to start; startish; skittish; -- said especially of a horse

statemonger.d: One versed in politics, or one who dabbles in state affairs

states-general.d: In France, before the Revolution, the assembly of the three orders of the kingdom, namely, the clergy, the nobility, and the third estate, or commonalty

statocracy.d: Government by the state, or by political power, in distinction from government by ecclesiastical power

stavewood.d: A tall tree (Simaruba amara) growing in tropical America. It is one of the trees which yields quassia

staymaker.d: One whose occupation is to make stays

stayship.d: A remora, -- fabled to stop ships by attaching itself to them

stearolic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid of the acetylene series, isologous with stearic acid, and obtained, as a white crystalline substance, from oleic acid

steatomatous.d: Of the nature of a steatoma

steelbow goods.d: Those goods on a farm, such as corn, cattle, implements of husbandry, etc., which may not be carried off by a removing tenant, as being the property of the landlord

steep-down.d: Deep and precipitous; having steep descent

steganographist.d: One skilled in steganography; a cryptographer

steganophthalmata.d: The Discophora, or Phanerocarpae. Called also Steganophthalmia

steganopodous.d: Having all four toes webbed together

stegocephala.d: An extinct order of amphibians found fossil in the Mesozoic rocks; called also Stegocephali, and Labyrinthodonta

stelene.d: Resembling, or used as, a stela; columnar

stellerida.d: An extensive group of echinoderms, comprising the starfishes and ophiurans

stellion.d: A lizard (Stellio vulgaris), common about the Eastern Mediterranean among ruins. In color it is olive-green, shaded with black, with small stellate spots. Called also hardim, and star lizard

stelography.d: The art of writing or inscribing characters on pillars

stem-clasping.d: Embracing the stem with its base; amplexicaul, as a leaf or petiole

stenoderm.d: Any species of bat belonging to the genus Stenoderma, native of the West Indies and South America. These bats have a short or rudimentary tail and a peculiarly shaped nose membrane

stenodermine.d: Of or pertaining to the genus Stenoderma, which includes several West Indian and South American nose-leaf bats

stenostome.d: Having a small or narrow mouth; -- said of certain small ground snakes (Opoterodonta), which are unable to dilate their jaws

stercoranism.d: The doctrine or belief of the Stercoranists

stercoranist.d: A nickname formerly given to those who held, or were alleged to hold, that the consecrated elements in the eucharist undergo the process of digestion in the body of the recipient

stercorianism.d: The doctrine or belief of the Stercoranists

stereo-chemic.d: Pertaining to, or illustrating, the hypothetical space relations of atoms in the molecule; as, a stereo-chemic formula

stereo-chemistry.d: Chemistry considered with reference to the space relations of atoms

stereoelectric.d: Of or pertaining to the generation of electricity by means of solid bodies alone; as, a stereoelectric current is one obtained by means of solids, without any liquid

stereotypery.d: The art, process, or employment of making stereotype plates

stereotypography.d: The act or art of printing from stereotype plates

stern-wheel.d: Having a paddle wheel at the stern; as, a stern-wheel steamer

sternocoracoid.d: Of or pertaining to the sternum and the coracoid

sterquilinous.d: Pertaining to a dunghill; hence, mean; dirty; paltry

sterrink.d: The crab-eating seal (Lobodon carcinophaga) of the Antarctic Ocean

sterve.d: To die, or cause to die; to perish. See Starve

stethal.d: One of the higher alcohols of the methane series, homologous with ethal, and found in small quantities as an ethereal salt of stearic acid in spermaceti

stewardly.d: In a manner, or with the care, of a steward

stian.d: A sty on the eye. See Styan

sticcado.d: An instrument consisting of small bars of wood, flat at the bottom and rounded at the top, and resting on the edges of a kind of open box. They are unequal in size, gradually increasing from the smallest to the largest, and are tuned to the diatonic scale. The tones are produced by striking the pieces of wood with hard balls attached to flexible sticks

stichomancy.d: Divination by lines, or passages of books, taken at hazard

stick-seed.d: A plant (Echinospermum Lappula) of the Borage family, with small blue flowers and prickly nutlets

stick-tight.d: any of several plants having seeds tipped with barbs that may cling to fur or clothing, especially those of the genus Bidens, also called bur marigold, beggar-ticks, and Beggar's ticks, which have prickly flattened achenes

stiddy.d: An anvil; also, a smith shop. See Stithy

stiff-neckedness.d: The quality or state of being stiff-necked; stubbornness

stigonomancy.d: Divination by writing on the bark of a tree

stilar.d: Of or pertaining to the style of a dial

still wine.d: a table wine which is not effervescent; a non-sparkling wine

still-burn.d: To burn in the process of distillation; as, to still-burn brandy

stillatitious.d: Falling in drops; drawn by a still

stillatory.d: An alembic; a vessel for distillation

stillion.d: A stand, as for casks or vats in a brewery, or for pottery while drying

stiltify.d: To raise upon stilts, or as upon stilts; to stilt

stilton cheese.d: A peculiarly flavored unpressed cheese made from milk with cream added; -- so called from the village or parish of Stilton, England, where it was originally made. It is very rich in fat

stimulism.d: The theory of medical practice which regarded life as dependent upon stimulation, or excitation, and disease as caused by excess or deficiency in the amount of stimulation

sting ray.d: Any one of numerous rays of the family Dasyatidae, syn. Trygonidae, having one or more large sharp barbed dorsal spines, on the whiplike tail, capable of inflicting severe wounds. Some species reach a large size, and some, esp., on the American Pacific coast, are very destructive to oysters

stipendiate.d: To provide with a stipend, or salary; to support; to pay

stirrage.d: The act of stirring; stir; commotion

stirte.d: imp. of Start, v. i. & t

stock-blind.d: Blind as a stock; wholly blind

stockdove.d: A common European wild pigeon (Columba aenas), so called because at one time believed to be the stock of the domestic pigeon, or, according to some, from its breeding in the stocks, or trunks, of trees

stomapoda.d: An order of Crustacea including the squillas. The maxillipeds are leglike in form, and the large claws are comblike. They have a large and elongated abdomen, which contains a part of the stomach and heart; the abdominal appendages are large, and bear the gills. Called also Gastrula, Stomatopoda, and Squilloidea

stomatoda.d: A division of Protozoa in which a mouthlike opening exists

stomatode.d: Having a mouth; -- applied to certain Protozoa

stomatopodous.d: Of or pertaining to the Stomatopoda

stonebird.d: The yellowlegs; -- called also stone snipe. See Tattler, 2

stonebrearer.d: A machine for crushing or hammering stone

stoneroot.d: A North American plant (Collinsonia Canadensis) having a very hard root; horse balm. See Horse balm, under Horse

stonerunner.d: The ring plover, or the ringed dotterel

stopping-out.d: A method adopted in etching, to keep the acid from those parts which are already sufficiently corroded, by applying varnish or other covering matter with a brush, but allowing the acid to act on the other parts

stopship.d: A remora. It was fabled to stop ships by attaching itself to them

storge.d: Parental affection; the instinctive affection which animals have for their young

stork-billed.d: Having a bill like that of the stork

storm-beat.d: Beaten, injured, or impaired by storms

stormglass.d: A glass vessel, usually cylindrical, filled with a solution which is sensitive to atmospheric changes, indicating by a clouded appearance, rain, snow, etc., and by clearness, fair weather

stormwind.d: A heavy wind; a wind that brings a storm; the blast of a storm

story-writer.d: One who writes short stories, as for magazines

stovain.d: A substance, C14H22O2NCl, the hydrochloride of an amino compound containing benzol, used, in solution with strychnine, as a local anaesthetic, esp. by injection into the sheath of the spinal cord, producing anaesthesia below the point of introduction.  Called also amylocaine hydrochloride.  Chemically it is the hydrochloride of the benzoyl ester of 1-(dimethylaminomethyl)-1-methyl propanol

stradometrical.d: Of, or relating to, the measuring of streets or roads

straight-pight.d: Straight in form or upright in position; erect

stramazoun.d: A direct descending blow with the edge of a sword

strangle hold.d: a hold by which one's opponent is choked. It is usually not allowed

strap-shaped.d: Shaped like a strap; ligulate; as, a strap-shaped corolla

strapple.d: To hold or bind with, or as with, a strap; to entangle

stratarithmetry.d: The art of drawing up an army, or any given number of men, in any geometrical figure, or of estimating or expressing the number of men in such a figure

strato-cumulus.d: Large balls or rolls of dark cloud which frequently cover the whole sky, esp. in winter, and give it at times an undulated appearance

stratonic.d: Of or pertaining to an army

straw-cutter.d: An instrument to cut straw for fodder

stream clock.d: An instrument for ascertaining the velocity of the blood in a vessel

stream gold.d: Gold in alluvial deposits; placer gold

stream wheel.d: A wheel used for measuring, by its motion when submerged, the velocity of flowing water; a current wheel

streamful.d: Abounding in streams, or in water

strelitz.d: A soldier of the ancient Muscovite guard or Russian standing army; also, the guard itself

strengthful.d: Abounding in strength; full of strength; strong

strepitores.d: A division of birds, including the clamatorial and picarian birds, which do not have well developed singing organs

strepsorhine.d: Having twisted nostrils; -- said of the lemurs

streptoneura.d: An extensive division of gastropod Mollusca in which the loop or visceral nerves is twisted, and the sexes separate. It is nearly to equivalent to Prosobranchiata

striges.d: The tribe of birds which comprises the owls

strigine.d: Of or pertaining to owls; owl-like

strigment.d: Scraping; that which is scraped off

strisores.d: A division of passerine birds including the humming birds, swifts, and goatsuckers. It is now generally considered an artificial group

strobiline.d: Of or pertaining to a strobile; strobilaceous; strobiliform; as, strobiline fruits

strombite.d: A fossil shell of the genus Strombus

structural shape.d: The shape of a member especially adapted to structural purposes, esp. in giving the greatest strength with the least material

strull.d: A bar so placed as to resist weight

strumstrum.d: A rude musical instrument somewhat like a cittern

struntian.d: A kind of worsted braid, about an inch broad

struse.d: A Russian river craft used for transporting freight

struthiones.d: A division, or order, of birds, including only the African ostriches

stryphnic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a complex nitrogenous acid, obtained by the action of acetic acid and potassium nitrite on uric acid, as a yellow crystalline substance, with a bitter, astringent taste

stuckle.d: A number of sheaves set together in the field; a stook

stud-horse.d: A stallion, esp. one kept for breeding

studdery.d: A stud, or collection of breeding horses and mares; also, a place for keeping a stud

stulp.d: A short, stout post used for any purpose, a to mark a boundary

stultiloquent.d: Given to, or characterized by, silly talk; babbling

stundist.d: One of a large sect of Russian dissenters founded, about 1860, in the village of Osnova, near Odessa, by a peasant, Onishchenko, who had apparently been influenced by a German sect settled near there. They zealously practice Bible reading and reject priestly dominion and all external rites of worship

stupration.d: Violation of chastity by force; rape

sturiones.d: An order of fishes including the sturgeons

sturionian.d: One of the family of fishes of which the sturgeon is the type

sturnoid.d: Like or pertaining to the starlings

styca.d: An anglo-Saxon copper coin of the lowest value, being worth half a farthing

stycerin.d: A triacid alcohol, related to glycerin, and obtained from certain styryl derivatives as a yellow, gummy, amorphous substance; -- called also phenyl glycerin

stylagalmaic.d: Performing the office of columns; as, Atlantes and Caryatides are stylagalmaic figures or images

stylaster.d: Any one of numerous species of delicate, usually pink, calcareous hydroid corals of the genus Stylaster

styloglossal.d: Of or pertaining to styloid process and the tongue

styphnic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, a yellow crystalline astringent acid, (NO2)3.C6H.(OH)2, obtained by the action of nitric acid on resorcin. Styphnic acid resembles picric acid, but is not bitter. It acts like a strong dibasic acid, having a series of well defined salts

suant.d: Spread equally over the surface; uniform; even

sub-bass.d: The deepest pedal stop, or the lowest tones of an organ; the fundamental or ground bass

subaction.d: The act of reducing to any state, as of mixing two bodies combletely

subah.d: A province; a government, as of a viceroy; also, a subahdar

subahdary.d: The office or jurisdiction of a subahdar

subaid.d: To aid secretly; to assist in a private manner, or indirectly

subapennine.d: Under, or at the foot of, the Apennine mountains; -- applied, in geology, to a series of Tertiary strata of the older Pliocene period

subarration.d: The ancient custom of betrothing by the bestowal, on the part of the man, of marriage gifts or tokens, as money, rings, or other presents, upon the woman

subarytenoid.d: Situated under the arytenoid cartilage of the larynx

subaud.d: To understand or supply in an ellipsis

subbrachiales.d: A division of soft-finned fishes in which the ventral fins are situated beneath the pectorial fins, or nearly so

subbronchial.d: Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the bronchi; as, the subbronchial air sacs of birds

subcarbureted.d: United with, or containing, carbon in less than the normal proportion

subchanter.d: An underchanter; a precentor's deputy in a cathedral; a succentor

subcompressed.d: Not fully compressed; partially or somewhat compressed

subcorneous.d: Situated under a horny part or layer

subcrustaceous.d: Occurring beneath a crust or scab; as, a subcrustaceous cicatrization

subdeposit.d: That which is deposited beneath something else

subdichotomy.d: A subordinate, or inferior, division into parts; a subdivision

subdititious.d: Put secretly in the place of something else; foisted in

subdiversify.d: To diversify aggain what is already diversified

subdivine.d: Partaking of divinity; divine in a partial or lower degree

subhornblendic.d: Containing hornblende in a scattered state; of or relating to rocks containing disseminated hornblende

subhumerate.d: To place the shoulders under; to bear

subindicate.d: To indicate by signs or hints; to indicate imperfectly

subindication.d: The act of indicating by signs; a slight indication

subinfer.d: To infer from an inference already made

subintestinal.d: Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the intestine

subjectist.d: One skilled in subjective philosophy; a subjectivist

sublative.d: Having power, or tending, to take away

sublevation.d: The act of raising on high; elevation

sublimification.d: The act of making sublime, or state of being made sublime

sublition.d: The act or process of laying the ground in a painting

subministrate.d: To supply; to afford; to subminister

subnect.d: To tie or fasten beneath; to join beneath

subnuvolar.d: Under the clouds; attended or partly covered or obscured by clouds; somewhat cloudy

subopercular.d: Situated below the operculum; pertaining to the suboperculum

subpentangular.d: Nearly or approximately pentangular; almost pentangular

subpodophyllous.d: Situated under the podophyllous tissue of the horse's foot

subpolygonal.d: Approximately polygonal; somewhat or almost polygonal

subprehensile.d: Somewhat prehensile; prehensile in an inferior degree

subquadruple.d: Containing one part of four; in the ratio of one to four; as, subquadruple proportion

subquintuple.d: Having the ratio of one to five; as, subquintuple proportion

subreader.d: An under reader in the inns of court, who reads the texts of law the reader is to discourse upon

subreligion.d: A secondary religion; a belief or principle held in a quasi religious veneration

subsacral.d: Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the sacrum

subsecute.d: To follow closely, or so as to overtake; to pursue

subsecutive.d: Following in a train or succession

subsemitone.d: The sensible or leading note, or sharp seventh, of any key; subtonic

subseptuple.d: Having the ratio of one to seven

subsesqui-.d: A prefix (also used adjectively) denoting the combination of constituents (especially electro-negative and electro-positive bodies) in the proportion of two to three; as, a subsesqui acetate, i. e., a salt having two equivalents of acetic acid to three of the base

subsignation.d: The act of writing the name under something, as for attestation

subsistence department.d: A staff department of the United States army charged, under the  supervision of the Chief of Staff, with the purchasing and issuing to the army of such supplies as make up the  ration. It also supplies, for authorized sales, certain articles of food and other minor stores. It is commanded by any officer of the rank of brigadier general, called commissary general, and the department is popularly called the Commissary Department

subsizar.d: An under sizar; a student of lower rank than a sizar

subsolary.d: Being under the sun; hence, terrestrial; earthly; mundane

subsphenoidal.d: Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the body of the sphenoid bone

subspherical.d: Nearly spherical; having a figure resembling that of a sphere

substruct.d: To build beneath something; to lay as the foundation

substyle.d: A right line on which the style, or gnomon, of a dial is erected; being the common section of the face of the dial and a plane perpendicular to it passing through the style

subsulphide.d: A nonacid compound consisting of one equivalent of sulphur and more than one equivalent of some other body, as a metal

subtartarean.d: Being or living under Tartarus; infernal

subtectacle.d: A space under a roof; a tabernacle; a dwelling

subtegulaneous.d: Under the roof or eaves; within doors

subterranity.d: A place under ground; a subterrany

subtilism.d: The quality or state of being subtile; subtility; subtlety

subtrihedral.d: Approaching the form of a three-sided pyramid; as, the subtrihedral crown of a tooth

subtriple.d: Containing a third, or one part to three

subulicornes.d: A division of insects having slender or subulate antennae. The dragon flies and May flies are examples

subulipalp.d: One of a group of carabid beetles having slender palpi

subumbonal.d: Beneath or forward of the umbos of a bivalve shell

subvitalized.d: Imperfectly vitalized; having naturally but little vital power or energy

successionist.d: A person who insists on the importance of a regular succession of events, offices, etc.; especially (Eccl.), one who insists that apostolic succession alone is valid

succinamic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid amide derivative of succinic acid, obtained as a white crystalline substance, and forming a series of salts

succinuric.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid amide, analogous to succinamic acid, which is obtained as a white crystalline substance by heating urea with succinic anhydride. It is known also in its salts

succision.d: The act of cutting down, as of trees; the act of cutting off

succula.d: A bare axis or cylinder with staves or levers in it to turn it round, but without any drum

suchospondylous.d: Having dorsal vertebrae with long and divided transverse processes; -- applied to certain reptiles

suchwise.d: In a such a manner; so

suckanhock.d: A kind of seawan. See Note under Seawan

sucken.d: The jurisdiction of a mill, or that extent of ground astricted to it, the tenants of which are bound to bring their grain thither to be ground

suent.d: Uniformly or evenly distributed or spread; even; smooth. See Suant

suf-.d: A form of the prefix Sub-

suffragator.d: One who assists or favors by his vote

suffraginous.d: Of or pertaining to the hock of a beast

sugar-house.d: A building in which sugar is made or refined; a sugar manufactory

suggillate.d: To beat livid, or black and blue

suicidism.d: The quality or state of being suicidal, or self-murdering

suillage.d: A drain or collection of filth

suiogoths.d: The Scandinavian Goths. See the Note under Goths

suist.d: One who seeks for things which gratify merely himself; a selfish person; a selfist

suleah fish.d: A coarse fish of India, used in making a breakfast relish called burtah

sulphacid.d: An acid in which, to a greater or less extent, sulphur plays a part analogous to that of oxygen in an oxyacid; thus, thiosulphuric and sulpharsenic acids are sulphacids; -- called also sulphoacid. See the Note under Acid, n., 2

sulphamic.d: Of or pertaining to a sulphamide; derived from, or related to, a sulphamide; specifically, designating an amido acid derivative, NH2.SO2.OH, of sulphuric acid (analogous to sulphonic acid) which is not known in the free state, but is known in its salts

sulphanilic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an anilene sulphonic acid which is obtained as a white crystalline substance

sulphantimonic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a hypothetical sulphacid of antimony (called also thioantimonic acid) analogous to sulpharsenic acid

sulphantimonious.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a hypothetical sulphacid of antimony (called also thioantimonious acid) analogous to sulpharsenious acid

sulpharsenic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a hypothetical sulphacid (called also thioarsenic acid) analogous to arsenic acid, and known only in its salts

sulpharsenious.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a hypothetical sulphacid (called also thioarsenious acid) analogous to arsenious acid, and known only in its salts

sulphato-.d: A combining form (also used adjectively) denoting a sulphate as an ingredient in certain double salts; as, sulphato-carbonate

sulphauric.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a hypothetical sulphacid of gold (aurum), known only in its salts

sulphinate.d: A salt of a sulphinic acid

sulphindigotic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a sulphonic acid obtained, as a blue solution, by dissolving indigo in sulphuric acid; -- formerly called also cerulic sulphuric acid, but properly called indigo-disulphonic acid

sulphine.d: Any one of a series of basic compounds which consist essentially of sulphur united with hydrocarbon radicals. In general they are oily or crystalline deliquescent substances having a peculiar odor; as, trimethyl sulphine, (CH3)3S.OH.  Cf. Sulphonium

sulphinic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, any one of a series of acids regarded as acid ethereal salts of hyposulphurous acid; as, methyl sulphinic acid, CH3.SO.OH, a thick unstable liquid

sulphionide.d: A binary compound of sulphion, or one so regarded; thus, sulphuric acid, H2SO4, is a sulphionide

sulphoarsenic.d: Of, pertaining to, or containing, sulphur and arsenic; -- said of an acid which is the same as arsenic acid with the substitution of sulphur for oxygen

sulphocarbonate.d: A salt of sulphocarbonic acid; a thiocarbonate

sulphocarbonic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a sulphacid, H2CSO2 (called also thiocarbonic acid), or an acid, H2CS3, analogous to carbonic acid, obtained as a yellow oily liquid of a pungent odor, and forming salts

sulphocyanate.d: A salt of sulphocyanic acid; -- also called thiocyanate, and formerly inaccurately sulphocyanide

sulphocyanic.d: Of, pertaining to, derived from, or designating, a sulphacid, HSCN, analogous to cyanic acid, and obtained as a colorless deliquescent crystalline substance, having a bitter saline taste, and not poisonous

sulphophosphoric.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a hypothetical sulphacid of phosphorus, analogous to phosphoric acid, and known in its salts

sulphophosphorous.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a hypothetical acid of phosphorus, analogous to phosphorous acid, and known in its salts

sulphostannic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a sulphacid of tin (more exactly called metasulphostannic acid), which is obtained as a dark brown amorphous substance, H&unr_;SnS&unr_;, forming a well-known series of salts

sulphotungstic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, hypothetical sulphacid of tungsten (called also sulphowolframic acid), analogous to sulphuric acid, and known in its salts

sulphovinic.d: Of, pertaining to, and formerly designating, ethylsulphuric acid

sulphur-bottom.d: A very large whalebone whale of the genus Sibbaldius, having a yellowish belly; especially, Sibbaldius sulfureus of the North Pacific, and Sibbaldius borealis of the North Atlantic; -- called also sulphur whale

sulphureity.d: The quality or state of being sulphureous

sulphydrate.d: A compound, analogous to a hydrate, regarded as a salt of sulphydric acid, or as a derivative of hydrogen sulphide in which one half of the hydrogen is replaced by a base (as potassium sulphydrate, KSH), or as a hydrate in which the oxygen has been wholly or partially replaced by sulphur

sulphydric.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, hydrogen sulphide, which is regarded as an acid, especially when in solution

sumatra leaf.d: A thin, elastic, uniformly light-colored tobacco leaf, raised in Sumatra and extensively used for cigar wrappers

summer-fallow.d: To plow and work in summer, in order to prepare for wheat or other crop; to plow and let lie fallow

summist.d: One who sums up; one who forms an abridgment or summary

summity.d: The height or top of anything

sun-burner.d: A circle or cluster of gas-burners for lighting and ventilating public buildings

sun-struck.d: Overcome by, or affected with, sunstroke; as, sun-struck soldiers

sunblink.d: A glimpse or flash of the sun

suncup.d: A yellow flowered evening primrose (Taraxia ovata, syn. Oenothera ovata) native of California

sundryman.d: One who deals in sundries, or a variety of articles

sunniah.d: One of the sect of Sunnites

sunnud.d: A charter or warrant; also, a deed of gift

supawn.d: Boiled Indian meal; hasty pudding; mush

superadvenient.d: Coming upon; coming in addition to, or in assistance of, something

superangelic.d: Superior to the angels in nature or rank

supercarpal.d: Situated above, or in the upper part of, the carpus

superchemical.d: Above or beyond chemistry; inexplicable by chemical laws

superessential.d: Essential above others, or above the constitution of a thing

superexalt.d: To exalt to a superior degree; to exalt above others

superfecundity.d: Superabundant fecundity or multiplication of the species

superfluitant.d: Floating above or on the surface

superinspect.d: To over see; to superintend by inspection

superinstitution.d: One institution upon another, as when A is instituted and admitted to a benefice upon a title, and B instituted and admitted upon the presentation of another

superlation.d: Exaltation of anything beyond truth or propriety

supermaterial.d: Being above, or superior to, matter

superparticular.d: Of or pertaining to a ratio when the excess of the greater term over the less is a unit, as the ratio of 1 to 2, or of 3 to 4

superpartient.d: Of or pertaining to a ratio when the excess of the greater term over the less is more than a unit, as that of 3 to 5, or 7 to 10

superpolitic.d: More than politic; above or exceeding policy

superreflection.d: The reflection of a reflected image or sound

superregal.d: More than regal; worthy of one greater than a king

superreward.d: To reward to an excessive degree

superroyal.d: Larger than royal; -- said of a particular size of printing and writing paper. See the Note under Paper, n

supersacral.d: Situated over, or on the dorsal side of, the sacrum

supersaliency.d: The act of leaping on anything

supersecular.d: Being above the world, or secular things

superseminate.d: To sow, as seed, over something previously sown

supersemination.d: The sowing of seed over seed previously sown

supersphenoidal.d: Situated above, or on the dorsal side of, the body of the sphenoid bone

superstruction.d: The act of superstructing, or building upon

superstructive.d: Built or erected on something else

supersulphurize.d: To impregnate or combine with an excess of sulphur

suppalpation.d: The act of enticing by soft words; enticement

supparasitation.d: The act of flattering to gain favor; servile approbation

supparasite.d: To flatter; to cajole; to act the parasite

supple-jack.d: A climbing shrub (Berchemia volubilus) of the Southern United States, having a tough and pliable stem

supplial.d: The act of supplying; a supply

suppositor.d: An apparatus for the introduction of suppositories into the rectum

suppute.d: To reckon; to compute; to suppose; to impute

supra-esophagal.d: Situated above, or on the dorsal side of, the esophagus; as, the supra-esophageal ganglion of Crustacea

supra-ethmoid.d: Above, or on the dorsal side of, the ethmoid bone or cartilage

supra-ilium.d: The cartilaginous cap at the sacral end of the ilium of some animals

suprabranchial.d: Situated above the branchiae; -- applied especially to the upper division of the gill cavity of bivalve mollusks

supraclavicle.d: A bone which usually connects the clavicle with the post-temporal in the pectorial arch of fishes

supraglotic.d: Situated above the glottis; -- applied to that part of the cavity of the larynx above the true vocal cords

supraloral.d: Situated above the lores; as, the supraloral feathers of a bird

supralunar.d: Beyond the moon; hence, very lofty

suprapubian.d: Situated above, or anterior to, the pubic bone

suprascalpular.d: Situated above, or on the anterior side of, the scapula

suprasphenoidal.d: Situated above the sphenoidal bone; as, the suprasphenoidal appendage, or pituitary body

supraspinate.d: Situated above a spine or spines; especially, situated above, or on the dorsal side of, the neural spines of the vertebral column, or above, or in front of, the spine of the scapula

supravulgar.d: Being above the vulgar or common people

suradanni.d: A valuable kind of wood obtained on the shores of the Demerara River in South America, much used for timbers, rails, naves and fellies of wheels, and the like

suraddition.d: Something added or appended, as to a name

surbate.d: To make sore or bruise, as the feet by travel

surbed.d: To set edgewise, as a stone; that is, to set it in a position different from that which it had in the quarry

surchargement.d: The act of surcharging; also, surcharge, surplus

surcle.d: A little shoot; a twig; a sucker

suresby.d: One to be sure of, or to be relied on

surface loading.d: The weight supported per square unit of surface; the quotient obtained by dividing the gross weight, in pounds, of a fully loaded flying machine, by the total area, in square feet, of its supporting surface

surfeit-water.d: Water for the cure of surfeits

surfel.d: To wash, as the face, with a cosmetic water, said by some to be prepared from the sulphur

surfoot.d: Tired or sore of foot from travel; lamed

suricat.d: A South African mongooselike viverrine (Suricata suricatta or Suricata tetradactyla) having a lemurlike face and only four toes; called also mierkat, yellow mongoose and zenick

suroxidate.d: To combine with oxygen so as to form a suroxide or peroxide

surquedous.d: Having or exhibiting surquedry; arrogant; insolent

surrebound.d: To give back echoes; to reecho

surrein.d: To override; to exhaust by riding

surreption.d: The act or process of getting in a surreptitious manner, or by craft or stealth

sursolid.d: The fifth power of a number; as, a&unr_; is the sursolid of a, or 32 that of 2

survene.d: To supervene upon; to come as an addition to

survenue.d: A sudden or unexpected coming or stepping on

surview.d: To survey; to make a survey of

suspensation.d: The act of suspending, or the state of being suspended, especially for a short time; temporary suspension

suspiral.d: A breathing hole; a vent or ventiduct

sustaltic.d: Mournful; -- said of a species of music among the ancient Greeks

susurringly.d: In the manner of a whisper

sutling.d: Belonging to sutlers; engaged in the occupation of a sutler

suturated.d: Sewed or knit together; united by a suture; stitched

suwarrow.d: The giant cactus (Cereus giganteus); -- so named by the Indians of Arizona.  Called also saguaro

swainmote.d: A court held before the verders of the forest as judges, by the steward of the court, thrice every year, the swains, or freeholders, within the forest composing the jury

swaip.d: To walk proudly; to sweep along

swallowfish.d: The European sapphirine gurnard (Trigla hirundo). It has large pectoral fins

swan's-down.d: The down, or fine, soft feathers, of the swan, used on various articles of dress

swankie.d: An active and clever young fellow

swanny.d: Swanlike; as, a swanny glossiness of the neck

sward-cutter.d: A plow for turning up grass land

swarmspore.d: One of innumerable minute, motile, reproductive bodies, produced asexually by certain algae and fungi; a zoospore

swartback.d: The black-backed gull (Larus marinus); -- called also swarbie

sway-backed.d: Having the back hollow or sagged, whether naturally or as the result of injury or weakness; -- said of horses and other animals

sway-bracing.d: The horizontal bracing of a bridge, which prevents its swaying

sweepwasher.d: One who extracts the residuum of precious metals from the sweepings, potsherds, etc., of refineries of gold and silver, or places where these metals are used

sweet-breasted.d: Having a sweet, musical voice, as the nightingale.  Cf. Breast, n., 6

sweet-sop.d: A kind of custard apple (Anona squamosa). See under Custard

sweetweed.d: A name for two tropical American weeds (Capraria biflora, and Scoparia dulcis) of the Figwort family

sweetwort.d: Any plant of a sweet taste

swimbel.d: A moaning or sighing sound or noise; a sough

swine-pox.d: A variety of the chicken pox, with acuminated vesicles containing a watery fluid; the water pox

swinesty.d: A sty, or pen, for swine

swingebuckler.d: A swashbuckler; a bully; a roisterer

swingel.d: The swinging part of a flail which falls on the grain in thrashing; the swiple

swingletail.d: The thrasher, or fox shark. See Thrasher

switching power supply.d: a device used as part of an electronic device, which transforms electrical current from an AC line circuit to DC for use in electronic devices, and which can use either 110 volt or 220 volt AC line curent

swough.d: A sound; a groan; a moan; a sough

sycoceric.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained by the oxidation of sycoceryl alcohol

syllabist.d: One who forms or divides words into syllables, or is skilled in doing this

sylvic.d: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, pine or its products; specifically, designating an acid called also abeitic acid, which is the chief ingredient of common resin (obtained from Pinus sylvestris, and other species)

symbranchii.d: An order of slender eel-like fishes having the gill openings confluent beneath the neck. The pectoral arch is generally attached to the skull, and the entire margin of the upper jaw is formed by the premaxillary. Called also Symbranchia

symmetrian.d: One eminently studious of symmetry of parts

symmetrist.d: One eminently studious of symmetry of parts

symphytism.d: Coalescence; a growing into one with another word

synallaxine.d: Having the outer and middle toes partially united; -- said of certain birds related to the creepers

synapta.d: A genus of slender, transparent holothurians which have delicate calcareous anchors attached to the dermal plates. See Illustration in Appendix

synartesis.d: A fastening or knitting together; the state of being closely jointed; close union

synchoresis.d: A concession made for the purpose of retorting with greater force

syndyasmian.d: Pertaining to the state of pairing together sexually; -- said of animals during periods of procreation and while rearing their offspring

synecphonesis.d: A contraction of two syllables into one; synizesis

synepy.d: The interjunction, or joining, of words in uttering the clauses of sentences

syngenesia.d: A Linnaean class of plants in which the stamens are united by the anthers

syngenesian.d: Having the stamens united by the anthers; of or pertaining to the Syngenesia

syngnathi.d: A suborder of lophobranch fishes which have an elongated snout and lack the ventral and first dorsal fins.  The pipefishes and sea horses are examples

synocil.d: A sense organ found in certain sponges. It consists of several filaments, each of which arises from a single cell

synomocy.d: Sworn brotherhood; a society in ancient Greece nearly resembling a modern political club

synteretics.d: That department of medicine which relates to the preservation of health; prophylaxis

syntonizer.d: One that syntonizes; specif., a device consisting essentially of a variable inductance coil and condenser with a pair of adjustable spark balls, for attuning the time periods of antennae in wireless telegraphy (called also syntonizing coil)

syrianism.d: A Syrian idiom, or a peculiarity of the Syrian language; a Syriacism

syriasm.d: A Syrian idiom; a Syrianism; a Syriacism

syrma.d: A long dress, trailing on the floor, worn by tragic actors in Greek and Roman theaters

syrphus fly.d: Any one of numerous species of dipterous flies of the genus Syrphus and allied genera. They are usually bright-colored, with yellow bands, and hover around plants. The larvae feed upon plant lice, and are, therefore, very beneficial to agriculture

systasis.d: A political union, confederation, or league

t connection.d: The connection of two coils diagrammatically as a letter T, chiefly used as a connection for passing transformers. When the three free ends are connected to a source of three-phase current, two-phase current may be derived from the secondary circuits. The reverse arrangement may be used to transform from two-phase

t'other.d: A colloquial contraction of the other, and formerly a contraction for that other. See the Note under That, 2

tabefy.d: To cause to waste gradually, to emaciate

tabellion.d: A secretary or notary under the Roman empire; also, a similar officer in France during the old monarchy

table work.d: Typesetting of tabular nmatter, or the type matter set in tabular form

table-land.d: A broad, level, elevated area of land; a plateau

taborite.d: One of certain Bohemian reformers who suffered persecution in the fifteenth century; -- so called from Tabor, a hill or fortress where they encamped during a part of their struggles

tac-au-tac.d: The parry which is connected with a riposte; also, a series of quick attacks and parries in which neither fencer gains a point

tachhydrite.d: A hydrous chloride of calcium and magnesium occurring in yellowish masses which rapidly deliquesce upon exposure.  It is found in the salt mines at Stassfurt

tachydidaxy.d: A short or rapid method of instructing

tachyglossa.d: A division of monotremes which comprises the spiny ant-eaters of Australia and New Guinea. See Illust. under Echidna

tachyscope.d: An early form of animated-picture machine, devised in 1889 by Otto Anschütz of Berlin, in which the chronophotographs were mounted upon the periphery of a rotating wheel

tacksman.d: One who holds a tack or lease from another; a tenant, or lessee

taeniata.d: A division of Ctenophora including those which have a long, ribbonlike body. The Venus's girdle is the most familiar example

taenioglossa.d: An extensive division of gastropod mollusks in which the odontophore is long and narrow, and usually bears seven rows of teeth.  It includes a large number of families both marine and fresh-water

taenioglossate.d: Of or pertaining to the Taenioglossa

taeniosomi.d: An order of fishes remarkable for their long and compressed form. The ribbon fishes are examples. See Ribbon fish, under Ribbon

tag-rag.d: The lowest class of people; the rabble.  Cf. Rag, tag, and bobtail, under Bobtail

tagliacotain.d: Of or pertaining to Tagliacozzi, a Venetian surgeon; as, the Tagliacotian operation, a method of rhinoplasty described by him

tagsore.d: Adhesion of the tail of a sheep to the wool from excoriation produced by contact with the feces; -- called also tagbelt

tagtail.d: A worm which has its tail conspicuously colored

tahaleb.d: A fox (Vulpes Niloticus) of Northern Africa

tail-bay.d: One of the joists which rest one end on the wall and the other on a girder; also, the space between a wall and the nearest girder of a floor.  Cf. Case-bay

taintworm.d: A destructive parasitic worm or insect larva

tajacu.d: The common, or collared, peccary (Tayassu tajacu).  Called also javelina and tayaussa

take the heat.d: To be assigned or to accept the blame for some misdeed; as, Mary broke the vase, but she acted innocent and young Johnny had to take the heat

taking-off.d: Removal; murder. See To take off (c), under Take, v. t

talegalla.d: A genus of Australian birds which includes the brush turkey. See Brush turkey

talewise.d: In a way of a tale or story

tallow-face.d: One who has a sickly, pale complexion

tallwood.d: Firewood cut into billets of a certain length

talook.d: A large estate; esp., one constituting a revenue district or dependency the native proprietor of which is responsible for the collection and payment of the public revenue due from it

tamaric.d: A shrub or tree supposed to be the tamarisk, or perhaps some kind of heath

tamine.d: A kind of woolen cloth; tammy

tampico fiber.d: A tough vegetable fiber used as a substitute for bristles in making brushes. The piassava and the ixtle are both used under this name

tampoon.d: The stopper of a barrel; a bung

tanagrine.d: Of or pertaining to the tanagers

tanak.d: A term used among Jews for the Hebrew Bible; the Old Testament

tanate.d: An Asiatic wild dog (Canis procyonoides), native of Japan and adjacent countries. It has a short, bushy tail. Called also raccoon dog

tandem cart.d: A kind of two-wheeled vehicle with seats back to back, the front one somewhat elevated

tangent spoke.d: A tension spoke of a bicycle or similar wheel, secured tangentially to the hub

tangent wheel.d: A worm or worm wheel; a tangent screw

tanglefish.d: The sea adder, or great pipefish of Europe

tanite.d: A firm composition of emery and a certain kind of cement, used for making grinding wheels, slabs, etc

tank warfare.d: combat between tanks of opposing armies

tantalism.d: A punishment like that of Tantalus; a teasing or tormenting by the hope or near approach of good which is not attainable; tantalization

tanystomata.d: A division of dipterous insects in which the proboscis is large and contains lancelike mandibles and maxillae. The horseflies and robber flies are examples

taotai.d: In China, an official at the head of the civil and military affairs of a circuit, which consists of two or more fu, or territorial departments; -- called also, by foreigners, intendant of circuit. Foreign consuls and commissioners associated with taotais as superintendants of trade at the treaty ports are ranked with the taotai

tapayaxin.d: A Mexican spinous lizard (Phrynosoma orbiculare) having a head somewhat like that of a toad; -- called also horned toad

tapestry beetle.d: A small black dermestoid beetle (Attagenus piceus) whose larva feeds on tapestry, carpets, silk, fur, flour, and various other goods

tapish.d: To lie close to the ground, so as to be concealed; to squat; to crouch; hence, to hide one's self

taplings.d: The strong double leathers by which the two parts of a flail are united

tapoa tafa.d: A small carnivorous marsupial (Phascogale penicillata) having long, soft fur, and a very long tail with a tuft of long hairs at the end; -- called also brush-tailed phascogale

tappet rod.d: A rod carrying a tappet or tappets, as one for closing the valves in a Cornish pumping engine

taqua-nut.d: A Central American name for the ivory nut

tarantulated.d: Bitten by a tarantula; affected with tarantism

tardation.d: The act of retarding, or delaying; retardation

tarheel state.d: North Carolina; -- used as a nickname

tarnisher.d: One who, or that which, tarnishes

tarpum.d: A very large marine fish (Megapolis Atlanticus) of the Southern United States and the West Indies. It often becomes six or more feet in length, and has large silvery scales. The scales are a staple article of trade, and are used in fancywork. Called also tarpon, sabalo, savanilla, silverfish, and jewfish

tarquinish.d: Like a Tarquin, a king of ancient Rome; proud; haughty; overbearing

tarrock.d: The young of the kittiwake gull before the first molt

tartarine.d: Potassium carbonate, obtained by the incineration of tartar

tartralic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained as a white amorphous deliquescent substance, C8H10O11; -- called also ditartaric, tartrilic, or tartrylic acid

tartramic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid which is the primary acid amide derivative of tartaric acid

tartrelic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an anhydride, C4H4O5, of tartaric acid, obtained as a white crystalline deliquescent substance

tartro-.d: A combining form (also used adjectively) used in chemistry to denote the presence of tartar or of some of its compounds or derivatives

tartronic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an organic acid (called also hydroxy malonic acid) obtained, by reducing mesoxalic acid, as a white crystalline substance

tartronyl.d: A hypothetical radical constituting the characteristic residue of tartronic acid and certain of its derivatives

tartrovinic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a certain acid composed of tartaric acid in combination with ethyl, and now called ethyltartaric acid

tasimer.d: An instrument for detecting or measuring minute extensions or movements of solid bodies. It consists essentially of a small rod, disk, or button of carbon, forming part of an electrical circuit, the resistance of which, being varied by the changes of pressure produced by the movements of the object to be measured, causes variations in the strength of the current, which variations are indicated by a sensitive galvanometer. It is also used for measuring minute changes of temperature

task wage.d: A wage paid by the day, or some fixed period, on condition that a minimum task be performed. When the workman is paid in proportion for excess over the minimum, the wage is one for piece-work

taslet.d: A piece of armor formerly worn to guard the thighs; a tasse

tasto.d: A key or thing touched to produce a tone

tatch.d: A spot or stain; also, a trick

tath.d: 3d pers. sing. pres. of Ta, to take

tattersall's.d: A famous horse market in London, established in 1766 by Richard Tattersall, also used as the headquarters of credit betting on English horse races; hence, a large horse market elsewhere

tatusiid.d: Any armadillo of the family Tatusiidae, of which the peba and mule armadillo are examples. Also used adjectively

taupie.d: A foolish or thoughtless young person, esp. a slothful or slovenly woman

tauricornous.d: Having horns like those of a bull

taurid.d: Any of a group of meteors appearing November 20-23; -- so called because they appear to radiate from a point in Taurus

taurocol.d: Glue made from a bull's hide

taurylic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid found of a urine of neat cattle, and probably identical with cresol

tautegorical.d: Expressing the same thing with different words; -- opposed to allegorical

tautoousian.d: Having the same essence; being identically of the same nature

tautophonical.d: Pertaining to, or characterized by, tautophony; repeating the same sound

tavernman.d: The keeper of a tavern; also, a tippler
