taxaspidean.d: Having the posterior tarsal scales, or scutella, rectangular and arranged in regular rows; -- said of certain birds

taxeopoda.d: An order of extinct Mammalia found in the Tertiary formations

taxiarch.d: An Athenian military officer commanding a certain division of an army

taxicorn.d: One of a family of beetles (Taxicornes) whose antennae are largest at the tip. Also used adjectively

taylor-white process.d: A process (invented about 1899 by Frederick W. Taylor and Maunsel B. White) for giving toughness to self-hardening steels. The steel is heated almost to fusion, cooled to a temperature of from 700° to 850° C. in molten lead, further cooled in oil, reheated to between 370° and 670° C., and cooled in air

tea-saucer.d: A small saucer in which a teacup is set

teache.d: Any one of the series of boilers or evaporating pans in which the cane juice is concentrated in making sugar; especially, the last boiler of the series

tear-thumb.d: A name given to several species of plants of the genus Polygonum, having angular stems beset with minute reflexed prickles

teatish.d: Peevish; tettish; fretful; -- said of a child. See Tettish

teaze-hole.d: The opening in the furnaces through which fuel is introduced

tebeth.d: The tenth month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, answering to a part of December with a part of January

tectibranch.d: One of the Tectibranchiata. Also used adjectively

tectibranchiata.d: An order, or suborder, of gastropod Mollusca in which the gills are usually situated on one side of the back, and protected by a fold of the mantle.  When there is a shell, it is usually thin and delicate and often rudimentary. The aplysias and the bubble shells are examples

tectibranchiate.d: Having the gills covered by the mantle; of or pertaining to the Tectibranchiata

tee-to-tum.d: A workingmen's resort conducted under religious influences as a counteractant to the drinking saloon

teenful.d: Full of teen; harmful; grievous; grieving; afflicted

teeswater.d: A breed of cattle formerly bred in England, but supposed to have originated in Holland and to have been the principal stock from which the shorthorns were derived

teeter-tail.d: The spotted sandpiper. See the Note under Sandpiper

tegulated.d: Composed of small plates, as of horn or metal, overlapping like tiles; -- said of a kind of ancient armor

teinland.d: Land granted by the crown to a thane or lord

teinoscope.d: An instrument formed by combining prisms so as to correct the chromatic aberration of the light while linear dimensions of objects seen through the prisms are increased or diminished; -- called also prism telescope

tel-el-amarna.d: A station on the Nile in Egypt, midway between Thebes and Memphis, forming the site of the ancient city of Akhetaton, capital of Amenophis IV. (Akhenaton, or Amenhotep IV., of the 18th dynasty, king 1353-1336 B. C.), whose archive chamber was discovered there during extensive excavations in 1887-1888.  A collection of about 300 clay tablets (called the Tel-el-Amarna tablets, or the Amarna tablets) was found here, forming the diplomatic correspondence (Tel-el-Amarna letters) of Amenophis IV. and

telary.d: Of or pertaining to a web; hence, spinning webs; retiary

tele-iconograph.d: An instrument essentially the same as the telemetrograph

telechirograph.d: An instrument for  telegraphically transmitting and receiving handwritten messages, as photographically by a beam of light from a mirror

telehydrobarometer.d: An instrument for indicating the level of water in a distant tank or reservior

telemeteorograph.d: Any apparatus recording meteorological phenomena at a distance from the measuring apparatus, as by electricity or by compressed air; esp., an apparatus recording conditions at many distant stations at a central office

telemetrograph.d: A combination of the camera lucida and telescope for drawing and measuring distant objects

telenergy.d: Display of force or energy at a distance, or without contact; now more commonly called telekinesis; -- applied to mediumistic phenomena

teleocephali.d: An extensive order of bony fishes including most of the common market species, as bass, salmon, cod, perch, etc

teleostomi.d: An extensive division of fishes including the ordinary fishes (Teleostei) and the ganoids

telepolariscope.d: A polariscope arranged to be attached to a telescope

telerythin.d: A red crystalline compound related to, or produced from, erythrin. So called because regarded as the end of the series of erythrin compounds

telescope bag.d: An adjustable traveling bag consisting of two cases, the larger slipping over the other

telesm.d: A kind of amulet or magical charm

telesmatic.d: Of or pertaining to telesms; magical

telestereograph.d: An instrument for telegraphically reproducing a photograph

telestic.d: Tending or relating to a purpose or an end

tellina.d: A genus of marine bivalve mollusks having thin, delicate, and often handsomely colored shells

tellureted.d: Combined or impregnated with tellurium; tellurized

tellurhydric.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, hydrogen telluride, which is regarded as an acid, especially when in solution

temper screw.d: A screw link, to which is attached the rope of a rope-drilling apparatus, for feeding and slightly turning the drill jar at each stroke

tempestivily.d: The quality, or state, of being tempestive; seasonableness

temptationless.d: Having no temptation or motive; as, a temptationless sin

ten-o'clock.d: A plant, the star-of-Bethlehem. See under Star

ten-pounder.d: A large oceanic fish (Elops saurus) found in the tropical parts of all the oceans. It is used chiefly for bait

tenaillon.d: A work constructed on each side of the ravelins, to increase their strength, procure additional ground beyond the ditch, or cover the shoulders of the bastions

tenebrose.d: Characterized by darkness or gloom; tenebrous

teneriffe.d: A white wine resembling Madeira in taste, but more tart, produced in Teneriffe, one of the Canary Islands; -- called also Vidonia

tenonian.d: Discovered or described by M. Tenon, a French anatomist

tentful.d: As much, or as many, as a tent will hold

tenthredinides.d: A group of Hymneoptera comprising the sawflies

tentory.d: The awning or covering of a tent

tentwort.d: A kind of small fern, the wall rue. See under Wall

tenuious.d: Rare or subtile; tenuous; -- opposed to dense

tephramancy.d: Divination by the ashes of the altar on which a victim had been consumed in sacrifice

teraconic.d: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained by the distillation of terebic acid, and homologous with citraconic acid

teracrylic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid of the acrylic series, obtained by the distillation of terpenylic acid, as an only substance having a peculiar cheesy odor

tercelet.d: A male hawk or eagle; a tiercelet

tercine.d: A cellular layer derived from the nucleus of an ovule and surrounding the embryo sac.  Cf. Quintine

terebilenic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a complex acid, C7H8O4, obtained as a white crystalline substance by a modified oxidation of terebic acid

terebinthic.d: Of or pertaining to turpentine; resembling turpentine; terbinthine; as, terbinthic qualities

terebratuliform.d: Having the general form of a terebratula shell

teretial.d: Rounded; as, the teretial tracts in the floor of the fourth ventricle of the brain of some fishes

tergeminal.d: Thrice twin; having three pairs of leaflets

terin.d: A small yellow singing bird, with an ash-colored head; the European siskin. Called also tarin

termatarium.d: Any nest or dwelling of termes, or white ants

terpenylic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid, C8H12O4 (called also terpentic acid), homologous with terebic acid, and obtained as a white crystalline substance by the oxidation of oil of turpentine with chromic acid

terre-verte.d: An olive-green earth used as a pigment. See Glauconite

terrestrify.d: To convert or reduce into a condition like that of the earth; to make earthy

terricolae.d: A division of annelids including the common earthworms and allied species

tertiate.d: To do or perform for the third time

tesselar.d: Formed of tesserae, as a mosaic

tessellata.d: A division of Crinoidea including numerous fossil species in which the body is covered with tessellated plates

tesseraic.d: Diversified by squares; done in mosaic; tessellated

testaceography.d: The science which treats of testaceans, or shellfish; the description of shellfish

testamentation.d: The act or power of giving by testament, or will

testicardines.d: A division of brachiopods including those which have a calcareous shell furnished with a hinge and hinge teeth. Terebratula and Spirifer are examples

testone.d: A silver coin of Portugal, worth about sixpence sterling, or about eleven cents

tete-de-pont.d: A work thrown up at the end of a bridge nearest the enemy, for covering the communications across a river; a bridgehead

tetel.d: A large African antelope (Alcelaphus tora). It has widely divergent, strongly ringed horns

tether-ball.d: A game played with rackets and a ball suspended by a string from an upright pole, the object of each side being to wrap the string around the pole by striking the ball in a direction opposite to the other

tethyodea.d: A division of Tunicata including the common attached ascidians, both simple and compound. Called also Tethioidea

tetrabranchiata.d: An order of Cephalopoda having four gills. Among living species it includes only the pearly nautilus. Numerous genera and species are found in the fossil state, such as Ammonites, Baculites, Orthoceras, etc

tetracolon.d: A stanza or division in lyric poetry, consisting of four verses or lines

tetractinellid.d: Any species of sponge of the division Tetractinellida. Also used adjectively

tetractinellida.d: A division of Spongiae in which the spicules are siliceous and have four branches diverging at right angles. Called also Tetractinellinae

tetradite.d: A person in some way remarkable with regard to the number four, as one born on the fourth day of the month, or one who reverenced four persons in the Godhead

tetradynamian.d: A plant of the order Tetradynamia

tetragynia.d: A Linnaean order of plants having four styles

tetragynian.d: Belonging to the order Tetragynia; having four styles

tetrakosane.d: A hydrocarbon, C24H50, resembling paraffin, and like it belonging to the marsh-gas series; -- so called from having twenty-four atoms of carbon in the molecule

tetrapharmacom.d: A combination of wax, resin, lard, and pitch, composing an ointment

tetrapla.d: A Bible consisting of four different Greek versions arranged in four columns by Origen; hence, any version in four languages or four columns

tetrapneumona.d: A division of Arachnida including those spiders which have four lungs, or pulmonary sacs. It includes the bird spiders (Mygale) and the trapdoor spiders. See Mygale

tetraptote.d: A noun that has four cases only

tetraspaston.d: A machine in which four pulleys act together

tetrathionic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a thionic derivative, H2S4O6, of sulphuric acid, obtained as a colorless, odorless liquid

tetrinic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a complex ketonic acid, C5H6O3, obtained as a white crystalline substance; -- so called because once supposed to contain a peculiar radical of four carbon atoms. Called also acetyl-acrylic acid

tetrodon.d: Any one of numerous species of plectognath fishes belonging to Tetrodon and allied genera. Each jaw is furnished with two large, thick, beaklike, bony teeth

tetrodont.d: Of or pertaining to the tetrodons

tetrolic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid, C3H3.CO2H, of the acetylene series, homologous with propiolic acid, obtained as a white crystalline substance

tetrylene.d: Butylene; -- so called from the four carbon atoms in the molecule

tetter-totter.d: A certain game of children; seesaw; -- called also titter-totter, and titter-cum-totter

tetterous.d: Having the character of, or pertaining to, tetter

tettigonian.d: Any one of numerous species of Hemiptera belonging to Tettigonia and allied genera; a leaf hopper

tewan.d: A tribe of American Indians including many of the Pueblos of New Mexico and adjacent regions

tewtaw.d: To beat; to break, as flax or hemp

textrine.d: Of or pertaining to weaving, textorial; as, the textrine art

textury.d: The art or process of weaving; texture

thalassinian.d: Any species of Thalassinidae, a family of burrowing macrurous Crustacea, having a long and soft abdomen

thallate.d: A salt of a hypothetical thallic acid

thallene.d: A hydrocarbon obtained from coal-tar residues, and remarkable for its intense yellowish green fluorescence

thamyn.d: An Asiatic deer (Rucervus Eldi) resembling the swamp deer; -- called also Eld's deer

thanksgive.d: To give or dedicate in token of thanks

tharos.d: A small American butterfly (Phycoides tharos) having the upper surface of the wings variegated with orange and black, the outer margins black with small white crescents; -- called also pearl crescent

thaumatolatry.d: Worship or undue admiration of wonderful or miraculous things

thaumaturgus.d: A miracle worker; -- a title given by the Roman Catholics to some saints

theatin.d: One of an order of Italian monks, established in 1524, expressly to oppose Reformation, and to raise the tone of piety among Roman Catholics. They hold no property, nor do they beg, but depend on what Providence sends. Their chief employment is preaching and giving religious instruction

thebaid.d: A Latin epic poem by Statius about Thebes in Boeotia

thecodactyl.d: Any one of a group of lizards of the Gecko tribe, having the toes broad, and furnished with a groove in which the claws can be concealed

thecophora.d: A division of hydroids comprising those which have the hydranths in thecae and the gonophores in capsules. The campanularians and sertularians are examples. Called also Thecata. See Illust. under Hydroidea

thelphusian.d: One of a tribe of fresh-water crabs which live in or on the banks of rivers in tropical countries

thenadays.d: At that time; then; in those days; -- correlative to nowadays

theobromic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid extracted from cacao butter (from the Theobroma Cacao), peanut oil (from Arachis hypogaea), etc., as a white waxy crystalline substance

theomachist.d: One who fights against the gods; one who resists God of the divine will

theophilanthropic.d: Pertaining to theophilanthropy or the theophilanthropists

theophilanthropism.d: The doctrine of the theophilanthropists; theophilanthropy

theophilanthropist.d: A member of a deistical society established at Paris during the French revolution

theophilosophic.d: Combining theism and philosophy, or pertaining to the combination of theism and philosophy

theopneusty.d: Divine inspiration; the supernatural influence of the Divine Spirit in qualifying men to receive and communicate revealed truth

theoric.d: Of or pertaining to the theorica

theorica.d: Public moneys expended at Athens on festivals, sacrifices, and public entertainments (especially theatrical performances), and in gifts to the people; -- also called theoric fund

theosophistical.d: Of or pertaining to theosophy; theosophical

therapeutae.d: A name given to certain ascetics said to have anciently dwelt in the neighborhood of Alexandria. They are described in a work attributed to Philo, the genuineness and credibility of which are now much discredited

therewhile.d: At that time; at the same time

therf.d: Not fermented; unleavened; -- said of bread, loaves, etc

theriodont.d: One of the Theriodontia. Used also adjectively

thermetograph.d: A self-registering thermometer, especially one that registers the maximum and minimum during long periods

thermifugine.d: An artificial alkaloid of complex composition, resembling thalline and used as an antipyretic, -- whence its name

thermoanaesthesia.d: Loss of power to distinguish heat or cold by touch

thermochemic.d: Of or pertaining to thermochemistry; obtained by, or employed in, thermochemistry

thermolyze.d: To subject to thermolysis; to dissociate by heat

thermoneurosis.d: A neurosis caused by exposure to heat

thermotype.d: A picture (as of a slice of wood) obtained by first wetting the object slightly with hydrochloric or dilute sulphuric acid, then taking an impression with a press, and next strongly heating this impression

thermotypy.d: The art or process of obtaining thermotypes

thesicle.d: A little or subordinate thesis; a proposition

thetical.d: Laid down; absolute or positive, as a law

thialol.d: A colorless oily liquid, (C2H5)2S2, having a strong garlic odor; -- called also ethyl disulphide. By extension, any one of the series of related compounds

thibet cloth.d: A fabric made of coarse goat's hair; a kind of camlet

thible.d: A slice; a skimmer; a spatula; a pudding stick

thick wind.d: A defect of respiration in a horse, that is unassociated with noise in breathing or with the signs of emphysema

thickskull.d: A dullard, or dull person; a blockhead; a numskull

thimbleeye.d: The chub mackerel. See under Chub

thinolite.d: A calcareous tufa, in part crystalline, occurring on a large scale as a shore deposit about the Quaternary lake basins of Nevada

thionol.d: A red or violet dyestuff having a greenish metallic luster. It is produced artificially, by the chemical dehydration of thionine, as a brown amorphous powder

thionoline.d: A beautiful fluorescent crystalline substance, intermediate in composition between thionol and thionine

thiosulphuric.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an unstable acid, H2S2O3, analogous to sulphuric acid, and formerly called hyposulphurous acid

third-penny.d: A third part of the profits of fines and penalties imposed at the country court, which was among the perquisites enjoyed by the earl

third-rail system.d: A system in which a third rail is used for carrying the current for operating the motors, the rail being insulated from the ground and the current being taken off by means of contact brushes or other devices

thirdings.d: The third part of the corn or grain growing on the ground at the tenant's death, due to the lord for a heriot, as within the manor of Turfat in Herefordshire

thitsee.d: The varnish tree of Burmah (Melanorrhoea usitatissima)

thomaean.d: A member of the ancient church of Christians established on the Malabar coast of India, which some suppose to have been originally founded by the Apostle Thomas

thomson process.d: A process of electric welding in which heat is developed by a large current passing through the metal

thoracostraca.d: An extensive division of Crustacea, having a dorsal shield or carapec&unr_; &unr_;&unr_;niting all, or nearly all, of the thoracic somites to the head. It includes the crabs, lobsters, shrimps, and similar species

thoral.d: Of or pertaining to a bed

thorn-headed.d: Having a head armed with thorns or spines

thorough-brace.d: A leather strap supporting the body of a carriage, and attached to springs, or serving as a spring. See Illust. of Chaise

thorough-lighted.d: Provided with thorough lights or windows at opposite sides, as a room or building

thoroughstitch.d: So as to go the whole length of any business; fully; completely

thousand legs.d: A millepid, or galleyworm; -- called also thousand-legged worm

thrack.d: To load or burden; as, to thrack a man with property

thrall-like.d: Resembling a thrall, or his condition, feelings, or the like; slavish

thranite.d: One of the rowers on the topmost of the three benches in a trireme

thrashel.d: An instrument to thrash with; a flail

thread-shaped.d: Having the form of a thread; filiform

threaden.d: Made of thread; as, threaden sails; a threaden fillet

threatful.d: Full of threats; having a menacing appearance

three-coat.d: Having or consisting of three coats; -- applied to plastering which consists of pricking-up, floating, and a finishing coat; or, as called in the United States, a scratch coat, browning, and finishing coat

three-flowered.d: Bearing three flowers together, or only three flowers

three-leafed.d: Producing three leaves; as, three-leaved nightshade

three-mile.d: Of or pertaining to three miles; as, the three-mile limit, or the limit of the marine belt (the three-mile belt or three-mile zone) of three miles included in territorial waters (which see) of a state

three-parted.d: Divided into, or consisting of, three parts; tripartite

three-pile.d: An old name for the finest and most costly kind of velvet, having a fine, thick pile

three-piled.d: Having the quality of three-pile; best; most costly

three-pointed.d: Having three acute or setigerous points; tricuspidate

three-torque system of control.d: Any system of rudders by which the pilot can exert a turning moment about each of the three rectangular axes of an aeroplane or airship

three-valved.d: Consisting of, or having, three valves; opening with three valves; as, a three-valved pericarp

throatboll.d: The Adam's apple in the neck

throw-crook.d: An instrument used for twisting ropes out of straw

thrum-eyed.d: Having the anthers raised above the stigma, and visible at the throat of the corolla, as in long-stamened primroses; -- the reverse of pin-eyed

thryfallow.d: To plow for the third time in summer; to trifallow

thunderproof.d: Secure against the effects of thunder or lightning

thurrok.d: The hold of a ship; a sink

thurst.d: The ruins of the fallen roof resulting from the removal of the pillars and stalls

thuyin.d: A substance extracted from trees of the genus Thuja, or Thuya, and probably identical with quercitrin

thwartingly.d: In a thwarting or obstructing manner; so as to thwart

thwartness.d: The quality or state of being thwart; obliquity; perverseness

thwite.d: To cut or clip with a knife; to whittle

thyine wood.d: The fragrant and beautiful wood of a North African tree (Callitris quadrivalvis), formerly called Thuja articulata. The tree is of the Cedar family, and furnishes a balsamic resin called sandarach

thymate.d: A compound of thymol analogous to a salt; as, sodium thymate

thymiatechny.d: The art of employing perfumes in medicine

thysanopterous.d: Of or pertaining to the Thysanoptera

thysanurous.d: Of or pertaining to the Thysanura

tibicinate.d: To play on a tibia, or pipe

tichorrhine.d: A fossil rhinoceros with a vertical bony medial septum supporting the nose; the hairy rhinoceros

ticker tape parade.d: A parade to honor a person or persons, held in New York City, during which people in the tall buildings of Manhattan throw large quantities of paper, confetti, paper ribbons, or the like onto the parading group.  The name comes form the ticker tape originally thrown onto the parade when it passed stockbrokers' offices in lower Manhattan, before stock tickers became obsolete; in subsequent years other types of waste paper were used to serve the honorary function, as well as paper tape distributed

ticklenburg.d: A coarse, mixed linen fabric made to be sold in the West Indies

tide-rode.d: Swung by the tide when at anchor; -- opposed to wind-rode

tidesman.d: A customhouse officer who goes on board of a merchant ship to secure payment of the duties; a tidewaiter

tien an men.d: a large plaza in Beijing, China

tienda.d: In Cuba, Mexico, etc., a booth, stall, or shop where merchandise is sold

tiers etat.d: The third estate, or commonalty, in France, answering to the commons in Great Britain; -- so called in distinction from, and as inferior to, the nobles and clergy

tiger's-foot.d: A name given to some species of morning-glory (Ipomoea) having the leaves lobed in pedate fashion

tiger-eye.d: A siliceous stone of a yellow color and chatoyant luster, obtained in South Africa and much used for ornament. It is an altered form of the mineral crocidolite. See Crocidolite

tigh.d: A close, or inclosure; a croft

tikor.d: A starch or arrow-root made from the tubes of an East Indian zinziberaceous plant (Curcuma angustifolia); also, the plant itself

tikur.d: An East Indian tree (Garcinia pedunculata) having a large yellow fleshy fruit with a pleasant acid flavor

tile-drain.d: To drain by means of tiles; to furnish with a tile drain

tileseed.d: Any plant of the genus Geissois, having seeds overlapping like tiles on a roof

tilly-vally.d: A word of unknown origin and signification, formerly used as expressive of contempt, or when anything said was rejected as trifling or impertinent

tilt hammer.d: A tilted hammer; a heavy hammer, used in iron works, which is lifted or tilted by projections or wipers on a revolving shaft; a trip hammer

tilt-mill.d: A mill where a tilt hammer is used, or where the process of tilting is carried on

tilt-yard.d: A yard or place for tilting

tim-whiskey.d: A kind of carriage. See Whiskey

timaline.d: Of or pertaining to the genus Timalus or family Timalidae, which includes the babblers thrushes, and bulbuls

timbuctoo.d: A city on the southern edge of the Sahara, in central Africa, some nine miles from the Niger.  It is about three miles around, and was formerly surrounded by a clay wall.  Timbuctoo has a large caravan trade, gold dust being the most important export.  The people are negroes, Tuariks, Mandingoes, Arabs, Foolahs, etc.  The city was founded in the 12th century, but was first seen by a white man in 1826.  Timbuctoo now belongs to France, and a railroad is proposed to connect Algiers, Timbuctoo and

timenoguy.d: A rope carried taut between or over obstacles likely to engage or foul the running rigging in working a ship

tinamides.d: A division of struthious birds, including the tinamous

tinchel.d: A circle of sportsmen, who, by surrounding an extensive space and gradually closing in, bring a number of deer and game within a narrow compass

tinean.d: Any species of Tinea, or of the family Tineidae, which includes numerous small moths, many of which are injurious to woolen and fur goods and to cultivated plants. Also used adjectively

tineman.d: An officer of the forest who had the care of vert and venison by night

tingid.d: Of or pertaining to the genus Tingis

tingis.d: A genus of small hemipterous insects which injure trees by sucking the sap from the leaves. See Illustration in Appendix

tintamar.d: A hideous or confused noise; an uproar

tippling-house.d: A house in which liquors are sold in drams or small quantities, to be drunk on the premises

tipstock.d: The detachable or movable fore part of a gunstock, lying beneath the barrel or barrels, and forming a hold for the left hand

tipula.d: Any one of many species of long-legged dipterous insects belonging to Tipula and allied genera. They have long and slender bodies. See Crane fly, under Crane

tipulary.d: Of or pertaining to the tipulas

tironian.d: Of or pertaining to Tiro, or a system of shorthand said to have been introduced by him into ancient Rome

tirrit.d: A word from the vocabulary of Mrs. Quickly, the hostess in Shakespeare's Henry IV., probably meaning terror

tisar.d: The fireplace at the side of an annealing oven

tisri.d: The seventh month of the Jewish ecclesiastical year, answering to a part of September with a part of October

titan crane.d: A massive crane with an overhanging counterbalanced arm carrying a traveler and lifting crab, the whole supported by a carriage mounted on track rails.  It is used esp. for setting heavy masonry blocks for piers, breakwaters, etc

titanitic.d: Pertaining to, or containing, titanium; as, a titanitic mineral

titano-.d: A combining form (also used adjectively) designating certain double compounds of titanium with some other elements; as, titano-cyanide, titano-fluoride, titano-silicate, etc

titanotherium.d: A large American Miocene mammal, allied to the rhinoceros, and more nearly to the extinct Brontotherium

tithonic.d: Of, pertaining to, or denoting, those rays of light which produce chemical effects; actinic

tithonicity.d: The state or property of being tithonic; actinism

tithonographic.d: Of, relating to, or produced by, the chemical action of rays of light; photographic

tithonometer.d: An instrument or apparatus for measuring or detecting tithonicity; an actinometer

tithymal.d: Any kind of spurge, esp. Euphorbia Cyparissias

titleless.d: Not having a title or name; without legitimate title

tiver.d: A kind of ocher which is used in some parts of England in marking sheep

tlinkit.d: The Indians of a seafaring group of tribes of southern Alaska comprising the Koluschan stock.  Previous to deterioration from contact with the whites they were the foremost traders of the northwest.  They built substantial houses of cedar adorned with  totem poles, and were expert stone carvers and copper workers.  Slavery, the potlatch, and the use of immense labrets were characteristic.  Many now (1913) work in the salmon industry

to-.d: An obsolete intensive prefix used in the formation of compound verbs; as in to-beat, to-break, to-hew, to-rend, to-tear. See these words in the Vocabulary. See the Note on All to, or All-to, under All, adv

to-break.d: To break completely; to break in pieces

to-brest.d: To burst or break in pieces

to-name.d: A name added, for the sake of distinction, to one's surname, or used instead of it

tobine.d: A stout twilled silk used for dresses

tockay.d: A spotted lizard native of India

toe hold.d: A hold in which the agressor bends back his opponent's foot

toftman.d: The owner of a toft. See Toft, 3

toilinette.d: A cloth, the weft of which is of woolen yarn, and the warp of cotton and silk, -- used for waistcoats

toison d'or.d: Lit., the golden fleece; specif., the order of the Golden Fleece, or its jewel

tolletane.d: Of or pertaining to Toledo in Spain; made in Toledo

tolsester.d: A toll or tribute of a sextary of ale, paid to the lords of some manors by their tenants, for liberty to brew and sell ale

tolsey.d: A tollbooth; also, a merchants' meeting place, or exchange

toluid.d: A complex double tolyl and toluidine derivative of glycocoll, obtained as a white crystalline substance

toluric.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, any one of three isomeric crystalline acids, C9H10ON.CO2H, which are toluyl derivatives of glycocoll

tom o' bedlam.d: Formerly, a wandering mendicant discharged as incurable from Bethlehem Hospital, England; hence, a wandering mendicant, either mad or feigning to be so; a madman; a bedlamite

tomaley.d: The liver of the lobster, which becomes green when boiled; -- called also tomalline

tomjohn.d: A kind of open sedan used in Ceylon, carried by a single pole on men's shoulders

tomopteris.d: A genus of transparent marine annelids which swim actively at the surface of the sea. They have deeply divided or forked finlike organs (parapodia). This genus is the type of the order, or suborder, Gymnocopa

tompon.d: An inking pad used in lithographic printing

tomrig.d: A rude, wild, wanton girl; a hoiden; a tomboy

ton mile.d: A unit of measurement of the freight transportation performed by a railroad during a given period, usually a year, the total of which consists of the sum of the products obtained by multiplying the aggregate weight of each shipment in tons during the given period by the number of miles for which it is carried

ton mileage.d: Ton miles collectively; esp., the total ton miles performed by a railroad in a given period

tonnihood.d: The female of the bullfinch; -- called also tonyhoop

tonsilotome.d: An instrument for removing the tonsils

tonsilotomy.d: The operation of removing the tonsils, or a portion thereof; -- called more commonly tonsillectomy

tool-post.d: The part of a tool-rest in which a cutting tool is clamped

tool-rest.d: the part that supports a tool-post or a tool

toothbill.d: A peculiar fruit-eating ground pigeon (Didunculus strigiostris) native of the Samoan Islands, and noted for its resemblance, in several characteristics, to the extinct dodo. Its beak is stout and strongly hooked, and the mandible has two or three strong teeth toward the end.  Its color is chocolate red. Called also toothbilled pigeon, and manu-mea

toothdrawer.d: One whose business it is to extract teeth with instruments; a dentist

toothshell.d: Any species of Dentalium and allied genera having a tooth-shaped shell. See Dentalium

top rake.d: The angle that the front edge of the point of a tool is set back from the normal to the surface being cut

top-armor.d: A top railing supported by stanchions and equipped with netting

top-block.d: A large ironbound block strapped with a hook, and, when used, hung to an eyebolt in the cap, -- used in swaying and lowering the topmast

top-chain.d: A chain for slinging the lower yards, in time of action, to prevent their falling, if the ropes by which they are hung are shot away

top-cloth.d: A piece of canvas used to cover the hammocks which are lashed to the top in action to protect the topmen

top-drain.d: To drain the surface of, as land; as, to top-drain a field or farm

top-draining.d: The act or practice of drining the surface of land

top-light.d: A lantern or light on the top of a vessel

top-rope.d: A rope used for hoisting and lowering a topmast, and for other purposes

top-shaped.d: Having the shape of a top

top-shell.d: Any one of numerous species of marine top-shaped shells of the genus Trochus, or family Trochidae

top-tackle.d: A tackle used in hoisting and lowering the topmast

top-timbers.d: The highest timbers on the side of a vessel, being those above the futtocks

top-tool.d: A tool applied to the top of the work, in distinction from a tool inserted in the anvil and on which the work is placed

topophone.d: A double ear trumpet for estimating the direction from which sounds proceed, esp. for the use of navigators

toppiece.d: A small wig for the top of the head; a toupee

tops-and-bottoms.d: Small rolls of dough, baked, cut in halves, and then browned in an oven, -- used as food for infants

torchon lace.d: a simple thread lace worked upon a pillow with coarse thread; also, a similar lace made by machinery

torchon paper.d: Paper with a rough surface; esp., handmade paper of great hardness for the use of painters in water colors

torchwort.d: The common mullein, the stalks of which, dipped in suet, anciently served for torches. Called also torch, and hig-taper

toreumatography.d: A description of sculpture such as bas-relief in metal

toreumatology.d: The art or the description of scupture such as bas-relief in metal; toreumatography

torilto.d: A species of Turnix (Turnix sylvatica) native of Spain and Northen Africa

tormentful.d: Full of torment; causing, or accompanied by, torment; excruciating

tormentry.d: Anything producing torment, annoyance, or pain

torpedinous.d: Of or pertaining to a torpedo; resembling a torpedo; exerting a benumbing influence; stupefying; dull; torpid

torpedo body.d: An automobile body which is built so that the side surfaces are flush

torpedo boom.d: A spar formerly carried by men-of-war, having a torpedo on its end

torpedo catcher.d: A small fast vessel for pursuing and destroying torpedo boats

torpedo shell.d: A shell longer than a deck-piercing shell, with thinner walls and a larger cavity for the bursting charge, which consists of about 130 pounds of high explosive. It has no soft cap, and is intended to effect its damage by the powerful explosion which follows on slight resistance. It is used chiefly in 12-inch mortars

torpedo station.d: A headquarters for torpedo vessels and their supplies, usually having facilities for repairs and for instruction and experiments. The principal torpedo station of the United States is at Newport, R.I

torpedo stern.d: A broad stern without overhang, flattened on the bottom, used in some torpedo and fast power boats. It prevents settling in the water at high speed

torpedoist.d: One skilled in the theory or use of torpedoes; also, one who favors the use of torpedoes

torrens system.d: A system of registration of titles to land (as distinct from registration of deeds) introduced into South Australia by the Real Property (or Torrens) Act (act 15 of 1857-58), drafted by Sir Robert Torrens (1814-84). Its essential feature is the guaranty by the government of properly registered titles. The system has been generally adopted in Australia and British Columbia, and in its original or a modified form in some other countries, including some States of the United States. Hence Torrens ti

torril.d: A worthless woman; also, a worthless horse

torsibillty.d: The tendency, as of a rope, to untwist after being twisted

torsion head.d: That part of a torsion balance from  which the wire or filament is suspended

torteau.d: A roundel of a red color

tortulous.d: Swelled out at intervals like a knotted cord

tortuoslty.d: the quality or state of being tortuous

torulaform.d: Having the appearance of a torula; in the form of a little chain; as, a torulaform string of micrococci

torvity.d: Sourness or severity of countenance; sternness

torvous.d: Sour of aspect; of a severe countenance; stern; grim

toscatter.d: To scatter in pieces; to divide

toshred.d: To cut into shreds or pieces

tossy.d: Tossing the head, as in scorn or pride; hence, proud; contemptuous; scornful; affectedly indifferent; as, a tossy commonplace

totalness.d: The quality or state of being total; entireness; totality

totear.d: To tear or rend in pieces

totipalmi.d: A division of swimming birds including those that have totipalmate feet

tottle.d: To walk in a wavering, unsteady manner; to toddle; to topple

tottlish.d: Trembling or tottering, as if about to fall; unsteady

touch up paint.d: A paint applied to small areas of a painted surface, to cover small blemishes, especially on an automobile

touch-box.d: A box containing lighted tinder, formerly carried by soldiers who used matchlocks, to kindle the match

touch-needle.d: A small bar of gold and silver, either pure, or alloyed in some known proportion with copper, for trying the purity of articles of gold or silver by comparison of the streaks made by the article and the bar on a touchstone

touch-paper.d: Paper steeped in saltpeter, which burns slowly, and is used as a match for firing gunpowder, and the like

tough-pitch.d: The exact state or quality of texture and consistency of well reduced and refined copper

tous-les-mois.d: A kind of starch with very large, oval, flattened grains, often sold as arrowroot, and extensively used for adulterating cocoa. It is made from the rootstocks of a species of Canna, probably Canna edulis, the tubers of which are edible every month in the year

tout-ensemble.d: All together; hence, in costume, the fine arts, etc., the general effect of a work as a whole, without regard to the execution of the separate perts

tow-head.d: An urchin who has soft, whitish hair

towilly.d: The sanderling; -- so called from its cry

town and gown.d: Of or pertaining to interactions between a college or university and the residents of the town in which the institution is located; as, a town and gown dispute

town-crier.d: A town officer who makes proclamations to the people; the public crier of a town

toxodon.d: A gigantic extinct herbivorous mammal from South America, having teeth bent like a bow. It is the type of the order Toxodonta

toxodonta.d: An extinct order of Mammalia found in the South American Tertiary formation. The incisor teeth were long and curved and provided with a persistent pulp. They are supposed to be related both to the rodents and ungulates. Called also Toxodontia

toyhouse.d: A house for children to play in or to play with; a playhouse

tozy.d: Soft, like wool that has been teased

trabea.d: A toga of purple, or ornamented with purple horizontal stripes. -- worn by kings, consuls, and augurs

trachearia.d: A division of Arachnida including those that breathe only by means of tracheae. It includes the mites, ticks, false scorpions, and harvestmen

trachelidan.d: Any one of a tribe of beetles (Trachelides) which have the head supported on a pedicel. The oil beetles and the Cantharides are examples

trachelipoda.d: An extensive artificial group of gastropods comprising all those which have a spiral shell and the foot attached to the base of the neck

trachelipodous.d: Having the foot united with the neck; of or pertaining to the Trachelipoda

trachelobranchiate.d: Having the gills situated upon the neck; -- said of certain mollusks

trachenchyma.d: A vegetable tissue consisting of tracheae

tracheobranchia.d: One of the gill-like breathing organs of certain aquatic insect larvae. They contain tracheal tubes somewhat similar to those of other insects

tracheophonae.d: A group of passerine birds having the syrinx at the lower end of the trachea

trackmaster.d: One who has charge of the track; -- called also roadmaster

tractator.d: One who writes tracts; specif., a Tractarian

traction wheel.d: A locomotive driving wheel which acts by friction adhesion to a smooth track

tractor airplane.d: An airplane having one or more tractor propellers; -- called also tractor

tractor screw.d: A propeller screw placed in front of the supporting planes of an airplane instead of behind them, so that it exerts a pull instead of a push. Hence, Tractor monoplane, Tractor biplane, etc.  This is the most common arrangement for propellers on modern airplanes

tradeful.d: Full of trade; busy in traffic; commercial

trades-unionist.d: A member of a trades union, or a supporter of trades unions

traducible.d: Capable of being derived or propagated

traduct.d: To derive or deduce; also, to transmit; to transfer

traffic mile.d: Any unit of the total obtained by adding the passenger miles and ton miles in a railroad's transportation for a given period; -- a term and practice of restricted or erroneous usage

tragi-comi-pastoral.d: Partaking of the nature of, or combining, tragedy, comedy, and pastoral poetry

tragi-comic.d: Of or pertaining to tragi-comedy; partaking of grave and comic scenes

tralation.d: The use of a word in a figurative or extended sense; ametaphor; a trope

tralatition.d: A change, as in the use of words; a metaphor

tralineate.d: To deviate; to stray; to wander

tralucency.d: Translucency; as, the tralucency of a gem

trammel wheel.d: A circular plate or a cross, with two or more cross grooves intersecting at the center, used on the end of a shaft to transmit motion to another shaft not in line with the first

trampoose.d: To walk with labor, or heavily; to tramp

tramrail.d: An overhead rail forming a track on which a trolley runs to convey a load, as in a shop

trangram.d: Something intricately contrived; a contrived; a puzzle

transanimate.d: To animate with a soul conveyed from another body

transcolate.d: To cause to pass through a sieve or colander; to strain, as through a sieve

transcolation.d: Act of transcolating, or state of being transcolated

transcur.d: To run or rove to and fro

transcursion.d: A rambling or ramble; a passage over bounds; an excursion

transdialect.d: To change or translate from one dialect into another

transfeminate.d: To change into a woman, as a man

transferography.d: The act or process of copying inscriptions, or the like, by making transfers

transfiguratien.d: A change of form or appearance; especially, the supernatural change in the personal appearance of our Savior on the mount

transfretation.d: The act of passing over a strait or narrow sea

transfrete.d: To pass over a strait or narrow sea

transfuge.d: One who flees from one side to another; hence, a deserter; a turncoat; an apostate

transfund.d: To pour from one vessel into another; to transfuse

transgressional.d: Of pertaining to transgression; involving a transgression

transhumanize.d: To make more than human; to purity; to elevate above humanity

translatorship.d: The office or dignity of a translator

translavation.d: A laving or lading from one vessel to another

transmeable.d: Capable of being passed over or traversed; passable

transmeation.d: The act of transmeating; a passing through or beyond

transmew.d: To transmute; to transform; to metamorphose

transmission dynamometer.d: A dynamometer in which power is measured, without being absorbed or used up, during transmission

transmissionist.d: An adherent of a theory, the transmission theory, that the brain serves to “transmit,” rather than to originate, conclusions, and hence that consciousness may exist independently of the brain

transmove.d: To move or change from one state into another; to transform

transnatation.d: The act of swimming across, as a river

transpare.d: To be, or cause to be, transparent; to appear, or cause to appear, or be seen, through something

transpass.d: To pass over; as, Alexander transpassed the river

transpassable.d: Capable of being transpassed, or crossed over

transpeciate.d: To change from one species to another; to transform

transplendency.d: Quality or state of being transplendent

transportal.d: Transportation; the act of removing from one locality to another

transportment.d: The act of transporting, or the state of being transported; transportation

transprint.d: To transfer to the wrong place in printing; to print out of place

transprose.d: To change from prose into verse; to versify; also, to change from verse into prose

transubstantiator.d: One who maintains the doctrine of transubstantiation

transumpt.d: A copy or exemplification of a record; a transcript

transumption.d: Act of taking from one place to another

transumptive.d: Taking from one to another; metaphorical

transvasate.d: To pour out of one vessel into another

transvasation.d: The act or process of pouring out of one vessel into another

transvert.d: To cause to turn across; to transverse

transvolation.d: The act of flying beyond or across

trap shooting.d: Shooting at pigeons liberated, or glass balls or clay pigeons sprung into the air, from a trap

trapezate.d: Having the form of a trapezium; trapeziform

trappous.d: Of or performance to trap; resembling trap, or partaking of its form or qualities; trappy

trapstick.d: A stick used in playing the game of trapball; hence, fig., a slender leg

traverse drill.d: A machine tool for drilling slots, in which the work or tool has a lateral motion back and forth; also, a drilling machine in which the spindle holder can be adjusted laterally

trawlwarp.d: A rope passing through a block, used in managing or dragging a trawlnet

tray-trip.d: An old game played with dice

treasuress.d: A woman who is a treasurer

treckschuyt.d: A covered boat for goods and passengers, used on the Dutch and Flemish canals

tredille.d: A game at cards for three

tree burial.d: Disposal of the dead by placing the corpse among the branches of a tree or in a hollow trunk, a practice among many primitive peoples

tree calf.d: A bright brown polished calfskin binding of  books, stained with a conventional treelike design

treebeard.d: A pendulous branching lichen (Usnea barbata); -- so called from its resemblance to hair

treeful.d: The quantity or number which fills a tree

tregetour.d: A juggler who produces illusions by the use of elaborate machinery

trekometer.d: A field range finger used in the British service

tremando.d: Trembling; -- used as a direction to perform a passage with a general shaking of the whole chord

trematodea.d: An extensive order of parasitic worms. They are found in the internal cavities of animals belonging to all classes. Many species are found, also, on the gills and skin of fishes. A few species are parasitic on man, and some, of which the fluke is the most important, are injurious parasites of domestic animals. The trematodes usually have a flattened body covered with a chitinous skin, and are furnished with two or more suckers for adhesion. Most of the species are hermaphrodite. Called also Trem

trematoid.d: Of or pertaining to the Trematodea. See Illustration in Appendix

tremex.d: A genus of large hymenopterous insects allied to the sawflies. The female lays her eggs in holes which she bores in the trunks of trees with her large and long ovipositor, and the larva bores in the wood. See Illust. of Horntail

trench-plow.d: To plow with deep furrows, for the purpose of loosening the land to a greater depth than usual

trencher-man.d: A feeder; a great eater; a gormandizer

trenchmore.d: A kind of lively dance of a rude, boisterous character. Also, music in triple time appropriate to the dance

trenton period.d: A subdivision in the lower Silurian system of America; -- so named from Trenton Falls, in New York. The rocks are mostly limestones, and the period is divided into the Trenton, Utica, and Cincinnati epochs. See the Chart of Geology

tres-tine.d: The third tine above the base of a stag's antler; the royal antler

tres-tyne.d: In the antler of a stag, the third tyne above the base. This tyne appears in the third year. In those deer in which the brow tyne does not divide, the tres-tyne is the second tyne above the base. See Illust. under Rucervine, and under Rusine

trevat.d: A weaver's cutting instrument; for severing the loops of the pile threads of velvet

triaconter.d: A vessel with thirty banks of oars, or, as some say, thirty ranks of rowers

triangulares.d: The triangular, or maioid, crabs. See Illust. under Maioid, and Illust. of Spider crab, under Spider

triarian.d: Occupying the third post or rank

tribual.d: Of or relating to a tribe; tribal; as, a tribual characteristic; tribular worship

tricarballylic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a complex tribasic organic acid, C3H5.(CO2H)3 occurring naturally in unripe beet roots, and produced artificially from glycerin as a white crystalline substance

tricennarious.d: Of or pertaining to thirty years; tricennial

trichiuriform.d: Like or pertaining to the genus Trichiurus or family Trichiuridae, comprising the scabbard fishes and hairtails

trichiuroid.d: Of, like, or pertaining to, Trichiurus

trichopterous.d: Of, pertaining to, or characterizing, the Trichoptera

trichoscolices.d: An extensive group of wormlike animals characterized by being more or less covered with cilia

tricliniary.d: Of or pertaining to a triclinium, or to the ancient mode of reclining at table

tricoccous.d: Having three cocci, or roundish carpels

tricurvate.d: Curved in three directions; as, a tricurvate spicule (see Illust. of Spicule)

tride.d: Short and ready; fleet; as, a tride pace; -- a term used by sportsmen

tridecatoic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, that acid of the fatty acids heterologous with tridecane. It is a white crystalline substance

tridecatylene.d: A hydrocarbon, C13H26, of the ethylene series, corresponding to tridecane, and obtained from Burmah petroleum as a light colorless liquid; -- called also tridecylene, and tridecene

triduan.d: Lasting three lays; also, happening every third day

triens.d: A Roman copper coin, equal to one third of the as. See 3d As, 2

trieterical.d: Kept or occurring once in three years; triennial

trifallow.d: To plow the third time before sowing, as land

trifasciated.d: Having, or surrounded by, three fasciae, or bands

trifloral.d: Three-flowered; having or bearing three flowers; as, a triflorous peduncle

triformity.d: The state of being triform, or of having a threefold shape

triger process.d: A method of sinking through water-bearing ground, in which the shaft is lined with tubbing and provided with an air lock, work being proceeded with under air pressure

trigesimo-secundo.d: Having thirty-two leaves to a sheet; as, a trigesimo-secundo form, book, leaf, size, etc

trigonocerous.d: Having horns with three angles, like those of some species of goats

trigrammatic.d: Containing three letters or characters, or three sets of letters or characters

trigynian.d: Having three pistils or styles; of or pertaining to the Trigynia

trihoral.d: Occurring once in every three hours

trikosane.d: A hydrocarbon, C23H48, of the methane series, resembling paraffin; -- so called because it has twenty-three atoms of carbon in the molecule

triliterality.d: The quality of being triliteral; as, the triliterality of Hebrew roots

trimaculated.d: Marked with three spots, or maculae

trimellic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a certain tribasic acid (called also trimellitic acid) metameric with trimesitic acid

trimembral.d: Having, or consisting of, three members

trimeran.d: One of the Trimera. Also used adjectively

trimesitic.d: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a tribasic acid, C6H3.(CO2)3, of the aromatic series, obtained, by the oxidation of mesitylene, as a white crystalline substance

trimyarian.d: A lamellibranch which has three muscular scars on each valve

tringoid.d: Of or pertaining to Tringa, or the Sandpiper family

trinoctial.d: Lasting during three nights; comprising three nights

triobolar.d: Of the value of three oboli; hence, mean; worthless

trioctile.d: An aspect of two planets with regard to the earth when they are three octants, or three eighths of a circle, that is, 135 degrees, distant from each other

trioecia.d: The third order of the Linnaean class Polygamia

trionychoidea.d: A division of chelonians which comprises Trionyx and allied genera; -- called also Trionychoides, and Trionychina

tripalmitate.d: A palmitate derived from three molecules of palmitic acid

tripartient.d: Dividing into three parts; -- said of a number which exactly divides another into three parts

tripersonality.d: The state of existing as three persons in one Godhead; trinity

triple-crowned.d: Having three crowns; wearing the triple crown, as the pope

triple-headed.d: Having three heads; three-headed; as, the triple-headed dog Cerberus

triple-tail.d: An edible fish (Lobotes Surinamensis) found in the warmer parts of all the oceans, and common on the southern and middle coasts of the United States. When living it is silvery gray, and becomes brown or blackish when dead. Its dorsal and anal fins are long, and extend back on each side of the tail. It has large silvery scales which are used in the manufacture of fancy work. Called also, locally, black perch, grouper, and flasher

tripodian.d: An ancient stringed instrument; -- so called because, in form, it resembled the Delphic tripod

tripoline.d: Of or pertaining to Tripoli or its inhabitants; Tripolitan

triptote.d: A noun having three cases only

tripudiary.d: Of or pertaining to dancing; performed by dancing

triquadrantal.d: Having three quadrants; thus, a triquadrantal triangle is one whose three sides are quadrants, and whose three angles are consequently right angles

trirhomboidal.d: Having three rhombic faces or sides

trisacramentarian.d: One who recognizes three sacraments, and no more; -- namely, baptism, the Lord's Supper, and penance. See Sacrament

triseralous.d: Having three sepals, or calyx leaves

tristoma.d: Any one of numerous species of trematode worms belonging to Tristoma and allied genera having a large posterior sucker and two small anterior ones. They usually have broad, thin, and disklike bodies, and are parasite on the gills and skin of fishes

trisulc.d: Something having three forks or prongs, as a trident

trithionic.d: Of or pertaining to, or designating, a certain thionic acid, H2S3O6 which is obtained as a colorless, odorless liquid

tritovum.d: An embryonic insect which has twice cast its skin previous to hatching from the egg

tritozooid.d: A zooid of the third generation in asexual reproduction

trituberculy.d: A theory of the development of mammalian molar teeth. The primitive stage is that of simple cones, as in reptiles. The simple cone then developed a smaller cone in front and another behind. Next, a cingulum was developed, and the three cones became arranged in a triangle, the two smaller cusps having moved to the outer side in upper and to the inner in lower molars. This primitive triangle is called the trigon or trigonid and this stage the tritubercular or trigonodont. The trigon being a cuttin

triungulus.d: The active young larva of any oil beetle. It has feet armed with three claws, and is parasitic on bees. See Illust. of Oil beetle, under Oil

triverbial.d: Pertaining to, or designating, certain days allowed to the pretor for hearing causes, when be might speak the three characteristic words of his office, do, dico, addico. They were called dies fasti

trocha.d: A line of fortifications, usually rough, constructed to prevent the passage of an enemy across a region

trochilidist.d: One who studies, or is versed in, the nature and habits of humming birds, or the Trochilidae

trochleary.d: Pertaining to, or connected with, a trochlea; trochlear; as, the trochleary, or trochlear, nerve

troco.d: An old English game; -- called also lawn billiards

troilus butterfly.d: A large American butterfly (Papilio troilus). It is black, with yellow marginal spots on the front wings, and blue on the rear; -- also called troilus

trois point.d: The third point from the outer edge on each player's home table

trolley wire.d: A heavy conducting wire on which the trolley car runs and from which it receives the current

trollopee.d: A kind of loose dress for women

tronage.d: A toll or duty paid for weighing wool; also, the act of weighing wool

tronator.d: An officer in London whose duty was to weigh wool

trophonian.d: Of or pertaining to Trophonius, his architecture, or his cave and oracle

tropologize.d: To use in a tropological sense, as a word; to make a trope of

trough-shell.d: Any bivalve shell of the genus Mactra. See Mactra

trousse.d: A case for small implements; as, a surgeon's trousse

troweled.d: Formed with a trowel; smoothed with a trowel; as, troweled stucco, that is, stucco laid on and ready for the reception of paint

trowelful.d: As much as a trowel will hold; enough to fill a trowel

truage.d: A pledge of truth or peace made on payment of a tax

truantship.d: The conduct of a truant; neglect of employment; idleness; truancy

trubu.d: An East India herring (Clupea toli) which is extensively caught for the sake of its roe and for its flesh

trucebreaker.d: One who violates a truce, covenant, or engagement

truckle-bed.d: A low bed on wheels, that may be pushed under another bed; a trundle-bed

true-born.d: Of genuine birth; having a right by birth to any title; as, a true-born Englishman

true-bred.d: Of a genuine or right breed; as, a true-bred beast

true-hearted.d: Of a faithful heart; honest; sincere; not faithless or deceitful; as, a truhearted friend

truismatic.d: Of or pertaining to truisms; consisting of truisms

truite.d: Having a delicately crackled surface; -- applied to porcelian, etc

trullization.d: The act of laying on coats of plaster with a trowel

trumpet-tongued.d: Having a powerful, far-reaching voice or speech

trumplike.d: Resembling a trumpet, esp. in sound; as, a trumplike voice

truncheoneer.d: A person armed with a truncheon

trundle-bed.d: A low bed that is moved on trundles, or little wheels, so that it can be pushed under a higher bed; a truckle-bed; also, sometimes, a simiral bed without wheels

trundlehead.d: One of the disks forming the ends of a lantern wheel or pinion

trundletail.d: A round or curled-up tail; also, a dog with such a tail

trunk steamer.d: A freight steamer having a high hatch coaming extending almost continuously fore and aft, but not of whaleback form at the sides

trunkwork.d: Work or devices suitable to be concealed; a secret stratagem

trustee process.d: The process of attachment by garnishment

trustee stock.d: High-grade stock in which trust funds may be legally invested

truttaceous.d: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a trout; as, fish of the truttaceous kind

try cock.d: A cock for withdrawing a small quantity of liquid, as for testing

try-square.d: An instrument used by carpenters, joiners, etc., for laying off right angles off right angles, and testing whether work is square

trygon.d: Any one of several species of large sting rays belonging to Trygon and allied genera

tschego.d: A West African anthropoid ape allied to the gorilla and chimpanzee, and by some considered only a variety of the chimpanzee. It is noted for building large, umbrella-shaped nests in trees. Called also tscheigo, tschiego, nschego, nscheigo

tsung tu.d: A viceroy or governor-general, the highest provincial official in China, with civil and military authority over one or more provinces

tsung-li yamen.d: The board or department of foreign affairs in the Chinese government. See Yamen

tube railway.d: an electrically powered railroad with tracks running through a tunnel underground; a subway

tube-shell.d: Any bivalve mollusk which secretes a shelly tube around its siphon, as the watering-shell

tubeform.d: In the form of a tube; tubular; tubiform

tubfish.d: The sapphirine gurnard (Trigla hirundo). See Illust. under Gurnard

tubicolae.d: A division of annelids including those which construct, and habitually live in, tubes. The head or anterior segments usually bear gills and cirri. Called also Sedentaria, and Capitibranchiata. See Serpula, and Sabella

tubinares.d: A tribe of sea birds comprising the petrels, shearwaters, albatrosses, hagdons, and allied birds having tubular horny nostrils

tubipora.d: A genus of halcyonoids in which the skeleton, or coral (called organ-pipe coral), consists of a mass of parallel cylindrical tubes united at intervals by transverse plates. These corals are usually red or purple and form large masses. They are natives of the tropical parts of the Indian and Pacific Oceans

tubipore.d: Any species of the genus Tubipora

tubiporite.d: Any fossil coral of the genus Syringopora consisting of a cluster of upright tubes united together by small transverse tubules

tubivalve.d: A shell or tube formed by an annelid, as a serpula

tubularia.d: A genus of hydroids having large, naked, flowerlike hydranths at the summits of long, slender, usually simple, stems. The gonophores are small, and form clusters at the bases of the outer tentacles

tubularian.d: Any hydroid belonging to the suborder Tubularida

tubularida.d: An extensive division of Hydroidea; the tubularians; -- called also Athecata, Gymnoblastea, and Tubulariae

tubulibranchiata.d: A group of gastropod mollusks having a tubular shell. Vermetus is an example

tubulicole.d: Any hydroid which has tubular chitinous stems

tubulidentate.d: Having teeth traversed by canals; -- said of certain edentates

tubulipore.d: Any one of numerous species of Bryozoa belonging to Tubulipora and allied genera, having tubular calcareous calicles

tuck pointing.d: The finishing of joints along the center lines with a narrow ridge of putty or fine lime mortar

tucuma.d: A Brazilian palm (Astrocaryum Tucuma) which furnishes an edible fruit

tuf-taffeta.d: A silk fabric formerly in use, having a nap or pile

tuggingly.d: In a tugging manner; with laborious pulling

tuko-tuko.d: A burrowing South American rodent (Ctenomys Braziliensis). It has small eyes and ears and a short tail. It resembles the pocket gopher in size, form, and habits, but is more nearly allied to the porcupines

tula metal.d: An alloy of silver, copper, and lead made at Tula in Russia

tulip-eared.d: Having erect, pointed ears; prick-eared; -- said of certain dogs

tulip-shell.d: A large, handsomely colored, marine univalve shell (Fasciolaria tulipa) native of the Southern United States.  The name is sometimes applied also to other species of Fasciolaria

tulipist.d: A person who is especially devoted to the cultivation of tulips

tullian.d: Belonging to, or in the style of, Tully (Marcus Tullius Cicero)

tum-tum.d: A dish made in the West Indies by beating boiled plantain quite soft in a wooden mortar

tumulate.d: To cover, as a corpse, with a mound or tomb; to bury

tumulosity.d: The quality or state of being tumulous; hilliness

tumulous.d: Full of small hills or mounds; hilly; tumulose

tumultuariness.d: The quality or state of being tumultuary

tumultuation.d: Irregular or disorderly movement; commotion; as, the tumultuation of the parts of a fluid

tun-bellied.d: Having a large, protuberant belly, or one shaped like a tun; pot-bellied

tun-great.d: Having the circumference of a tun

tungsten lamp.d: An electric glow lamp having filaments of metallic tungsten, and contained in a glass bulb which is evacuated or has an inert gas, to avoid oxidation of the tungsten; a common form of light bulb. Such lamps, owing to the refractory nature of the metal, may be maintained at a very high temperature and require an expenditure of only about 1.25 watts per candle power, depending on the total wattage and the design of the bulb.  By mid-20th century tungsten lamps became the most common type of incand

tunnel stern.d: A design of motor-boat stern, for  use in shallow waters, in which the propeller is housed in a tunnel and does not extend below the greatest draft

tupaiid.d: Any one of several species of East Indian and Asiatic insectivores of the family Tupaiidae, somewhat resembling squirrels in size and arboreal habits.  The nose is long and pointed

tupman.d: A man who breeds, or deals in tups

tupperware party.d: a social gathering at which the host (or more typically hostess) entertains the guests, and provides them with an opportunity to order Tupperware.  This was used as an effective sales strategy by the Tupperware manufacturer, and provided income to the host(ess) from commissions on sales

turacoverdin.d: A green pigment found in the feathers of the turacou. See Turacin

turban-shell.d: A sea urchin when deprived of its spines; -- popularly so called from a fancied resemblance to a turban

turban-top.d: A kind of fungus with an irregularly wrinkled, somewhat globular pileus (Helvella esculenta syn. Gyromitra esculenta.)

turbinella.d: A genus of large marine gastropods having a thick heavy shell with conspicuous folds on the columella

turbinite.d: A petrified shell resembling a member of the genus Turbo

turcism.d: A mode of speech peculiar to the Turks; a Turkish idiom or expression; also, in general, a Turkish mode or custom.  Same as Turkism

turdiformes.d: A division of singing birds including the thrushes and allied kinds

tureenful.d: As much as a tureen can hold; enough to fill a tureen

turgesce.d: To become turgid; to swell or be inflated

turk's-head.d: A knot of turbanlike form  worked on a rope with a piece of small line

turkey-trot.d: An eccentric ragtime dance, danced with the feet well apart and with a characteristic rise on the ball of the foot, followed by a drop upon the heel. The original form, owing to the positions assumed by the dancers, is offensively suggestive.  Similar dances are the bunny hug and grizzly bear, so called in allusion to the movements and the positions assumed by the partners in dancing

turko-iranian.d: Designating, or pert. to, a mixed racial type including the Afghans, and characterized chiefly by stature above mean, fair complexion, dark, or sometimes gray, eyes, brachycephaly, and very long, prominent, and moderately narrow nose

turlupin.d: One of the precursors of the Reformation; -- a nickname corresponding to Lollard, etc

turn-buckle.d: A loop or sleeve with a screw thread at one end and a swivel at the other, -- used for tightening a rod, stay, etc

turnbull's blue.d: The double cyanide of ferrous and ferric iron, a dark blue amorphous substance having a coppery luster, used in dyeing, calico printing, etc.  Cf. Prussian blue, under Prussian

turnicimorphae.d: A division of birds including Turnix and allied genera, resembling quails in appearance but differing from them anatomically

The long magnetic tape in the videocasette is moved between two spindles, and a small portion of the tape at any one time is passed over a recording or playback head

videocasette recorder.d: an electronic device which can record electronic signals, as from a television program, on magnetic tape contained in a videocassette, and can also play back the recording.  It is used, for example, to record television programs broadcast at some particular time, which can then be viewed at any subsequent time by attaching the videocasette recorder to a television receiver and playing the signals throught the television receiver.  Also called VCR

virgouleuse.d: An old French variety of pear, of little value

vitamin k3.d: menadione, (C11H8O2) being chemically 2-methyl-1,4,-naphthoquinone.  Having no side chain in the 3 position, it cannot exert all functions of a true K vitamin and the designation as vitamin K3 has been discouraged

It inhabits grassy plains, and is noted for its extensive burrows and for heaping up miscellaneous articles at the mouth of its burrows. Called also biscacha, bizcacha, vischacha, vishatscha

vizier-azem.d: A grand vizier.  See under Vizier
