vocule.d: A short or weak utterance; a faint or feeble sound, as that heard on separating the lips in pronouncing p or b

vodanium.d: A supposed element, afterward found to be a mixture of several metals, as copper, iron, lead, nickel, etc

volapuek.d: Literally, world's speech; the name of an artificial language invented by Johan Martin Schleyer, of Constance, Switzerland, about 1879.  For more about “planned languages”, see Esperanto

volapükist.d: One who is conversant with, or who favors adoption of, Volapük

volcanic neck.d: A column of igneous rock formed by congelation of lava in the conduit of a volcano and later exposed by the removal of surrounding rocks

volcanic wind.d: A wind associated with a volcanic outburst and due to the eruption or to convection currents over hot lava

volcanity.d: The quality or state of being volcanic, or volcanic origin; volcanicity

volcanization.d: The act of volcanizing, or the state of being volcanized; the process of undergoing volcanic heat, and being affected by it

volge.d: The common sort of people; the crowd; the mob

volksraad.d: A legislative assembly or parliament of any one of several countries colonized by the Dutch, esp. that of the South African Republic, or the Transvaal, and that of the Orange Free State

volley ball.d: A game played by volleying a large inflated ball with the hands over a net 7 ft. 6 in. high

volow.d: To baptize; -- used in contempt by the Reformers

volt-amp.d: A unit of electric measurement equal to the product of a volt and an ampere. For direct current it is a measure of power and is the same as a watt; for alternating current it is a measure of apparent power

volta-electric.d: Of or pertaining to voltaic electricity, or voltaism

volta-electrometer.d: An instrument for the exact measurement of electric currents

voltagraphy.d: In electrotypy, the act or art of copying, in metals deposited by electrolytic action, a form or pattern which is made the negative electrode

voltaplast.d: A form of voltaic, or galvanic, battery suitable for use electrotyping

voltigeur.d: A tumbler; a leaper or vaulter

volumist.d: One who writes a volume; an author

volunteer navy.d: A navy of vessels fitted out and manned by volunteers who sail under the flag of the regular navy and subject to naval discipline. Prussia in 1870, in the Franco-German war, organized such a navy, which was commanded by merchant seamen with temporary commissions, with the claim (in which England acquiesced) that it did not come within the meaning of the term privateer

volunteers of america.d: A religious and philanthropic organization, similar to the Salvation Army, founded (1896) by Commander and Mrs. Ballington Booth

voluta.d: Any one of numerous species of large, handsome marine gastropods belonging to Voluta and allied genera

volutation.d: A rolling of a body; a wallowing

voortreker.d: One who treks before or first; a pioneer

voraginous.d: Pertaining to a gulf; full of gulfs; hence, devouring

vortex filament.d: A vortex tube of infinitesimal cross section

vortex fringe.d: The region immediately surrounding a disk moving flatwise through air; -- so called because the air has a cyclic motion as in vortex ring

vortex line.d: A line, within a rotating fluid, whose tangent at every point is the instantaneous axis of rotation as that point of the fluid

vow-fellow.d: One bound by the same vow as another

vowelish.d: Of the nature of a vowel

vulcan powder.d: A dynamite composed of nitroglycerin (30 parts), sodium nitrate (52.5), charcoal (10.5), and sulphur (7), used in mining and blasting

vulneration.d: The act of wounding, or the state of being wounded

vulpic.d: Pertaining to, derived from, or designating, an acid obtained from a lichen (Cetraria vulpina) as a yellow or red crystalline substance which on decomposition yields pulvinic acid

vulpinism.d: The quality of being cunning like the fox; craft; artfulness

vultern.d: The brush turkey (Talegallus Lathami) of Australia.  See Brush turkey

vulturism.d: The quality or state of being like a vulture; rapaciousness

vyce.d: A kind of clamp with gimlet points for holding a barrel head while the staves are being closed around it

wa'n't.d: A colloquial contraction of was not

waahoo.d: The burning bush; -- said to be called after a quack medicine made from it

waddywood.d: An Australian tree (Pittosporum bicolor); also, its wood, used in making waddies

wag-halter.d: One who moves or wears a halter; one likely to be hanged

wagati.d: A small East Indian wild cat (Felis wagati), regarded by some as a variety of the leopard cat

wagenboom.d: A south African proteaceous tree (Protea grandiflora); also, its tough wood, used for making wagon wheels

waggel.d: The young of the great black-backed gull (Larus marinus), formerly considered a distinct species

wagon-headed.d: Having a top, or head, shaped like the top of a covered wagon, or resembling in section or outline an inverted U, thus &unr_;; as, a wagonheaded ceiling

wagon-roofed.d: Having a roof, or top, shaped like an inverted U; wagon-headed

wagonful.d: As much as a wagon will hold; enough to fill a wagon; a wagonload

wagonry.d: Conveyance by means of a wagon or wagons

wai wu pu.d: The Department of Foreign Affairs in the Chinese government

waid.d: Oppressed with weight; crushed; weighed down

waistcoateer.d: One wearing a waistcoat; esp., a woman wearing one uncovered, or thought fit for such a habit; hence, a loose woman; strumpet

wait-a-while.d: One of the Australian wattle trees (Acacia colletioides), so called from the impenetrability of the thicket which it makes

waketime.d: Time during which one is awake

wakf.d: The granting or dedication of property in trust for a pious purpose, that is, to some object that tends to the good of mankind, as to support a mosque or caravansary, to provide for support of one's family, kin, or neighbors, to benefit some particular person or persons and afterward the poor, etc.; also, the trust so created, or the property in trust

waldheimia.d: A genus of brachiopods of which many species are found in the fossil state. A few still exist in the deep sea

wall-eye.d: An eye in which the iris is of a very light gray or whitish color; -- said usually of horses

wall-plat.d: The spotted flycatcher. It builds its nest on walls

wall-sided.d: Having sides nearly perpendicular; -- said of certain vessels to distinguish them from those having flaring sides, or sides tumbling home (see under Tumble, v. i.)

wallaba.d: A leguminous tree (Eperua falcata) of Demerara, with pinnate leaves and clusters of red flowers. The reddish brown wood is used for palings and shingles

walleteer.d: One who carries a wallet; a foot traveler; a tramping beggar

walm.d: To roll; to spout; to boil up

wamble-cropped.d: Sick at the stomach; also, crestfallen; dejected

wammel.d: To move irregularly or awkwardly; to wamble, or wabble

wanderment.d: The act of wandering, or roaming

wanghee.d: The Chinese name of one or two species of bamboo, or jointed cane, of the genus Phyllostachys. The slender stems are much used for walking sticks

wanhope.d: Want of hope; despair; also, faint or delusive hope; delusion. [Obs.] Piers Plowman

wanhorn.d: An East Indian plant (Kaempferia Galanga) of the Ginger family.  See Galanga

wantonize.d: To behave wantonly; to frolic; to wanton

wantrust.d: Failing or diminishing trust; want of trust or confidence; distrust

wantwit.d: One destitute of wit or sense; a blockhead; a fool

wapacut.d: The American hawk owl.  See under Hawk

wapatoo.d: The edible tuber of a species of arrowhead (Sagittaria variabilis); -- so called by the Indians of Oregon

wapinschaw.d: An exhibition of arms. according to the rank of the individual, by all persons bearing arms; -- formerly made at certain seasons in each district

warburg's tincture.d: A preparation containing quinine and many other ingredients, often used in the treatment of malarial affections. It was invented by Dr. Warburg of London

ward-corn.d: The duty of keeping watch and ward (see the Note under Watch, n., 1) with a horn to be blown upon any occasion of surprise

wardcorps.d: Guardian; one set to watch over another

warega fly.d: A Brazilian fly whose larvae live in the skin of man and animals, producing painful sores

wariangle.d: The red-backed shrike (Lanius collurio); -- called also würger, worrier, and throttler

warine.d: A South American monkey, one of the sapajous

warish.d: To protect from the effects of; hence, to cure; to heal

warling.d: One often quarreled with; -- &unr_; word coined, perhaps, to rhyme with darling

warmful.d: Abounding in capacity to warm; giving warmth; as, a warmful garment

warmthless.d: Being without warmth; not communicating warmth; cold

warty-back.d: An American fresh-water mussel (Quadrula pustulosa). Its shell is used in making buttons

warye.d: To curse; to curse; to execrate; to condemn; also, to vex

wash-off.d: Capable of being washed off; not permanent or durable; -- said of colors not fixed by steaming or otherwise

washoe process.d: The process of treating silver ores by grinding in pans or tubs with the addition of mercury, and sometimes of chemicals such as blue vitriol and salt

wasite.d: A variety of allanite from Sweden supposed to contain wasium

wasium.d: A rare element supposed by Bahr to have been extracted from wasite, but now identified with thorium

wastebook.d: A book in which rough entries of transactions are made, previous to their being carried into the journal

wastel.d: A kind of white and fine bread or cake; -- called also wastel bread, and wastel cake

watch meeting.d: A religious meeting held in the closing hours of the year

water agrimony.d: A kind of bur marigold (Bidens tripartita) found in wet places in Europe

water ballast.d: Water confined in specially constructed compartments in a vessel's hold, to serve as ballast

water barometer.d: A barometer in which the changes of atmospheric pressure are indicated by the motion of a column of water instead of mercury. It requires a column of water about thirty-three feet in height

water battery.d: A voltaic battery in which the exciting fluid is water

water blackbird.d: The European water ousel, or dipper

water breather.d: Any arthropod that breathes by means of gills

water buck.d: A large, heavy antelope (Kobus ellipsiprymnus) native of Central Africa. It frequents the banks of rivers and is a good swimmer. It has a white ring around the rump. Called also photomok, water antelope, and waterbok

water can.d: Any one of several species of Nuphar; the yellow frog lily; -- so called from the shape of the seed vessel.  See Nuphar, and cf. Candock

water celery.d: A very acrid herb (Ranunculus sceleratus) growing in ditches and wet places; -- called also cursed crowfoot

water cell.d: A cell containing water; specifically (Zool.), one of the cells or chambers in which water is stored up in the stomach of a camel

water cock.d: A large gallinule (Gallicrex cristatus) native of Australia, India, and the East Indies. In the breeding season the male is black and has a fleshy red caruncle, or horn, on the top of its head. Called also kora

water color.d: A color ground with water and gum or other glutinous medium; a color the vehicle of which is water; -- so called in distinction from oil color

water course.d: A stream of water; a river or brook

water craft.d: Any vessel or boat plying on water; vessels and boats, collectively

water crane.d: A goose-neck apparatus for supplying water from an elevated tank, as to the tender of a locomotive

water cress.d: A perennial cruciferous herb (Nasturtium officinale) growing usually in clear running or spring water. The leaves are pungent, and used for salad and as an antiscorbutic

water deck.d: A covering of painting canvas for the equipments of a dragoon's horse

water devil.d: The rapacious larva of a large water beetle (Hydrophilus piceus), and of other similar species.  See Illust. of Water beetle

water dock.d: A tall, coarse dock growing in wet places. The American water dock is Rumex orbiculatus, the European is Rumex Hydrolapathum

water doctor.d: One who professes to be able to divine diseases by inspection of the urine

water drain.d: A drain or channel for draining off water

water engine.d: An engine to raise water; or an engine moved by water; also, an engine or machine for extinguishing fires; a fire engine

water feather.d: The water violet (Hottonia palustris); also, the less showy American plant Hottonia inflata

water flag.d: A European species of Iris (Iris Pseudacorus) having bright yellow flowers

water flannel.d: A floating mass formed in pools by the entangled filaments of a European fresh-water alga (Cladophora crispata)

water fox.d: The carp; -- so called on account of its cunning

water frame.d: A name given to the first power spinning machine, because driven by water power

water furrow.d: A deep furrow for conducting water from the ground, and keeping the surface soil dry

water gall.d: A cavity made in the earth by a torrent of water; a washout

water gang.d: A passage for water, such as was usually made in a sea wall, to drain water out of marshes

water gavel.d: A gavel or rent paid for a privilege, as of fishing, in some river or water

water germander.d: A labiate plant (Teucrium Scordium) found in marshy places in Europe

water gilding.d: The act, or the process, of gilding metallic surfaces by covering them with a thin coating of amalgam of gold, and then volatilizing the mercury by heat; -- called also wash gilding

water god.d: A fabulous deity supposed to dwell in, and preside over, some body of water

water grass.d: A tall march perennial grass (Paspalum dilatatum) of the southern United States and the American tropics

water gruel.d: A liquid food composed of water and a small portion of meal, or other farinaceous substance, boiled and seasoned

water hare.d: A small American hare or rabbit (Lepus aquaticus) found on or near the southern coasts of the United States; -- called also water rabbit, and swamp hare

water lizard.d: Any aquatic lizard of the genus Varanus, as the monitor of the Nile.  See Monitor, n., 3

water measure.d: A measure formerly used for articles brought by water, as coals, oysters, etc. The water-measure bushel was three gallons larger than the Winchester bushel

water measurer.d: Any one of numerous species of water; the skater.  See Skater, n., 2

water mite.d: Any of numerous species of aquatic mites belonging to Hydrachna and allied genera of the family Hydrachnidae, usually having the legs fringed and adapted for swimming. They are often red or red and black in color, and while young are parasites of fresh-water insects and mussels.  Called also water tick, and water spider

water mole.d: The shrew mole.  See under Shrew

water monitor.d: A very large lizard (Varanaus salvator) native of India. It frequents the borders of streams and swims actively. It becomes five or six feet long. Called also two-banded monitor, and kabaragoya. The name is also applied to other aquatic monitors

water monkey.d: A jar or bottle, as of porous earthenware, in which water is cooled by evaporation

water mouse.d: Any one of several species of mice belonging to the genus Hydromys, native of Australia and Tasmania. Their hind legs are strong and their toes partially webbed. They live on the borders of streams, and swim well. They are remarkable as being the only rodents found in Australia

water murrain.d: A kind of murrain affecting cattle

water newt.d: Any one of numerous species of aquatic salamanders; a triton

water ousel.d: Any one of several species of small insessorial birds of the genus Cinclus (or Hydrobates), especially the European water ousel (Cinclus aquaticus), and the American water ousel (Cinclus Mexicanus). These birds live about the water, and are in the habit of walking on the bottom of streams beneath the water in search of food

water plate.d: A plate heated by hot water contained in a double bottom or jacket

water poa.d: Meadow reed grass.  See under Reed

water pocket.d: A water hole in the bed of an intermittent stream, esp. the bowl at the foot of a cliff over which the stream leaps when in the flood stage

water radish.d: A coarse yellow-flowered plant (Nasturtium amphibium) related to the water cress and to the horse-radish

water rail.d: Any one of numerous species of rails of the genus Rallus, as the common European species (Rallus aquaticus).  See Illust. of Rail

water rattle.d: The diamond rattlesnake (Crotalus adamanteus); -- so called from its preference for damp places near water

water rocket.d: A cruciferous plant (Nasturtium sylvestre) with small yellow flowers

water sail.d: A small sail sometimes set under a studding sail or under a driver boom, and reaching nearly to the water

water snail.d: Any aquatic pulmonate gastropod belonging to Planorbis, Limnaea, and allied genera; a pond snail

water soldier.d: An aquatic European plant (Stratiotes aloides) with bayonet-shaped leaves

water souchy.d: A dish consisting of small fish stewed and served in a little water

water spider.d: An aquatic European spider (Argyoneta aquatica) which constructs its web beneath the surface of the water on water plants. It lives in a bell-shaped structure of silk, open beneath like a diving bell, and filled with air which the spider carries down in the form of small bubbles attached one at a time to the spinnerets and hind feet. Called also diving spider

water tabby.d: A kind of waved or watered tabby.  See Tabby, n., 1

water telescope.d: A telescope in which the medium between the objective and the eye piece is water instead of air, used in some experiments in aberration

water tender.d: In the United States navy, a first-class petty officer in charge in a fireroom. He “tends” water to the boilers, sees that fires are properly cleaned and stoked, etc. There is also a rating of chief water tender, who is a chief petty officer

water thermometer.d: A thermometer filled with water instead of mercury, for ascertaining the precise temperature at which water attains its maximum density. This is about 39° Fahr., or 4° Centigrade; and from that point down to 32° Fahr., or 0° Centigrade, or the freezing point, it expands

water tiger.d: A diving, or water, beetle, especially the larva of a water beetle.  See Illust. b of Water beetle

water torch.d: The common cat-tail (Typha latifolia), the spike of which makes a good torch soaked in oil

water tree.d: A climbing shrub (Tetracera alnifolia syn. Tetracera potatoria) of Western Africa, which pours out a watery sap from the freshly cut stems

water tupelo.d: A species of large tupelo (Nyssa aquatica) growing in swamps in the southern of the United States.  See Ogeechee lime

water tuyere.d: A tuyère kept cool by water circulating within a casing. It is used for hot blast

water twist.d: Yarn made by the throstle, or water frame

water vine.d: Any plant of the genus Phytocrene, climbing shrubs of Asia and Africa, the stems of which are singularly porous, and when cut stream with a limpid potable juice

water willow.d: An American aquatic plant (Dianthera Americana) with long willowlike leaves, and spikes of small purplish flowers

water wing.d: One of two walls built on either side of the junction of a bridge with the bank of a river, to protect the abutment of the bridge and the bank from the action of the current

water-colorist.d: One who paints in water colors

water-laid.d: Having a left-hand twist; -- said of cordage; as, a water-laid, or left-hand, rope

water-ret.d: To ret, or rot, in water, as flax; to water-rot

water-rot.d: To rot by steeping in water; to water-ret; as, to water-rot hemp or flax

water-withe.d: A vinelike plant (Vitis Caribaea) growing in parched districts in the West Indies, and containing a great amount of sap which is sometimes used for quenching thirst

waterhorse.d: A pile of salted fish heaped up to drain

waterie.d: The pied wagtail; -- so called because it frequents ponds

waterlander.d: One of a body of Dutch Anabaptists who separated from the Mennonites in the sixteenth century; -- so called from a district in North Holland denominated Waterland

watertath.d: A kind of coarse grass growing in wet grounds, and supposed to be injurious to sheep

watteau back.d: The back of a woman's gown in which one or more very broad folds are carried from the neck to the floor without being held in at the waist, while the front and sides of the gown are shaped to the person and have a belt or its equivalent

waveringness.d: The quality or state of wavering

wawaskeesh.d: The wapiti, or wapiti, or American elk

way-wise.d: Skillful in finding the way; well acquainted with the way or route; wise from having traveled

waybung.d: An Australian insessorial bird (Corcorax melanorhamphus) noted for the curious actions of the male during the breeding season. It is black with a white patch on each wing

waymaker.d: One who makes a way; a precursor

wayment.d: To lament; to grieve; to wail

waywode.d: Originally, the title of a military commander in various Slavonic countries; afterwards applied to governors of towns or provinces. It was assumed for a time by the rulers of Moldavia and Wallachia, who were afterwards called hospodars, and has also been given to some inferior Turkish officers

waywodeship.d: The office, province, or jurisdiction of a waywode

weak-hearted.d: Having little courage; of feeble spirit; dispirited; faint-hearted

weal-balanced.d: Balanced or considered with reference to public weal

wealdish.d: Of or pertaining to a weald, esp. to the weald in the county of Kent, England

weasiness.d: Quality or state of being weasy; full feeding; sensual indulgence

weather signal.d: Any signal giving information about the weather. The system used by the United States Weather Bureau includes temperature, cold or hot wave, rain or snow, wind direction, storm, and hurricane signals

weather-bit.d: A turn of the cable about the end of the windlass, without the bits

weather-bitten.d: Eaten into, defaced, or worn, by exposure to the weather

weather-driven.d: Driven by winds or storms; forced by stress of weather

weather-fend.d: To defend from the weather; to shelter

weatherbit.d: To take another turn with, as a cable around a windlass

wedge gauge.d: A wedge with a graduated edge, to measure the width of a space into which it is thrust

wedge gear.d: A friction gear wheel with wedge-shaped circumferential grooves

wedge-formed.d: Having the form of a wedge; cuneiform

wedge-shell.d: Any one of numerous species of small marine bivalves belonging to Donax and allied genera in which the shell is wedge-shaped

wedge-tailed.d: Having a tail which has the middle pair of feathers longest, the rest successively and decidedly shorter, and all more or less attenuate; -- said of certain birds.  See Illust. of Wood hoopoe, under Wood

wedgwood ware.d: A kind of fine pottery, the most remarkable being what is called jasper, either white, or colored throughout the body, and capable of being molded into the most delicate forms, so that fine and minute bas-reliefs like cameos were made of it, fit even for being set as jewels

weeding-rhim.d: A kind of implement used for tearing up weeds esp. on summer fallows

weepful.d: Full of weeping or lamentation; grieving

weeping-ripe.d: Ripe for weeping; ready to weep

weet-bird.d: The wryneck; -- so called from its cry

wegotism.d: Excessive use of the pronoun we; -- called also weism

weigh-house.d: A building at or within which goods, and the like, are weighed

weiss beer.d: A light-colored highly effervescent beer made by the top-fermentation process

wekau.d: A small New Zealand owl (Sceloglaux albifacies). It has short wings and long legs, and lives chiefly on the ground

weld steel.d: A compound of iron, such as puddled steel, made without complete fusion

well-seen.d: Having seen much; hence, accomplished; experienced

well-willer.d: One who wishes well, or means kindly

wellat.d: The king parrakeet See under King

welldrain.d: To drain, as land; by means of wells, or pits, which receive the water, and from which it is discharged by machinery

wellwisher.d: One who wishes another well; one who is benevolently or friendlily inclined

weltschmertz.d: Sorrow or sadness over the present or future evils or woes of the world in general; sentimental pessimism

wemless.d: Having no wem, or blemish; spotless

wen-li.d: The higher literary idiom of Chinese, that of the canonical books and of all composition pretending to literary standing.  It employs a classical or academic diction, and a more condensed and sententious style than Mandarin, and differs also in the doubling and arrangement of words

wenlock group.d: The middle subdivision of the Upper Silurian in Great Britain; -- so named from the typical locality in Shropshire

wernerian.d: Of or pertaining to A. G. Werner, The German mineralogist and geologist, who classified minerals according to their external characters, and advocated the theory that the strata of the earth's crust were formed by depositions from water; designating, or according to, Werner's system

weroole.d: An Australian lorikeet (Ptilosclera versicolor) noted for the variety of its colors; -- called also varied lorikeet

west india.d: Belonging or relating to the West Indies

wet-shod.d: Having the feet, or the shoes on the feet, wet

wetbird.d: The chaffinch, whose cry is thought to foretell rain

whaap.d: The European curlew; -- called also awp, whaup, great whaup, and stock whaup

whachamacallit.d: Any object whose name is forgotten, or not known

whahoo.d: An American tree, the winged elm. (Ulmus alata)

whala.d: To lash with stripes; to wale; to thrash; to drub

whall.d: A light color of the iris in horses; wall-eye

whally.d: Having the iris of light color; -- said of horses

wharl.d: A guttural pronunciation of the letter r; a burr.  See Burr, n., 6

wharp.d: A kind of fine sand from the banks of the Trent, used as a polishing powder

whate'er.d: A contraction of what-ever; -- used in poetry

whealworm.d: The harvest mite; -- so called from the wheals, caused by its bite

wheat sawfly.d: A small European sawfly (Cephus pygmaeus) whose larva does great injury to wheat by boring in the stalks

wheatbird.d: A bird that feeds on wheat, especially the chaffinch

wheatstone's rods.d: Flexible rods the period of vibration of which in two planes at right angles are in some exact ratio to one another. When one end of such a rod is fixed, the free end describes in vibrating the corresponding Lissajous figure. So called because devised by Sir Charles Wheatstone

wheel of fortune.d: A gambling or lottery device consisting of a wheel which is spun horizontally, articles or sums to which certain marks on its circumference point when it stops being distributed according to varying rules

wheel-worn.d: Worn by the action of wheels; as, a wheel-worn road

whelky.d: Having whelks, ridges, or protuberances; hence, streaked; striated

whenceforth.d: From, or forth from, what or which place; whence

whereform.d: From which; from which or what place

wherret.d: To hurry; to trouble; to tease

whetile.d: The green woodpecker, or yaffle.  See Yaffle

whidah bird.d: Any one of several species of finchlike birds belonging to the genus Vidua, native of Asia and Africa. In the breeding season the male has very long, drooping tail feathers. Called also vida finch, whidah finch, whydah bird, whydah finch, widow bird, and widow finch

whiggamore.d: A Whig; -- a cant term applied in contempt to Scotch Presbyterians

whigling.d: A petty or inferior Whig; -- used in contempt

whilere.d: A little while ago; recently; just now; erewhile

whilk.d: A kind of mollusk, a whelk

whinock.d: The small pig of a litter

whip-shaped.d: Shaped like the lash of a whip; long, slender, round, and tapering; as, a whip-shaped root or stem

whip-tom-kelly.d: A vireo (Vireo altiloquus) native of the West Indies and Florida; -- called also black-whiskered vireo

whipparee.d: A large sting ray (Dasybatis Sayi, or Trygon Sayi) native of the Southern United States. It is destitute of large spines on the body and tail

whipperin.d: A huntsman who keeps the hounds from wandering, and whips them in, if necessary, to the of chase

whipstaff.d: A bar attached to the tiller, for convenience in steering

whirlbat.d: Anything moved with a whirl, as preparatory for a blow, or to augment the force of it; -- applied by poets to the cestus of ancient boxers

whisket.d: A basket; esp., a straw provender basket

whiskey ring.d: A conspiracy of distillers and government officials during the administration of President Grant to defraud the government of the excise taxes. The frauds were detected in 1875 through the efforts of the Secretary of the Treasury B. H. Bristow, and most of the offenders were convicted

whistlefish.d: A gossat, or rockling; -- called also whistler, three-bearded rockling, sea loach, and sorghe

whistlewood.d: The moosewood, or striped maple.  See Maple

white fly.d: Any one of numerous small injurious hemipterous insects of the genus Aleyrodes, allied to scale insects. They are usually covered with a white or gray powder

white slaving.d: The action of one who procures or holds a woman or women for unwilling prostitution

white-face.d: A white mark in the forehead of a horse, descending almost to the nose; -- called also white-blaze

white-foot.d: A white mark on the foot of a horse, between the fetlock and the coffin

white-fronted.d: Having a white front; as, the white-fronted lemur

white-heart.d: A somewhat heart-shaped cherry with a whitish skin

white-pot.d: A kind of food made of milk or cream, eggs, sugar, bread, etc., baked in a pot

whiteboyism.d: The conduct or principle of the Whiteboys

whitecoat.d: The skin of a newborn seal; also, the seal itself

whiteweed.d: A perennial composite herb (Chrysanthemum Leucanthemum) with conspicuous white rays and a yellow disk, a common weed in grass lands and pastures; -- called also oxeye daisy

whitling.d: A young full trout during its second season

whitster.d: A whitener; a bleacher; a whitester

whitten tree.d: Either of two shrubs (Viburnum Lantana, and Viburnum Opulus), so called on account of their whitish branches

whittlings.d: Chips made by one who whittles; shavings cut from a stick with a knife

whitworth ball.d: A prejectile used in the Whitworth gun

whity-brown.d: Of a color between white and brown

whoremasterly.d: Having the character of a whoremaster; lecherous; libidinous

whurry.d: To whisk along quickly; to hurry

why-not.d: A violent and peremptory procedure without any assigned reason; a sudden conclusive happening

widegap.d: The angler; -- called also widegab, and widegut

widow-hunter.d: One who courts widows, seeking to marry one with a fortune

widow-maker.d: One who makes widows by destroying husbands

widow-wail.d: A low, narrowleaved evergreen shrub (Cneorum tricoccon) found in Southern Europe

widual.d: Of or pertaining to a widow; vidual

wieldance.d: The act or power of wielding

wieldless.d: Not to be wielded; unmanageable; unwieldy

wieldsome.d: Admitting of being easily wielded or managed

wike.d: A temporary mark or boundary, as a bough of a tree set up in marking out or dividing anything, as tithes, swaths to be mowed in common ground, etc.; -- called also wicker

wild-cat.d: Unsound; worthless; irresponsible; unsafe; -- said to have been originally applied to the notes of an insolvent bank in Michigan upon which there was the figure of a panther

wildgrave.d: A waldgrave, or head forest keeper.  See Waldgrave

wilfley table.d: An inclined percussion table, usually with longitudinal grooves in its surface, agitated by side blows at right angles to the flow of the pulp; -- so called after the inventor

willow-weed.d: A European species of loosestrife (Lysimachia vulgaris)

willy nilly.d: Whether I (he, she, they) want to or not.  See Will I, nill I, etc., under 3d Will

wind-fertilized.d: Anemophilous; fertilized by pollen borne by the wind

wind-rode.d: Caused to ride or drive by the wind in opposition to the course of the tide; -- said of a vessel lying at anchor, with wind and tide opposed to each other

windbore.d: The lower, or bottom, pipe in a lift of pumps in a mine

wing-handed.d: Having the anterior limbs or hands adapted for flight, as the bats and pterodactyls

wing-leaved.d: Having pinnate or pinnately divided leaves

wing-shell.d: Any one of various species of marine bivalve shells belonging to the genus Avicula, in which the hinge border projects like a wing

winkingly.d: In a winking manner; with the eye almost closed

winkle-hawk.d: A rectangular rent made in cloth; -- called also winkle-hole

winninish.d: The land-locked variety of the common salmon

winter-beaten.d: Beaten or harassed by the severe weather of winter

winter-ground.d: To coved over in the season of winter, as for protection or shelter; as, to winter-ground the roods of a plant

winter-proud.d: Having too rank or forward a growth for winter

winter-rig.d: To fallow or till in winter

winterweed.d: A kind of speedwell (Veronica hederifolia) which spreads chiefly in winter

wire tapper.d: One that taps, or cuts in on, telegraph wires and intercepts messages

wire-drawer.d: One who draws metal into wire

wire-heel.d: A disease in the feet of a horse or other beast

wire-tailed.d: Having some or all of the tail quills terminated in a long, slender, pointed shaft, without a web or barbules

wire-worker.d: One who manufactures articles from wire

wise-hearted.d: Wise; knowing; skillful; sapient; erudite; prudent

wise-like.d: Resembling that which is wise or sensible; judicious

wiseling.d: One who pretends to be wise; a wiseacre; a witling

wishable.d: Capable or worthy of being wished for; desirable

wishedly.d: According to wish; conformably to desire

wishly.d: According to desire; longingly; with wishes

wispen.d: Formed of a wisp, or of wisp; as, a wispen broom

wisse.d: To show; to teach; to inform; to guide; to direct

wistit.d: A small South American monkey; a marmoset

wit-cracker.d: One who breaks jests; a joker

wit-snapper.d: One who affects repartee; a wit-cracker

wit-starved.d: Barren of wit; destitute of genius

witchuck.d: The sand martin, or bank swallow

witcraft.d: Art or skill of the mind; contrivance; invention; wit

withdrawing-room.d: A room for retirement from another room, as from a dining room; a drawing-room

withe-rod.d: A North American shrub (Viburnum nudum) whose tough osierlike shoots are sometimes used for binding sheaves

wither-wrung.d: Injured or hurt in the withers, as a horse

witherband.d: A piece of iron in a saddle near a horse's withers, to strengthen the bow

witherling.d: A withered person; one who is decrepit

withernam.d: A second or reciprocal distress of other goods in lieu of goods which were taken by a first distress and have been eloigned; a taking by way of reprisal; -- chiefly used in the expression capias in withernam, which is the name of a writ used in connection with the action of replevin (sometimes called a writ of reprisal), which issues to a defendant in replevin when he has obtained judgment for a return of the chattels replevied, and fails to obtain them on the writ of return

withsay.d: To contradict; to gainsay; to deny; to renounce

witworm.d: One who, or that which, feeds on or destroys wit

wizen-faced.d: Having a shriveled, thin, withered face

woad-waxen.d: A leguminous plant (Genista tinctoria) of Europe and Russian Asia, and adventitious in America; -- called also greenwood, greenweed, dyer's greenweed, and whin, wood-wash, wood-wax, and wood-waxen

wodegeld.d: A geld, or payment, for wood

woe-begone.d: Beset or overwhelmed with woe; immersed in grief or sorrow; woeful

wolf's-claw.d: A kind of club moss.  See Lycopodium

wolf's-milk.d: Any kind of spurge (Euphorbia); -- so called from its acrid milky juice

woman's christian temperance union.d: An association of women formed in the United States in 1874, for the advancement of temperance by organizing preventive, educational, evangelistic, social, and legal work.  It is also known as the Women's Christian Temperance Union and by its acronym WCTU or W.C.T.U..  It was one of the political forces leading to passage of the constitutional amendment, later repealed, which prohibited the sale of alcoholic beverages

wood partridge.d: Any of several small partridges of Java, Sumatra, Borneo, and neighboring regions belonging to the genera Caloperdix, Rollulus, and Melanoperdix

wood-layer.d: A young oak, or other timber plant, laid down in a hedge among the whitethorn or other plants used in hedges

wood-note.d: A wild or natural note, as of a forest bird

wood-sare.d: A kind of froth seen on herbs

wood-sere.d: The time when there no sap in the trees; the winter season

woodbury-type.d: A process in photographic printing, in which a relief pattern in gelatin, which has been hardened after certain operations, is pressed upon a plate of lead or other soft metal. woodhole.d: A place where wood is stored

woodly.d: In a wood, mad, or raving manner; madly; furiously

woodrock.d: A compact woodlike variety of asbestus

wool-dyed.d: Dyed before being made into cloth, in distinction from piece-dyed; ingrain

wordsman.d: One who deals in words, or in mere words; a verbalist

working-day.d: Pertaining to, or characteristic of, working days, or workdays; everyday; hence, plodding; hard-working

workways.d: In a working position or manner; as, a T rail placed workwise, i.e., resting on its base

workyday.d: A week day or working day, as distinguished from Sunday or a holiday. Also used adjectively

world-wide web.d: The collective total of all computer installations that are connected to the internet and provide access to other computers connected to the internet, using hypertext transfer protocol, to computer files called web pages, which may have text, graphics, audio or animated video data, as well as pages which may provide data or information in all those forms

wormian.d: Discovered or described by Olanus Wormius, a Danish anatomist

worshipability.d: The quality of being worthy to be worshiped

worshipable.d: Capable of being worshiped; worthy of worship

woteth.d: 3d pers. sing. pres. of Wit, to know

wou-wou.d: The agile, or silvery, gibbon; -- called also camper.  See Gibbon

woundily.d: In a woundy manner; excessively; woundy

wowf.d: Disordered or unsettled in intellect; deranged

wraprascal.d: A kind of coarse upper coat, or overcoat, formerly worn

wreath-shell.d: A marine shell of the genus Turbo.  See Turbo

wringbolt.d: A bolt used by shipwrights, to bend and secure the planks against the timbers till they are fastened by bolts, spikes, or treenails; -- not to be confounded with ringbolt

wrong-timed.d: Done at an improper time; ill-timed

wrongless.d: Not wrong; void or free from wrong

wung-out.d: Having the sails set in the manner called wing-and-wing

wurbagool.d: A fruit bat (Pteropus medius) native of India. It is similar to the flying fox, but smaller

wurraluh.d: The Australian white-quilled honey eater (Entomyza albipennis)

xanthose.d: An orange-yellow substance found in pigment spots of certain crabs

xenomi.d: A suborder of soft-rayed fresh-water fishes of which the blackfish of Alaska (Dallia pectoralis) is the type

xenylic.d: Pertaining to, derived from, designating, certain amido compounds obtained by reducing certain nitro derivatives of diphenyl

xeraphim.d: An old money of account in Bombay, equal to three fifths of a rupee

xyloplastic.d: Formed of wood pulp by molds; relating to casts made of wood pulp in molds

y current.d: The current through one branch of the star arrangement of a three-phase circuit

yalah.d: The oil of the mahwa tree

yardful.d: As much as a yard will contain; enough to fill a yard

yardline.d: Any of the lines parallel to the goal lines indicating distance from the goal line on a football the field; as, the twenty-five yardline

yarnen.d: Made of yarn; consisting of yarn

yarr.d: To growl or snarl as a dog

yarwhip.d: The European bar-tailed godwit; -- called also yardkeep, and yarwhelp.  See Godwit

ycleped.d: Called; named; -- obsolete, except in archaic or humorous writings

year 2000 bug.d: an error in the coding of certain computer programs in which the year portion of dates was represented by only two decimal digits, assuming that the first two digits are “19”.  In such a program the the year 1975 is represented as “75”.  This was a common practise in computer programming even into the 1990's, as many programmers failed to consider that their programs would be used after the year 1999.  Thus, with such a program, a person born in 2000 would be considered as 101 years old in 2001;

year 2000 compliant.d: having dates fully and properly represented, and not susceptible to failure due to the year 2000 bug

year-old.d: having reached an age as specified; as, a two-year-old toddler

yeara.d: The California poison oak (Rhus diversiloba).  See under Poison, a

yedding.d: The song of a minstrel; hence, any song

yeldrin.d: The yellow-hammer; -- called also yeldrock, and yoldrin

yellow-golds.d: A certain plant, probably the yellow oxeye

yellowfish.d: A rock trout (Pleurogrammus monopterygius) found on the coast of Alaska; -- called also striped fish, and Atka mackerel

yellowseed.d: A kind of pepper grass (Lepidium campestre)

yelting.d: The Florida and West Indian red snapper (Lutianus aya); also, sometimes, one of certain other allied species, as Lutianus caxis

yeomanlike.d: Resembling, or suitable to, a yeoman; yeomanly

yernut.d: An earthnut, or groundnut.  See Groundnut (d)

ygdrasyl.d: See in the Dictionary of Noted Names in Fiction

young one.d: A young human being; a child; also, a young animal, as a colt

young'un.d: A young human being; -- a contraction of young one

youngthly.d: Pertaining to, or resembling, youth; youthful

ypres lace.d: Fine bobbin lace made at Ypres in Belgium, usually exactly like Valenciennes lace

yttro-cerite.d: A mineral of a violet-blue color, inclining to gray and white. It is a hydrous fluoride of cerium, yttrium, and calcium

yttro-columbite.d: A tantalate of uranium, yttrium, and calcium, of a brown or black color

yunx.d: A genus of birds comprising the wrynecks

zaimet.d: A district from which a Zaim draws his revenue

zamite.d: A fossil cycad of the genus Zamia

zampogna.d: A sort of bagpipe formerly in use among Italian peasants. It is now almost obsolete

zarnich.d: Native sulphide of arsenic, including sandarach, or realgar, and orpiment

zealotical.d: Like, or suitable to, a zealot; ardently zealous

zealotism.d: The character or conduct of a zealot; zealotry

zebrinny.d: A cross between a male horse and a female zebra

zendik.d: An atheist or unbeliever; -- name given in the East to those charged with disbelief of any revealed religion, or accused of magical heresies

zeolitiform.d: Having the form of a zeolite

zeuzerian.d: Any one of a group of bombycid moths of which the genus Zeuzera is the type. Some of these moths are of large size. The goat moth is an example

ziment-water.d: A kind of water found in copper mines; water impregnated with copper

zimocca.d: A sponge (Euspongia zimocca) of flat form and fine quality, from the Adriatic, about the Greek islands, and the coast of Barbary

zincking.d: The act or process of applying zinc; galvanization

zinco-polar.d: Electrically polarized like the surface of the zinc presented to the acid in a battery, which has zincous affinity

zincongraphic.d: Of or pertaining to zincography; as, zincographic processes

zip + 4.d: a full nine-digit zip code.  See zip code

zoanthodeme.d: The zooids of a compound anthozoan, collectively

zoanthoid.d: Of or pertaining to the Zoanthacea

zoilean.d: Having the characteristic of Zoilus, a bitter, envious, unjust critic, who lived about 270 years before Christ

zoilism.d: Resemblance to Zoilus in style or manner; carping criticism; detraction

zonar.d: A belt or girdle which the Christians and Jews of the Levant were obliged to wear to distinguish them from Mohammedans

zonaria.d: A division of Mammalia in which the placenta is zonelike

zonure.d: Any one of several of South African lizards of the genus Zonura, common in rocky situations

zoocytium.d: The common support, often branched, of certain species of social Infusoria

zoodendrium.d: The branched, and often treelike, support of the colonies of certain Infusoria

zooerythrine.d: A peculiar organic red coloring matter found in the feathers of various birds

zooidal.d: Of or pertaining to a zooid; as, a zooidal form

zoomelanin.d: A pigment giving the black color to the feathers of many birds

zoophorous.d: The part between the architrave and cornice; the frieze; -- so called from the figures of animals carved upon it

zwanziger.d: An Austrian silver coin equivalent to 20 kreutzers, or about 10 cents

zygenid.d: Any one of numerous species of moths of the family Zygaenidae, most of which are bright colored. The wood nymph and the vine forester are examples. Also used adjectively

zygobranchia.d: A division of marine gastropods in which the gills are developed on both sides of the body and the renal organs are also paired. The abalone (Haliotis) and the keyhole limpet (Fissurella) are examples

zygodactylae.d: The zygodactylous birds. In a restricted sense applied to a division of birds which includes the barbets, toucans, honey guides, and other related birds

zygodactylic.d: Yoke-footed; having the toes disposed in pairs; -- applied to birds which have two toes before and two behind, as the parrot, cuckoo, woodpecker, etc

zymogene.d: One of a physiological group of globular bacteria which produces fermentations of diverse nature; -- distinguished from pathogene
